First Chapter.
Having prostrated before Śaṅkara and Gaurī—who ever increases bliss, who bestows happiness and liberation, and who is beautiful—along with the wise Mahākāla; (1)
This great tantra, the supreme essence of all tantras, is now composed;
therein, Pārvatī first questioned Śambhu as follows.
On the delightful Mount Kailāsa, endowed with various minerals,
that best of mountains frequented by hosts of Siddhas and Gandharvas.
It was crowded with various sages, frequented by various gods,
strewn with networks of creepers, and endowed with various trees.

On that best of mountains, which is golden and composed of the letters of the alphabet (mātṛkā), which is worshipped by the embodied [deities], and served by hosts of gods beginning with Brahmā; || 5 ||
In that place beautified by many stones closely set with the spray of the Ganges' cascades,
Pārvatī spoke to the Lord of Gods, who delights in the welfare of all beings.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, expert in the Yoga scriptures,
O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, I wish to ask you about a certain secret.
O best of gods, O Lord of Devas, tell me directly whatever secret is more secret than the secret itself, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain. (8)
The creation, characterized by the origin of the yantras and the syllables of the mantras,
as well as whatever exists among the stationary and moving beings produced during the rains according to the Smṛti scriptures— [all this is his work].
The past, the present, and the future are the supreme characteristics of this recitation;
[it contains] the majesty of the Śālagrāma, of the sacred fords (tīrthas), and of the mountain.
O Maheśvara, [you have described] the greatness of the sixfold ritual, the supreme greatness of power,
and [the greatness] of the mantras, the practitioners, and the means of accomplishment.
The greatness of the annual observance and likewise that of the eclipse,
as well as the greatness of leaves and flowers, and similarly that of the goal to be accomplished.
The greatness of the offering of sacrifice (balidāna), as well as that of animals, birds, and the like;
likewise the performance of ritual action, and similarly the nature of the body.
[He taught] the mudrās, the āsanas, yoga, and the retention and study [of mantras],
as well as the greatness of the phonemes (varṇas) and the duties to be performed.
Furthermore, [he knows] the dharma and adharma ordained by the Lord,
as well as the measurement of the yugas and the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra).
The greatness of the science of poetry, the Brahman of Sound which is beyond that,
the body, the union of the body, the sacrificial pit, and the performance of sacrifice.
And the majesty of the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), of the past, present, and future;
likewise of that body, and indeed of the world beyond.
Thereafter, he spoke of the greatness of Āyurveda, as well as of mantras and codes of conduct, for her who was devoted day and night;
having heard those words of hers, the Lord of the World smiled.
He related all of that, including the most excellent question among all questions.
The illustrious Lord said:
"Excellent, O Goddess, is that which you have asked; it is most excellent and supremely beneficial for the world. I shall indeed speak of this well-guarded secret; listen and be attentive."
O beloved of the gods, I shall describe the greatness of the Yoga-śāstra:
without yoga, no human being can attain awakening.
It has come from the mouths of Śiva and gone into the mouth of the Daughter of the Mountain;
because it removes the three impurities, it is therefore called Āgama.
First, I shall explain the body; listen to that according to its various types.
Without the body, from where could the manifestation of the scripture (āgama) arise?
The Supreme Brahman is the cause, while the effect indeed consists of the expressive word;
by virtue of being merely the expressed and the expresser, everything becomes an expresser.
By whatever means the Supreme Brahman is inferred through speech and that which is beyond speech—
Hari is indeed directly the designator (vācaka), and the Supreme Lord is the designated (vācya).
There was a God endowed with power, known as Sadāśiva;
he is pure, eternal, constant, and of the nature of existence, consciousness, and bliss.
He is the imperishable, supreme Brahman, the infallible, pure and stainless;
consisting of the three qualities, white in color, he is declared to be the root of creation.
He is renowned as Sadāśiva and remembered as the very nature of consciousness (citsvarūpa);
he is Viṣṇu, whose essence is the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman), the lord of yogis, and the leader of the gods.
Through his playful manifestation, this creation is extended;
then, at the proper time, he who delights in Māyā brings forth the world of moving and non-moving beings.
Through my power of illusion (māyā), I likewise contemplate the reality (tattva) of that [illusion];
and from that reality, undergoing transformation, I manifest the entire universe, including all things mobile and immobile.
The Lord of the World creates the entire universe— the whole world consisting of the moving and the stationary, all of which is composed of ego— merely as a sport.
In ancient times, many beings possessing desires were born after being cast forth;
likewise, obstacles were born first, and thereafter the performance of dharma.
For Dharma, O beloved, arises through yoga in the form of the scriptures;
therefore, one should perform the worship of the obstacles there according to the prescribed rule.
Now I shall explain the application of the purpose; listen, O lotus-faced one!
From Sadāśiva arises the Will, endowed with the conjunction of Time.
She is the agitator of the *guṇas*, the deluder of all,
the primordial Supreme Māyā, eternal, and the destroyer of what is undesirable.
She is the giver of happiness, the giver of auspiciousness, eternal, and established within all beings;
this creation would not come to be through one joined with the yoga of illusion.
When Māyā becomes pleased, then one should obtain success;
for she is divine, composed of the qualities (guṇas), and endowed with all beings.
Through the division of her play, this creation shall come to be—
that in which everything originated and in which it still exists even today.
Salutations again and again to that Goddess who, at the end of time, will enter into dissolution—
she who is Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, Raudrī, as well as the Goddess Prajñā and Śivā.
Homage again and again to that Goddess, the Māyā residing in all beings,
who is perceived as an illusion like a reflection in a mirror.
O Pārvatī, just as the many are false and impermanent, so too is creation within these worlds;
yet Māyā is always to be sprinkled with water, Māyā is eternally real, and Māyā is always to be worshipped, O Beloved.
O Goddess, Māyā is always to be praised and worshipped again and again;
for without Māyā, there is no cause for the production of creation.
Everywhere, among all beings— whether stationary or moving—
one perceives the Goddess, who is the light consisting of Brahman, pervading all that is mobile and immobile.
Greed, delusion, desire, and anger— whether with qualities or without qualities—
are all ordained as such when they are joined with Time.
Becoming composed of Time and Māyā, he should always bring about the agitation of the Guṇas;
through Time, he impels Māyā for the sake of the origin of creation.
That which is called the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti) is proclaimed to be Māyā;
and he who is called Sadāśiva is indeed the supreme Puruṣa.
The one Brahman, having become twofold, this creation is thus ordained:
by one half he became the male, and likewise by the other half the female.
The wise one, having made both of them equal, should bring about the manifestation of creation;
as Sadāśiva is described, so too is Māyā proclaimed.
As is Māyā, so is Ārddhā, and so indeed is Sadāśiva;
just as a wife is seen in the house by the husband and the protector of the household.
Likewise, she is the eternal Śivā, the primordial form of Śiva;
she is the consort of the one who is without [another], just as a wife is the refuge of a householder.
O Goddess of the gods, Sadāśiva is exactly as she is;
therefore, Māyā, who is higher than the highest, should always be revered and worshipped.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and all others who are supreme—all of them assume a body through Māyā; there is no doubt in this matter.
Just as the rays of the sun on the earth are worthy of worship,
so too has the great Brahman become all-pervasive through its illusory power (māyā).
But the world, both stationary and moving, is not distinct from Brahman;
for all, including Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, are under the control of Māyā.
No one is under the power of illusion, according to the words of Mahākāla;
rather, illusion should always and in every way be cultivated day and night.
One should reveal the subtle through the gross, and one should resort to the subtle meaning through the gross;
for indeed, O Goddess, without the gross, the subtle does not attain manifestation.
If there is bone here, it is elsewhere; that which is not here is nowhere.
A text equal to the Āgama never exists; thus, there is no bone here on the surface of the earth.
What is the use of other worthless talk, O Goddess, when life is wasted for the sake of food, while sleep carries away one's vitality and sexual indulgence consumes one's vital breaths?
O Goddess, [I am] here for the sake of my daily activities, and for the support of my family;
everywhere and at all times—in waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
O Daughter of the Mountain, Māyā is always to be saluted, always to be praised, and always to be worshipped; she is to be heard and to be celebrated eternally.
When Māyā is pleased— she who bestows primordial consciousness—
then Hari, Brahmā, Śiva, and all others shall attain supreme satisfaction.
O Maheśvarī, Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, women,
and all others should listen to and glorify the Māyā of Hari day and night.
Now I shall explain the process of emanation for the sake of attaining knowledge of the gross;
having mastered the self within the gross, one should then enter the subtle through the intellect.
But that which is subtle, O Great Goddess, does not indeed fall within the range of creation;
it must be understood through inference, and all of that according to the path of the scriptures.
That subtle, supreme Brahman is indeed not within the range of perception in difficult circumstances;
yet it is entirely present in meditative absorption and entirely accessible through the path of the scriptures.
O Maheśānī, that subtle and supreme Brahman which is indeed not within the range of the individual self— that must be thoroughly contemplated through every path of the scriptures.
O Goddess, they declare this scripture of wisdom to be the eye for all;
it should be studied with a steady mind, with devotion, and with those who are free from worldly attachment.
The scripture, which is the traditional authority (āgama), should always be heard at all times;
from hearing it, devotion arises, and through devotion, one should indeed perform worship.
From worship arises knowledge; through knowledge one should purify the elements.
Having attained purity of self, one becomes firm-minded.
When the mind is firm, there will be meditative absorption; from meditative absorption, liberation is said to arise.
Without the practice of illusion, there can be neither liberation nor excellent gnosis.
There should be a fourfold arrangement in the directions starting from the east in due order;
and on whatever part of the earth it may be, Mount Sumeru stands there.
This rule regarding the conduct of mantras and yantras in different regions should be understood as applying everywhere, in all those scriptures beginning with the Pūrva.
O Mahākāla, one should act toward all things according to these words:
whether it be knowledge or ignorance, both of these are enveloped by illusion.
Knowledge alone should always be cultivated, and never ignorance in any way;
that which is knowledge is Mahāmāyā, and she should always be served by the wise.
Ignorance constitutes the bondage of karma; from bondage, knowledge perishes. From the destruction of knowledge comes loss, and upon that loss, there is further transmigration.
From cyclic existence, however, there arises terrible ruin and even hell;
therefore, one who desires liberation should never resort to ignorance anywhere.
Śiva is said to be of two kinds: with attributes (saguṇa) and likewise without attributes (nirguṇa).
The one without attributes is beyond primordial nature (prakṛti), while the one with attributes consists of all things.

O Pārvatī, listen: this creation was described by Brahmā in ancient times as consisting of both the qualified (saguṇa) and the unqualified (nirguṇa). It is said to be composed of all things; hear now how it is so described.
Whatever was spoken by Brahmā in the past, whatever was spoken by Viṣṇu of old,
and whatever was proclaimed by Sadāśiva— all that I shall now relate.
In ancient times, the sages spoke of the auspicious characteristics of the goddess Bhāratī;
I shall tell you all of that, so listen, O lotus-faced one.
The Supreme Brahman is indeed the signified, while the syllables are traditionally known as the signifiers;
I shall explain all of that through the relationship of the substratum and the dependent.
That which perishes is declared to be "the perishable" (kṣara), as it is found in all systems of thought; that which does not exist therein is proclaimed to be "the imperishable" (akṣara).
Just as the origin of the body within the elements has been fully described,
I shall now declare all that regarding the Supreme Brahman therein.
Sadāśiva becomes the fire; beyond that is the voiced (ghoṣa), and then the unvoiced (aghoṣa) and the resonant (saṃghoṣa); beyond that is the aspirated (mahāprāṇa).
From Mahāprāṇa comes Sughoṣa, and from him indeed comes Anāhata;
from Anāhata comes Dhvani, and from that, O Goddess of the Suras, comes Nāda.
Then, from that *nāda* arises the *bindu*, which is the *bindu* of both the Moon and the Sun;
this creation, whose nature is Śiva, is known as the threefold creation.
That auspicious, sattvic creation is celebrated in all tantras;
now, the creation consisting of Śiva is described according to the sequence of yoga.
Śiva is manifestly united with Śakti, and she is endowed with the power of ego (ahaṅkāra);
for indeed, O Goddess, this creation is not brought about without Śakti.
Just as the production of a seed is not seen without a field,
O Goddess, when the Will of Power arises, then creation occurs.
O Maheśvarī, that which is the reflection within reflections in a mirror—this, O Pārvatī, is called "sṛṣṭi," or emanation; listen.
Creation was of two kinds: mental and sexual;
in the ancient Kṛta Yuga, the creation of Prajāpati was mental.
Therefore, she who was devoted to Vāsudeva desired desires and ritual actions;
therein arose the wrath of Viṣṇu, and after that, the creation of forms.
But driven by their wrath, they all became intent on the destruction of the world; at that time, creation became dominated by the quality of passion (rajas).
The *bindu* consists of the moon and the sun, and the *nāda* consists of the three qualities (*guṇas*);
the mantras consisting of the moon and the sun have been proclaimed by the Lotus-born One.
The Bindu should be known as having the nature of Śiva, and the Nāda as the Mistress of the World (Jagadīśvarī). Through the mere enjoyment of Śakti, the Nāda arises, intent upon action.
From Nāda arises Mahābindu, and that is devoted to action;
Bindu is proclaimed in all the scriptures as the soul of all.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are proclaimed as the threefold [deities]; likewise, rajas, sattva, and tamas are universally acknowledged as the three qualities (guṇas).
Among all classes of beings, the three qualities are proclaimed;
O Goddess, the deities are of three kinds, characterized by the predominance of tamas, rajas, or the state of equilibrium.
O Great Goddess, I shall later describe all their respective characteristics; they exist within the Bindu, which is of the nature of Śiva as the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
The three qualities (guṇas) exist within the Bindu, as do the auspicious Siddhis;
it is there alone, O lotus-faced one, that the Yoga-shastras are born.
After that, the treatises on reality; after that, the treatises on liberation;
after that, the treatises on knowledge; and after that, the Purāṇas.
After that, the great Purāṇa scriptures arise, which are worthy of being mastered; following those, the scriptures concerning the hundredfold principles for the destitute come into being.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—all are remembered as being of the nature of the Bindu.
The Vedas, the Śāstras, and all else—all are remembered as being of the nature of the Bindu.
Then, through the division of the Bindu, there arises the one great Sound (Śabda),
which is the supreme Brahman beyond speech and especially invisible.

Those who are experts in all the scriptures have declared that it is indeed the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahman); for it is that reality which, through knowledge, is fully extolled as the fulfillment of all desires.
Those proficient in all philosophical systems call that very [reality] Śabdabrahman;
it is not described as such because it descends from the states of sleep and waking.
The Lord Sadāśiva himself has declared you to be the "field of sound" (śabdakṣetra);
that sound is proclaimed to reside within the unstruck (anāhata) cakras.
The unstruck great wheel is in the hearts of all living beings;
there, the syllable Oṃ is said to reside, endowed with the three qualities.
Śiva, Brahmā, and likewise Viṣṇu are established within the syllables of Oṃ;
the letter A is Brahmā, and the letter U is of the nature of existence and consciousness (saccidātman).
"The letter *ma* is said to be Rudra"—such is the conceptualization of the phonemes;
in the letter *a* there is Viṣṇu, and in the letter *ru* there is Prajāpati.
"And when there is the letter *ma*, there is Rudra"—such is the determination of the phonemes;
thus has it been declared in all the Tantras by the Lotus-born One.
At that very moment, O beloved, that Bindu becomes twofold;
"the Bindu consists of the nature of devotion"—this is the certainty established in the Vedas.
Raudrī, Vāmā, and Jyeṣṭhā are the threefold, supreme Śakti. Raudrī is the Śakti beloved by Rudra, always endowed with the qualities of Rudra.
Vāmā is the power (śakti) of Viṣṇu, endowed with his qualities;
Jyeṣṭhā, however, is the power of Brahmā, characterized by creation and origination.
The eldest creation, endowed with the quality of rajas, is possessed of all things;
the power of Viṣṇu, endowed with the quality of tamas, is esteemed by all.
That fierce great power (mahāśakti) which is Raudrī is proclaimed to be auspicious;
that great power is of the nature of sattva, according to the word of Śiva.
Beyond Sadāśiva, O Goddess, that which is called Śivameru exists;
its power, O Goddess, is considered to be the Tāmasī Śakti.
O Queen of the Gods, the powers of Sadāśiva are remembered as manifold:
the power of will (icchā-śakti), the power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti), and the power of action (kriyā-śakti), which is supreme.
Śiva’s manifold powers—Vimalā and the others—are bestowers of auspiciousness:
Vimalā, Utkarpiṇī, Jvālā, Kriyā, Satyā, and beyond that, Parā.
Yogā, Prahvī, and likewise Aiśānī, and Ugrāṇī again and again;
these, beginning with Brahmāṇī, are the Śaktis, as is this entire world of moving and unmoving things.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī;
likewise Vārāhī, Anantendrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā, and again Kamalā.
Then there are indeed various kinds of powers considered to be manifold;
the power that consists of all the castes always preceded that of Śiva.
O Goddess of gods, whatever has been, is, or will be produced within the cosmic egg—
all that is the power (śakti) of Śiva, endowed with all things.
Indeed, without power (śakti), the universe is not perceived for even a single moment;
the entire universe, including all things mobile and immobile, is filled with powers.
Having attained the state of being the support and the supported, she remains even now;
furthermore, that power whose essence is the *bindu* is celebrated as Raudrī.
Now, that power whose nature is sound (nāda) is proclaimed as Jyeṣṭhā;
and that power arising from the seed-syllable (bīja) is proclaimed as Vāmā.
Vāmā is the auspicious power (śakti) of Vāmadeva; she is Prakṛti, whom people who know all the Vedas call Śabdabrahman.
But sound would be mere sound; how can oneness with Brahman, the supreme state, be realized through the word "Brahman"?
O beloved, by means of the words "the signified" and "the signifier," or by the word "Brahman," all is perceived as one; that is called Śabdabrahman.
Just as, O Goddess, the body cannot be sustained without the elements,
so too, O Goddess, the element does not become manifest without the life-force (jīva).
Just as the identity of the elements, the individual soul, and the Self is sung among the gods,
so too is the one Śabdabrahman proclaimed from the word.
In the union with the body in one place, the individual soul is [united] with the supreme soul;
likewise, in all the Tantras, it is celebrated as Śabdabrahman.
For without Brahman, sound itself could not exist as the nature of manifestation;
all that has been, is, and will be is indeed the Śabdabrahman.
Just as the sun is clearly perceived day and night,
so too should one, through inference and by means of the intellect, recollect all that [is indicated] and the meaning of words.
For when an inconceivable light arises that is [identical to] Brahman,
then even for that [light], direct perception of the meaning of the word arises.
All that arises with respect to those objects occurs through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Now, O Great Goddess, the characteristic of the *bindu* is proclaimed.
From the light of the Moon, all the feet of Time (Kālapāda) and so forth arise in succession;
from Time arises the Great Bindu, and the Bindu is of the nature of Śakti and Sadāśiva.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and the others, who are witnesses to the world, are born [from it].
Through the conjunction of time, Nāda arises, and it is endowed with all qualities.
Then, O Goddess, from Nāda arise these bestowers of the yoga of action;
then, O Goddess, from Nāda arise the fifty Mātṛkās in sequence.
The vowels beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa' are accompanied by the Tantras;
those preceding [the consonants] are short, while those following are long, and immediately after them follow the six ending in 'ṣ'.
Likewise, the seven vowels—ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, and the others—are endowed with all the Tantras;
the consonants from *ka* to *ma* are also endowed with all the Tantras.
Those letters ending with *y* that constitute the *dikṣānta* class are the letters approved in the Tantras;
in all Tantras, the consonants from *y* to *v* are the elements (*dhātu*) that bestow auspiciousness.
The *uṣman* sounds are to be known as *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, and *h*; the bones, marrow, and so forth are the auspicious [elements].
The two letters *la* and *kṣa* are the supreme self and the individual self, respectively—the *paramātman* and the *jīvātman*.
Indeed, the principles ending with the letter *ma* are proclaimed as the phonemes;
they reside in the individual soul (*jīva*), in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and in the mind (*manas*) and intellect (*buddhi*), conjoined with the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the ego (*ahaṅkāra*).
The Great Elements, ending with the mind, reside in the ear, the skin, and the eye;
in the tongue, the nose, the organ of speech, the hands, the anus, the feet, and the generative organ.

One should contemplate the three maṇḍalas, beginning with *ṅa* and ending with *ṇa*, within the heart among the elements (*bhūta*); and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), beginning with *ra* and ending with *va*, within the constituents (*dhātu*).
Thus, O Mistress of the Gods, the characteristics of the origin and production of the phonemes through such contemplation are always known as Śabdabrahman in all the Tantras.
Through the differentiation of its phonemic nature, it manifests as lotus-like verses;
this entire world of moving and non-moving beings is said to have the fifty phonemes as its seed-syllables.
O Goddess, the deities and brahmins are remembered as being composed of all the castes;
furthermore, all beings—gods and asuras alike—are born from the *bindu* and have the elements as their essence.
Then from the drop arises sound; from that, space is produced.
From space arises touch, and from touch, wind is born.
Alternatively, from wind arises fire, and from fire arises the origin of light;
from light arises taste, and from that taste arises the origin of water.
From water, fragrance arises; therefore, it is known as earth (pṛthivī).
O Goddess of the gods, the qualities of earth consist of the five, beginning with fragrance.
Water is to be known as having four qualities; fire has three qualities;
and space is said to have two qualities, characterized by their defining marks.
Air is said to be twice the size of space;
beyond that, fire is twice the size of air, and water is twice the size of fire.
Earth is proclaimed to be twice the size of water, or else equal to it;
now the element endowed with qualities, together with its Tantric application, has been declared.
From the earth, herbs are born; from herbs, food is produced.
From that food, O Goddess, the cosmic egg of the moon and sun then comes into being.
This entire world, consisting of the mobile and the immobile, is composed of the Moon and the Sun.
O Goddess, the immobile is manifold, distinguished by mountains, trees, and so forth.
All of them, however, are to be known as moving beings, as spoken by Śaṅkara;
they exist in various forms, distinguished as animals, birds, and so forth.
Mobile beings are to be known as threefold: sweat-born, egg-born, and womb-born.
Sweat-born are insects and the like; egg-born are serpents and the like.
And many are those born from a womb, namely all humans and so forth;
in all the Tantras, it is held that a human is one born from a womb.
The Lotus-born One has declared that everything consists of the five elements;
all that is moving and unmoving is pervaded by these five great elements.
Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are proclaimed;
O Goddess of gods, these are declared by the wise to be the great elements (mahābhūtas).
O Pārvatī, space, air, fire, water, and earth—
these elements have indeed been described in their gross forms.
The body of a living being is to be known as fourfold, according to the distinction of its origin:
born from a sprout (udbhijja), born from sweat (svedaja), born from an egg (aṇḍaja), and the fourth is born from a womb (jarāyuja).
Having burst through the earth and risen up, it is called "udbhida" (the sprouting); that which is stationary is designated by its trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth.
Everything, consisting of the five elements, arises depending upon the earth as its substrate,
through the combination of water, fire, wind, and space.
The sweat-born arises from earth, fire, and water while they are being heated;
these include insects such as the *śūkmat* and *kunakī*, as well as *priyā* and others, all of which are subject to momentary destruction.
From the egg, which has become a sphere produced from semen and blood,
the complete self, emerging once it is broken by time, shall proceed forth.
Those such as the iguana and the lizard, and those such as the frog and the *siṇḍamāra*,
which are born from a womb (*jarāyuja*), are produced through the process of creation once they have entered a village.
One is born possessing a body composed of the twenty-four principles;
and from the semen fallen from its own location, the vital air (māruta) takes up the drop.
In this way, O beloved of Śiva, [beings] born from a womb arise throughout all bodies, through the forms of origination, maintenance, and dissolution.
Having become Brahmāṇī and Vaiṣṇavī, she likewise becomes the supreme Raudrī;
listen as I describe the portions of the five elements that bestow all perfections.
Śāntātītā, Śānti, Vidyā, and Saṃpratiṣṭhitā—
this is declared to be Nivṛtti, O beloved, consisting of the five elements.
O Supreme Goddess, this process of emanation has been described in the Tantras;
the process of withdrawal is proclaimed to proceed by the reverse order, ending with space.
Listen now to how the mandalas among the elements are measured:
the mandala of space is said to be circular, as is agreed by all.
The maṇḍala of Vāyu is hexagonal, that of Vibhāvasu (Fire) is triangular,
that of Varuṇa is octagonal, and that pertaining to the Earth is square.
"The triangle belongs to Vāyu and the triangle belongs to Varuṇa;
thus it has been declared in all the Tantras by the Lotus-born One."
O Dear One, the [mandala] of water is circular and resembles a half-moon;
that of fire is triangular, endowed with a svastika, and brings all happiness.
The circle of the sky is a sphere marked with six dots;
that of water is white in color, and others are likewise pale yellow.
The wise have declared that all beings exist within all beings;
upon the earth, all beings—both moving and unmoving—are born.
The ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose are the organs of perception;
and speech, hands, feet, the organ of excretion, and the organ of generation are the organs of action.
Speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure are declared to be the objects of speech and the other senses.
Furthermore, the mind, intellect, ego, and consciousness are the causes;
and when the elements, the senses, and the objects of the senses are included, twenty-five principles are observed.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are proclaimed as the primary constituents;
by these, all beings are said to be composed, as declared by the wise.
Now, all modifications arising from the *bindu*— beginning with the immobile and so forth—
as well as the mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and consciousness (*citta*), are entirely composed of it.
Desire, anger, greed, envy, old age, death, and so forth,
as well as violence, lack of compassion, and all such states, are governed by the quality of darkness (tamas).
Those high-souled ones who have desisted, yet are endowed with the quality of goodness (sattva),
and all those who are possessed of desire— they are all considered to be of the nature of passion (rājasa).
Therefore, O Great Goddess, in the Kali age there are many who are rajasic and tamasic;
O Devi, in the Kali age there is no man endowed with sattva anywhere.
The qualities of rajas are the paths of action; they consist of the perception of happiness within sufferings.
It is here that the accomplishment of karma and other such matters occurs, as declared by the Lotus-born One.
Those who are characterized by passion (rājasa) and darkness (tāmasa) are considered the lowest;
they are the powers (śaktis) of the Great Goddess residing in the senses, endowed with those qualities.
Now, all the elements in all the tantras are proclaimed to be of the nature of the drop;
therein they arise, endowed with all living beings.
Skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the constituents (dhātus);
wind, bile, and phlegm are the humors (doṣas), and these together constitute the seven constituents of the body.
The five seed-syllables beginning with *ha* and ending with *la* belong to you;
I shall proclaim them according to the ritual procedure and in their sequential order of elemental manifestation.

O lotus-faced one, one should then contemplate, in sequence, the letters Ha, Ṣa, Va, Ra, and La; from these, O lady of beautiful countenance, arise the peaceful [syllables] whose essence is the Bindu.
In one place, the birth of the embodied soul within the body occurs through union with Yoga;
furthermore, all [deities] such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and others are essentially identical with the body.
When that Great Soul was being divided, all the Brahmins and others emerged;
among them, O Goddess, those who were knowers of the Vedas were equal to the gods.
O Goddess, Śiva himself is directly proclaimed to have two bodies, namely knowledge and ignorance;
that which is endowed with knowledge, O Goddess, is worshipped by the leaders of the gods.
That which is called the subtle body (tanu) of ignorance is likewise to be experienced by the bound soul (paśu), as well as the bindu,
the orb, the three times, and the characteristics of the Supreme Self and so forth.
And all that is inexhaustible, joined with the most subtle of the subtle;
likewise the moments (nimiṣa) and so forth, as well as illusions (māyā), days, and nights.
The fortnights and months, the seasons, the two solstices, and again the year; the yuga, the measurement of the yugas, and likewise the Manvantaras.
Everything up to the end of the great dissolution is remembered as being of the nature of the Bindu;
or else, O Maheśānī, the universe may consist of both Bindu and Nāda.
From that unmanifested primordial source, which is the supreme reality beyond modification,
there indeed arose the principle of Mahat, born of the nature of transformation.
From the principle of Mahat, the threefold Ahaṅkāra is proclaimed;
it is of various kinds and of three types according to the measurement of the qualities (guṇas).
The ego (ahaṃkāra) is threefold: the *vaikārika*, the *taijasa*, and the *tāmasa*.
From the *vaikārika* ego arise the guardians of the gods.
O beloved, all the lords of the gods, beginning with Indra, arise from the ego (ahaṅkāra); likewise, all the incarnations are considered to be of the nature of the vaikārika [sāttvika] ego.
O beloved, for those whose intellects are deluded by *māyā* and who desire all states of existence,
the true form does not manifest through the prior service of *māyā*.
Having placed the seed with water, one should simultaneously enter the sky;
one should place speech in the mouth, the moon and sun in the eyes, and Varuṇa in the dwelling.
The nose is in the fire [element], while the two nostrils are endowed with the quality of sound;
likewise, greed and delusion are in the lips, and Yama is in the teeth.
The quarters [of the sky] are his ears, likewise Maghā; Kāla’s noose is on his arm, and Indra is on his pair of bodies; Dharma is in his chest, while Adharma is the maker of his deeds.
Brahmā is in the navel, likewise Lakṣmī in the generative organ;
beyond that, Mitra in the private parts, and Viṣṇu himself in the feet thereafter.
O Pārvatī, having entered the assembly with all one's qualities,
one should experience transformation while showing compassion for the body.
From the Vaikārika [tattva], as an ornament, there are likewise eleven deities:
those of the quarters, Vāta, Arka, Pracetas, Agni, Hara, Indra, Upendra, Mitra, and Ka.
From the taijasa ego, however, the ten sense organs arose;
through the sequential application of the subtle elements (tanmātras), everything therein possesses both qualities and non-qualities.
From the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) consisting of the primary elements (bhūtādi), the five gross elements were born;
O Goddess, everything—both the stationary and the moving—is composed of the ego-sense.
The eight [vowels] ending with *ṛ* were non-existent, while those ending with *y* are immutable;
that which is pure and stainless is proclaimed as "joined" (*yukta*).
A living being is born through karma and perishes through karma alone;
when the body has perished, that karma is obtained again in another body.
The body is said to be composed of karma, and that is established in the Veda; yet,
O Goddess of Gods, it was declared by the Lotus-born One that everything is entirely false, just as the self of a child does not exist in the preceding moment.
O Goddess, hear that all this world, both moving and unmoving, consists of karma.
The mother is action, the father is action; for action is the supreme teacher.
Whether heaven or hell, one obtains that body through action alone.
O Maheśānī, one should perform day and night that very action which has been prescribed;
now listen to the supreme characteristics of human beings.
First, O lotus-faced one, I shall explain birth; listen!
When the time of the menses has arrived for a woman through union with a man, [birth occurs].
At the proper time, one should approach the deity, and likewise a woman or a man;
having engaged in sexual union at that time, the act of intercourse is performed according to the prescribed rule.
Then Vāyu, the son of Dhananjaya, having placed that seed within the womb,
would cause it to descend again through the path of the birth canal.
In one day it becomes a bubble; in five days, a membrane;
thus, by this sequence, one should gradually cause that body to grow by means of the vital air.
From that time forward, O Maheśānī, his lifespan also consists of eight hundred years; at the beginning, his body is composed of the five elements.
One should always contemplate that body as possessing qualities and as a whole—
whatever is non-existent and whatever is existent, and whatever is within the palm of the hand.
O Goddess, one should contemplate all that according to the word of Śiva;
at the end of existence, at all times, and at the time of ritual action, this is ordained.
O Maheśānī, at the beginning, the entire body arises through yoga;
or else, birth occurs from the feet in reverse order.
In former times, O Māyā, all the Mahākālamata was sequentially meditated upon by Brahmā and Śaṅkara through his creative power.
O beloved, when every ritual procedure has been performed by Viṣṇu even out of sequence,
then from the mantra, the two eyes arise upon the head.
Then its two ears and its two tongues come into being;
then, through the formation of the body, the two nostrils arise there.
From the neck, those two shoulders; after that, the breast-suckling infant; then the hips and the body; and after that, the navel and the trunk.
Then, at the outset, this is the procedure for the secret of the *liṅga* in all tantras:
the differentiation of the *liṅga* arises in accordance with one's previous karma.
O Goddess of the gods, where the body of fire arises, there the hairs grow;
they emerge from the navel, and from the navel arise those that nourish the field.
The channel of the nature of fire is Piṅgalā, located in the right region.
Iḍā is on the left side of the portion of the earth, and Piṅgalā is auspicious on the right.
In the center, O Goddess, the Suṣumnā channel is to be known as having the nature of the vowels;
from it, infinite channels have emerged within the five joints of the Suṣumnā.
That great channel called Suṣumnā, which consists of the nature of both fire and moon,
becomes the Piṅgalā channel, consisting of the nature of fire, in the right region.
The channel of the nature of the Moon, which carries all happiness, is on the left;
it is Gāndhārī, Hastijihvā, Sapuṣā, Lambuṣā, and Mahā.
Yaśasvinī, Śaṅkhinī, and Kuhū—these are the seven nāḍīs;
all the vital breaths (prāṇas) situated in the mūlādhāra are sustainers of the winds.
O Supreme Goddess, these ten Vāyarāstras are proclaimed among the fields (kṣetras);
they should be understood in due order as having the nature of the served and the server.
Prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna are declared to be the primary vital airs (vāyus); furthermore, their attendants are now described.
I shall subsequently explain the practice of the vital breaths according to their true nature;
regarding the practice-mantra known as Haṃsa, I shall declare its essential meaning to you.
The Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya—these are the fires; the ten vital airs (vāyus) are dissolved within those [elements] corrupted by defects.
The Prāṇa [wind], located in the heart region, has a luster like a ruby;
and the Apāna is said to be in the secret region, resembling an Indragopa insect.
The Samāna wind, having the appearance of cow's milk, is located at the region of the navel;
and the Udāna wind, of a smoky color, is proclaimed to be in the region of the throat.
Vyāna is seen in all bodies in the form of light;
the prāṇa wind is in the heart, while apāna is directed toward the anus.
Listen, O lotus-faced one, to the sequence of the sense organs:
vision is the object of the eyes, and sound is that of the ears.
Odor is to be known by the nose; it is associated with all the [other] tantras.
Grasping occurs in the pair of hands, and taste is said to be in the tongue.
The emission (visarga) is to be known in the secret place, while bliss (ānanda) is in the generative organ;
and movement is said to be in the pair of feet, O Supreme Goddess.
Hunger and thirst are established in the region of the vital breath;
mental grief and delusion, as well as fever and death, reside in the body.
At the time of destruction, when all living beings are dissolved within the body,
those great-souled ones of immense strength and prowess are themselves withdrawn at the end.
The body of all beings is proclaimed to consist of six sheaths:
marrow, bone, feces, semen, skin, and blood.
Thus, there is a division among embodied beings known as the six sheaths (ṣaṭkoṣika). Now, bliss is proclaimed to exist in the generative organ and the womb.
The destruction of all castes is proclaimed to occur during the *vipanta* period;
likewise, the birth of living beings is declared to be their physical manifestation.
Within the single Brahman, multiplicity is proclaimed as the state of being a living soul (jīva);
the cessation of that [state] is its death, as is consistent with all philosophical systems.
For Brahmā there is no death, nor indeed does he possess life;
those women who, in all the tantras, are the auspicious wives of Śiva—
And those men who have been mentioned, they are all forms of Rudra;
this entire world of moving and non-moving beings consists of the essence of Hara and Gaurī.
The destruction of all elements arises from that very transformation;
the body is conceptually constructed from the union of semen and blood.
Semen is produced from food, and food [resides] upon the surface of the earth;
from that which resides in semen and so forth arises marrow, O Supreme Goddess.
Skin, blood, flesh, and hair are proclaimed to arise from the blood;
likewise, O Goddess, the semen is the essence of all the principles (*tattva*), consisting of their vital sap.
In men as well as in women, the body is conceptually constructed,
just as the nature of a lamp is seen through its connection with oil.
In this way, having encountered karma, a body is fully produced;
when that karma is exhausted, there occurs for him the destruction of the body's movement.
Just as a grass-hut, having abandoned one blade of grass, moves on to another blade of grass,
so too the living being, having abandoned one field, takes refuge in another field.
The channel named Āpyāyanī is established at the navel of women;
during the period of pregnancy, it nourishes the accumulation of the embryo within the womb.
Among those women and men, there were some who were similar to Iḍā;
however, all the other women were of an unsuitable nature, though they possessed every [other] quality.
Now, all persons are proclaimed to be of the nature of the *liṅga*;
the distinction between *liṅgas* is declared according to the influence of prior karma.
Now, O beloved, the body is described according to the union of the erotic sentiment:
therein, when rajas is predominant, one becomes female; when semen is predominant, one becomes male.
After this, O Goddess, their common mass—the constituent parts of the body—is formed;
then, by the process of sequential development, the sense organs arise.
Then there is that which is internal, external, and celestial;
furthermore, existence and non-existence, fever and death—whatever arises from the sacrificial pit.
Listen to all of that, O Goddess of gods: it is always present within the bodies of men. There is an aperture in the region of the genitals, from which the root of the navel is certainly fixed.
Those who know all the tantras call that the "remnant of the embryo";
it remains there as "moistening" (undana), and it is produced within that body.
One should prescribe the manifestation according to the nature of the application of karma;
having manifested the fruit of karma, which was produced in each preceding birth.
When the fifth or likewise the seventh month has arrived,
one should perform the sprinkling of water for the living, recollecting the fruits of previous actions.
Through meditation and the practice of yoga, one should constantly recollect the yoga of meditation;
having practiced thus for three months, one should then fall upon the ground once more.
Then the embryo, being praised by Īśa, remembers its auspicious and inauspicious deeds from previous births;
remaining there for a moment, it certainly becomes motionless.
Then, when the ten months in his womb were complete,
the embodied being, remembering his past karma, remained within the womb for as long as his stay there continued.
Then, by its own power, the individual soul (jīva) departs from that body of Sadāśiva;
having clearly deposited that field, it should then lead it to an external location.
But having reached that foreign land, his previous knowledge perishes;
then, however, he performs worldly actions according to this procedure prescribed by the scriptures.
Then, in accordance with past karma, one becomes embodied;
and thus that Śiva-śakti, the sovereign of the gods, takes on that very form.
One should protect the field by relying [on it], just as a mother herself protects her child;
for the guardians of the quarters are indeed uninterrupted, existing through the various states resulting from the differentiation of the body.
An infant, a child, a youth, and likewise a teenager; beyond that, a young man, and after that, an adult.
The very mature, the old, and the very aged beyond that,
as well as the gray-haired and death— these are declared to be the stages of life.
Childhood, youth, adolescence, early manhood,
full maturity, extreme maturity, old age, and thereafter, grey hair.
The ten stages ending in death have been declared in accordance with all the tantras;
however, within those ten, nine are declared according to the Mahākāla system.
Thus has that stage been described by Śaṅkara according to his own opinion:
[the stages of] conception, the embryo, birth, infancy, childhood, and youth.
The middle of the Varas is birth and death; these nine are the positions of the Aras. Then, these Antardashas were described by the Lotus-born One (Brahmā).
Waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth state (turiya) are universally accepted;
through the division of the higher and the lower, this is considered Śiva-Śakti.
Dancing in the heart-lotus of yogins, she appears in the form of a preta;
she is established upon the support of the deer for all classes of beings.
Born from the fire of lightning, her body like that of a slumbering serpent, the Goddess is composed of all the Vedas and consists of all the Tantras; she is auspicious.
She consists of all tantras, she is eternal, and her very nature is all tantras;
she is either the embodiment of eternal bliss or the form of the lamp of the inner self.
She is manifestly composed of all reality, more subtle than the subtle, all-pervading,
the mother of the three abodes, and the very embodiment of the Śabdabrahman.
She is the worshipful form of fifty letters, endowed with all tantras;
she destroys various sounds within all classes of beings.
Consciousness resides in all beings, just as Mahākāla has declared;
likewise, there are the powers of Brahmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī.
Vārāhī, Anantā, Indrāṇī, Cāmuṇḍā as the seventh,
as well as Mahālakṣmī, Mahādevī, Vikṛtā, and Prākṛtā.
Atomicity, levitation, extension, as well as lightness,
mastery, lordship, and thereafter the power to fulfill desires at will.
Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Prahvī, Satyā, and beyond her [is] Parā;
Īśānā, Anugrahā, Nityā, and that other one is remembered as being manifold.
Likewise, these nine planets, the world-protectors, and the lords of the gods;
the astrological instruments (karaṇas), diseases, the jhaṅkas, and the zodiac signs.
The Lunar dynasties, the Solar dynasties, and likewise the other lineages of Manu;
as well as the Nāgas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, Kinnaras, Cāraṇas, and so forth.
All weapons, all scriptures, and whatever secret treasures there may be—
whether natural or artificial, existent or non-existent.
The five elements, the beings, and the great elements—
whatever has been mentioned or not mentioned, whether stationary or moving.
Flowers, scents, and the like, as well as tastes, are functions of the fiery element;
time, months, and all else originate from the vessel of the cosmic egg.
By the power of Mahāmāyā, this entire universe is proclaimed [to be her manifestation]:
the girl, the young woman, the tree, the adolescent, and likewise the maiden.
The young woman, the delicate one, the mature one, and the very experienced; then the highly experienced, the experienced, the overgrown, and the one beyond that.
O Pārvatī, those ten [vowels] are white at their extremities in all fields;
then, having projected that body consisting of the sky (the letter *ha*), the bestower of divine boons [is established].
From that time onwards, she herself becomes Mahāmāyā in her menses;
she remains so for twelve years until she reaches the number twenty.
She is called Sukumārī, endowed with all the tantras;
she abides in the form of light within gems, stones, and minerals.
O Goddess of the gods, what more need be said regarding living beings?
Where Mahāmāyā is not present, nothing at all exists there.
Mahāmāyā, whose nature consists of the phonemes and who embodies the essence of all tantras—
Śrī Pārvatī said:

"O Lord of the gods of gods, who are the castes (varṇas), and what is the power (śakti) esteemed by all? O Lord of the gods of gods, what is the creative digit (kalā)? Please explain this in accordance with reality."
Having heard those words of hers, the Lord of the World smiled and related that entire secret, which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
The illustrious Lord said: "Well asked, O Mahāmāyā! This is supremely beneficial for the world of the virtuous.
You are blessed, you have performed meritorious deeds; you are blessed, O you who are affectionate toward the world!"
I shall declare that secret which is to be heard throughout the three worlds:
the fifty phonemes known as letters, beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'.
O Goddess, in the former Kṛta Yuga, on Kailāsa, the best of mountains, Mahāvidyā was proclaimed as your form, beginning with Maheśa.
O lotus-faced Goddess, through the yoga of meditation, I meditate upon your pair of feet; may my perfection be attained at the end of the age, O Divine One.
Immediately thereafter, great joy arose in that field;
first there was dancing and singing, and then the playing of hand-drums.
Then, O Goddess, at that moment, [the place] was adorned with the Brahman of Sound (Śabdabrahman),
filled with the entire collection of Vedas, and endowed with all times.
Just as Viṣṇu is the life-force of the universe and the repository of all qualities, so too,
having reached that drum, it would then become his radiance.
Then, having gone there to the abode of the gods,
they began to teach that [scripture] through the combination of fifty letters, by means of the relationship between the signifier and the signified.
All mantras, great mantras, great vidyās, and the most supreme ones, arise through secret syllables; all of that I shall now proclaim.
Your command ends with a long vowel, while my royal command is beyond that;
both yours and mine are proclaimed to consist of the letters from *ka* to *ma*.
Among these, the letter *ma* is proclaimed to be Puruṣa; O Maheśānī, the two letters *ha* and *kṣa* are the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*).
The letter *ha* is Śiva himself, manifest and endowed with all the Tantras;
following that are *a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, e, ai*.
O, Au, Aṃ, Aḥ— these are declared to be the vowels, endowed with all the Tantras,
through the union of the signified and the signifier, and by means of the qualities of the tongue in every respect.
For that which is one is indeed perceived as supreme multiplicity,
just as sparks from a fire are seen to take on various forms.
Just as fire, though previously latent within wood, appears when it is separated from its body and its form is manifested; so too does the one appear when the connection with the material is severed.
O Goddess of the gods, the deity of the long vowels is Bhuvaneśvarī;
O Goddess of the gods, the deity of the short vowels is Śaṅkara himself.

O Goddess, the letters from *ka* to *kṣa*, along with *ha* and *m*, have been declared as being endowed with all the tantras; their meanings are explained according to the application of substances in the *Ajma*.
The ploughs are all the seed-syllables, and the pegs are the vowels;
O Goddess, without these pegs, this creation would not attain stability.
O Goddess, action cannot exist without the vital breaths, just as a body cannot exist without them;
each of these is to be discerned through the intellect, being directly perceived within the range of vision.
In various regions, the meanings of words are proclaimed to be manifold;
by means of vowels and consonants, the designation of all substances and their functions is established.
The Suṣumnā is located in the middle region, and it is known as the Vaikharī channel;
that channel, which is of the nature of air, produces sound through the movement of the vital breath.
In the body at its root is the Suṣumnā, which is the cause of the production of sound;
differentiated by the organs of the throat and so forth, the Great Goddess takes the form of the phonemes.
The vowels (varṇas) and the pervasive consonants (sparśas) manifest;
likewise, those beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'ma' are the vowels, while those beginning with 'ya' are known as the pervasive consonants.
The hot [syllables] and the vital breaths are to be known as endowed with all the tantras;
O Goddess of gods, I shall tell you the deities of the seven groups.
The deities of the ka-group are red in color and have the form of the sun; Kāvya is the progenitor of the ka-group, and Rudra is remembered as the progenitor of the ṭa-group.
O Goddess, the Guru is the deity of the *tavarga* group, Śanaiścara is the deity of the *pavarga* group,
and likewise, the Moon is the deity of the *ṣavarga* group, accomplishing all aims.
One should worship the presiding deities of the consonant groups (varga-adhiṣṭhā-bhū-devatās) on the ground for the *śa*-group and on the earth for one's own group;
these should be worshipped upon the body during the ritual placement of the groups (*varganyāsa*) for the attainment of the fruit of all accomplishments.
O Goddess, there should be five groups of five, consisting of the letters from *ka* to *la* in sequence;
O Queen of the Gods, for the group beginning with *ha* and *kṣa*, Nṛsiṃha is universally accepted.
Ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa; ca, cha, ja, jha, ña; ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa;
ta, tha, da, dha, na; pa, pha, ba, bha, ma; and after that:
The letters ya, ra, la, va, śa, ṣa, sa, ha, and kṣa are proclaimed [to belong to the northeast].
A, ā, e, ka, ca, cha, ta, pa, and ṣa-sa are proclaimed as belonging to the northwest (vāyavya).
Ḷ, ḹ, aṃ, ṅ, ña, ṇa, na, ma, va, kṣma, and ā are proclaimed as the elements of space (ākāśa).
Ī, ū, ai, kha, cha, ṭha, tha, pa, va, kṣa, and ā are proclaimed as the elements of fire (āgneya).
Ṛ, ṝ, au, gha, jha, ca, dha, bha, ba, and mā are proclaimed as the Varuṇas; u, ū, o, ga, ja, ḍa, da, ra, na, and nā are proclaimed as the Pārthivas.
The vowels and consonants (ajjhalāḥ) are proclaimed to consist of the five elements;
that the phonemes consist of the five elements is hidden in all the tantras.
The Mātṛkā, joined with the fifty phonemes, is established within the wheels;
the mantras consist of the six wheels, and she is the embodied one who culminates in the Mātṛkā.
One should always contemplate Vaikuṇṭha within one's own body as being in the seven wheels:

in the Ādhāra, the Liṅga, the navel, the heart-lotus, the root of the palate, the forehead, the two-petaled wheel, the sixteen-spoked wheel, the twenty-petaled wheel, the twelve-spoked wheel, and the four-petaled wheel.

I bow to that form of letters which consists of the vowels joined with the consonants ḍa, pha, ka, and ṭha at the tips and middle of the petals, the syllable *ha-kṣa* at the region of the throat, and all the phonemes pervading every petal, endowed with the true meaning of reality.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the power of the letters, which is manifested through the consonants;
beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', they are endowed with all the tantras.
Power (śakti) is said to be twofold, and the kalās are remembered as being twofold:
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and beyond that [Śāntyatītā].
Iksikā, Dīpikā, Vācikā, and likewise Mocikā;
Sukṣmā, Asukṣmā, Amṛtā, Jñānā, and likewise Amṛtāpyāyanī.
She is all-pervading and of the nature of space, remembered as consisting of vowels and consonants;
she is Sṛṣṭi, Ṛddhi, Smṛti, Medhā, Kānti, Lakṣmī, Dyuti, and Sthirā.
Sthitir, Buddhi, Jarā, Gālinī, Śānti, Īśvarī, Rati, Kāmikā, Vasudā, and Ādinī.
Prīti, Dīrghā, likewise Atīkṣṇā, Raudrī, and Abhayā;
Nidrā, Tantrī, Kṣudhā, Krodhī, and thereafter Kriyā and Utkārī.
Likewise, Death itself, as well as Śvetā, Pītā, Vāruṇī, Sitā,
and all the infinite kalās, whose essence consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
O Maheśvarī, all these digits (kalās) are of the nature of Sadāśiva;
their lotus-like hands are enriched with an axle, a mace, a svastika, a bowstring, and a skull-cup.
In the rite of placement (nyāsa), one should apply all [the mantras] according to the rules for their respective locations:
in the skull, the face, the two eyes, the two ears, the nose, and the two cheeks.
Upon the upper and lower lips, the two rows of teeth, and the tongue within the lunar disc,
the vowels beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa' are fully present.
One should place the letters from *ka* to *ṅa*, ending with *vidha*, upon the right shoulder, the elbow, the hollow of the wrist, the base of the fingers, and the tips of the fingers.
Then, in the place of the left arm, according to the rule, are the letters from *ca* to *ña*;
likewise on the hip, the circle of the knee, the root of the shank, and the waist.
One should place the letters from *a* to *ṇa* on the tip of one's right index finger;
likewise, according to the prescribed rule, one should place the other letters from *ta* to *na* on the left side.
One should place the letters from *pa* to *ma* according to the prescribed rule upon the body: on the right side, the left side, the back at two parts, the navel, and likewise the abdomen.
In the heart, the right shoulder, the base of the neck, and the left shoulder;
then from the heart down to the right foot, and likewise from the heart to the abdomen.
O Pārvatī, one should place [the mantras] on the hands and feet according to the prescribed rule;
likewise, from the heart to the genitals, and from the heart to one's own head.
To be known as skin, blood, and so forth, and endowed with all the tantras,
the letter *kṣa* resides sequentially within the self consisting of the essence of *rasa*, and finally in the Supreme Self.
One should place the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) within one's own body, [distributing them] among the skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen.
In these locations within the body, one should apply the ritual placement of the *kalās*;
all those forms, beginning with Nīlakaṇṭha, are universally esteemed.
One should install them according to the sequence and their respective places by means of this rite:
Śrīkaṇṭha and the others, as well as Anūpama, Sūkṣma, Trimūrti, and Amareśvara.
Arghīśa is Bhāvabhūti; Hara is situated in the place of Tithīśa;
Jhiṇṭāśa is Bhautika; Sadyojāta is Anugraheśvara.
Arjuna and Mahāsena are the sixteenth; these are the forms of the vowels. Also Krodhīśa, Caṇḍeśa, Pañcātmaka, and Śivottama.
Ekarudra, Kurma, Ekanetra, and Ekaśṛṅga;
Ajeśa, Sarvasomaśa, as well as Lāṅgula and Dāruka.
Ardhanārīśvara, Umākānta, Aṣāḍha, Daṇḍin,
Abhrī, Mīna, the one named Madhu, Lohita, and again Śikhī.
Chagalaṇḍa, Dviraṇḍeśa, Mahākāla, Sukālina,
Bhujaṅgeśa, Pinākīśa, the one known as Khaḍgīśa, and likewise Kunta.
Śvetā, Bhūgīśā, Nakulī, Śivā, Saṃvartukā, and likewise Śunakharparā—
all these powers are of the nature of Rudra.
All of these should be assigned as white in color during the ritual placement of colors (varṇanyāsa).
Pṛṇodarī, Virajā, and Śālmalī follow immediately after that.
The Lolākṣī, the Vartulākṣī, and after her the Dīrghaghoṇā;
then the Sudīrghamukhī, the Gomukhī, and after her the Dīrghajihvā.
Then there was Daṇḍodarī, with hair standing erect and a deformed face;
after her, Jvālāmukhī, Śucimukhī, and then Ulkāmukhī.
Vidyāmukhī, however, should be known as the final powers of the gods:
Sarasvatī, Mahākālī, and Gaurī, the Enchantress of the Three Worlds.
The power of mantra, the power of the self, and beyond that the Mother of Beings;
likewise Lambodarī, Drāviṇī, Nagarī, and Khecarī.
Mañjarā, Rūpiṇī, and Vidhinī immediately after her;
then Kākodarī, Putanā, and Bhadrakālī following that.
Yoginī, Śaṅkhinī, Gandhinī, Kālarātrikā, Kūjinī, Kavardinī, and likewise Kriyā.
Sumukhī, Īśvarī, and Revatī after her;
then Māyavī, Vāruṇī, Vāyasī, and Vakṣavidāriṇī.
Sahajā, Lakṣmī, Vyāpinī, and the supreme one beyond her—these reside in the Brahma-pīṭha; they are red in color and bestow auspiciousness.
One should always visualize the Rudrāṇīs as being richly adorned with red lotuses and skull-bowls, their lotus-hands beautifully decorated; they are known by all as the Siddhas.
Keśava, Nārāyaṇa, Govinda, Viṣṇu,
Madhusūdana, Trivikrama, Vāmana, and likewise Śrīdhara.
Mādhava, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and thereafter Dāmodara; Vāsudeva and Saṅkarṣaṇa—these are remembered as the forms of Viṣṇu’s power.
Pradyumna and Aniruddha, endowed with all their weapons—
the wielder of the discus, the mace, the Śārṅga bow, the sword, the conch, and furthermore the plow.
Muṣalī, Śūlī, Pāśī, and Aṅkuśī follow after him;
then Mukunda, Nandaja, Nandī, Nara, Narakajit, and Hari.
The friend of Kṛṣṇa, the eternal one, the son of Sūrya, the heroic Janārdana;
the upholder of the earth, the universal form, Vaikuṇṭha, and the supreme Puruṣa.
Vali, Valānuja, Bāla, Vṛṣaghna, and again Vṛdhī;
Haṃsa, Varāha, Vimala, and Nṛsiṃha, who is honored by all.
One should place all these [deities], beginning with Keśava, during the worship of Viṣṇu;
they are all dark-complexioned, bestowers of auspiciousness, and have hands shining with the conch and discus.
Fame, Beauty, Contentment, Nourishment, Memory, Peace, Action, Compassion,
Intelligence, Fortitude, Faith, Modesty, Fortune, and Sarasvatī.
Joy, Delight, and all those powers are the leaders of the gods:
Jayā, Durgā, Prabhā, Satyā, Caṇḍā, Vāṇī, and Vilāsinī.
Vijayā, Vinadā, Viśvā, Vinodā, Śūladā, Smṛti, Ṛddhi, Samṛddhi, Śuddhi, Buddhi, Bhakti, Mati, and Kṣamā.
Varāmā, Kledinī, Klinnā, Vasudā, Vasudhā, Parā, Parāyaṇā, as well as Sūkṣmā, Sandhyā, Prajñā, and Niśā.
These two powers, Amoghā and Vicyutā, are located on the body of the Goddess;
they are equal in splendor to the flash of lightning, with arms like two lotuses.
Equal in splendor to the single Goddess, with beautiful smiles and bestowing all accomplishments,
the Mantras and Vidyās were born from the various divisions of the letters of the Mātṛkā.
For Mātṛkā, O Great Goddess, is the very nature of all seeds;
just as in the body, the mind is the preeminent among the senses.
Just as the sun is the most excellent among lights in the sky,
so too is Mātṛkā, in the form of seed-syllables, the most excellent among all mantras.
Having assigned the mantras to the limbs of the mantra and the auspicious powers (*śakti*) to the limbs of the *vidyā*,
one who is approved by all should perform the placement (*vinyāsa*) of the self through the yoga of the field (*kṣetra*).
The powers of the mantra reside in the limbs of the mantra; the powers of the deity reside in the limbs of the goddess.
In this mantra, the limbs of the mantra are present, and the auspicious powers reside in the limbs of the vidyā.
One should assign the zodiac signs, beginning with Aries, upon the body according to the prescribed rule;
one should assign them in sequence to the head, the mouth, the two arms, and the abdomen.
The hips, the secret organ, the thighs, the knees, the shanks, and the feet—
in this sequence is the Mahākālamata placement (nyāsa) of the zodiac signs, which bestows accomplishment.
The splendors are, respectively: crimson, black, green, pale-red, pale-white, variegated, white, yellowish-brown, tawny, brindled, earthy, and soiled.
One should contemplate the signs beginning with Aries in their respective places, by means of the vargas,
in the head, the mouth, the throat, the heart, and the two arms.
On the back, the navel, the abdomen, the genitals, the private parts, and likewise on the pair of feet; [these correspond to] Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, and thereafter Leo.

One should assign the signs beginning with Virgo— namely Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and ending with Pisces— to the body, each followed by the syllable *oṃ* and joined with the word *namaḥ*.
One should place the constellations there, beginning from the head and ending at the feet;
these are the twenty-eight known as beginning with Aśvinī and ending with Revatī.
Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Rohiṇī,
Mṛgaśiras, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Aśleṣā, and Maghā.
Pūrvaphalgunī and Uttaraphalgunī, Hastā, Citrā following that,
Svātī, Viśākhā, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Mūlā following that.
Pūrvāṣāḍhā and Uttarāṣāḍhā, then Śravaṇā and Abhijit; Dhaniṣṭhā and Śatabhiṣā, and then Pūrvabhādrapadā.
Uttarabhādrapadā and likewise those ending with Revatī are proclaimed;
one should assign them to one's own body, beginning with the syllable Om and ending with "namaḥ."
On the crown of the head, the two eyebrows, the eyes, the ears,
the nose, the cheeks, on the tongue, at the base of the neck, on the pair of breasts, and likewise in the heart.
One should place [the mantras] in sequence on the back, the navel, the penis, the private parts, and the glans;
these lunar days (tithis), beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, bestow all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
One should place the seats upon the body for the sake of accomplishing all undertakings:
on the head, the face, the throat, the feet, the navel, the belly, and the hips.
One should place [the mantras] upon the body at the two feet for the sake of accomplishing all undertakings:
Kāmarūpa, Kāmakaṭa, and immediately after that, Uḍḍīśa.
O Dear One, for the sake of attaining all perfections, one should place Jālandhara, Āsrataka, as well as Jvālāmukhī, Śrīśaila, and Malaya.
One should meditate upon the foundational power (Ādhāraśakti), then upon the Boar (Varāha),
followed by the Great Frog (Mahāmaṇḍūka), and thereafter upon the one known as Rudra, the Fire of Time (Kālāgni).
Then, beyond that, one should meditate upon that entire infinite earth,
as well as the jeweled pavilion, the wish-fulfilling tree, and thereafter the golden lion.
Then, [one should meditate upon] the seat of consciousness (saṃvit), which is infinite and the essence of all principles (tattva);
likewise, the lotus with its petals as the limbs and Keśava as the pericarp.
There, one should mentally place a lotus composed of all the principles (tattvas),
as well as sattva, rajas, and tamas, and the self (ātman) which is the supreme self (paramātman).

Then, one should gradually place the inner self, whose nature is knowledge, starting from the *mūlādhāra* and ending at the *ājñā*, beginning with the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*. It consists of the pure self.
One should place the Dharma-seat there and worship oneself as the deity;
immediately thereafter, one should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya.
One should always place [the mantras] on the right shoulder, likewise on the left, at the base of the foot, on the face, on the sides, and on the navel and the right side.
Then, by means of the prescribed method, he likewise [attained] unprecedented non-dharma and dispassion,
as well as ignorance and unprecedented sovereignty, in due order.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) at all times, beginning with the syllable *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*;
thereafter, one should perform the placement of the principles (*tattva-nyāsa*), starting from the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth.
In all classes of mantras, the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa) is prescribed;
for without the principles, the arising of the reality of the principle is not understood.

In Aries, Dharma; in Taurus, Śyāmavahni; in Gemini, Marut and Pitta; in Cancer, Vairāgya; in Leo, Jñāna; in Virgo, Bhūtāgāra; in Libra, Dvirada; in Scorpio, Tattva; in Sagittarius, Aiśvarya; and in Pisces, Kṛṣṇa.
May the variegated seats of the limbs in the eastern direction beginning with Na, E, and Ña be victorious;
this ritual placement (nyāsa) bestows all desires among all mantra-sciences.
One should install the *mātṛkā* within the body according to this procedure;
likewise, the wise practitioner should perform the internal sacrifice (*antaryāga*), as well as the yoga and the breath-control (*vāyu*).
The reciter should first perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) according to this procedure,
by means of inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka), following the ritual rule with the letters beginning with 'ya' and ending with 'va'.
One should slowly fill the breath through the *iḍā* channel, the respiratory passage, with exactly sixteen measures; thereafter, one should perform the *kumbhaka*.
After that, having performed the *kumbhaka* (retention) in the *suṣumnā* with the mantra consisting of sixty-four [syllables], one should perform the *recaka* (exhalation) through the *piṅgalā*.
Having recited the mantra four times along with the seed-syllable *raṃ*, one should perform the immersion;
then, through the channel of breath-restraint, one should slowly exhale the air.
Long ago, while still within the womb, he was contemplated as a sinner by the wise:
the murder of a Brahmin as his head, and the theft of gold as his two arms.
The heart is joined with the drinking of liquor, and the two hips with violating the teacher’s bed;
from association with those, the two feet [are affected], and thus there is sin in every limb and sub-limb.
With body hair like that of a minor sinner, red beard and eyes,
bearing a sword and shield, and the size of the left thumb.
One should visualize [the syllable] as black in color and facing downwards in the left side of the belly;
I shall now describe in due order those sages who have been mentioned in relation to these.
O Goddess of the gods, in Purakā and the other [cities], the sages universally honored are Kiṣkindha, Kaśyapa, and thereafter Hiraṇyagarbha.
The inner controller (antaryāmī) is remembered as the seer (ṛṣi) of this sinful body;
having meditated thus, one should burn the entire body with the fire-channel (vahnināḍī).

Then one should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma), and immediately thereafter the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi). Having performed the purification of the elements, one should likewise impart the meditative visualization (bhāvanā).
One should contemplate one's own body from the feet up to the head,
enriched with the seed-syllables of the fifty letters and joined with the great elements and so forth.
One should then meditate upon smell, taste, touch, form, and sound,
as well as one's own body, because from that [body] arises a thousand lotuses.
One should meditate upon the eternal Goddess within the great thousand-petaled lotus,
united with Sadāśiva and engaged in the inverted act of love.

And having dissolved the elements according to the prescribed rule into the Great Primordial (Mahāpūrva), one should establish them within that lotus-foot; then, one should contemplate the phonemes and so forth.
The teacher has taught the wheel of withdrawal (saṃhāracakra), which consists of the letters from *kṣa* down to *a* in reverse order, and which is endowed with all the tantras.
The teacher should contemplate the six chakras within the body according to this procedure:
Mūlādhāra, Svādhiṣṭhāna, Maṇipūra, and Anāhata.
The Ājñā [cakra] is called Viśuddha; in due order within one's own body, the thousand-petaled great lotus is proclaimed as Viśuddhākhya.
The root support (mūlādhāra), likewise the generative organ, then the region of the navel;
thereafter the heart, the region of the throat, and immediately after that the pair of eyebrows.
The seven cakras within the body are said to end with the thousand-spoked [cakra]:
namely, Ḍākinī, Hākinī, Rākinī, and likewise Lākinī.
Kākinī and Śākinī are indeed the deities of the six cakras;
Hākinī is declared to be the deity of the thousand-spoked [cakra], the sovereign goddess of the gods.
There, one should indeed contemplate with the intellect, in due order, that which consists of the colors of the petals:
the four-petaled root-support (mūlādhāra), O Great Goddess, containing the letters from *va* to *sa*.
One should contemplate the six chakras ending with Vādilā;
Mūlādhāra is at the anus and Svādhiṣṭhāna is at the genitals.
One should contemplate the region of the navel as the ten-petalled Maṇipūra, the great wheel, adorned with the Śabdabrahman and consisting of the letters from *ḍa* to *pha*.
The pure double-petaled [lotus] is said to be adorned with the letters *ha* and *kṣa*;
the petal consisting of the essence of all letters is proclaimed by the Lord of Lotuses (*Padmanābha*).
One should mentally contemplate the writing by means of a clockwise rotation;
it is in the direct order at the time of emanation, and in the reverse order during withdrawal.
Having reflected thus, one should contemplate one's own body and the individual soul (jīvātman);
one should contemplate the individual soul situated in the *mūlādhāra*, established in the form of *kuṇḍalinī*.
Arising from the fire of lightning, with a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning,
it should then be uttered once more from the *mūlādhāra* by means of the syllable *hūṃ*.
Just as a lamp remains steady even when possessed of a body in a windless place,
so should one contemplate oneself as the individual soul (jīvātman) whose body consists of mantra.
One should contemplate gradually through meditation and the practice of yoga;
having thus contemplated one's own body, one should thereafter perform breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
And having likewise contemplated the deity and the individual soul as being of equal weight,
one should perform inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka) [while meditating] on the sequence from the letter 'A' to the letter 'KṢa'.
Then, the performer of the rite for the deceased should perform this procedure three times according to the following rule:
one should slowly fill [the breath] with the letters from *a* to *kṣa* through the *iḍā* [left nostril].
Having reflected thus upon one's own body, one should thereafter perform breath control (prāṇāyāma);
then, by means of the letters beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'ma', one should fill [the body] within the suṣumnā according to the prescribed rule.
One should exhale through the Piṅgalā [nāḍī] slowly with the letters from ya to pha;
this is declared to be prāṇāyāma, in accordance with all tantras.
Holding the breath for three repetitions is proclaimed as *prāṇāyāma*. Having retained the breath, one should recite the *mātṛkā* [vowels] and the *mātṛkā* [consonants] in their natural order.
One should contemplate the five elements, the great elements, and one's own life-force;
having placed the life-force endowed with its qualities [within], one should utter the *prāṇa* [mantra].
Having encased [the deity] with the vowel and consonant [mantras] that pervade all [limbs],
one should perform the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) in the heart, conjoined with the body.
That which is joined with the body of Dakṣa has been declared by the knower of mantras;
it is the face joined with the bindu and adorned with the half-moon.
O Goddess of the gods, this seed-syllable of Lajjā was proclaimed by Akṣobhya;
it is joined with the Bindu of Brahmā and endowed with the seed-syllable of Fire.
This first [syllable] with the tenth vowel is proclaimed as the hook (aṅkuśa).
The deities of the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā mantra are the Brāhmaṇas and the others.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are proclaimed as the Ṛṣis;
at that time, there shall also be the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as the meters.
The first seven [syllables] ending in *sakāra*, joined with the *atri-mantra*;
[the next] joined with the half-head and the teeth, and joined with the *haṃsa-mantra*.
Having brought that Kuṇḍalinī back by that same path,
the wise practitioner, having established her in the Mūlādhāra, should mutter the Haṃsa-mantra.
One should contemplate the fifty seed-syllables of the phonemes joined with the nasal bindu:
"My vital breaths are here; my life-force is established here."
One should contemplate all the sense faculties, the elements, and sentient beings,
as well as the primary elements and the principles, according to this procedure.
"Having come here, may Vahnisundarī remain happily for a long time. This is declared to be the life-force mantra (prāṇamanu), endowed with all the tantras."
The entry of the vital breath (prāṇa) is traditionally taught to be performed with the seed-syllable of Nṛsiṃha;
at that time, one who is restrained and pure should meditate upon the visualization of the prāṇa.
And Sundarī should impart the life-mantra of the external deity.
Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Origin of the Body," in the venerable Viśvasāra Tantra. || 1 ||
The Second Chapter. Now I shall proclaim the Yoga; listen, O lotus-faced one!
It was spoken by Brahmā in former times to Nārada in the Kṛta Yuga.
Listen to that, O Great Goddess, for the purification of the form of the mantra:
the knowledge of the five elements is the primary and supreme yoga.
Having reflected upon their destination, one should then contemplate one's chosen deity.
O Pārvatī, listen as I describe the destination of living beings within one's own body.
At that time, O Great Goddess, the Yogaśāstra, along with its ancillaries, which bestows liberation, becomes the auspicious path for those who are servants of Kāla’s Kāla.
One should contemplate with the intellect the identity of the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman);
this is samādhi, the supreme yoga, which is consistent with all philosophical systems.
One should contemplate that which is pure, stainless, eternal, and devoid of the states of existence and non-existence,
through mind, speech, and indeed through body.
One should contemplate day and night that very supreme Yoga, which was formerly meditated upon by Śiva—
the pure deity endowed with pure qualities.
One should always contemplate Sadāśiva, united with Śakti and seated upon a thousand-petaled lotus, within meditative absorption (samādhi) with a mind purified by devotion.
