The practitioner should always meditate upon the Lord as consisting of the syllables of the mantra, and Śivā as consisting of the syllables of the mantra, through the yoga of mental practice.
When the teacher acts amidst the behavior of cows, crows, and deer— motionless, free from ego, beyond dualities, and without possessions.
One should always, at all times, meditate upon that God and that Goddess worshipped by the gods within all principles (tattvas), according to this rite.
Eternal, pure, originating from purity, devoid of the states of existence and non-existence,
she brings about the destruction of all time and is established within all mantras.
One should contemplate her as the eternal essence of the science of weapons, dwelling in various sounds, free from old age and death, and having the nature of the daughter of Dakṣa.

O Dear One, having conquered the enemies of one's own self, such as desire, anger, and the like, one should contemplate the Goddess, whose nature is the light of Brahman, through the yoga of meditation.
Desire, anger, as well as delusion, greed, violence, and the like,
as well as Indra and the other gods— all these were [subdued] by the sage through meditation according to the prescribed method.
One should meditate upon the Śakti seated upon the mental lotus, united with Śiva,
adorned with various ornaments, and endowed with manifold virtues.
Then, with the tongue restrained from the six sense-objects, one should meditate upon the Mother of the World;
O Goddess of Gods, desire and the like have been described by you as sufferings.
Having conquered this [state] through the eight limbs of yoga, the yogi shall attain union;
he beholds Śiva within his own body in the thousand-petaled lotus and should meditate upon Him.
Thus, having reflected upon the Puruṣa as complete and upon Māyā as dependent on him,
one should then practice the yoga of meditative absorption (samādhi).
Just as the power of burning resides within a coal by taking it as its substratum,
so too does that very [power] reside in Śrī Sadāśiva when he has entered the fire of the Yamādi-tantras.
And this scripture is proclaimed through its division into limbs:
Yama, Niyama, Āsana, and thereafter Prāṇāyāma.
Withdrawal, concentration, meditation, and absorption—
this is called the eightfold yoga, endowed with all the scriptures.
Non-violence, truthfulness, self-restraint, celibacy, compassion, straightforwardness, forgiveness, fortitude, moderation in diet, purity, and likewise self-control.
O Maheśānī, these are the restraints (yamas) endowed with all the tantras:
austerity, contentment, faith, charity, and the worship of the Deity.
Constantly listening to the established doctrine, modesty, intelligence, and the recitation of the heart-mantra—
these ten are declared to be the observances (niyamas) in accordance with all the Tantras.
The wise one should know these five postures in their proper order: the lotus posture (padmāsana), the one called the auspicious (svastika), and likewise the hero posture (vīrāsana).
O Dear One, having properly placed both feet upon the broad and auspicious vajra-seat,
one should bind the two big toes together at the back in the reverse order.
This is declared to be the *padmāsana*, which is consistent with all tantras:
having properly placed the soles of the feet between the knees once again.
The yogi should sit with an upright body in what is called the svastika posture;
he should place his two ankles very firmly at the sides of the perineum.
One should mark the lower sides of the thighs with the two hands;
this is called Bhadrāsana, which is heart-pleasing to yogins.

O Goddess of gods, one should place the feet shoulder-width apart, the knees facing each other, and the fingers turned inward; the hands should be placed [in this manner]—this is declared to be the Vajrāsana posture.
Placing one foot below and resting the other upon it, with the body held straight, the yogi should enter [the posture]; this is declared to be the vīrāsana.
O Pārvatī, there are indeed many postures mentioned in the Vedas;
however, that which is called Svastika is declared to be the best among them all, as it brings great comfort.
One should fill [the body] with air through the *iḍā* while reciting the syllable *yaṃ* sixteen times;
it is taught that one should then retain it within the *suṣumnā* for sixty-four [mātrās].
One should expel the breath through the Piṅgalā for thirty-two measures;
those who know all the tantras declare this to be the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Having performed inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka) by means of the *raṃ* mantra in reverse order,
one should then recite the *ṭhaṃ* mantra according to that same procedure.
Having recited [the mantra] according to that very same procedure, one should cast it into ashes for the sake of purifying sins;
one should contemplate the body as joined with the fifty letters using the syllable *laṃ*.
Then, having strengthened that body with the seed-syllable *dharā* (laṃ),
one should oneself recite [the mantra] twelve or sixteen times according to the sequence of increasing the *mātrās*.
Having performed the placement of mantras (*nyāsa*) and other rites such as recitation (*japa*), a person shall obtain all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
As he practices in this sequence, the supreme state of dharma arises for him.
The middling [type] is associated with the aeon; thereafter is the abandonment of the ground.
For the superior [type], the attainment of qualities is maintained as long as ethical discipline is practiced.
Pratyāhāra (withdrawal) is defined as the forceful drawing back of the senses from their objects, which wander among various sensory domains and are divided into two types.
[One should contemplate] in the thumb, the ankle, the knee, the thigh, the mind, the genitals,
the navel, the heart, the region of the head and throat, the uvula, and likewise in the nose.
The procedure is the same at the center of the eyebrows, on the forehead, at the crown of the head, and at the dvādaśānta;
the retention of the vital breath (prāṇamarut) is proclaimed as dhāraṇā.
Those who know meditation understand that meditation consists of the visualization of one's chosen deities within the self by means of a concentrated mind abiding therein.
O Goddess, the constant cultivation of the equality between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) is declared to be samādhi, in accordance with all the scriptures.
In the rectum, which measures two finger-breadths, the body is of a dual nature;
however, they know the height of the anus at the end of the rectum to be two finger-breadths.
Twice its width, it is situated in a circular form;
there, three principal channels are said to have arisen.
The channel Iḍā is situated on the left, and Citrā is auspicious for yogins;
O Dear One, they know the Brahma-randhra within it to resemble the fiber of a lotus stalk.
And they know the support there to be endowed with all the Tantras;
they call this divine path characterized by the bliss of immortality.
One should contemplate the moon in the iḍā and the sun in the piṅgalā;
O Goddess of gods, one should contemplate both of them within the body in the suṣumnā.
The Suṣumnā channel, consisting of fire and moon, is accepted in the Tantras;
it is the center of the Ādhāra-lotus, a most beautiful triangle.
And that abode of the luminaries was described by the Lotus-born;
there resides the Supreme Deity, Kuṇḍalinī, in the form of a flash of lightning.
Within this body, which has the appearance of a sleeping serpent, the Kuṇḍalinī adorns herself;
through the Haṃsa-mantra, she sustains the body as her very self.
Born from the syllable *haṃ*, Kuṇḍalī is the mistress of the *kula*;
for going and coming, one should employ the mantra *haṃ* along with *laṃ*.
The seed-mantra of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) has been declared there as follows:
it is eternally the refuge of the *haṃsa*-breath, resting upon the path of the vital channels (*prāṇanāḍī*).
The wind flows from the base according to its nature for all embodied beings;
having reached the body through the excellent channels, it carries out the outward departure.
From that, the person of the vital breath (prāṇa) is twelve finger-breadths in measure;
this living soul (jīva), in the form of wind, is traditionally held to be all-knowing and all-pervading.
Kuṇḍalinī remains pervading from the Mūlādhāra to the Sahasrāra;
and Suṣumnā resides in the middle of the body, having a form subtler than the subtlest.
Having the nature of wind, she remains established upon the vital air;
the Kuṇḍalinī, the supreme deity, constantly comes and goes.
On a pleasant, holy, and soft seat covered with cloth, an antelope skin, and kuśa grass,
one should assume the svastika posture and become intent upon the path of yoga.
Having correctly understood the arising of the elements within the body by means of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu),
O beloved, one should always meditate on her in the form of Śakti at the left side of the navel.
O Great Goddess, one should meditate with the intellect upon Śambhu in the form of the sun within the Piṅgalā [nāḍī], and upon Śivānī in the form of the moon within the Vāmanā nāḍī.
Now hear concerning the emergence of all elements within this body, which consists of the primary elements;
the wise person should contemplate by means of this wind for the attainment of all perfections.
What is the use of kingdoms or idle talk, when this life must pass away?
One should contemplate their movement through the channels by means of the cessation of the breath.
Having meditated upon this body as being of the nature of the Self, the consort of Śambhu should nourish it;
her movement upon the ground takes the form of a staff, and she has a desire for her own [true] self.
The upward movement is that of fire; the transverse movement is known as that of wind;
the intermediate movement of space is endowed with all the principles.
Having meditated upon this body as being of the nature of the Self, one should nourish it as having the form of wind;
the Great Māyā resides in the skin, while the auspicious Śivā resides in the blood.
Likewise, that Goddess resides in the flesh; likewise, being present in the fat;
she, the consort of Śiva, resides in the bone; and Śambhu’s beautiful lady resides in the marrow.
She is known as the essence of semen, the form of wind, and likewise the nature of vital breath;
she is the eternal soul of the individual life-force, residing within all fields of being.
O Dear One, when the [appropriate] signs arise, the wise man should perform rites such as killing;
he should always contemplate the movement of that [deity] within his own body.
O Dear One, when the rising of the syllable Varaṇa occurs at the time of water, one should perform the universally esteemed rites of stambhana, śāntika, and pauṣṭika.
One effects the killing of an enemy through the conjunction with the rising of fire;
however, during the rising of wind, one should perform the universally acclaimed rite of immobilization (stambhana).
Then, at the rising of Ākāśa, the wise practitioner should perform the rite of eradication (uccāṭana) according to all the tantras; he should effect the destruction of fields and other such things.
Starting from the rising of the Asura [period] and continuing for two ghaṭikās,
having understood it in this sequence, one should contemplate it in relation to the six rites.
Having established the wind-constellation (vāyurnakṣatra) in this manner, one should contemplate the yoga;
the practitioner of yoga, through the practice of meditation, should contemplate the vital air (māruta) within the body.
Having meditated upon the wind within one's own body, one should contemplate the Supreme Deity;
O Supreme Goddess, the *nāda* arises in that field through the wind.
At first, it is like the sound of intoxicated bees; then, the sound of the flute is heard.
Then the sound of a bell arises, and after that, the sound of clouds. For one who practices in this manner, there is no suffering born of defects such as grief.
For him there shall be fear; yet there shall be accomplishment, the supreme accomplishment of all.
From that, the *nāda* arises; it is traditionally held that the *bindu* consists of the nature of the moon and the sun.
Some of the most eminent sages say that the *bindu* consists of the nature of the *nāda*.
This entire world, including all that is moving and unmoving, consists of *bindu* and *nāda*.
*Bindu* is the male principle, while *nāda* is universally accepted as being female in form.
The Lotus-born One has declared that Nāda is the cause of the worlds;
without the practice of sexual union, success can never be attained in any way.
There, a pair consisting of male and female arose, as recognized in the Tantras.
In the *haṃ* mantra, the male is proclaimed, and the letter *sa* is remembered as the primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
These two pervade the entire universe and the sacrificial pit as well;
when one attains that state, then one is said to be "That I am."
He alone is the supreme Brahman, the immutable germ of the universe;
likewise, all the gods, the Vedas, the directions, the winds, and so forth, are He.
The divisions of time, such as the *truṭi* and so forth, as well as the respective deities who constitute them,
all go to their destruction within that [Supreme Reality], O Mistress of the Universe, toward whom they direct their devotion.
In whom creation is eternally produced, and in whom even today it continues to arise—he alone is the Supreme Brahman; by his very hand, he is born.
One should direct the syllable of power, which is the same color as the *bindu*, with joy;
this *praṇava* has been declared by the Lotus-born One in all the tantras.
O Dear One, within the center of one's own body resides Brahman, which consists of supreme bliss, adorned with the Śabdabrahman, and is the essence of all tantras.
One should meditate according to this method upon that which consists of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva,
which is declared to be the cause of the worlds and the cause of the Vedic mantra.
This is the rule in all tantras regarding the Gāyatrī and the Praṇava;
furthermore, the meaning of the mantra of the Gāyatrī-Praṇava was [revealed] by Brahmā in ancient times.
One who has not reached the culmination in the four Vedas and the Shastras cannot attain this;
for this is indeed called Samadhi-yoga by the Lotus-born One.
One should contemplate the Goddess in meditative absorption (samādhi) and perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and so forth;
having then executed the entire network of ritual placements (nyāsa), one should always worship her within that absorption.
"Whatever kind of worship or libation with water one performs in meditative concentration, one should perform that same kind externally; so it was spoken by Śaṅkara."
Henceforth, O Śaṅkarī, I shall describe the yoga of action (karmayoga); listen.
Among those, the various stages of life (āśramas) were described by the Lotus-born One (Brahmā).
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are entitled to all systems;
they are entitled to ritual action and thus entitled to all systems.
And those others who are called mixed castes (*saṅkara*), as well as the Śūdras, O Maheśvarī—
all of them are proclaimed to be servants of those who perform ritual actions.
Having obtained half of their fruit, he rejoices in heaven like a god.
One should not give the sacred teaching to a Śūdra, nor the Praṇava, which is the core of the Veda.
A practitioner should never give the mantra, nor the yoga of the mantra, nor the ancillaries of the mantra,
to Śūdras or to women.
If Valāmbā were ever to perform any other ritual action,
she would surely fall from heaven, like a sandcastle washed away by its own protection.
O beautiful one, listen as I shall describe the ritual acts beginning with the worship of the deity;
first, among those, I will explain the characteristics of the teacher and the disciple.
Devoted to all scriptures, skillful, and always knowing the meaning of all treatises;
young, handsome, with all his limbs intact, of noble birth, and of auspicious appearance.
A Brahmin who has conquered his senses, speaks the truth, possesses a tranquil mind,
is devoted to the welfare of his father and mother, and is dedicated to all his duties.
The preceptor is ordained to be one who belongs to a spiritual stage of life (*āśramin*) and resides in a sacred region (*deśasthāyin*);
at the conclusion of the *Śiva*-mantra, such a person should be known as the universally accepted practitioner (*sādhana*).
That which was previously spoken regarding the sacrifice has been communicated out of affection for you;
now I shall declare what is to be eaten—listen, O lotus-faced one!
Food, milk, as well as a tree, milk-rice, cakes,
fresh butter, and various fruits combined with jaggery and milk-rice.
One who knows the ritual rules should consume all fruits and flowers;
likewise, garlic, *guñjana*, neem, *asura*, and *śūraṇa*, as well as *jambīra*,
*nakuca*, bell-metal, gourd, and *mayathu*.
Seed-meat, as well as meat, garlic, and onions.
Food offerings consist of red lentil dishes and the like, as well as betel leaf with a firebrand;
and milk that has been kept overnight, such as *tāla*, *garjuna*, and *muṣita*, along with *braṣṭa* and other such items.

One should avoid food that has turned sour, that which has lost its six qualities, and sacrificial oblations that have been left over; likewise, one should avoid a person in tattered clothes, oil, sour liquids, and [food containing] nails or hair.
A woman who maintains the sacrificial fire should avoid food that is tasteless and improper conversation.
Now I shall declare the opinion of the Goddess; listen to the flowers, O Pārvatī.
Tulsi, lotuses, jasmine, ketaki, karavira,
and red water-lilies— these flowers are praised for subjugation.
Blue lotuses, red lotuses, white water lilies, and night-blooming lilies, as well as jasmine, white water lilies, aṅgāra, nandyāvarta, and other such flowers.
There were thickets of *palāśa* and *vetra*, as well as *balā* and *vaṭaka* trees; and among the *bilva* trees growing on the mountain slopes were those produced from *karṇikāra*.
O beloved, these and other flowers indeed exist in this tantra; they may originate from various countries and bloom at all times.
One should especially offer leaves and flowers to the deities.
Now, O Maheśvarī, I shall explain the flowers used in the application of ritual action.
Listen with supreme devotion to what was spoken by me and Brahmā in the past:
[the worship] of Kamala, Karavīra, Deva, Kumuda, and the two types of Tulasī.
There are two species of *ketakī*, two types of *kahlāra*, as well as *campaka*,
*utpala*, *kunda*, *mandāra*, *panāga*, *paṭala*, *nāgacampaka*, and [the others].
Aruṣkara, karṇikāra, pārvantī, navamallikā,
saugandhika, sokavaṇḍa, palāśa, aśoka, and majjakā.
Dhustūra, varjaka, nimba, arjuna, maṇipuṣpaka, sindhuvāra, apāmārga, kālapuṣpa, and nikāmajam.
Then vyāghrāṭaka, damanaka, and maruvaka; thereafter lavaṅga, water, camphor, tagara, and likewise javā.
The *bilva* flower, the *droṇa* flower, the *kāmarāja*, the *suhoḍaka*,
and the petals of the *karavīra*, whether growing in water or on land.
Beyond these are the mountain-born flowers, the country-born flowers, and various other flowers;
this has been declared in all the tantras, and especially in the Viśvasāra.
Kavya, kāruṣkara, āmalaka, ḍumbura, and that known as jambu;
khadira, kṛṣṇalāpā, puṣpāṇa, nāgara, and rauhiṇa.
Palāśa, plakṣa, āmrātaka, ikṣu, arjuna, vikakṣata, vañjula,
vikalā, sajjā, bandhūka, panasa, and ārkaka.
Trees such as the *śamī*, *kadamba*, *nimba*, mango, and those with honey-like fragrance increase longevity and bring about prosperity; one should never cut them down.
O Goddess of the gods, Śiva himself is eternally present in these trees.
Now, O Pārvatī, I shall describe the sacred site according to the application of ritual action.
Ayodhyā, Mathurā, Māyā, Kāśī, Kāñcī, Avantikā,
Dvārakā, Haridvāra, and likewise Godāvarī, O beloved.
Setubandha, Sarayū, Kurukṣetra, and likewise Gayā;
the lake named Dvaipāyana, and beyond that, Survāruka.
Rohitāśva, Śoṇabhadrā, Viṣṇupadī, Gayā, Phalgu, and Udīcī; beyond that is the place Kañcana.
O beloved, [he visited] Mānasarovara and likewise Vindhyeśvara,
Kailāsa, Bhṛṇḍapura, Mandara, and Himālaya.
Carmannatī, Vetravatī, Bāhu, and likewise Dāsurasā;
and Prayāga, which arose from ten horse-sacrifices and is the refuge of Pūlaha.
The Yamunā, the Candrabhāgā, the Gaṅgā, and likewise the Panasa;
Jālandhara, Badarikā, and also the Sarasvatī.
It is said that Saṅketāśrama is the abode of Kapila;
likewise Purobodha, Vyāsanī, and Priyaṃvadā.
Kāmarūpa, Gokarṇa, together with Vakāryā, O beloved;
Guhyakanyāśrama, O Goddess, and Naṭikālaya as well.
Hāṭakācala, as well as Ekaliṅga and Nanda,
Gandhamādana, Kimpuruṣa, and after that, Durgāpīṭha.
The site of a Tulasī plant, which is the abode of the Purāṇas, the Mahābhārata, and other scriptures; a cow-pen; the root of a Bilva tree; and a reservoir of water excavated by oneself.
A place dug by deities, a riverbank, and beyond that,
a temple site, a cremation ground, and the root of a family tree.
The temple of the deity and the hermitage of Śiva,
as well as others, O Maheśānī, which are celebrated in Bhārata.
That which is proclaimed in the Purāṇas, the Yāmala, the Tantra, and other scriptures—
the entire Siddhāśrama as well as the seven oceans— [is all contained herein].
Gaṅgādvāra, the Gaṅgā, and the very confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean;
likewise Saptagodāvarī and the hermitage of Nārada.
O noble lady, whatever sacred fords (tīrthas) are proclaimed in the Vedas and the Rāmāyaṇa,
one should perform initiation and auspicious rites in the vicinity of a Śālagrāma stone.
O Goddess of the gods, those locations have been declared by the wise;
in all auspicious rites, this procedure is desired everywhere.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should worship Bhairava, the host of Bhairavas, and Vāntīśa in the east with this mantra, preceded by the syllable Om and followed by "namaḥ."
Adorned with various offerings, oblations, barley-gruel, and other such items:
Oṃ! O you with sharp fangs and great body, who resemble the fire at the end of an aeon!
Salutations to you, O Bhairava; you should grant me permission. Accept, accept this offering, O Lord, surrounded by your own host of attendants.
O Lord of the Gods, destroy all calamities and obstacles!
O lotus-faced one, listen as I describe the sacrificial pit.
The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is said to be of eight kinds, as prescribed in all the Tantras:
square, triangular, semi-circular, crescent-shaped, three-cornered, and circular.
The six-cornered [mandala] has the form of a lotus, while the eight-cornered is approved by the Tantras;
the four-cornered square is endowed with all the Tantras.
The wise know that a pit shaped like a half-moon is called an *ardhacandra*;
a triangle is designated as *tryasra*, in accordance with all the tantras.
A circular pit is round in shape; one joined with six sides is hexagonal;
and that which is situated within eight angles is proclaimed as octagonal.
One should construct a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) according to the prescribed rules on ground measuring one cubit;
the pit should be square, in accordance with all the tantric traditions.
One should prepare a cord of six [fathoms] that appears long; that very same cord, when measured by the span (*vitasti*), shall be consistent with all the tantras.
In this manner, one should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) up to twelve [fingers] in size,
such that it appears exceedingly beautiful upon the earth.
Therefore, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) has been fully described for the benefit of practitioners;
one should construct the pit according to the prescribed rules on ground measured by the proper dimensions.
Just as the bathing of the sacrificial pits is prescribed, so too is their excavation;
one should perform the laying of the three cords at the base, the middle, and the top regions.
One should construct a beautiful pit according to the prescribed rite, which is pleasing to the mind of the practitioner;
it should have three girdles (mekhalās) in accordance with all the tantras.
One should fashion a beautiful girdle with an interval of one finger-breadth;
it should be made according to the prescribed rule for as long as the [stūpa] may extend up to ten cubits.
One should gradually increase the girdle by the measure of one finger-width at a time;
that girdle should be well-fashioned for the practitioner and captivating to the mind.
One should increase it by one finger-breadth, two finger-breadths, and three finger-breadths respectively; this is the procedure taught by Śaṅkara.
One should place a very beautiful yoni directly in front of the *kuṇḍa*;
one should gradually increase the tip of the yoni by the measure of a *paramātra*.
O Great Goddess, from hand to hand, by means of the measure of two sixes (twelve),
one makes the yoni complete with its apertures, endowed with all the tantric principles.
The excavation of the pit should extend as far as that; at its end, one should fashion a beautiful and most enchanting lotus within the vaginal cavity.
One should also dig a pit beneath the *kuṇḍa* on all sides;
it should be somewhat slanted in sequence, and then filled with earth once again.
One should fashion the vulva according to the prescribed rule, having the shape of a horse's hoof-tip;
it should be made beautiful and symmetrical, so as to be pleasing to the sight.
Once the field has been made square, one should construct every fire-pit (kuṇḍa) within it;
whatever the shape of the pit may be, the girdle (mekhalā) is prescribed to be of that same shape.
The measurement of a hasta is said to be twenty-four aṅgulas;
one aṅgula consists of eight yavas, according to the consensus of all tantras.
Whatever the measurement of the fire-pits (kuṇḍas) may be, the excavation is prescribed to be of that same measure;
or one may dig the pit to half that size, as this is in accordance with all the Tantras.
For a hundred oblations, the pit should be one cubit; for a thousand, one cubit;
for ten thousand, it should be two cubits, or one may calculate it as four cubits.
For one hundred thousand repetitions, it should be four cubits; for two hundred thousand, it is traditionally held to be double that.
For ten million, it should be six cubits, and for a crore, it is traditionally held to be eight cubits.
A sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring one cubit is prescribed for the recitation of one hundred thousand [mantras];
up to ten lakhs, one should increase it by one cubit for each lakh.
A sacrificial pit measuring ten cubits is prescribed for a *koṭi-homa*;
however, O Maheśānī, in the Kali age, there is no possibility of performing such a great sacrifice.
When the great homa is performed, the worlds shall attain the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice;
O Maheśvarī, the quadrangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) brings about all perfections.
The *pūrṇa* (full) shape bestows prosperity; the *yoni* (womb) shape brings wealth; the *ardhacandra* (half-moon) brings riches;
the *triśūla* (trident) shape causes the destruction of enemies; and the *vartula* (circular) shape is for rites of pacification (*śāntika*).
A six-cornered pit is prescribed for killing; the lotus-shaped pit is supreme for bestowing nourishment;
and the square pit, O Maheśvarī, destroys diseases.
For Brahmins it is square, and for kings it is circular in shape.
For Vaiśyas, it is indeed a half-moon shape endowed with all structural elements;
for all others, however, it is a square—this is the consensus of the learned.
One should know the form of the *kuṇḍa* to be the supreme primordial body;
its head is said to be in the east, while the heart is in the south and north.
The *kuṇḍa* should be known as the belly, while the womb and the feet are in the west;
thus one should understand the *kuṇḍa*, which is concealed in all tantras.
One should perform the daily and occasional rites upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila),
having fashioned it from sand to a measurement of six finger-breadths.
Thus, O Goddess, it has been described in manifold ways in various tantras;
variegated with diverse and brilliant colors, it is exceedingly beautiful.
Equipped with a neck like a Guṇḍī drum and joined with the feet of a deer and so forth, it has the face of a boar,
a camel, a deer, and a camel, as well as the body of an elephant, a camel, and a tortoise.
One should fashion [the vessel] in this manner according to the prescribed rule, provided with an elephant’s frontal globe;
thus one should understand the *śruva* ladle, and after that, the mandalas.
The mandala is said to be of four kinds, encompassing all tantras:
the five-goat (pañcāja), the nine-navel (navanābha), and the sarvatobhadra.
The field known as Laghusarvatantra, which is endowed with all systems,
is made four-cornered and divided into equal parts.
One should divide the central body into five or four parts,
and according to the rule, allocate the four [parts] in the four directions by means of equal portions.
In the center of that, one should draw a beautiful and very charming lotus,
provided with filaments, a pericarp, eight petals, and a whorl.
Outside the lotus, the pedestal (pīṭha) should be formed according to the rules in the four directions;
it is adorned with a pathway arranged in rows and beautified by primary and secondary ornaments.
The practitioner should always draw the maṇḍala according to the prescribed rite, endowed with all its ritual components,
using various colored powders in that manner.
One should color the most beautiful maṇḍala with five powders:
yellow turmeric powder and white powder derived from śāli rice.
Kauśāmbha salt is said to be black, produced from burnt chaff;
alternatively, it may be a blue powder, described as being black in color.
The dark-colored [lotus] made from the leaves of the *bilva* and other such plants is said to consist of five colors;
one should fashion that lotus with various powders according to this procedure.
The pericarp is described as yellow in color, the filaments as reddish,
and the petals as white with red tips.
The wise one should adorn it with a yellowish-white color and dark green for the living beings;
or else, he should fashion the pericarp with a red color.
One should fashion that lotus in its respective place, wherever it belongs, according to the sequence;
this has been taught for the sake of beauty and is consistent with all tantras.
Regarding that, it is stated there: the lotuses are born of white;
the doors are white in color, while the intermediate spaces are said to be red like gold.
The *upaśobhā* is yellow in color and the corners are reddish;
immediately after the pedestal (*pīṭha*), one should provide the creeper known as *kalpa*.
It should not be made with uneven colors, but should be provided with fruits and flowers;
the wise one should construct the mandala everywhere with equal proportions.
Since all the tantras are seen to be most enchanting,
one of vast intelligence should first worship the Rākṣasa, the lord of the site (Vāstu).
By performing which act the knower of mantras enjoys the fruit of initiation— namely,
by slaying the *rākṣasa* named Vāstunāman and taking possession of that body.
He had terrible fangs, a massive body, tawny eyes, and three eyes;
he carried a skull-cup and a staff topped with a skull, and was endowed with his own inherent qualities.
One should worship with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, combined with red meat and other offerings;
having first obtained his permission, the Vāstuyāga is then performed.
That which is called Sarvatobhadra was taught by the Lotus-born;
having abandoned the secondary ornamentation, it is briefly known everywhere by that name.
Having made the ground square and divided it into equal parts,
O Pārvatī, the preceptor should draw a nine-petaled lotus there according to this procedure.
The instructor should fashion it beautifully and symmetrically using various colors;
this mandala, which bestows all accomplishments, is said to bring new gain.
One should draw a lotus with excellent characteristics in the center of the four-cornered directions;
this is declared to be the five-navelled maṇḍala, most beautiful to behold.
In whatever manner the ritual for the worship of the deity is performed,
the mandala must necessarily be constructed according to this procedure.
Then that goddess Bhavasundarī becomes well-pleased;
the auspicious [mandala] known as Sarvatobhadra is seen everywhere.
In all tantras, the mandala is joined with various powders;
now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe the most beautiful Vāstuyāga.
In all auspicious rites, the preceptor should first perform the Vāstuyāga;
he should first prostrate to the Earth with this mantra:
Oṃ! O Earth, strewn with all kinds of jewels, girdled by the oceans—O Mother of the World, grant me success for the attainment of the fruits of all my desires!
O Goddess, one should not perform any ritual action without the sacrifice of the *cāsta*;
one should prepare a square ground with straight, sharp, and auspicious lines.
The preceptor should provide this ear-ornament with equal proportions;
it should be beautifully drawn with various colors, exquisite and most captivating.
The preceptor should color it with five colors according to this rite;
there, the preceptor should worship those deities according to their respective portions.
The preceptor, according to the prescribed method, should worship the deities in their respective places with this ritual procedure, using perfumes, flowers, sandalwood, and other offerings.
The wise one worshipped according to the prescribed rite with various food offerings, oblations, and sacrifices, as well as with incense, lamps, and fresh water.
One should worship Brahmā there in the four central squares;
thereafter, one should worship [the deities] in the four directions, starting from the east, according to the prescribed rite.
One should worship with supreme devotion for the sake of accomplishing all tasks;
O Goddess, one should perform the sacrifice by pairing them two by two for the attainment of the fruit of all siddhis.
One should worship [the deities] in the directions, starting from the east, according to the prescribed rule;
O Dear One, all that has been told regarding the space between the deity and the practitioner.
The practitioner should first worship Āryāman, Vivasta, as well as Mitra and Mahādhava, according to the previously stated ritual procedure.
The wise practitioner should worship [the deities] all around in the pairs of half-cones starting from the southeast (vahni):
Sāvitrī and Savitṛ, Śukra, Indra, and Yama.
Rudra, Rudravana, Āpa, Āpya, and Āpavatsaka—
these are again placed in the squares surrounding both sides of the ear-ornament (karṇasūtra).
One should worship, in due order starting from the east, according to this rite:
Sarva, Śuddha, Cāryamana, Jambhaka, and Nipipitsaka.
One should worship [the deities] in the directions starting from the east;
then, in the remaining compartments, [one worships] Aparjanya starting from Īśāna, followed by Jaya, Śatru, and Bhāskara.
Then the wise one should worship Sadyovṛta and Antariksha in the east;
then Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, Yama, and Graharakṣaka.
One should worship Gandharva and Bhuṇḍarāṇa, as well as Mṛga, on the south;
likewise, Nimi, Dvārapālaka, Sugrīva, and Varuṇa.
Puṣpadanta is situated in the northeast; Sureśa, Īśa, Raudra, and Gopa are in the east; Vāyu, Nāga, Mukhya, Soma, and Bhalāṭa are likewise [in the north].
Maṅgalā, Adhya, Diti, and Aditi are established in the direction of Soma.
Thus, with many kinds of perfumes, flowers, food, and water— (p. 15b) [one should worship].
One should worship with supreme devotion that jeweled mandala, described of old by Brahmā, which is adorned with various colors and variegated hues.
One should fashion canopies, leafy garlands, and so forth according to the prescribed rules;
one should also construct a beautiful banner with flags in the four directions.
The wise one should arrange eight jars in the eight directions within the pavilion; he should construct the fire-pit for the preceptor in the center according to the prescribed rules.
One should place sprouted shoots here and there in the four directions;
then, in due order, the *pālikās*, the five-faced vessels, and the *savas*.
These [fingers] are respectively sixteen, twelve, and eight finger-breadths in length;
when filled with fragrant water, it is declared to be the "sprouted" (jātāṅkura) vessel.
One should scatter seeds there on all sides with the *sudhā* seed-syllable;
one should appoint a preceptor according to the rules, who has mastered the meaning of all the scriptures.
Śyāmāka, māyaka, and kandhu rice are all universally approved;
on the seventh day prior to the initiation, one should always remain self-restrained.
For seven nights, one should perform worship for all the deities;
one should worship the Supreme Goddess with various offerings and oblations.
One should worship the Supreme Goddess with mantras beginning with *praṇava* (Om) and ending with *namaḥ*.
[She is] the elements, the ancestors, the yakṣas, the nāgas, Brahmā, Śiva, and the sacrificial oblation.
The preceptor should worship all [the deities] in sequence over seven nights;
for all seven nights, the deity is universally esteemed.
O Pārvatī, I shall describe those offerings with which one should worship them:
one should worship the bhūtas with parched grains (lājā), as well as perfumes, flowers, and sandalwood paste.
One should worship those— the Lord of Beings (Bhūtādhipa), the Host of Beings (Bhūtagaṇa), and the Master of Beings (Bhūteśa)—
in sequence with offerings consisting of sesame, turmeric, curd, and parched grain flour.
One should constantly worship the ancestors with rice mixed with sesame seeds and accompanied by food and flowers; this was declared by the Lotus-born One.
To the Yakṣas who have nets of rays for hands, [offer] coconut water,
a single ball of jaggery, and jaggery-rice accompanied by various flavors.
Having offered curd, milk, milk-rice, and whatever else is greatly dear to him to Viṣṇu, a person shall then obtain all perfections.
Then, for the sake of accomplishing one's rites, one should worship the Ālokeśvarī-bhās;
there, one should worship the Mātṛkās and all the deities beginning with Gaurī.
Gaurī, Padmā, Śacī, Medhā, Sāvitrī, Vijayā, Jayā,
Devasenā, Svadhā, Svāhā, Śānti, Puṣṭi, Dhṛti, and Kṣamā.
One should always worship one's own deity and the family deity in due order;
one should worship Gaṇeśa and the others, and say "forgive me" to them in sequence.
Then the stream of wealth (vasordhārā), which destroys all obstacles, should be offered;
one should worship Rudra, who dwells above the door, with supreme devotion.
Then one should perform the Nāndī-śrāddha according to this procedure for the father,
the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather.
While his father is still alive, he should perform the Śrāddha beginning with that father;
thereafter, [he should offer it] to the maternal grandfather, the great-grandfather, and the great-great-grandfather.
O Goddess, one should cast six lumps [of food] according to one's own capacity, without specific designation;
then one should perform the śrāddha rite according to the rules, in accordance with the names and lineages.
One should first perform the *śrāddha* for the deities, and then the *nāndīmukha* rite;
Purūravas and Mādravas are the deities in all ritual undertakings.
One should offer handfuls of water in the śrāddha according to the sequence of all the deities;
having caused the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be made, one should then designate all the ritual acts.
In all matters and for all undertakings, one should first worship Gaṇeśa and the water-pot;
thereafter, one should worship Gaṇeśa, the Sun, and Śiva.
One should worship Viṣṇu with diligence for the sake of accomplishing all undertakings and goals,
as well as Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and the destroyer of obstacles (Vighnanāśinī).
Then, O Pārvatī, [he saw] the guardians of the directions, the elephants of the quarters, the gods, the sages, and clusters of jewels;
as well as the days, lunar dates, yogas, and karaṇas.
One should worship with supreme devotion, endowed with all the tantras;
then the preceptor shall kindle that fire in the sacrificial pit according to this rite.
In the aforementioned groups of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas),
the excellent practitioner should kindle the fire according to the prescribed rite, preceded by the recitation of the mantra.
One should consecrate that sacrificial pit with the root mantra according to this procedure;
and the Guru should bestow whichever mantra belongs to whichever world, according to the prescribed rite.
That should be known as the root mantra, endowed with all the tantras;
or else, O lotus-faced one, listen as I shall explain it to you.
The digging of that pit is prescribed with the *kavaca* and *astra* mantras;
one should sprinkle it with water from one's own feet, in accordance with all the tantras.
The wise know the mantra "pāntaṃ" (the letter *pa*) joined with "halaṭa" (the letter *ha*);
having extracted the seed-syllable of Śiva (*śa*), it is endowed with the sixth vowel (*ū*).
That which is joined with the *bindu* and the *nāda* is proclaimed as the armor (*kavaca*);
one should know that to be the *māyābīja*, according to the words of Mahākāla.
One should perform the leveling according to the rules with the seed-syllable of Māyā and the Astra-mantra;
the smearing of that pit is proclaimed to be done with the seed-syllable of Lajjā.
The letter ŚA (śānta) joined with fire (RA), adorned with NĀDA and BINDU—
this is declared to be the seed-syllable of Lajjā, endowed with all the Tantras.
Then, one should sprinkle that pit with the seed-syllable of Māyā and the Astra-mantra;
there, three lines should be drawn in sequence, three by three.
With their tips pointing eastward and northward, they are provided with all the necessary components;
as great as the width of the sacrificial pit is, so great shall be their equal divisions.
O Dear One, the preceptor should fashion those [images] from kuśa grass and the roots of kuśa grass in equal proportions,
using the root mantra as well as the armor mantra.
Alternatively, one should perform the rite for the crest-lock (śikhā) according to the prescribed rule using the armor-mantra (kavaca) alone;
the deities residing at the tips pointing eastward are traditionally held to be Mukunda, Īśa, and Puraṃdara.
One should worship Brahmā, Vaivasvata, and Indu with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings within the interior space of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) that possess prominent lines.
One should worship the deities upon the lines; thereafter, one should begin the hexagon.
One should fashion a most beautiful hexagon in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
There too, O Pārvatī, one should worship the fire preceded by the invocation,
using the *praṇava* alone for everything and likewise with the *kavaca*.
One should likewise fashion the lines endowed with all the tantric principles;
then [one should worship] Vāgīśvarī, who has bathed after her menses and possesses a subtle form.
She is joined with Vāgīśvara, endowed with a taste for the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa),
adorned with all ornaments, and resembling a cloud out of season.
One should worship with various offerings and oblations, and with perfumes and sandalwood;
having thus meditated and performed the worship, one should direct the blazing fire there.
Four-armed and red in color, adorned with all ornaments,
produced from the sun-stone or made of iron.
Whether it originates from a cow, or likewise from stone,
one should fashion it from the mouth [of the image] according to the injunctions of the Vedic mantras.
Then, one should carefully bring fire produced from lightning or from a forest conflagration;
likewise, one may bring fire from the house of a twice-born man, accompanied by a Brāhmaṇa.
The preceptor should perform the consecration according to the ritual procedure with this mantra;
he should extract the mantra beginning with the *kavaca* (the protective syllable), preceded by the *praṇava*, and ending with the *astra*.
The wise one should cast what has been rejected into the southern part of the enemy's domain;
at the time of discarding the portion for the flesh-eaters, he should utter this mantra.
O Maheśvarī, with the arrow-mantra, the seed-syllable of fire, and the armor-mantra,
one should ignite that auspicious fire within the center of the sacrificial pit.
Then, one should display the Denumudrā there upon the head of the fire;
one should protect the fire in the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) with the Astra-mantra according to this procedure.
Having enveloped it with the Kavaca mantra, one should then circumambulate above the fire-pit;
having circled it with the Praṇava, one should worship it with the seed-syllable of Fire (Raṃ).
Then, O Dear One, one should wash the goddess Vāgīśvarī with perfumes, flowers, and so forth,
using this mantra accompanied by the fire element.
One should extract the seed-syllable (bīja) ending with the letter *sa*, conjoined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*;
this is declared to be the seed of Śiva, endowed with all the Tantras.
Then the preceptor should kindle the fire there with this mantra: "O Cit Piṅgala, burn, burn! Cook, cook! having uttered this pair [of words].
Reveal everything there, joined with the wife-ending [letter] of fire;
the seed-syllable of the moon joined with the letter *na* and endowed with the *mukhavṛtta* [vowel].
Likewise, having extracted the seed-syllable of Śiva, one should join it with the circular face (the letter *u*);
this is declared to be the consort of Fire (*svāhā*), endowed with all the Tantras.
The best of fire-practitioners should meditate upon [the deity] as golden-hued;
then, he should sequentially place the seed-syllable and other elements upon all the limbs of the fire.
The preceptor should place the vajra upon the head, as well as upon the breath, anus, and genitals;
he should place the pair of eyes and the tongue of fire for the sake of accomplishing all limbs.
One should sequentially place those letters from *sa* to *va*, joined with the *bindu* and *nāda*,
conjoined with the sixth vowel (*ū*), and combined with the letter *ya* in due order.
In ancient times, Brahmā spoke of the various tongues of fire;
they are indeed sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa, bestowing all accomplishments.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) everywhere with the fire-mantra for the sake of all accomplishments.
[The five fires are] Hiraṇyā, Gaganā, Aruṇā, Kṛṣṇā, and Suprabhā.
Bahūrūpā and Rūpā should be well-employed for the sake of the karma of sentient beings;
likewise Padmarāgā, Suparṇā, and Bhadralohitā.
Lohitā, Śvetā, Dhūmrā, and Karālikā—all of these are endowed with the quality of rajas; one should employ them in all ritual activities.
Viśvamūrti, Sphuliṅginī, Dhūmravarṇā, Jarā, Lohitā, Karālā, and Kālī follow immediately after her.
These seven [syllables] are employed according to the prescribed rite for cruel rites;
they are the tongue and the deity of the syllable—listen, O beloved of Hara!
The tongue is said by those who know the tantras to consist of the letters *gu*, *ṇa*, *va*, and *r*.
The immortals, all the gandharvas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and piśācas [are its presiding deities].
The deities of the seven tongues have been proclaimed along with their mantras;
one should worship them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as incense, lamps, and the highest offerings.
The preceptor should perform the installation of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) with the prāṇa-mantra;
the most excellent of preceptors should then perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) of the eight mantras upon the eight limbs.
One should place the mantras, complete with all their constituent parts, upon the head, the shoulders, the hips, the two sides, the region of the waist, and the heart.
Jātavedas, Saptajihva, the one known as Havyavāhana,
another known as Aśvodaraja, and the one called Pūrvaviśvanara.
Kaumāratejā should be placed there, and then Vimukha is remembered; Agnimukha is likewise known.
These are the steps based on the Tārā-mantra, and they are not those various forms of Fire.
One should indeed perform the placement according to this ritual procedure in the sequence beginning with the thumb:
the thumb, the index finger, the middle finger, the ring finger, and the little finger.
Next, with both hands joined so that all the fingers are turned in the reverse direction,
one should perform the rites beginning with the invocation and then provide a seat.
Having uttered "Obeisance to Vahni" as the beginning of the seat preceded by the Praṇava,
the preceptor should then meditate upon that Fire with this mantra.
O Goddess of the gods, one should protect the fire from others with those waters by means of the seed-syllable of fire and the auspicious armor-mantra.
One should offer a line of water by means of the *praṇava* ending with *namaḥ* or *phaṭ*, according to the prescribed rule,
using a clockwise motion.

Likewise, the excellent practitioner, in accordance with the ritual injunctions, should touch all the kusha grass in the four directions with both the roots and the tips, keeping the tips pointing toward the east.
Then, one should perform the strewing of grass according to the measure of one's own right arm; the spreading of *kuśa* grass in the four directions is prescribed to be done with the *kavaca* mantra.
Having avoided [the rite] in the presence [of the deity], it was said by the Lotus-born One:
"Then one should perform the dismissal of the Goddess, and then the dismissal of the God."
With the mantra "Forgive me," according to the tradition of all the Vedas, [one should say]:
"O Goddess of gods, may Sadāśiva, joined with Śakti, go to his own abode."
Then, the practitioner should invoke Vaiśvānara Jātavedas from the place of purchase and so forth,
reciting the words "lohitākṣa" and others in sequence for the accomplishment of all rites.
The Vidyā beginning with the letter *ra*, which extends as far as the wife of Fire (*vahni*), bestows all accomplishments.
This extraction of the mantra of Fire consists of twenty-one syllables.
This mantra for invocation was spoken by the Lotus-born One;
one should worship those tongues of flame in sequence within the six-cornered sacrificial pit.
One should worship the eight guardians of the world according to the previously mentioned procedure, using perfumes, flowers, food offerings, incense, lamps, and sandalwood paste.
One should worship the Lord— Indra, Vahni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, and Nabhasvat— as well as Svadhānta, together with their weapons, vehicles, and ornaments.
One should worship Brahmā there in the northeast and the King of Serpents in the southwest upon their respective seats for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
The wise one should meditate on Ananta in the four directions of the fire: first as black-colored, then as dark blue.
The vajra, the śakti, and likewise the staff, then the sword and the noose;
[they are] smoke-colored, white-colored, and then black-colored.
One should worship the pure-colored and likewise pure [deity] on the crown through yoga;
then Brahmā of red color, and thereafter the white-colored one.
The wise one should contemplate the infinite [space] and likewise the four weapons of Fire in the four directions:
the thunderbolt (vajra), the spear (śakti), the staff (daṇḍa), and thereafter the sword (khaḍga) and the noose (pāśa).
The goad, the mace, the trident, the lotus, and then the discus—
this is declared to be [the sequence] for the guardians of the directions, complete with their respective mantras and tantras.
I shall describe the excellent colors of the missiles; listen, O Pārvatī:
yellow, snow-white, white-shining, radiant, and the color of a kanda root.
One should visualize them in sequence as blue, the seed-syllable of Kara (yellow), fair (yellowish-white), white, slightly red, and then whitish-red.
There, one should worship the vehicle according to the prescribed rite in its own place:
namely, Airāvata, the goat, the man, and the crocodile.
The preceptor [should visualize] a deer, a horse, a bull, a swan, and a tortoise in sequence;
everywhere, he should likewise [use] the root mantra and the armor mantra.
Having performed the purification of the *śruva* ladle, one should cast it in the western direction;
with that same *astra-mantra*, one should consecrate the *śālī* rice.
One should cast two *kuśa* leaves there with the root mantra;
for the purpose of the fire offering (*homa*), one should cast clarified butter there while reciting the mantra.
Thereafter, one should burn two *kuśa* leaves in the fire according to the ritual injunctions;
this was taught by the Lotus-born One using the very *hṛdaya* mantra.
One should rub all the limbs there for the complete prosperity of the fire,
as well as the channels, the vital breaths, the teeth, the mouth, or the belly and the ears.
Having recollected the cheeks, the lips, the fire, the anus, the generative organ, the waist, the hips, the belly, the pair of knees, and the two sides of the waist;
The two arms, the two nostrils, the tongue, the back, and after that the two breasts,
the base of the neck, and after that the pores of the skin.
Then, having meditated, one should offer clarified butter for the sake of prosperity;
with these mantras, O Great Goddess, one should crush Indrāṇī.
The armor (kavaca) is with the *praṇava* alone, and thereafter the word "Agni";
this vidyā is said to end with *svāhā*, through its connection with the southern [face] of Agni.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of reality (tatvabīja), one should offer an oblation from the left eye to Soma with the beloved of Fire for the sake of all accomplishments.
Then, for Agni and Soma, [the mantras] ending in *svāhā* are approved by all;
one should extract the seed-syllable of fire (*raṃ*) followed by *agniṃ* ending in *ṅe*.
Then, from the purchase [of the Soma], the offerings for Agni-Sviṣṭakṛt are made; all [mantras] are agreed upon as ending with "svāhā.
The wise one should offer into the mouth of that [fire] with "svāhā" for the sake of complete prosperity.
Having recollected the two previous seeds, one should extract the fire [seed] ending in the dative case (Ṅe);
for each individual limb, there is a collection of mantras ending in Svāhā.
Having then extracted that [essence], one should employ it for the perfection of the limbs of Agni;
one should perform the invocation (āvāhana) sequentially into each limb by means of the seed-syllable of Fire.
Furthermore, the wise one should offer oblations repeatedly from all sides with the fire-seed mantra (*vahni-bīja*);
he should give each individual oblation for the purpose of severing every limb.
One should offer twenty-five oblations there into the fire with the root mantra;
by this method, one should contemplate the identity of the fire and the deity.
Then one should offer [the oblation] to Brahmā, the creator, and to Prajāpati;
[these mantras] begin with Oṃ, end with Namaḥ, and are endowed with the power of Svāhā.
O Dear One, the blazing of the fire is declared as *iḍā*, and it is considered to be Mahākāla.
Now I shall describe the procedure for the substances, together with the mental [visualization], for the purpose of the *homa*.
One karṣa of ghee is prescribed; that same measure is recorded for milk.
The five nectars (pañcāmṛta) are of that same measure, as are honey and milk.
That which is derived from cow's milk should be the same; a handful of parched grain and so forth is considered a standard measure.
Rice grains should be of the size of a handful, and its derivatives should be likewise.
Sugar and other such substances should be half a *pala* each, in accordance with all the scriptures;
likewise, there should be one smooth fruit, one leaf, and one flower for each.
One should break the *vṛhatphala* into pieces as prescribed, joining them together; one should make it equal in size to a mouthful, endowed with all the tantric properties.
One *sukti* measure of salt and twenty *marica* peppers are prescribed;
likewise, *guggulu*, *tintiḍī* seeds, and *hiṅgu* are recorded as being of the same measure.
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, kastūrī, and saffron—
these are declared in all Tantras to be the standard measure for the oblation (homa) in every instance.
Then one should offer the Aghora mantra, and after that, the Pratyaghora;
having raised the foot for Indra, one should first cast the tip of the ladle toward the west.
Having raised the *ṣamāṣa* footprint with its tip facing east, one should likewise place [the footprints of] Varuṇa and Soma; then, one should offer them at all four doors in every direction.
One should prepare a seat by means of the clockwise-turning yoga;
thereupon, one should always meditate upon the chosen deity according to the prescribed rite.
Now, O Pārvatī, I shall describe the fruit of the limb-oblation (aṅgahoma);
one should always meditate upon Viśvānara during the oblations with fuel-sticks, O Pārvatī.
In all oblations of clarified butter (ājya), the wise practitioner should meditate upon the Fire;
he should offer everything into its mouth for the sake of complete prosperity in every rite.
If [the fire] is drawn toward the ear, there will be disease; if toward the eye, it will take the form of Mars;
if toward the nose, there is mental distress; and if toward the head, there is the loss of wealth.
In all matters and everywhere, the wise man should prescribe the fire-oblation (homa) at the beginning;
O lotus-faced one, listen as I shall declare the names of the fires.
In rites performed for specific desires as well as in obligatory rites, the preceptor should perform [the fire-laying] with effort;
in the rite of conception (garbhādhāna), the fire named Marut is prescribed.
Candramas is to be known for the *puṃsavana* rite; the one named Śṛṅga for rites of nourishment (*pauṣṭika*); Maṅgala by name for the *sīmantonnayana*; and Pragalbha for the *jātakarman*.
By name he is indeed Pārthiva-vahni; likewise, he is Śuci on the seat, Satyanāman on the crest-lock, and Samudbhava at the time of the vow.
In the Gomedha sacrifice he is known as Dhṛti, and in marriage he is remembered as Yojaka;
in all rites and in every undertaking, he is the Yojaka, approved by Brahmā.
He is the bearer of oblations for the gods and the carrier of funeral offerings for the ancestors;
however, for the Raudra-homa, the name of Agni is prescribed as Tejas.
In the *śāntihoma* the fire is named Śikhin; in the *utsarga*, Jātavedas; for purification of the ground, Hasu; and for one's own kindred, Dhanañjaya.
In a *lakṣa*-homa, the fire is Vahni; in a *koṭi*-homa, it is Hūtaśana.
For the purpose of pacification (*śānti*), it is named Agni, and in a *vāruṇa* rite, it is Hūtaśana.
In the Viṣṇu-homa, the names of the fire are indeed Huta and Kalyāṇa, as well as Bhadra;
these names of the fire have been proclaimed in accordance with all the Tantras.
He who engages others in various rites for desired objects is honored by all.
Now, O lotus-faced one, I shall describe the fire-colored [mantra]; listen.
Resembling gold, vermilion, the morning sun, saffron, and honey—
the color of Suvarṇaretas is proclaimed to be beautiful.
Now I shall explain the sound of the fire, which bestows all prosperity:
the intense, rushing roar of the fire, as if burning Bhairava and the other [deities], brings auspiciousness.
It was filled with *nāga*, *campaka*, *punnāga*, *pāṭalā*, and *yūthikā* flowers;
it also possessed *puṣpa*, *indīvara*, and *kahlāra* lotuses, as well as the fragrance of *guggulu*.
The auspicious fragrance of the fire is consistent with all treatises;
its flames move clockwise, are free from trembling, and the crest of the fire possesses the luster of an umbrella.
Smoke as white as a kunda flower or the moon brings auspiciousness to the sacrificer and especially to the kingdom; it brings about auspiciousness for all undertakings.
Fire that has entered the black fire will cause total destruction;
when joined with the sound of a crow, even one's lifespan there shall perish.
If the fire is equal in sound to the sound of a dog, everything is destroyed at that very moment;
if the fire has a foul odor, it will cause the destruction of all.
Thus, many kinds of defects have been described in various tantras;
for the sake of pacifying all defects, one should perform one hundred and eight oblations.
Having meditated upon the identity of the fire, the deity, and the tree,
one should then offer oblations into the mouth of the fire, which is the form of the deity, according to the prescribed ritual.
Now I shall proclaim the Cakra, which is endowed with all the Tantras;
I shall explain the Cakra of Siddhi and the rest—listen, O lotus-faced one!
The wise one should draw a square grid consisting of four compartments;
furthermore, he should draw another set of four [compartments] there in sequence.
The wise one should write the letters from *a* to *kṣa*, starting from the root-square, in their proper sequence, each preceding one following the one before it.
One should write the letters of the squares in sequence by means of the fourfold method starting from the south;
it is taught that the counting should be performed in the very same manner as the writing.
The wise one should contemplate, in due order, the Siddhi, the Sādhya, the Susuddha, and the Ari;
and again and again, right there, he should focus on that which he desires through yoga.
Then, in that very same manner, the wise one should contemplate according to the prescribed rule;
by means of a clockwise rotation, he should count them in sequence.
Success is achieved in time through recitation; the *sādhya* [deities] are won by means of summoning (*āhvāna*) and other rites.
Those who are well-perfected (*susiddha*) should be known as nourishers; they cut through obstacles without delay.
Resembling the *dhustūra* flower, joined with the twelve signs (*rāśis*); [the letters] *va*, *na*, *ga*, *ra*, *kha*, *ra*, *ga*, *ū*, *ṇa*, *śa*, *mī*, and *śo*bhā [are assigned] to the signs.
The vowels, when divided in sequence, are known as the daughters, beginning with *ka* and ending with *śa*;
these, from *a* to *kṣa*, are associated with the zodiac signs starting from Aries.
The best of instructors should write the letters ending with *mīna* within the squares;
the wise one should write those letters by means of the left-and-right arrangement.
One should perform the calculation by that very [method]; this is known as the "conjunction with one's own sign.
Wherever the first letter of one's own name occurs, there that conjunction is said to be.
The relatives are remembered as being one, five, and nine; and two, six, ten, and finally eleven.
Fire (three), Rudra (eleven), the root (one), and six are the nourishers; twelve, eight, and four are the destroyers.
The vital breath of Rudra has fallen away from the mountain;
O you who possess vast hands, the worlds have perished, for destruction has come upon those who rise as the wicked.
The vowels in order, followed by *ya* and *ra*, and likewise *sva* in *Revatī*;
this is called the "Wheel of the Nakṣatras," which one should draw according to the measure of the syllables.
The most excellent practitioner should draw nine squares in three rows in sequence;
he should worship the groups of vowels and the favorable squares for the houses with the mantra.
Birth, death, calamity, security, enemy,
accomplisher, slayer, friend, and great friend— these states, beginning with birth, recur again and again.
The presiding deities of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) are as follows: Aśvin, Yama, Agni, Dhātṛ, Śaśin (Candra), Rudra, Aditi,

Guru (Bṛhaspati), Ahi (Sarpa), Pitṛs, Bhaga, Aryaman, Anu, Kṛt, Tvaṣṭṛ, Pavana (Vāyu), Indra-Agni, Mitra, Indu (Candra), Nirṛti, Jala (Varuṇa), Viśvedevas, Hari (Viṣṇu), Vāsava (Indra), Varuṇa, Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, and Pūṣan.
The impurity of a zodiacal sign is declared according to its own constellation, the deity, and its friend through the conjunction of signs; this is in accordance with all the Tantras.
O Pārvatī, listen as I shall explain the sequence of one's own family and the non-family;
the wheel consisting of the elements and colors is known as one's own family and the other family.
One should reveal the mantra-syllable consisting of the elements to the practitioner;
one’s own family is said to be the wheel conjoined with the letters of one’s own name.
One should divide the mantra according to one's own family (kula), and not according to any other family whatsoever;
for the wind is the friend of fire, as they are mutually agreed upon by their very nature.
If one should know that one's own family has a single elemental deity, it is as follows:
the Pārthiva [belongs to] Varuṇa, the Maitra to Agni, and the Āgneya to Marut.
The Māruta [varga] is remembered as the enemy of the Pārthiva [varga] and of the vowels;
the Antastha [varga] is the enemy of the Āgneya [varga], as are the Nacabha and Tejas [vargas].
Among all these [elements], that which is ethereal (nābhasa) is non-contradictory;
a wise man should not cause impurity among those that are mutually contradictory.
The wise know that water is unfavorable for the color of fire. (p.
19) Multiply the Sādhya numbers by fourteen, twelve, two, twelve, five, six, four, three, five, eight, and nine.
One should multiply the letters of the practitioner's name by ten, eight, four, three, seven, four, six,

and three respectively; then, having added the letters from the name "Nāmājha" and the letters from "Nādaka," the remainder— whether it be a deficit or a surplus— of the two sums shall be known as the debt or the wealth.
The debtor should perform the deity-syllable according to the method of investigation;
otherwise, by doing it contrarily, all of that will become fruitless.
One should increase the limbs by means of houses through gradual application;
having first considered the positions of Indra, the Sun, and so forth, this sequence is approved in the Tantra.
Six, six, six, and then "void"—thus it is said; then two groups of three and four, then void, then them, then void, and finally, one should present the three at the end.
This is declared to be the limb of the deity, endowed with all the tantras:
two, two, five, and indeed zero; two, one, and zero as well.
Four, four, and one are declared to be the marks of the practitioner;
the calculation is proclaimed to be performed by means of these very syllables.
I shall describe the Kūrmacakra, which bestows the fruit of success in recitation;
without piercing [the vital points], one can never attain that accomplishment by any means whatsoever.
The wise man should draw a circular diagram divided into nine compartments in the shape of a tortoise,
[marking] again the two hands, the two feet, the back, the face, the belly, and the pair of sides.
The practitioner himself should write [the letters] according to the sequence starting from the east;
he should write the syllables in nine squares according to the sequence starting from the east.
One should draw the eight groups [of letters] in order starting from the east;
five, five, and five [letters] form each group, beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṅa*, according to this sequence.
First is the group ending in *ñ* and *t*, then that ending in *ṭ* and *n*;
after that, the group ending in *p* and *m*, and immediately following that, the group ending in *ṣ* and *v*.
One should form [the letters] from *śa* to *sa* with three [repetitions], followed by the syllables *ha* and *kṣa*.
This is declared to be the eight groups (*vargāṣṭaka*), which is consistent with all Tantras.
Having divided the belly and the stomach, one should fashion nine compartments;
there, having placed two in each starting from the east in sequence, one should write the vowels.
The enumeration of the directions, beginning with the east according to the prescribed rule, has been fully described.
Wherever the first syllable of the field (*kṣetra*) and so forth is located, there action is said to be easy;
it is declared that for those of short life, success-bestowing [mantras] are held in the mouth or in the hand.
When situated in the belly, it is indifferent; when at the feet, it brings only suffering.
When located in the tail, it effects salutation and expulsion in all rites.
This is declared to be the Kūrma-cakra, which bestows the fruit of all accomplishments.
One should draw two lines from east to west, and from their center, one line toward the south and another toward the direction of Kuvera (the north).
Having likewise pierced through in the sequence of Maheśa, Rakṣas, Adhipati, Vāyu, and Hūbhāśana;
One should write the vowels, excluding the neuter ones, starting from the beginning; such that *ka*, *ḍa*, and *ma* appear in the first square.
Having written [the consonants] starting with *meṣa* (me), this is the procedure, until the final dedication at the end of the *aṇḍaja* (vowels).
Regarding this as well, the investigation of the zodiacal sign (*rāśi*) has been established by Parāśara, Vyāsa, Vaśiṣṭha, and other leading authorities;
O Great Goddess, just as the calculation and ritual application of the sign were prescribed by the ancients, so it remains even now.
Without investigation, as it is, success is not achieved even in the four ages;
a mantra that has not purified the six chakras does not exist within the midst of saṃsāra.
Having satisfied the guru, one of vast intelligence should bestow initiation, whether it involves gold, silver, or especially a divine weapon.
In cases such as debt, however, one should perform four times the number of recitations due to the intense suffering.
The word "namaḥ" is for the heart, while "vahnisundarī" is for the head.
Having uttered "Vaṣaṭ" for the crest (śikhā), "Hūṃ" is said for the armor (kavaca);
one should apply "Vauṣaṭ" to the eyes, and "Phaṭ" for the weapon (astra) on all limbs is prescribed.
Now I shall explain the generation of the mantra as approved by the Tantras,
knowing which a person becomes a master of mantras that have attained accomplishment.
From the various phonemes of the *mātṛkā*, all mantras were born.
A "peak-syllable" (*kuṭākṣara*) is said to be that which is joined with one of the vowels (*aj*), the semi-vowels (*hal*), or the sibilants (*sa*).

The *kuṭa* is manifested as the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and is traditionally considered equivalent to the technical term (*paribhāṣā*). That which is the *kuṭa* is the seed-syllable; it is known as the seed-syllable of the *kuṭa*-syllables.
Mantras are to be known as male deities, while Vidyās are remembered as female deities;
all mantras are declared to have the nature of either female or neuter.

Mantras for males should end with *phaṭ* and their limbs (*aṅga*) likewise; those for females are considered to end with *svāhā*; and those for neuters should end with *namaḥ*. Thus has mantra been declared by Manu to be of three kinds.
Whether they be women or men, these castes have been proclaimed;
at the end of the *śānta* [section], there are three kinds of mantras for the purposes of subjugation (*vaśya*), pacification (*śānti*), and malevolent rites (*abhicāra*).
Mantras should be understood as consisting of the nature of fire and moon for the purpose of fierce rites and desired objects;
the classes of mantras are of two kinds according to the division of mantra and vidyā.

The syllable *raṃ* is prescribed for action; it bestows nourishment when properly uttered. The *vayava* breaths are fiery (*āgneya*), while those established on earth are lunar (*saumya*) and consist of the immortal syllable *indum*.
The Āgneya stations are established on the right, and the Saumya stations are assigned to the left;
all these awaken the wise within the Suṣumnā.
This field (kṣetra) is of the nature of mantra; the channels (nāḍīs) are remembered as being essentially mantra;
the constituent elements (dhātus) are conjoined with mantra; and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is supreme.
The internal organ, the mantra, and the words are joined with mantra;
day and night consist of mantra, and the entire world consists of all mantras.
Without mantras, nothing would exist within the cosmic egg; listen, O fortunate lady!
One should perform everything according to the procedures prescribed in the Agamas, without being bound by [worldly] constraints.
All awakened mantras always bestow their fruit upon the practitioner;
however, those mantras that are defective due to being cut or otherwise corrupted do not protect the sādhaka.
One whose limbs are severed, one devoid of power, one who has turned away,
one who is called out, one who is blood-stained, one who is eyeless, one who is pinned down, and likewise one who is bound by cords.
Burning, trembling, soiled, and humiliated;
pierced, emitting the cry of a peacock, and deprived of life.
Smoky, marked, deluded, afflicted by hunger,
deprived of limbs due to excessive thirst, and thereafter exceedingly cruel.
One who is excessively hunchbacked, as well as one who is shameless, one whose mind is tranquil,
one who has fallen from his position, one who is incapacitated, and thereafter, one who is very old.
Being devoid of affection and even afflicted, I shall now describe their characteristics:
that [mantra] in whose beginning, middle, and end the blue seed-syllable (*nīlabīja*) is conjoined with a vowel is called *chinna* (severed).
That in which there is a pair of earth-seed syllables (*bhūbījadvandva*) at the beginning, middle, and end is declared to be *ruddha* (obstructed).
The Praṇava, deprived of the syllable *māyā* (the letter *m*) and the letter *ra*, is said by the Lotus-born One to be "deprived" (*hīna*).
The seed-syllable of desire (KĀM) at the mouth, Māyā (Hrīṃ) situated on the head, and Aṅgula (Śrīṃ) facing away— this is the mantra as taught by the Lotus-born One.
The syllable *hūṃ* joined with a *bindu*, yet devoid of the moon, seed-syllable, beginning, end, and middle—
that very mantra is "deaf," being bereft of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
That mantra which consists of five syllables, is devoid of the letter *ra*, the sun (*arka*), and the moon (*indu*),
and lacks the eyes (*netra*), is a mantra bereft of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
[Furthermore,] at the beginning, middle, and end, there are the *haṃsa*, *prasāda*, and *vāgbhava* [bījas].
The syllable *ha* joined with the *bindu*, or likewise the syllable *phaṭ*.
Likewise, [if] the goad or the illusion [is misplaced], I bow to that which follows;
indeed, that mantra is pinned down and deprived of all accomplishments.
One [syllable] in the middle, two at the head, and the letters *ṣa* and *mminnidra* [followed by] *purandara*:
if these are not accompanied by the mantra, one will be paralyzed and deprived of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
That mantra at the head of which the fire [letter *ra*] joined with the first [vowel *a*] is seen seven times is called a *dagdha* (burnt) mantra.
A weapon-mantra (astra) is seen to consist of two, three, six, or eight syllables;
that mantra is called "stambha" (paralyzing) and is devoid of all spiritual accomplishments (siddhis).
That mantra in whose mouth there is no *māyā* or the *praṇava* according to the prescribed rule is said to be "frightened"; it is devoid of all accomplishments.
That mantra which possesses four *sān* (anusvāras) at its beginning, middle, and end is indeed impure and beset by all obstacles.
He in whose [mantra] the letter *da* appears in the middle, or the armor (*kavaca*) is seen at the head,
and the threefold weapon (*astra*) is seen, is declared to be "transcendent" (*tiraṣkṛta*).
The pair "hā" is at the heart and the head, while "vaṣaṭ" and "vauṣaṭ" are in the middle;
that very mantra, when thus differentiated, is free from all [other] scriptures.
That which consists of three phonemes but lacks the *haṃsa* is declared to be deep sleep (*suṣupta*).
Furthermore, a mantra or a *vidyā* consisting of seventeen syllables [is also so described].

The syllable *phaṭ*, beginning with the fifth [letter], is declared to be "Intoxicated with Pride" (*madonmatta*). O Dear One, these mantras consisting of seventeen syllables are always the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*).
A mantra that is uttered with a fainting tone is said to be devoid of all accomplishments;
likewise, a mantra that consists of five *phaṭ*s and is joined with pauses at the points of rest is ineffective.
He is called Kṛtavīrya; for him there is no further purpose.
The arrow should consist of seven syllables, while the youth is remembered as having eight syllables.
A mantra of sixteen syllables is called "youthful" (yuvan) and is devoid of all supernatural accomplishments (siddhi);
that which consists of forty letters is proclaimed as "mature" (prauḍha).
A mantra that possesses four *aṣkas* at the beginning, middle,
and end is indeed a *chīna-mantra*, as is one consisting of eighteen syllables.
The mantra consisting of twenty syllables, arranged in a triangle and enriched with the seed-syllables of Hṛllekhā and Aṅkuśa— by this, you are declared to be utterly destroyed.
The twenty-two-syllable Vidyā is Māyā devoid of Kāma;
that Vidyā is of destroyed form and is devoid of all siddhis.

A spell (vidyā) consisting of thirty syllables, a mantra of sixty-four syllables, or a mantra of one hundred syllables is said to be "fainted" (mūrcchita), which causes the destruction of [the practitioner's] mantras.
Furthermore, that which consists of four hundred syllables is proclaimed as the "Vṛddha" (the aged).
The nine-syllable mantra joined with the Dhruva is the deity of the thirty [gods].
At the end of which is the heart [mantra], and the two Śivas [the seed-syllables] are in the middle;
it is joined with the śikhā and varma, as well as the utterances vaṣaṭ and vauṣaṭ.
Or, that which is devoid of the syllables of Śiva and Śakti is declared to be "seedless" (nirbīja);
likewise, that in which the syllable *phaṭ* does not occur six times in these positions [is also so called].
That mantra will be devoid of accomplishment and abandoned by all tantras;
if it consists of two syllables, it is lacking in essence, but if it consists of four syllables, it is one-eyed.

The six-syllabled mantra is devoid of a seed-syllable, and that seven-syllabled mantra consists of twelve and a half letters, marked by the syllables *dhu* and *mi*, and gladdened by the essence of living beings (*satva*).
Likewise, there are those known as the twenty-one with three seeds,
the twenty-syllable, and that which consists of thirty syllables, which is remembered as being embraced [by the seed].
The thirty-two-syllable mantra is proclaimed as the Deluded (Mohita);
this twenty-four-syllable mantra consists of twenty-seven phonemes.
He who is afflicted by hunger should be known as one who has abandoned all tantras;
he consists of twenty-four syllables and is designated as the twenty-seventh.
O Dear One, whether it consists of eleven syllables, twenty-five,
or twenty syllables, that mantra is one that is deficient in its limbs.
The mantra consists of twenty-six syllables, or likewise twenty-six letters;
or it may consist of thirty-one syllables, and that very same [mantra] is also devoid of limbs.
That which consists of twenty-eight syllables, or even twenty-one, should be known as excessively cruel; it is censured in all ritual activities.
