Those mantras that consist of sixty-five syllables are peaceful in mind;
from sixty-five syllables up to ninety-nine syllables [they are likewise].
All of those should be known as fruitless— whether one hundred and fifty,
or two hundred, or ninety-three, or even eighty-nine.
Up to three hundred in number, they are proclaimed to be without essence;
likewise, from four hundred up to a thousand syllables.
That mantra which exceeds [the prescribed length] is considered too old and is rejected in all scriptures;
mantras exceeding one thousand syllables are designated as *daṇḍaka* and *pīḍita*.
Whether the mantras consist of two thousand syllables or are divided into hundreds of fragments,
these mantras should be understood as being in the form of hymns, exactly as they exist.
In the same way, the vidyās should be understood through the mantras in rites performed for specific desires.
A wise person who resorts to a mantra without recognizing its defects [will fail].
Success does not arise for that practitioner even in hundreds of millions of eons,
when a person, failing to recognize a defect, resorts to a mantra or vidyā.
Success does not arise for him even in hundreds of millions of eons,
regarding those mantras described in various tantras that have been broken or corrupted.
All these attain purification through the power of the letters of the Mātṛkā;
especially by encasing the mantra or vidyā within the letters of the Mātṛkā.
One should first recite [the mantra] one hundred and eight times for the sake of attaining the fruit;
then the mantra becomes a great vidyā that bestows the fruit as described.
Having encased [the syllables] within the *mātṛkā* and having placed the letters in the middle, one should then perform the awakening of the mantra-syllables; this is approved by all.
Then, having performed the *yonimudrā* preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*),
one should first feed one hundred and eight Brahmins, O Dear One.
Then, O Great Goddess, one should offer substances according to this procedure:
first, O Beloved, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of jaggery and cinnamon bark.
Then, O Goddess, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations of parched grain;
likewise, one hundred and eight oblations of various fragrant substances.
There, one should offer eight thousand oblations of combustible materials according to the prescribed rite,
along with garments and ornaments in accordance with one's wealth.
One should offer betel leaves, camphor, and so forth, according to one's means,
as well as gold, silver, and a cow to the preceptor.
Then there shall be the accomplishment of the mantra, endowed with all tantras—
the single-syllable [mantra] of Bhuvaneśvarī, Gaṇeśa, and Śiva.
Viṣṇu, Ekākṣara, Sūryāsya, Praṇava,
as well as those such as the Siddhividyā and others belonging to Śrī Rāma and Agni.
Merely by accepting them, one does not incur the fault of being a perfected master (siddha) or the like;
rather, whether out of delusion or by chance, one should examine them for the sake of one's own purification.
According to the opinion of Laṅkara, that very [initiate] becomes a deity.
Now, O lotus-faced one, listen as I shall explain initiation,
by the mere knowledge of which a man attains divinity.
Because it bestows divine knowledge and because it effects the destruction of sin,
that is called *dīkṣā*, endowed with all the tantras.
That *dīkṣā* was declared by Brahmā in the past to be of four kinds.
Active, consisting of color, possessing arts, and also consisting of piercing—
these auspicious [energies], which bestow all prosperity, [are described] in sequence at the conclusion of the narrative.
The practitioner should always perform the invitation of the Guru on the preceding day,
according to the prescribed rite, with garments, ornaments, gold, and even cows.
According to the doctrine of Śaṅkara, there is no purification whatsoever for the Chinnādi mantras and vidyās, nor even for the Mahāvidyās.
When Kālikā has been severed, so too are Sundarī and Tripurā;
likewise Ugratārā among the Vidyās, as well as those consisting of a single syllable.
In the mantras of the Yakṣiṇīs, in the groups of Viṣṇu-mantras,
in the Nārasiṃha mantras, and in those of Maheśa and Gaṇapati;
Especially in the mantra of the Goddess, no fault whatsoever arises;
in the Kali age, Caṇḍī is the means for men, having purified the abode of Śiva.
On earth, among one's own groups, there is no doubt that one should perform the morning rites according to the prescribed rule, having first performed the ritual bath.
A river, a natural lake, a long pond, the ocean,
or all rivers such as the Gaṅgā— these are recommended by the wise at their respective locations.
Indeed, all the sacred fords (tīrthas) such as Kāśī and others that exist in Bhārata are praised for bathing; they are truly the removers of all sins.
In the event of another's death, the wise should perform the rite of lifting the five lumps (pañcapiṇḍoddhāra), [reciting]:
"Arise, arise, O mud! Abandon the merit of another!"
May my sins be destroyed; grant me peace forever, O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Godāvarī, and Sarasvatī!
O Narmadā, Sindhu, and Kāverī, establish your presence in these waters;
for by your excellent hands, the holy tirthas within the belly of the universe have been touched.
Therefore, O Goddess, grant me truth; O Divākara, grant me the sacred fords (*tīrtha*).
Vows and sacred fords are most beneficial when established within the rays of the Sun.
Having come here and set down the sacrificial vessel (ava), the wise one should ask me for all accomplishments; having fashioned a square there, he should prescribe the ritual bath.
Having bathed in the Mṛdgosara and the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rules,
one should perform the ritual ablution according to the procedure as stated by Mahākāla.
Oṃ! Stepped upon by the horse, stepped upon by the chariot, stepped upon by Viṣṇu, O Earth, bearer of wealth! O Clay, take away my sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me.
You were lifted up by Kṛṣṇa, who possesses a hundred arms;
salutations to you, O source of destruction for all beings, O lady of excellent vows!
Having ascended upon my limbs, release me from all evil;
there, one should perform your ablution according to the rules within a square enclosure.
Having turned toward the north, one should enter facing the east;
one should then meditate upon the Lord, the lotus-eyed one, who stands firm and is the embodiment of the mantra.
One should contemplate that stream born from the water of His feet falling upon one's own head,
entering one's own body through the aperture of Brahmā (the *brahmarandhra*).
Then one should wash away the impurity within the body with water and mantras;
at that very moment, the mantra becomes free from dust—of this there is no doubt.

The sevenfold bath is proclaimed as follows: that performed with mantras, that on the ground, as well as that pertaining to fire, that pertaining to wind, the celestial, that pertaining to water, and the mental.
Having bathed in this manner according to the prescribed rule, one becomes pure; it is not otherwise.
Thereafter, one should perform the Vṛddhi-śrāddha preceded by the worship of Gaṇeśa and the water-pot (ghaṭa).
One should worship Gaṇeśa there for the pacification of all obstacles, preceded by the invocation with mantras beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*.
And there, in that house at the place of initiation, one should perform the worship according to the ritual rules,
having covered the hands and feet with clean cloth for the sake of purification.
Having sipped water according to the rule, O wise one, one should then worship the deities of the doorway,
followed by the Lord of the Field (Kṣetrādhipa), the Guardian of the Field (Kṣetrapāla), and thereafter the Goddess of the House (Gṛhadevī).
One should offer incense, flowers, lamps, and food offerings;
for without performing this worship, there shall be no success in any age.
First, one should offer a portion to Gaṇeśa,
Vighnarāja, Lakṣmī, Durgā, and Sarasvatī, as well as to the foremost Upavāras.
Having worshipped Vināyaka, Vaṭuka, Gaṅgā, Yamunā,
and Bhogavatī, he should then touch the left branch for a short while.
Having entered the house according to the prescribed rite, one should destroy those respective obstacles;
then, with palms joined in reverence, one should utter this mantra.
Oṃ! The Sun, the Moon, Yama, Time, and the five great elements—these are the witnesses to the auspicious, inauspicious, and delusive actions of men.
The preceptor should perform the installation of the jar with this mantra;
and this is the mantra for the installation of the jar, which is in accordance with all the Tantras.
There, one should first cause the auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be proclaimed, preceded by the recitation of blessings (*svastivācana*), and then invoke Gaṇeśa, the son of Śiva.
One should dispel terrestrial obstacles with the Astra-mantra and the Phaṇa-mantra,
and one should also dispel celestial and other obstacles in the four directions.
Vision with unblinking eyes is proclaimed as divine vision (divyadṛṣṭi);
this is accomplished by subsisting for a month on food consisting of boiled barley (yāvaka).
Having worshipped according to the prescribed ritual with the blood, milk, and honey of a goat-earred animal, one should accomplish [the rite] at the gateway.
Having expelled all those obstacles by reciting the armor-mantra and the seed-syllable seven times, one should then again bestow protection.
One should protect oneself there by means of the enclosure of fire;
indeed, one should mentally visualize an enclosure in the four directions using the seed-syllable of fire.
Then the preceptor should perform three claps with the fire-seed syllable (raṃ) and,
by means of the sequential yoga of ascending and descending, instruct [the disciple] in prostration to the Guru.
Oṃ, perpetual salutation to the gurus, and likewise to the sandals of the guru—
supreme, more supreme, the highest, beyond the highest, and more supreme than that.
O wise one, one should prostrate in sequence, accompanied by the syllable *oṃ* and the word *namaḥ*,
having bowed to Gaṇeśa on the right and one’s chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*) at the front of the face.
The wise one should install Gaṇeśa there under the banyan tree as previously described;
I shall now invoke the god Gaṇeśa, the son of Śiva.
The god, who wears a tiger skin as his garment and has a black sacred thread,
is surrounded by ten million attendants and is a consumer of sweetmeats.
I invoke that fierce Lord, the Lord of Obstacles, of massive form, uniquely worshipped by all the worlds, for the sake of the purpose of all teachers.
Come, come, O Blessed Lord, O God, destroyer of all obstacles!
Accept this worship and make everything of mine fruitful.
One should worship the Son of Śiva with vermilion, red flowers, and other offerings;
first, one should invoke him with joined palms—this is remembered as the rule for all cases.
Then, having offered a welcome and so forth, along with questions and their corresponding answers,
and having provided a seat, one should then present water for the feet (pādya) and the respectful offering (arghya).
Please accept this fragrant and sweet water for washing the feet, which brings nectar to all beings and removes the fatigue of a long journey.
"Obeisance" (namaḥ) for the water for the feet at the base of the feet; "Svāhā" for the water for the guest-offering (arghya) placed upon the head;
"Svadhā" for the honey-mixture (madhuparka); and again "water for sipping" (ācamanīyaka).
One should say "namas" for the bathing water, and then again for the perfume and so forth;
one should likewise offer the garment and the sacred thread with "namas" at the end.
One should sequentially place food and eatables with "svadhā," and incense and lamps with "svadhā namaḥ" there for the deity according to this rite.
And then one should offer it into the arghya vessel; listen now, O fair-faced one:
the arghya water should be placed in a conch shell with *śyāmā*, *arka*, barley, and *durvā* grass.
One should offer the *arghya* in a conch shell, consisting of kusha grass tips, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, *viṣṇukrāntā*, and barley, combined with various fragrances.
In all instances, the practitioner should offer the *arghya* with the root mantra preceded by *Oṃ* and followed by *namaḥ*,
and also with the mantra beginning with *kāṇḍāt caiva*.

The best of practitioners should perform the water for the feet with the *pādya* mantra, and likewise perform the sipping of water (*ācamana*) again; he should then offer the water for bathing with the *Puruṣasūkta*.

The knower of mantras should again perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and offer fragrance with the mantra "Gandhadvārām. For the sake of auspiciousness, he should also offer flowers with the mantra "Śrīśca te."
Endowed with various delicious flavors for the sake of attaining the fruit of Brahmanhood, I have offered this madhuparka with devotion; please accept it from me.
The *madhuparka* is proclaimed to consist of curd, honey, and clarified butter;
it is the supreme fragrance arising from the essence of the forest trees, possessing a most excellent scent.
May this incense, worthy of being smelled by all the gods, be accepted;
and may this great lamp, brilliantly shining and dispelling darkness in every direction, be accepted.
"May this lamp, whose light extends both within and without, be accepted.
Thereafter, the wise one should cast the vessel away for the washing of his hands."
One should place rows of lamps nearby, along with incense and oil-lamps;
the wise man should construct a pavilion filled with gold.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśa, one should then worship Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Śivā,
and Śiva according to the prescribed rite in that jar for the sake of all prosperity.
Thereafter, one should perform the *vṛddhi-śrāddha*, preceded by the worship of the Mothers;
in the *nāndīmukha* śrāddha, the wise man should say "namas" in place of "puṣṭi."
Then, having offered the *vasudhārā*, the disciple should perform the rite of initiation (*dīkṣākarma*) according to the prescribed rule by his own Guru, O Goddess of Gods.
The preceptor should cause the ritual action to be performed; the wise disciple should carry out everything.
He should fumigate the sacrificial pavilion with sandalwood, agallochum, and camphor.
Then one should stabilize the banyan tree until the ritual of initiation takes place;
one should perform the stabilization with the mantra: "Oṃ, be firm! (oṃ sthiro bhava).
Then, having joined his palms in reverence, he should recite this mantra:
"Oṃ namo gaṇebhyaḥ.
He should offer a monthly meal-oblation (māsabhakta-bali) to the bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas.
Oṃ! The bhūtas, pretas, and piśācas who dwell in the netherworld (pātāla) and upon the surface of the earth— [may they be pacified].
May all those who dwell upon mountain peaks, on trees, or in houses, fields, and so forth, be satisfied; may they all accept this bali offering from me.
With barley-grains, red flowers, the blood of goats and buffaloes,
fish, meat, and other such offerings, one should perform [the rite] according to this procedure.
There too, one should offer the oblation and then commence the auspicious rite;
one should present the sacred thread with the *yajñopavīta* mantra.
Crafted from various jewels and fashioned by Viśvakarman and others,
accept this ornament that beautifies every limb for the sake of attaining the fruit.
In this case, one should again offer the bali-oblation for the obstacles according to the opinion of Viṣṇu;
elsewhere, however, one should give everything according to the prescribed rule using the root mantra.
Or, as approved by Śiva, one may offer [the oblation] beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*;
first, the excellent practitioner should cast a handful of sacrificial grass (*kuśa*) with the *phaṭ*-mantra.
Sesame seeds, *kuśa* grass, and white mustard seeds constitute what is proclaimed as a "handful of *kūrca*";
one should scatter these, having consecrated them seven times with the *parātman* mantra.
Roasted grain, sandalwood, white mustard, barley, durva grass, kuśa grass, and unbroken rice—
these are designated as the *vikira* offerings, which destroy all obstacles.
Having worshipped the eight pitchers filled with water for protection and satisfaction in the eight directions,
one should honor the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī, together with all their attendants.
Having meditated upon these according to this rite with perfumes, flowers, food, and water,
[one should then visualize them] holding a staff and a water-pot, and subsequently bearing a rosary and a book.
Bearing a golden luster, Brāhmī is radiant with a black antelope skin.
Bearing a trident, a skull, a club, and a charming young deer, the auspicious Māheśvarī, who resembles snow, should be meditated upon. (2)
Holding a goad, a staff, a khaṭvāṅga, and a noose in her hands, Kaumārī—resembling the bandhūka flower and bestowing happiness—is to be meditated upon. (3)
Bearing a discus, a bell, a mace, and a sword, she is enchanting;
dark as the tamāla tree, the Vaiṣṇavī goddess who bestows happiness should be meditated upon. (4)
Vārāhī, possessing the complexion of a dark cloud, should be meditated upon as holding a pestle, a sword, a shield, and a fruit with her four hands. (5)
Holding a goad, a javelin, lightning, and a thunderbolt in her hands,
Indrāṇī, who resembles a sapphire, should be meditated upon as the bestower of all prosperity.
Holding a trident, a sword, a human head, and a skull in her hands, adorned with severed heads and blood, Cāmuṇḍā should be meditated upon as having a red body.
Holding a rosary of beads, a seed-vessel, a skull, and a lotus in her hands,
Mahālakṣmī, the beloved of Hari, shines with the luster of gold.
Thus, one should perform the auspicious rite according to the prescribed procedure,
having received the blessings of the Brahmin women and the Brahmins.

Having gratified the Brāhmaṇas with shouts of "Victory! and recitations of the Veda, and having likewise satisfied his circle of kinsmen, he should then perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa).
With this mantra and these substances, in the proper sequence, the supreme practitioner should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) of Śiva with great care.
Having first uttered the syllable *Oṃ*, one should offer [the earth] with the word *namaḥ* at the end;
then the Guru should cast the clay while reciting the mantra *bhūr asi*.

The preceptor should offer incense with the mantra *gandhadvārā*. And those ships which travel upon the back of the bull of the great mountain, moving as far as Īśāna, have returned from the lower cosmic egg, following the serpent-path while seeking their prey.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should sprinkle the stone with this mantra according to the prescribed rite:
"O you who are the stride of Viṣṇu, the wise one; you are the stride, you belong to Viṣṇu, you are of Viṣṇu.
With this mantra, grain endowed with all the Tantras should be placed [upon it].
One should offer *dūrvā* grass according to the prescribed rite, reciting the mantra beginning with "oṃ kāṇḍāt."
With the mantra "Oṃ Śrīśca te ca," one should offer a flower upon the head.
With the mantra "Oṃ yā kalinī," one should offer fruit upon the head of the rabbit-marked moon.

Oṃ! The two worlds, the heaven and earth, which possess the splendor of all beings, are wide, vast, yielding sweetness, and well-fashioned. By the law of Varuṇa, they are held apart—ageless, possessing abundant seed.
With this mantra, one should offer clarified butter upon the head of the child.
And one should offer a svastika with the mantra beginning "svasti naḥ."
Oṃ, "Siddhoriva" means the *sinduvāra* flower.
One should apply *laṅgha* to the head of the child with the mantra: *oṃ laṅghaṃ veti*.
And with the mantra "oṃ samiddhā," one should offer the kārṣmarya wood.
Oṃ. "They harness the ruddy steed; they stand around the moving Marut. With this mantra, the preceptor should bestow the light upon the light in the sky, surrounding the light.
O Lord of Food, grant us food that is abundant and strengthening;
further the giver, and provide nourishment for our bipeds and quadrupeds.
The touching of the food with this mantra is prescribed;
one should surround the gold with the mantra beginning with "hiraṇyagarbha."
May Viśvavedas distribute your form by means of [his] form; may he divide those who are foremost among you.
By this path, which leads toward the white moon as the sacrificial fee, proceed through the intermediate space together with those who occupy their seats.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should offer silver according to the prescribed rite with this mantra;
the wise man should offer copper with the mantra "asau yaḥ."
Having given the *siddhārtha* with the mantra "rakṣohan," he should place *darbha* grass upon the head of the disciple.
With the mantra "ākṛṣṇena" and the mantra "manojyotiḥ," he should offer a lamp according to the prescribed rite.

Having practiced the practice, having followed the following, having accomplished the accomplishment, having blazed with brilliance, having reached the goal, and having attained the attainment—you are the goal;
you are the vessel of success. Make everything pleasing for me; the pair of feet of the Goddess is worthy of worship.
This is declared to be the ritual of formal acceptance (adhivāsa), complete with all its scriptural traditions.
Then, at the time for the supreme initiation, the disciple, having bathed and sipped water according to the rules, [should proceed].

Having entered the house according to the prescribed rule, the Lord of Sacrifice (Yajñeśvara) should receive the benedictions and auspicious rites of the twice-born accompanied by women; and he should worship Viṣṇu in the water-pot with perfumes,
flowers, and jaggery-water.

Having worshipped Hari there with offerings of food, flowers, water for the feet, and so forth, preceded by the invocation (āvāhana), one should perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) and the subsequent rites.
Having prostrated to the Guru according to the prescribed rite, one should then perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi):
"Oṃ, for me who am blinded by the darkness of ignorance, with the lamp of knowledge..."
Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom the eye was opened;
salutation be to that Guru who is the very embodiment of the chosen deity.
One should worship the Guru— who possesses speech that destroys the poison of ignorant worldly existence—
as the two-eyed, twice-natured one, white and unborn, upon the head at dawn.
One should meditate upon him as peaceful, with hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, preceded by the recitation of his name;
having thus first prostrated, one should then perform the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Then, one should assign Brahmā, Kṣetrapāla, Vāstveśa, and Nairṛta in the corners starting from the northeast (Īśāna), and thereafter instruct the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
One should fill [the body] with sixteen repetitions of the seed-syllable *yaṃ*, which is the seed of air (*vāyu*);
then, one should retain the breath in the *suṣumnā* channel by means of the channel for the cessation of respiration.
One should purify the sinful body with that very [mantra] repeated sixty-four times;
by means of that seed-syllable and according to the prescribed rule, one should exhale through the Piṅgalā [nāḍī].
Having slowly applied ash thirty-two times along the path of the breath, performing this three times is known as the purification of the elements (bhūta-śodhana).
The preceptor should fill [the breath] with the fire-seed (ra) conjoined with the moon (sa);
having held it for sixteen or sixty-four [counts], he should then exhale.
The cremation is proclaimed to be performed with thirty-two measures;
then, having offered twenty-four [measures], one should recite the syllables of reality (tattvavarṇa) in sequence.
Drying, burning, and flooding are thus proclaimed. Kiskanna, Kaśyapa, and likewise Hiraṇyagarbha.
The lotus-eyed sages have declared these to be the seeds;
the best of teachers should perform them in sequence, concluding with breath control (prāṇāyāma).
The instructor should meditate upon the chosen deity within the great thousand-petaled lotus,
according to the prescribed meditation and by means of the path taught by the guru.
Then the elements situated therein, together with their qualities,
according to the prescribed rule, are endowed with the power of desire (*kāma-śakti*) through the sequence of phonemes and measures (*mātrā*).
Having withdrawn [the breath] in reverse order, like a cowherd with the elements joined together,
from the *mūlādhāra* to the *sahasrāra* by means of the sequential yoga of the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*).
Then, having meditated upon the thousand-spoked wheel in reverse order according to the ritual procedure,
one should lead the life-force (jīva) into the *hūṃ* mantra by means of the sequential yoga of the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*).
Having contemplated oneness in that place, one should practice this mantra;
having uttered the mantra "So'ham," one should contemplate the subtle Brahman.
At that moment, one should contemplate with the mind, through the yoga of devotion, the body as stainless, free from conflict, devoid of possessions, and non-dual.

One should contemplate the garland of letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa' in their proper sequence, by means of the restraint of breath through inhalation (pūraka), retention (kumbhaka), and exhalation (recaka).
Having reflected thus upon them all, one should then remember the Moon-mantra (candramanu),
consisting of the letter *ṭha* joined with the nasal bindu and adorned with the half-moon.
The wise one should mentally recite the mantra four times with the breath;
he should then recite the seed-syllable of Indra, followed by the seed-syllable of the Earth.
Having strengthened it according to the prescribed rite and sustained it again with the stream of nectar,
one should then contemplate the body as previously described, consisting of the Mātṛkās.
Then, [one should contemplate] that which is joined with the entire beginningless [reality], together with its powers,
endowed with the fifty phonemes, and accompanied by the great elements.
One should contemplate the body as consisting of the five elements in their natural order;
his success is unimpeded, and his vital breaths are said to be deities.
The preceptor should carefully place his right hand upon the chest with the previously mentioned *prāṇamantra*, accompanied by its seer (*ṛṣi*) and meter (*chandas*).
With the *haṃsa* mantra, that vital breath (*prāṇa*) is said to be invoked:
"O beings together with their elements, come here and dwell happily for a long time."
One should extract this mantra ending with the wife of fire (svāhā);
it is joined with the fifty letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'.
Having contemplated the body with the mind, a person then becomes two bodies;
by means of the threefold breath-control (prāṇāyāma), one should deposit strength into the vital breaths.

One should bring forth the vital breath (prāṇa) by contemplating it through the letters from *a* to *kṣa*, using inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*), both in reverse and direct order.
At that very moment, the minister shall become manifest as Sadāśiva himself;
by means of the Nṛsiṃha seed-syllable alone, he should cast the life-force into the body.
Then one should contemplate the individual soul (jīvātman) as having reached the mūlādhāra,
manifested in the form of Kuṇḍalinī and possessing a radiance like lightning and fire.
Stainless, abiding in the changeless state, and endowed with all perfections,
one should then place the Mātṛkā, in the form of phonemes, within the body.
Having meditated upon her with this mantra, one should place [the letters] throughout the entire body:
"Oṃ, with the fifty letters.
Having thus meditated, the best of practitioners should perform the placement of the garland of phonemes (varṇamālā).
First, one should indeed place [the mantras] upon one's own body according to the sequence of the garland of letters.
I bow to the red goddess, who is seated upon a blazing, crimson lotus; she possesses three eyes and holds in her hands a noose, a goad, a spear, a skull-cup, a sugarcane bow, and arrows.
One should assign the letters, adorned with the colors of the elements, to the six cakras,
as well as the petals together with their respective deities, in their proper order.

Just as one should assign the phonemes to their respective places according to the procedure beginning with the head, one should first assign them internally and then direct the assignment externally.
The preceptor should place the syllables on the head and other external locations.
[She is] seated upon a radiant, red lotus that rises from a blood-red ocean.
Holding in her hands a noose, a bow, a sugarcane arrow, a bowstring, a goad, and five arrows,

as well as a skull filled with blood; together with the Goddess who possesses three eyes and radiant, full breasts, and whose complexion is like the rising sun— may that Supreme Power of Life (Prāṇa-śakti) bring me auspiciousness.
Then, with the vital power of the elements and joined with that power, the preceptor should perform the ritual placement with supreme devotion, so that he may always become like the Divine.
The preceptor should place the noose and the goad upon the body according to this procedure:
he should place the seed-syllable of the noose on the pair of feet and the goad on the head.
The practitioner, with a restrained mind, should place the seed-syllable of Śakti in the heart according to this procedure,
having meditated upon the Goddess according to the prescribed rule.
I worship the Primordial Goddess, who is seated upon a lotus throne, holding a boar-tusked goad, a noose, and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands;
she resembles ten million rising suns, possesses three eyes, and dwells in the abode of Hara.
Having thus assigned [the mantras] to one's own body, one should then perform the preliminary binding (ādigbandhana);
with the mantra "Astrāya Phaṭ," one should offer protection in the four directions.
By snapping the fingers in sequence— either ten or twelve times in order—
one should then perform the infinite *lakṣa* rite again according to the prescribed rule.

Having applied the Aghora-weapon mantra ending in the dative case and joined with the seed-syllable of Kartṛkā in the four directions, one should then perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) again and again.
One should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) according to the rules with the root mantra—
three times, four times, and again three times there, O Dear One.
One should perform inhalation (pūraka), exhalation (recaka), and retention (kumbhaka) according to this procedure;
then, one should sequentially place the *hṛllekhā* mantra upon the six limbs beginning with the heart.
In all cases, one should apply the six-limbed [mantra] with a long vowel through diligent practice;
however, within the groups of five-limbed mantras, one should mentally provide it without the eye (netra).
Then the mantra-practitioner should imagine a Dharma-throne within his own body,
and subsequently, he should fashion a ritual peg (kīlaka) conjoined with the syllables of the mantra.
The wise practitioner should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon this body, beginning with the foundation (ādhāra), as previously described;
he should then duly place the principles (tattvas) taught by Śiva within the body according to the prescribed ritual.
The principles (tattvas) associated with the paths [of mantra] lead to the attainment of the fruit of mantra-perfection;
O Pārvatī, these are the path of the digits (kalādhvan), the path of the principles (tattvādhvan), and the foundation of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan).
The path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), the path of words (padādhvan), and thereafter the path of mantras (mantrādhvan);
[these consist of] the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning, the suffix *-ī* (*ṅe*), and the word *namaḥ* at the end, according to their established order.
One should install everything according to the prescribed rite and in accordance with the doctrine of Śaṅkara;
the five kalās beginning with Nivṛtti are proclaimed as the path of kalās (kalādhvan).
One should deposit the five elements in their respective locations according to this procedure;
then, one should deposit the ether (gagana) from the space down to the throat.
One should place the wind element according to the rule from the throat down to the navel;
one should then place the fire element from the navel down to the base of the spine.
Then one should assign Varuṇa from the navel down to the knees;
thereafter, one should assign Dharaṇī (the Earth) from the knees down to the feet in due order.
This placement of the parts (kalānyāsa) has been proclaimed, endowed with all the Tantras;
as for the path of the principles (tattvādhvan), O Maheśānī, it has been described in many ways by the wise.
O Pārvatī, there are thirty-six Śiva-tattvas, thirty-two Vaiṣṇava-tattvas,
and twenty-four Brahma-tattvas.
Likewise, there are seven principles (tattvas) plus ten;
I shall describe those Śiva-principles—listen, O lotus-faced one.
Sadāśiva, Śiva-Śakti, Vidyā, and Īśvara—
these five pure principles have been declared by the wise in this Śaiva system.
Māyā, Kāla, Niyati, Kalā, Vidyā,
Rāga, and Puruṣa— these seven are both pure and impure.
Nature consists of intellect, ego, mind, the organs of cognition,
the organs of action, the five subtle elements, and the five gross elements.
O Maheśānī, the wise have declared the Śiva-tattvas to be impure; O Queen of the Gods, they are pure-impure in every respect.
The classification of the Śaiva principles has been proclaimed here;
O lotus-faced one, listen as I shall now describe the Vaiṣṇava principles.
The individual soul (jīva), the vital breaths (prāṇa), the intellect (dhī), the mind (citta), knowledge (jñāna), the organs of action (karmendriya),
the five subtle elements (tanmātra), the five gross elements (bhūta), the heart-lotus (hṛtpadma), and the triad of fires (tejas)— [these constitute the aggregate].
Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha—
all these principles of Viṣṇu have been declared by the wise.
The five elements, the heart-lotus, and likewise the six sense organs, along with ego, intellect, and primordial matter— these, O Pārvatī, are the Śiva-tattvas.
The five digits (kalās) beginning with Nivṛtti, and then the digit of the Bindu,
as well as Nāda, Śakti, and Śiva, have always been proclaimed as before.
Self-knowledge is Śiva, and Śakti is indeed Śiva himself;
furthermore, all principles (tattvas) as well as the individual principles are proclaimed to belong to Śivā.
In this manner, O Goddess of the Gods, one should place the principles (tattvas) within one's own body:
Atala, Vitala, Sutala, and Talātala.
Then one should assign Mahātala and Pātāla to the navel;
thereafter [the worlds] Bhūr, Bhuvas, Svar, Mahar, Jana, Tapas, and Satya follow.
One should place [the mantras] within one's own body, from the heart up to the crest-lock (śikhā);
this is called the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan), consisting of the fourteen worlds.
The wise call the letters from *a* to *kṣa* the "path of phonemes" (*varṇādhvan*).
Together with these phonemes, there are words; one should always install them within one's own body.
One should assign the mantras upon the body according to the prescribed rules for their respective locations.
Having thus assigned [the mantras] to one's own body, one should kindle the fire in the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).
And according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should worship the Goddess in a jar filled with the water of the Gaṅgā, which has been placed in the northeast.
There too, one should worship the Goddess— who bears the sword and the shield— with perfumes, flowers, food, water, and various offerings and oblations.
The goddess Śivaśaktimaṣī, endowed with three eyes, possessing a radiance like ten million rising suns, and adorned with all ornaments.
[He saw] Mahādeva in the form of a Śava, most beautiful, with [the Goddess] stationed in his heart,
clad in a tiger skin, and possessing sprout-like limbs reddened by saffron.
Having worshipped Maheśānī, who has withered flesh and terrible fangs, and is accompanied by a host of Yoginīs, one should then offer oblations according to the prescribed rite.
Then, on the following day, the knower of the tantra should always perform the concluding rite of initiation;
at that time, he should give a tooth-stick to the disciple who is self-restrained.
Then, having produced [the paste] from dried *śākhin* wood, and thereafter adding bitter *akuñca*,
one should cast it forward facing east, measuring twelve finger-breadths.
Facing north, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth;
during the day, indeed facing south, with pure water.
Oṃ! For the sake of eating food, spread yourselves out; this King Soma has arrived.
Wipe clean my face with glory and with fortune.

Then, having made the disciple drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) from the south side, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on his body according to this aforementioned procedure as before.
Having brought [the disciple] to the region of the heart, one should begin the consecration by means of mantra:
first birth (janana), then life-giving (jīvana), followed by striking (tāḍana), and thereafter awakening (bodhana).
Now, consecration, purification, nourishment,
as well as satiation, illumination, and sleep— these ten are the ritual purifications of mantra.
The extraction of mantras from the midst of the Mātṛkā is known as knowledge;
for one should write them according to the rule of short and long vowels.
Thus, the extraction of the mantra-syllables is declared to be performed in sequence.
Having placed the Praṇava between each [syllable], one should recite ten [times] for each.
O Supreme Goddess, the "Life" (jīvana) has been described in all the Tantras:
having written the syllables of the mantra, one should strike them with sandalwood water.
O Goddess of the gods, listen as the tenfold method of striking is proclaimed according to the ritual procedure, complete with all the tantric systems, using horse-ear leaves.
Immediately thereafter, one should awaken each [syllable] with the seed-syllable of Vāyu;
having written the letters of the mantra, [one should worship them] with Karavīra flowers of that same color.
One should perform the awakening while moving; that is declared to be "awakening.
One should consecrate that mantra twenty-five times.
Consecration with auspicious water and milk is thus described;
it consists of the Praṇava and the seed-syllable of Śiva, joined with the fourteen vowels.
Having cast [the syllables] three times at the end of the root-mantra and likewise within the belly,
one should recite the mantra twenty-five times according to the prescribed rule.
The purification (vimalīkaraṇa) has been declared in accordance with all tantras; one should recite the mantra encased by the union of Tāra, Māyā, and Ramā.
The best of practitioners should kindle [the mantra] with one hundred and eight recitations;
this is called the "kindling" (dīpana) of the mantra, while its "concealment" (gopana) consists in not revealing it.
Or else, having dissolved even the auspicious [nature] of Bhadra within the mouth of the Guru,
it is not disclosed anywhere, even at the cost of one's life.
Having performed the ten purificatory rites (saṃskāras) and the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the Ṛṣis and so forth,
one should worship her, who is in the form of water, within the jar with supreme devotion.
Then, having worshipped with *arghya* and other offerings, a person shall obtain all perfections (*siddhi*); thus,
worship is declared to be threefold in the ritual procedure for the adoration of the deity.

Sandalwood paste, flowers, unbroken rice, barley, tips of kuśa grass, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and sprouts of dūrvā grass— these eight divine items are declared to be the arghya offerings in their respective order.
The water for washing the feet (pādya) is said to consist of śyāmāka, dūrvā grass, and viṣṇukrāntā;
the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka) is colored with jāti, lavaṅga, and kakkola.
With well-purified water alone, one should first offer the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka);
then, one should present the vessel for the respectful offering (arghyapātra) in sequence upon a triangular mandala on the left.
Having worshipped the fire there, one should then contemplate its six parts:
Dhumrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, and Visphuliṅginī.
Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, and Havyakavyavahā; likewise, one should worship the three-footed [pedestal] with: "Oṃ, obeisance to Śaṅkhādhāra."
Having diligently washed the conch with the mantra "Astrāya Phaṭ," one should then worship the digits of the Sun itself within the union of the conch.
Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci, Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā.
O Lord of the Gods, these digits (kalās) reside within the solar orb of the Sun;
all these digits begin with the syllable Om and end with "namaḥ."
Having worshipped with the *tīrtha* mantra, [one should worship] beyond the lunar disc (*somamaṇḍala*):
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Puṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, and Dhṛti.
Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, Aṅgadā, Pūrṇā,
and Pūrṇāmṛtā— these bestowers of desires are born from the gods.
Having displayed the fish-mudrā, one should then display the cow-mudrā;
having displayed the hook-mudrā, one should then scatter fragrant flowers.
O Goddess, I shall hereafter explain with effort the sequence ending with the mudrās according to the ritual;
one should perform the mudrās by that very same ritual in accordance with the tantras.
One should offer a lamp according to the prescribed rite using either ghee or sesame oil;
the most excellent of preceptors should place the lamp high on his own right side.
There, the wise one should recite the root mantra eight times according to the rule;
indeed, he should recite the Mātṛkās in reverse order by that same sequence.
One should perform the placement of the mantra-limbs there according to the measure of the six limbs;
for that water, one should pour it into the food offerings, the scents, and the flowers.
In the worship of the deity, the food offering (naivedya) consists of various kinds of rice and other grains, products of the cow, along with sweets (sandeśa), and is endowed with various flavors.
Then the preceptor should offer incense and lamps according to this rite;
indeed, various types of incense are prescribed as being composed of the natures of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
The incense that is proclaimed as being of the nature of Brahman for all [deities] consists of agallochum,
guggulu, sugar, honey, and sandalwood.
Then, O Dear One, one should fumigate with resin of the *sarja* tree mixed with clarified butter,
as well as with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, *cora*, saffron, and yellow pigment (*rocanā*).
They know the eight fragrant substances (*śaktigandhāṣṭaka*) to be *jaṭāmāṃsī*, *māṃsī*, *kapikacchū*,
sandalwood, *aguru*, camphor, *uśīra*, *kuṣṭha*, and saffron.
They know the eight fragrances of Viṣṇu to be jaṭāmāṃsī, māṃsī, and surabhi; as well as sandalwood, aguru, camphor, tamāla leaves, and saffron.
They know the eight-fold fragrance (gandhāṣṭaka) to consist of *kusita*, combined with *kuṣṭha* and *śaiva*.
Clarified butter mixed with curd and honey is proclaimed as *madhuparka*.
Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and clarified butter— in this sequence,
the "five products of the cow" (pañcagavya) and so forth are proclaimed as being in accordance with all Tantras.
One should offer curd, milk, and ghee, and then coconut water;
by combining these with sugar and other ingredients, it is declared as the "five nectars" (pañcāmṛta).
These, along with their ancillaries, have been described by the wise;
therein, the primary [set] is sixteenfold, and the secondary is remembered as tenfold.
One must certainly perform the fivefold service; listen now to that supreme [instruction].
Without the services, worship does not bring about grace.
A seat, a welcome, water for the feet, the arghya offering,
water for sipping, the madhuparka, further sipping water, a bath, garments, and ornaments.
Fragrant flowers, incense, a lamp, and then an offering of food;
linen garments and sandalwood—this is the sixteenfold oblation.
Water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), the honey-mixture (madhuparka),
water again, fragrant flowers, incense, a lamp, food offerings (naivedya), and sandalwood paste.
In ancient times, Manu declared that there are ten modes of service;
however, worship consisting of fragrant flowers and other such items is known as the five-fold service (pañcopacārikā).
The sixteenth, however, is the primary one; it is recollected in ten ways and attained in five ways. It should be practiced by one who desires prosperity.
Thus, O Goddess, it has been described in manifold ways in various tantras:
one should offer that object which is beneficial to oneself during the worship of the deity.
The deities long for many things within their own bodies;
therefore, whatever object one desires, that one should employ in the worship of the deity.
On an auspicious lunar day and under a favorable constellation, the wise teacher should impart the mantra;
specifically on the full moon, the seventh, the eighth, or likewise the ninth lunar day.
The fourteenth, the tenth, and especially the fifth—
these lunar days are declared to be auspicious for the rites of initiation.
Aśvinī, Maghā, Mūlā, and likewise the three Pūrvas; Svātī, Viśākhā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Rohiṇī bring auspiciousness.
And between those two, O beautiful lady, the merchant has vavakola and vata oil; all these Karaṇas are indeed auspicious in every Tantra.
And during the time of the preeminence of the bears (the month of Mārgaśīrṣa), one should perform initiation according to the rule;
initiation [is performed] on an auspicious lunar day, under a fixed, soft, or gentle nakṣatra, and on a favorable weekday.
When the auspicious lunar mansion is favorable, the moon is benefic, Venus and Jupiter occupy the quadrants or trines, and the ninth house is likewise occupied,
then at such a general time, initiation is performed with a tranquil mind.
On an auspicious lunar day and under a favorable constellation, one who is discerning should receive the mantra.
The commencement of mantra practice during the months beginning with Vaiśākha bestows auspicious results.
In Vaiśākha there shall be all success; in Jyeṣṭha, the destruction of everything;
in Āṣāḍha, the gain of a son; and in Śrāvaṇa, the accumulation of wealth.
In Bhādrapada there will be the destruction of subjects; in Āśvina it shall be auspicious;
in Kārttika there will be the splendor of the Vasus; and in Mārgaśīrṣa there shall be all prosperity.
In the month of Pauṣa, it causes the loss of knowledge; in Māgha, one is endowed with intelligence;
in Phālguna, there shall be all success; and Caitra is not an indicator of auspiciousness.
O beloved, on the thirteenth day of the month of Caitra, the initiation of Madana should also be performed;
one obtains that merit which belongs to the meritorious [day] of the year.
Furthermore, during the transit of the sun into the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) and at the great equinox (mahāviṣuvaka),
one should perform the unsurpassed rite of initiation during that great festival.
An eclipse of the moon or sun at times other than those prescribed is recorded;
such a time, equal to a solar eclipse, is difficult to find at any other time.
Indeed, a thousand lunar eclipses are proclaimed for the sun;
there is no fault in the day of the week, nor in the asterism, nor in the lunar date and so forth.
Nor is there the performance of yoga according to the doctrine of Śaṅkara;
[these are] Sūrya, Soma, the son of Śaśin (Budha), Śukrācārya, and the Lord of the Gods (Indra).
It should be performed on the Nandā and Bhadrā days, in accordance with all the tantras;
through the grace of a pure-minded guru, one shall always obtain [the results] for kings.
By the mere grace of him, a person shall obtain the fourfold aims of life;
his sandals are the givers of dharma, accompanied by both father and son.
O Pārvatī, I consider even the bile-humors (pitta) to be more significant than these [other humors] in the Tantras;
for what is the use of their kinsmen, what use their servants, or their sons and relatives?
He who may receive [this] from the Guru at all times and regarding all things, even for kings—
initiation shall be of three kinds, endowed with all the Tantras.

The great initiation (mahādīkṣā), as well as the initiation (dīkṣā) and the instruction (upadeśa) beyond that, are to be understood in each respective age; however, O beloved, it is the instruction that prevails in the Kali age.
O twice-born ones, in the Kṛta age, the path was as previously described; in the Tretā, it was the Smṛti of the Mahābhārata;
in the Dvāpara, it was that spoken in the Purāṇas; and in the Kali age, it is according to the Āgamas.
Thus, O Goddess, many kinds [of initiations] have been described in various tantras;
in the Kali age, initiation should be performed according to the specific place and time.
One who is destitute should not perform initiation for the sake of auspiciousness or for the two [types of] welfare;
at that time, the mantra, complete with its seer (*ṛṣi*) and other attributes, should be placed in the right ear.
Then, at that moment, O Goddess, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times;
then one should offer oblations into the fire-pit one thousand and eight times.
For the sake of protecting one's good rebirth, one should recite the mantra together with the guru;
one should worship that deity there, so that success (siddhi) is not destroyed.
Then the wise man should worship the Goddess with perfumes, flowers, food, and water;
he should offer ten flowers there to the Goddess according to the prescribed rite.
Tulsi, the two types of lotus, jasmine, ketakī, and karavīra—
these ten flowers are recommended, as are red lotuses.
Having joined these together according to their respective rules, the supreme practitioner, through union with the mantra,
shall obtain the grace of the excellent mantra just as it was previously described by the Guru when [the rite] was performed.
One should fashion the Goddess, adorned with various ornaments, according to the prescribed rite;
then, at that very moment, the Guru should always bestow a blessing.
Oṃ! May there be auspiciousness; may Śrī Mahālakṣmī be gracious.
May the supernatural powers (siddhis) be ever present for you, bestowing the fruits of your desires.
One should adorn oneself and the preceptor with various ornaments:
with bracelets during the rite of punishment, and with crowns and armlets during the fire-oblation.
One should offer necklaces, armlets, bracelets, and anklets according to the prescribed rule; one should also give a sacred thread made of silk cloth or golden threads.
A person of vast intellect should have the Guru adorned with various ornaments;
he should offer land that provides a livelihood, and cows by the hundreds of millions.
One should offer one's body, wealth, and even all one's life to him;
and until the end of one's life, one must not reveal the mantra to anyone.
O beloved, one should give a hundred thousand recitations to the guru and offer gold as a sacrificial fee;
indeed, a wise person must certainly give gold to the guru according to the prescribed rite.
The practitioner must perform the five-limbed initiation (*pañcāṅgadīkṣā*) for the sake of attaining all perfections (*sarvasiddhi*),
[bestowing] the four syllables of the deities and those of the four [states] in their proper sequence.
Śaṅkara, Gaṇeśa, and likewise the fourth, Hari;
[these names] are joined with the letter 'sa' at the end and 'satya' at the end, with their heads adorned by the bindu.
The wise know Gaṇapati to be the seed-syllable consisting of the moon (the letter *sa*) and the end of the five (the letter *ha*);
it is conjoined with fire (*ra*) and the syllable of Parā.
The mantra for Svarga-Kṛṣṇa is considered to be joined with Vahni (3), Vasu (8), and Svara (7).

When Śambhu is in the middle, there are Havi (3), Naha (2), Ra (25), Bhū (1), and Iṣṭi (14) [for the mantra of Hari]. In Śaṅkara, there are Bhāṣya (14), Nāga (8), and Yuta (2) [for the mantra of Avināśin]. Gaṇapa, Śrī, Īśa, Śeṣa, and Durgā are situated [within their respective mantras].

In the case of the Goddess, Viṣṇu, Hara, and Gaṇeśa are the younger [deities], while the son of Gaurī is Śaṅkara; indeed, the Vaiṣṇava is superior to Śaṅkara and the others, for those [others] are the cause of loss to him.
This sequence of worship has been declared as bestowing auspiciousness upon men.
One should feed the Brahmins there according to the path prescribed by Vedic knowledge.
Among thousands of fools, one wise man is distinguished;
and having fed learned scholars, one becomes a lord among great queens.
O beloved, one should always provide food for the maiden according to the prescribed rite;
and by worshipping the maiden, a man shall obtain all accomplishments.
"O beloved, having taken up the Great Vidyā, one should recite it until the end of one's life;
death shall occur within the portion of the mantra—so it was spoken by Śaṅkara."
Wherever one may be and in whatever place, one should live and recite for the sake of accomplishing all aims;
there is no fault in mental recitation at any time or on any occasion.
One should recite the Mahāvidyā day and night with supreme devotion;
there should be no doubt in that regard, nor any consideration of whether one is an outcaste (brātya) or not.
A wise man should not speak of what is distant, nor should he ever speak of the Aśvin;
he should never engage in idle conversation there in any way whatsoever.
In the event of the downfall of a great guru or similar misfortune, there is no room for hesitation regarding worship;
whether out of delusion, by chance, or through destiny, the practitioner must perform the worship.
Then Sadāśiva shall destroy everything belonging to him and slay him,
whether in impurity or purity, at all times and on every occasion.
One should worship with supreme devotion for the sake of success in all undertakings;
one should always adopt the attire of the Kaulas according to the ritual procedure for the worship of the Goddess.
In a solitary linga, or in a cremation ground, or in an empty house, or at a crossroads,
or standing upon a corpse, one should recite the vidyā with undistracted mind.
At the root of a bilva tree, or at a pond, in a cow-pen, or in a temple;
likewise at a crossroads, in a house, on a ritual seat (pīṭha), and in the Supreme Self.
The wise practitioner should recite the mantra until its accomplishment is attained;
likewise, [one should strive] through sacrifices, gifts, fire-oblations, and the feeding of Brahmins.
One should always recite [the mantra] according to the prescribed measure for the *pūrva-caraṇa* (preliminary practice) and with strict discipline;
the number of recitations must be performed, and it should never be done without counting.
Even for one who performs [the rite] countless times, everything becomes fruitless;
the accomplishment of a mantra is desired only when its specific fruit is attained.
Once the mantra has been mastered, one should always perform whatever else is prescribed;
then the commencement of the *pūrva-caraṇa* rite is ordained.
O Goddess of the gods, by the authority of Śaṅkara, at that very moment he first attains perfection in mantra, and thereafter the procedure for the fruits of his desires.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Viśvasāra Tantra.
The third chapter:
Now I shall proclaim the mantras; listen, O lotus-faced one!
By whose mere grace a person may obtain the fourfold aims of human life.
O Supreme Goddess, in all four directions of Vaiśākha, there exist everywhere Tantras of four kinds concerning the practice of mantras.
And there are tens of millions upon tens of millions of mantras, yantras,
and means of accomplishment on the earth, in the worlds of the gods, among the gandharvas, and in the subterranean realm of Rasātala.
In the world of the Nāgas, the world of the Ṛṣis, among the Kuṣmāṇḍas, and among the Rākṣasas,
there exist Tantras of various forms and indeed of specialized characteristics.
Among all tantras and mantras existing here among humans,
those which have been requested by deities are preeminent.
A birth like that of a human being does not exist anywhere else;
all the gods and ancestors desire human birth.
A human body is difficult to obtain at all times among all bodies;
even therein, birth in the land of Bhārata is indeed very difficult to attain.
In that case, birth in a household devoted to knowledge is exceedingly rare; and therein, O lady, it is especially difficult to find one who can dispel doubts.
In that regard, even such a person who possesses the mantra is extremely difficult to find;
among them, the one who knows the Āgamas is the best, honored in all the Vedas.
Even there, O Pārvatī, the best among practitioners, who is hidden in all tantras,
is the most excellent Śmaśānavāsinī among the Deva-tantras.
Moving among the yakṣas, gandharvas, and nāgas, she dwells there;
in the worlds of the Kuṣmāṇḍas and Vighnas, Bhairava is universally honored.
O Goddess, among men, Sadāśiva himself may appear as a god;

he stands with five faces— red, yellow, white like a cloud, pearl-white, and the color of the *javā* flower— each with three eyes, embracing his consort who wears a moon upon her crest and possesses the splendor of ten million full moons.
I worship him who holds a trident, a hammer, a sword, a vajra, fire, a serpent-king, a bell, a goad, a noose, and the destroyer of fear, his body blazing with immeasurable ornaments and garments.
Having prostrated, I shall declare that which is supremely beneficial for all the world;
for whatever practice is followed in a particular mantra, such indeed is the dharma therein.
By that, one becomes one who has accomplished the goal, established in heaven and liberation;
yet, even while speaking, success arises only through the practice of *bhrānti*.
One should become pure in mind here; through this, accomplishment shall arise by way of liberation.
Having bowed to the Goddess Trailokyasundarī according to the Mahācīnakrama, [one attains this].
One who is intent upon all perfections should worship the mantra every day;
for there, neither the Śruti nor the Smṛti applies, nor does ritual action, which arises from desire.
One should constantly worship the supreme deity with single-minded devotion;
he proclaimed every mantra for the sake of the liberation of the goddess's mouth.
Among the Yakṣas and Gandharvas, they know [the deity] to be on the Nyāsa with a yellow face;
among the Kuṣmāṇḍas and the worlds of the Vighnas, indeed with a face like a cloud.
O Goddess of the Suras, it is said among men that you, teaching the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā) to your disciples, possess a face like the Java flower and are adorned with pearls.
It is said that this is the most excellent of all for the purpose of human beings according to the prescribed rule;
indeed, even the deities will long for the mantra of a human being.
O Goddess, among the millions of mantras, those secret rites intended for human beings still exist on the surface of the earth even today; such humans are the five deities.
They seek [it] through austerities, as described by the Lotus-born;
they seek it through austerities, as described by the Lotus-born.
Thus addressed, all the sciences, endowed with the authority of the Vedas, were born forth:
the Great Science (Mahāvidyā) preceded by the Great [Vidyās], as well as meditation, ritual placement, and recitation.
I shall describe to you, in due order, the ritual of worship, as well as the hymn, the armor, the eulogy, the conduct, and the means of accomplishment.
And the specific mantra-vidyās have been described in various tantras;
O Maheśvarī, those great vidyās have entered into ten million living beings.
O Maheśānī, those who have entered the ten million divine abodes and are endowed with all the tantras are proclaimed as the Great Vidyās, the deities of life.
The accomplishment of a living being occurs through a living being; divinity is sought through a deity.
These two are employed among men in all tantras.
This mantra, which seizes upon the supreme contemplation, liberates the practitioner from the bonds of existence;
therefore, it is proclaimed by the virtuous as the mantra that cuts through saṃsāra.
Now I shall proclaim the Vidyā; listen, O lotus-faced one!
I shall describe Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā, who bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
By the mere knowledge of which, O Indra among the lords of the earth,
you obtained wealth, grain, sons, a wife, as well as horses and elephants.
A person shall obtain the Vasundharā, the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), and the eight supernatural powers (siddhis);
from the various divisions of the letters of the Mātṛkā, all mantras were born.
O beautiful lady, the Great Vidyā, the Great Primordial,
and the Great Mantra are said to be the seed of all things, according to the doctrine of Śaṅkara.
And there are various great vidyās endowed with all tantras;
both the primary and the modified forms are recognized in all tantras.
The seed-syllable Śrī is Nature (prakṛti) and Lajjā is Transformation (vikṛti), as is Māyā;
Vāgbhava is both Nature and Transformation.
The vocative case, the *kīla*, the pair of *māyā*, the *prakṛti*, and *phaṭ*.
The *prakṛti* and *vikṛti*, and *vahnīndarī*. Then the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī, the seed-syllable of Māyā, and after that Vāgbhava; immediately following that, *vajravairocanīye*.
The pair of Māyās ending with *phaṭ*, and at the end of that, Vahnisundarī.
O Goddess, in the section on primordial illusion (pūrvamāyāpada), the seed-syllable of desire (kāmabīja) is expounded;
this is declared to be the Mahākālamata, which brings about the auspicious extraction of mantras.

The wise practitioner should worship the Vidyā that bestows the fruits of the four aims of life—beginning with Kāmā, or beginning with Vāgabhavā, or beginning with Māyā; or he may worship the Vidyā beginning with Lajjā.
Lakṣmī and the others are for the sake of attaining prosperity; Kāmā and the others for the attainment of desires;
Māyā and the others for acts of subjugation; and Lajjā and the others for the destruction of enemies.
One should recite the vidyā in the west from the southern side of Meru;
likewise, one should recite the vidyā in the north and especially in the east.
In the west are those associated with Māyā, and in the south are those of Śrīvidyā;
in the north are Vāgbhava and the others, and immediately following that are Kāmā and the others.
Bhairava declared that ritual procedure during the Kṛta Yuga;
thus, one should recite the Vidyā according to the rules before the assembly of those deities.
A hundred thousand mantras are described in various tantras;
the Great Vidyā Śyāmā is proclaimed in manifold ways according to the tantric scriptures.
The wise man should mutter the Gāyatrī according to the prescribed rule; listen to that.
One should mutter this Vidyā, beginning with "Kāma," for the attainment of the fruits of all desires.
Immediately after that, we meditate upon her whose nature is consciousness (citsvarūpā), ending in the feminine suffix -ī;
and immediately after that, we meditate upon Vajravairocanī, ending in the feminine suffix -ī.
"May that Mother Gāyatrī, the bestower of all accomplishments, inspire us.
The wise one should then utter "Vairocanīm," ending with the syllable *ṅ*, followed by "vidmahe."
Likewise, we meditate upon that which ends in *chinnam* and that which ends in *ṅi*;
thereafter, may the Goddess lift us up from that and impel us toward the purchase.
The goddess Gāyatrī, the intention of Mahākāla, is honored by all; one should always recite her mantra beginning with *lajjā* (hrīḥ), or beginning with *kāma* (klīm), or beginning with *māyā* (hūṃ).
One should recite the Vidyā beginning with the syllable *Vāgbhava*, which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
through the Gāyatrī, it protects all those practitioners from the bondage of worldly existence.
By that very [method], the Gāyatrī, which is approved by all, is sung by the virtuous;
one should perform four hundred thousand recitations for the rite of *puraścaraṇa*.
Lakṣmī, Lajjā, Māyā, Mātrā, and also Dvādaśikā—
[these are] with "Vajravairocanīye," "Mātre Phaṭ," and joined with "Svāhā."
The syllable consisting of the letter 'va', joined with the vowel 'u' (v-u) and adorned with the bindu of passion (anusvāra), is designated as "Rati" by the wise because it is the fourth vowel.
This is declared to be the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī, endowed with all the Tantras;
it is joined with the left eye (the letter *i*) and fire (the letter *r*), and adorned with the Bindu and Nāda.
O Maheśānī, the seed-syllable of Śiva is proclaimed as the seed-syllable of Lañjā (Lajjā).
Having extracted Īśāna, one should take the seed-syllable of the Enemy of Pura (Rudra), adorned with the Bindu and the Nāda.
Having arranged the twelve vowels around the left ear, one should produce here the state of a wise sage,
endowed with the resonance (nāda) and the bindu of the phonemes.
The seed-syllable Vāgbhava is said to be for the purification of all speech;
O Goddess, in the vocative case, it is declared to be the very form of the deity.
Beyond this, one should join the seed-syllable of Māyā at its end, followed by the Astra-mantra;
one should employ these with supreme devotion, for Śakti is Vahnisundarī.
Whatever other various sciences there may be, they are indeed that Goddess, the Sovereign of the Gods;
she alone is the transformation whose form is sound, endowed with all the Tantras.
Bhairava is the seer (ṛṣi), while the other [verses] are declared to have the Samrāṭ as their meter;
the deity is named Sarvasiddhā, known in the three worlds by the name Tribhuvaneśvarī.
The seed-syllable of Māyā and the power of Svāhā have been declared by the Lotus-born One.
Now I shall describe the meditation; listen, O lotus-faced one!
Dhyāna is said to be threefold: sakala, niṣkala, and likewise kalātīta; listen hereafter, O Goddess, to it exactly as it is.
The partless [vow] is to be performed by ascetics, while the one with parts is for householders;
the celibacy that transcends all parts was thus described by the Lotus-born One.
One should meditate on the syllable *nī* within one's own navel, which is the metre and possesses a blossoming smile;
and in the center of that lotus bud is the mandala of the fierce-rayed sun.
Resembling the Javā flower and similar to the red Bandhūka,
it is the dust [of passion] marked by the lines of *sattva* and *tamas*, adorned with the circle of the womb.
In the center, however, is that Great Goddess, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
who holds in her left hand the severed head of Chinnamastā.
The goddess, with her mouth wide open and her fierce tongue lolling out,
drinks the stream of blood flowing forth from her own throat.
With her mass of hair disheveled and adorned with various flowers,
she holds a flaying knife in her right hand and is decorated with a garland of severed heads.
She is naked, most terrible, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture,
radiant while wearing a garland of bones, and having a serpent as her sacred thread.
And the practitioners of mantra always meditate upon her as seated for the sake of pleasure,
eternally sixteen years of age, with full and elevated breasts.
One should meditate on Rati and Manobhava standing in reverse union,
joined with Ḍākinī and Rūpiṇī through the yoga of the left and right [channels].
And on the left side, the goddess [beholds] a Ḍākinī, who is drinking streams of flowing blood and resembles the blazing fire at the end of an aeon.
Her eyes flash like streaks of lightning, her rows of teeth are like a flight of cranes;
her face is terrifying with its fangs, and her breasts are full and elevated.
The Great Goddess, with disheveled hair, most terrible, and naked,
holds a skull and a chisel in her hands through the union of the left and right [hands].

The wise practitioner should meditate upon that primordial Goddess, who is being served by [her attendants], who is exquisitely adorned with a skull held in her hand, and who causes the drinking of streams of blood flowing from her throats.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the Goddess for the attainment of the fruit of all siddhis.
I shall proclaim the meditation taught by Bhairava, which destroys all sins:
[one should meditate on her] possessing the brilliance of ten million rising suns, holding a terrifying skull-bowl filled with her own blood in her left hand,
and with a face intent upon drinking it.

One should always meditate upon the beautiful goddess, whose thighs are as lovely as the body of the Lord of Serpents, who holds a sword in her right hand, stands in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, and has the quarters of the sky for her garment.

One should arrange the body as before, perform the purification of the elements as before, and likewise perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) as before; after that, [one should prepare] the vessel for the offering water (arghyapātra).
One should prepare the requisites for worship for the sake of accomplishing external yoga;
having designated a location as before, one should constantly recite [the mantra] in a secluded place.
There is no need for ritual worship or adoration of her; one should always merely recite the mantra.
Regarding this particular Great Vidyā, no further deliberation is required.
In the event of the death of a great guru or similar circumstances, there is no fault whatsoever;
whether in an impure or pure place, the wise person should recite at all times.
One should perform the consideration of the *lekhavakṣa* (the writing-tablet) as approved by the Tantras;
there should be no consideration of the body (*dehavicāra*), nor even the gladdening of friends and others.
Everywhere and at all times, one should always recite the mantra-vidyā;
having drawn the wheel according to the rule, the wise practitioner should worship the Śakti.
First, one should draw a triangle adorned with a yoni-maṇḍala;
therein, one should fashion the three worlds with eight petals according to the proper proportions.
One should present three skull-cups provided with vajras and tridents;
one should present a skull-bowl and a chisel, joined to the left and right [hands].
In the center, having written a pair of *kūrca* syllables (*hūṃ*) ending with *svāhā* or *phaṭ*,
one should mentally worship it with the mantra "To the Great Wheel" (*mahācakrāya*), ending with *namaḥ*.
Now I shall describe another yantra; listen and be attentive. One should draw an eight-petalled lotus, and in its center, a triangle.
One should draw a mandala; at its center is the yoni-mandala.
Therein, within the triangle, one should write the seed-syllable of Māyā (Hrīṃ) accompanied by the syllable Phaṭ.
There, one should invoke the Goddess by means of the mantras of their respective vehicles;
one should perform the worship beginning with the Supportive Power (Ādhāraśakti) for the sake of all prosperity.
One should worship Ādhāraśakti, who holds two lotuses,
is seated upon the Kūrma-āsanā below, and resembles the autumnal moon.
Above that, one should worship the deity Kūrma, who resembles the color of a blue sapphire;
one should worship the god who wears a single earring as being situated below him.
O Goddess, one should worship her who is endowed with a thousand hoods and served by gods and gandharvas; upon her head, one should worship the earth bounded by the ocean and girt by the sea.
One should worship the earth, the island of jewels, and the wish-fulfilling tree (kalpavṛkṣa) beyond that;
beneath them, one should worship the divine and auspicious lion-throne of heaven.
One should worship [the deity] endowed with various wonders according to this procedure;
right there is the Root of Bliss (Ānandakanda), and beyond that is the Supreme Sambinnāla.
Therein is a most beautiful lotus, the essence of all reality;
one should worship the quality [of nature] there, which consists of rajas, sattva, and tamas.
There, one should worship oneself as the inner self;
then, desiring pleasure, one should remain there in the inverted posture.
There, one should always worship the Goddess who is the embodiment of the three powers;
she is the power whose nature is the quality of rajas, who possesses color, and resides in the right region.
One should always worship on her left side the Śakti who possesses a beautiful form, who is endowed with all the Tantras, and whose nature consists of the quality of Tamas.
In the center is the eternal goddess known as Ḍākinī Sarvasiddhā,
born from pure sattva and adorned with various colors.
One should utter the mantra of Siddhi-Ḍākinī, which begins with Oṃ and ends with Namaḥ, bestows the fruit of mantra-accomplishment, and consists of syllables that grant all excellent attainments.
One should utter the Vajravairocanī mantra ending with "sambuddhā," according to the ritual procedure;
one should worship her with the mantra: "Come here! Stay here! Stay! (ihāvaha iha tiṣṭha tiṣṭha).
O lotus-faced one, one should perform the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breaths) as before;
then, one should offer the seat with the *āsana-mantra*, followed by the invocation (*āvāhana*).
Then, having performed the imposition of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga-nyāsa), the excellent practitioner should worship the Goddess;
then, O Goddess, he should worship the Goddess with mantras for the offering of oblations (bali) and so forth.
One should utter the word ending in "sambuddhi" (vocative), followed by the two words "dehi" and "ehi";
then one should say "gṛhṇa gṛhṇa" and after that the word "bali."
Having addressed the word "mama," one should utter the two words "siddhiṃ dehi";
then, having spoken the second [mantra], "kavacaṃ," followed by the word "karālike."
The great mantra ending in *phaṭ* and *svāhā* is for the procedure of offering the *bali*.
Thereafter, one should offer various kinds of *bali*, both raw and cooked.
Raw rice, fine rice-pudding, and products made from molasses;
likewise, red meat, fried foods, and various kinds of liquor.
The Gauḍī, the Pauṣṭī, the Tāla, the Kharjūrī produced from flowers,
the well-ripened Kājñikā, and the women who offer gifts and fans.
Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—all are eligible recipients.
One should give various kinds of animals, and especially human beings.
Having first worshipped Bali with perfumes, flowers, sandalwood, and other offerings,
and having obtained his permission, one should then worship the deities residing in the limbs.
The principal female forms have bodies as white as frost or crystal, with blue, black, and reddish rays,
and they hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The best of practitioners should worship the Goddess in sequence beginning with the heart:
he should utter "To the sword, the heart," and "To the sword, upon the head."
Then, one should place that noose upon the face with the Śrī mantra, the noose upon the topknot with the Kavaca mantra, the goad upon the pair of eyes, and finally, [the goad] upon all the limbs.
The wise one should place [the mantra] on all limbs for the sake of destroying the Asuras;
he should worship the Śaktis upon the eight petals according to the ritual procedure beginning with the syllable *Oṃ*.
One should worship Oṃkārī and Vartinī, and immediately after them, Ḍākinī; then one should worship Mahābhairavī, Bhairavī, and Indrākṣī.
One should worship Piṅgalākṣī and Saṃhāriṇī according to the sequence starting from the east,
and in the center, one should worship the pair of armor-mantras ending with *phaṭ* in due order.
The worship of the Goddess is prescribed to be performed at all times at the conclusion of the *svāhā* mantra;
one should worship the god Bhairava in front [of her] according to this procedure.
The wise practitioner should worship the *samrāṭ* metre in the south, the words of the mantra in the north, and the seed-syllable and power (*bīja-śakti*) in the southern direction, in due order.
And the Mothers, beginning with Brahmāṇī, who bestow all accomplishments, [should be worshipped] within the petals;
having worshipped them in due order according to the previously mentioned meditation and ritual placement (nyāsa).
There, the worship of those beginning with Indra and ending with the World-Protectors is performed;
having worshipped them in the *bhūpura* according to the sequence starting from the east.
Indra and the others have been mentioned previously; their forms are now described:
Pārvatī is yellow, red, white, dark-blue, smoke-colored, and white.
She is black, fair, red, and white-complexioned beyond that;
likewise, the goddess Brahmāṇī is proclaimed as Lakṣmī of Hari.
There too, one should worship these forms of those mantras:
Vajra and the others, as enjoined for the weapons, endowed with all the tantras.
Yellow, white, pale-blue, lightning-red, black, and dark-blue;
resembling the *kāravella* and the *pāṭala* flower—these are proclaimed by the wise as the types of vajras.
Now, this mantra for the seat was spoken by the Lotus-born One:
one should utter the word ending in "Sambuddha," followed by the two words "dehi" and "ehi."
Having raised this seat, seize, seize the two feet;
having raised that perfection, give, give the two feet.
Having addressed my enemies, she again utters "māraya dvitayam" (slay the pair), followed by "kartṛkā dvitayam" (the two knives); thus ends the beautiful goddess of weapons.
This knowledge concerning the seat has been declared by the Lotus-born One;
having thus worshipped according to the rule, up to the offering of food (naivedya), in accordance with the ritual procedure.
One should perform the worship of the wheel in the cardinal directions according to the prescribed rule,
with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings, by means of this ritual procedure.
O Goddess of the Gods, one should worship Karāla, Vikarāla, Atikarāla, and thereafter Mahākarāla, ending with the dative case (caturthī).
Having performed the preliminary rites beginning with the seed-syllable of Māyā, one should always worship at the end of the word "namas.
O lotus-faced one, listen as I describe the five-limbed deities.

"Thus, without this, there can be no accomplishment; so it was spoken by Śaṅkara. Then, one should perform the ritual contemplation according to the prescribed rule with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings."
The one of vast intellect should worship the Great Vidyā with supreme devotion;
having first performed the internal sacrifice (antaryāga), he should thereafter perform the external sacrifice (vahiryāga).
Then, at the time of recitation, one should perform the ritual placement of the mantras (mantranyāsa) according to the prescribed rule;
one should perform it from the feet to the head, both in reverse and in direct order.
Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma), one should recite the mantra according to the prescribed rule,
after having meditated upon oneself as being of the nature of the deity according to the prescribed rule.
