she is short-lived, emaciated, and increases the joy of others.
Suprītā, Ślokinī, Ślokā, Cāṇḍālī, and likewise Vāyasī;
she who causes the destruction of all asuras, Kālī, the dweller in Koṇa.
Mākarī, Bhaumī, Horānaṭakā, Nirjharā, Kulaghnā,
Yāvatī, Kolā, Nikolā, and Trāsarūpiṇī.
Terrifying and fearful of the end of time, Sāvitrī is the bestower of liberation;
she is Mātā, Skandamātā, Jiyamātā, and Jinendrarī.
Clad in a deer-skin and dressed in rags, she conceals herself with the skin of a tiger; she possesses the three powers, is the embodiment of power, and is likewise the Ḍākinī and Varṇinī.
Daṃṣṭrābhīmā, Piṅgalākṣī, Kaṃśinī, Audarī, Oṃkārī, Varṇamātā, Kṣemaṅkarī, and Svarūpiṇī.
Prāṇaśīlā, Suśīlā, Suraktā, Raktavāhinī, Celinī,
Siṃhasaṃsthā, Vyāghrasthā, and Jagavāhinī.
Pārijātaharā, the one dwelling in the mortal realm and Satyaloka,
Surabhī, Vāmanī, Nindakā, and Nandinī.
Lakṣmī, Satyabhāmā, Hiḍambā in the form of a crane,
Jvaramātā, Jvarī, Jvālā, Jvālinī, Jvaladā, and Jvalā.
She is the three-headed, the triple-pathed, the threefold, the dweller in the limbs of action, the ritual act itself;
she is the slow-moving, the dull-witted, the possessor of enjoyment, and she who goes to the netherworld.
Gaganāśvā and Gaṇāśvā, Āśvāmbā, and Sukulīmahi;
Kumadā, endowed with devotion, is eternal and delightful through her devotion.
She who is free from desire and yet possesses desire, she who dwells within the limbs of all desires,
she who destroys the body of desire, she who is moist, the mind-born one, and the increaser of nourishment.
Auṣadhī is the mother of physicians and the destroyer of all death;
she is that which is spoken of and that which is unsaid—whatever exists, whether stationary or moving.
There dwells eternally the goddess Chinnamastā, the beloved of Śiva.
Thus ends this Thousand Names of Śivā as spoken by Śiva.
Whoever should recite [this] upon waking at dawn, at the time of morning, at the beginning of night,
at midnight, at night, or at the time of worship, O Maheśvarī.
In a cremation ground, in a wilderness, in a formidable fortress, in fetters and bonds,
on a boat, in a mountain pass, in danger, or when life is at stake—
Whenever fear arises— whether from poison, fire, or other such dangers—
and when the sun has entered Leo, whoever worships the Supreme Goddess [shall be protected].
Having recited it and having caused others to recite it, one shall destroy all malevolent beings;
and they shall not see the practitioner at any time whatsoever.
O Goddess, having recited this hymn of armor according to the prescribed rite,
wherever one may go, one remains as if held in the hand of Jayanta.
Whether on Ketu or on Dundubhi, one should always enter the abode of heaven;
having conquered all the kings, one should bring them back to one's own home.
On the new moon day falling on a Tuesday, a man who has gone to a crossroads or traveled to a cremation ground in a desolate wilderness should [take] a burnt fish along with it.
Having offered an oblation of milk-rice, that best of practitioners who recites [the mantra] upon the funeral pyre on a Tuesday becomes like Kubera among men.
Having recited the armor-verse (*kavaca*) there, one should then recite the *Nāmasahasraka*;
through the practice of recitation for six months, one quickly becomes invisible.
O Great Goddess, one should recite the mantra of Caṇḍadevī according to the prescribed rite;
having completed ten thousand times eight recitations, one shall become a wise poet like Vāṇī herself.
Having offered an oblation of food mixed with meat in a deserted garden or likewise in a house,
and having performed recitation and study, one shall become a supreme Lord of Speech.
Upon seeing the vulva of a menstruating woman, the practitioner himself should mutter [the mantra] six thousand times; having muttered it thus, he shall become a lord of the earth.
Having recited the armor-armor (kavaca) with his own semen and blood, and having offered an oblation, the wise man should mutter the mantra; he shall become the abode of all prosperity.
One should recite the mantra in the womb of another; he shall become the abode of all prosperities.
[The substances are: a scorched fish, a hen’s egg, a rat, a buffalo, and a human [flesh].
At the onset of night, one should offer an oblation of honey, meat, and flour-cakes;
being personally intent on dancing, one may do so in whatever place is available.
Naked and with disheveled hair, he shall become the abode of all prosperities;
he should recite the mantra at all times and on every occasion within the supreme female organ.
A person seeking dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa shall obtain the fourfold aims by offering liquor,
meat, and sacrificial oblations at night together with practitioners.
Having recited the great vidyā, Sundarī Bhavasundarī,
the wise man should satisfy Caṇḍikā with water used for washing the vulva.
The world shall abide under his control by means of six thousand [recitations].
Having reflected and then contemplated thoroughly, one should recite the target mantra with undistracted mind for one hundred thousand times.
One should offer all of those to the Goddess day after day according to the prescribed rite;
whatever food one offers to the Goddess, a man should eat a portion of that.
Then, O one of great wisdom, he shall be honored by all truths;
[he should avoid] fish that are burnt, meat that is burnt, and the flesh of crows, cocks, and mice.

Having offered the bali-oblation during the portion of the night, the practitioner, most excellent among seekers, should offer [the remains] with the substance that is the residue of the food offering; thus he becomes Nārāyaṇa himself.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite at midnight during the portion of the night,
and having praised the eternal Goddess, the Blessed One, who is the very form of the Root Mantra;
Within six months, one shall attain a perfection difficult even for the gods to obtain—
by means of the *bhaga* and *liṅga*, by those things called *bhaga*, and by that which is designated by the word *bhaga*.
The best of practitioners should offer the food offering with the nectars of the bhaga and the liṅga;
by the grace of the goddess Caṇḍā, he shall become a son of Pārvatī.
One should always sprinkle a little water from the washing of the vulva [with the mantra]:
"This is my own, O Blessed Lady; it is the nectar of the vulva and the phallus."
Whether by his own power or through the power of another, the wise man should recite [the mantra] at all times;
whether by night or by day, he should increase the Goddess’s delight.
Within just one month, you shall attain a perfection difficult even for the gods to obtain;
the wise man should worship the goddess Chinnamastā with wine and meat.
And by consuming a portion of it, one becomes a lord of the earth;
it effects killing, incites hatred, and likewise brings about subjugation.
The practitioner shall always paralyze Yama, the sun, the moon, the wind, and so forth;
thus the man shall accomplish the six rites, including enchantment and eradication.
O lotus-faced one, even a king behaves like a slave before her;
and upon seeing her, even a skilled debater becomes speechless and shorn of his luster.
The Vaksas, Bhūtas, Piśācas, and others, the Ḍākinīs who are honored by the gods,
the Kuṣmāṇḍas who create obstacles, and Yama himself, the self-ruling lord— [all these are present].
They neither see nor hear, O you who delight in the rules of right conduct,
whether in heaven, among mortals, in the netherworld, or upon the earth, including the Gandharvas and the Kinnaras.
No fear of the Nivātakavacas and others shall arise for them;
a wise person should write this hymn with gorocanā and saffron.
With white *svayambhū* flowers, on a birch leaf, under Mars or Saturn,
during an auspicious conjunction, in a favorable lunar mansion, on a good lunar day, and in an empty house.
And immediately one should write out the mantra-armor and the auspicious hymn;
at the end of the night, one should worship the Vidyā in its source according to the ritual injunctions.
One should praise the Supreme Goddess with garments, ornaments, perfumes, and other offerings;
likewise, having meditated upon the Protectress Goddess according to the prescribed rite, one should offer her protection.
By wearing [this] on the head or on the arm, a person shall obtain all accomplishments (siddhi),
using vermilion and sandalwood as ornaments for the Goddess’s own adornments.
Having worshipped the maiden, he himself became Śrī Sadāśiva,
[uniting with] Svaratī, the charming Kulaṭā, and Vālikā, who was filled with passion.
Having worshipped and recited [the mantra], one shall bring the entire world under control;
there is no inciting of enmity there, for all gods and asuras are friends.
Wherever the planet is situated, there Lakṣmī resides;
there is no fear of teachers and the like, nor is there poverty or diseases there.
Famine is pacified, and one certainly attains long life;
there shall be no grief, nor old age, nor disease, nor any harm from malevolent planets, and so forth.
There is no fear of thieves there, nor is a person afflicted by disease or grief;
even when [the deity] has departed due to fire, burning, or other such calamities, O fair-faced one, [this remains so] through the power of this hymn and yantra.
One should perform a month-long fast to increase the pleasure of the Goddess,
having worshipped her according to the prescribed rite with goats, sheep, cattle, and other offerings.
With ruru deer, antelopes, bears, elephants, boars, jackals, and mice;
with lions, horses, restless monkeys, coconuts, and tortoises.
Having offered oblations and having performed worship, Caṇḍikā becomes pleased;
one should always offer the bali-oblation to the Goddess month after month according to the prescribed rule.
Having offered liquor into each and every jar daily according to the prescribed rite,
the wise one should satisfy Pārvatī, Caṇḍī, Chinnamastā, and Virūpīṇī.
Having offered the *śivāvali*, one should then satisfy the Mother of the World;
by constantly uttering the word "bhaga," one shall become possessed of the *bhagas*.
A person of vast intelligence, while menstruating, should constantly recite this vidyā one hundred thousand times,
or half of that, or half of that again, or half of that once more, within the vulva.
One should worship the Goddess, the daughter of the mountain, as a young maiden during the night;
then Sarasvatī, the mother of Skanda, becomes well-pleased.
One should always recite the vidyā beginning with "kāma," or one may always recite it beginning with "lakṣya.
One should recite the vidyā beginning with "oṃ," and one should always recite it beginning with "lajjā."
Having worshipped the Kumārikā according to the prescribed rite— she who, at all times and in all seasons, bestows all perfections upon those who perceive her— the wise man [attains his goal].
One should recite the vidyā six thousand times daily within its source;
no fault exists therein, as was spoken by Brahmā in the past.
O Goddess, there is doubt as to whether [this] is in the form of the eightfold conduct or in the form of the Siddhas; what more need be said further regarding these many things?
Thus ends the hymn of a thousand names of Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā in the Viśvasāra Tantra.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the mantra worshipped by the three worlds;
it is a great vidyā preceded by the word "Mahā," spoken of old by Brahmā.
This knowledge was told by Viṣṇu to Brahmā in the lotus of his navel;
thereafter, this knowledge was told by Brahmā to Nārada.
Nārada [gave it] to Asita; Asita to Devala;
Devala to Gautama; and Gautama to Kaśyapa.
One should always recite this six-syllable vidyā taught by Kaśyapa in the past;
then one becomes greatly wise, like another Prajāpati.
Then, having become Prajāpati, he went to heaven with his physical body;
at that very time, Bhairava became filled with anxiety.
Having received the knowledge, that sage prepared to go to heaven;
then [the Goddess said], "O Maheśānī, how can it be so in the world of men?"
Thinking that all those there were wealthy, learned in the Vedas, and devoted to righteousness, Kaśyapa arrived at that place.
Having performed that, Kaśyapa spoke to the gods concerning that great six-syllabled vidyā, the vidyā of Chinnamastā, the sovereign of the gods.
Then those worlds become bestowers of the fruits of the four aims of life.
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim the enchanting mantra of the Goddess.
I shall explain the extraction of the mantra, which is well-guarded, supremely meritorious, and the bestower of all siddhis; listen, O lotus-faced one.
O Mistress of the Gods, for whom Gaṅgādhara himself becomes manifest through mere consciousness alone— what need is there for other [deities], since whatever is desired is supreme?
O Goddess, by means of the knowledge of the mantra, the preceptor obtains all that,
having extracted the seed-syllable of Śiva adorned with the drop of passion (ratibindu).
One should make it endowed with the seed-syllable of fire; this is declared to be the [first] letter.
The first of the groups (varga), mounted upon the seed-syllable of Indra, is thus proclaimed.
The seed-syllable of Kāma, joined with the drop of passion (ratibindu) and composed of concentrated focus;
then the previously mentioned seed-syllable of Lakṣmī, and immediately after that, the Vāgbhava syllable.
The seed-syllable of Māyā, as well as the Astra-mantra, are proclaimed to consist of six syllables:
Hṛllekhā, Madanā, Lakṣmī, Vāgbhava, and Kūrca.
The great vidyā of Chinnamastā is proclaimed to be unsurpassed by any other weapon;
indeed, no vidyā equal to her exists even within the three worlds.
This six-syllabled mantra is the manifest bestower of liberation; there is no doubt in this matter.
All its procedures, such as recitation and worship, are like those of the sixteen-syllabled mantra.
The Vidyā, whose nature is that of Devakuṭā, bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life;
O lotus-faced one, listen as I describe her meditation.

Śiva always joyfully beholds her, who stands with her left leg extended in the *ālīḍha* posture, holding a severed *kartṛkā* knife, clad only in the directions as her garment, drinking with delight the streams of nectar-like blood from Skanda,
her head adorned with a wreath of serpents, possessing three eyes, and having cast the gods into her heart.
With a mind whose power is intoxicated by wine, one should meditate within the heart upon [the deity] who resembles a flame arising from meditation.
In her right hands she holds a very white, variegated mace, a spear, and likewise a skull-bowl; born from the quality of rajas, she is known by the name Sāvarṇī.

Is she to be meditated upon by the gods and those who know the Mantras as follows: joyfully drinking the stream of blood falling from the severed headless trunk (kavandha) of the Goddess, her arms bound with serpents; likewise holding a dark-colored body in her left hand, as well as a sword and a skull-bowl?
Standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture, joyfully drinking the blood trickling from the headless trunk (*kavandha*),
she is the *tāmasī* [form] capable of devouring the entire universe at the end of the dissolution (*pralaya*).
That very power is the supreme goddess; she is also known by the name Ḍākinī.
Having thus meditated upon that goddess, one should always recite [the mantra] as before.
One should perform [the rite] as before according to the traditional practice, or else equally with Kālikā;
having performed the ṛṣinyāsa and so forth, and having carried out the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi).
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall proclaim the King of Hymns (Stavarāja), which brings auspiciousness and bestows the fruits of all desires; listen with supreme devotion.

With the expansive, lotus-like faces adorned by pairs of shimmering earrings, with eyes like the water-lilies of the sky, and with prominent fangs emerging from broad cheeks that reveal loud, boisterous laughter, [the Goddess] makes manifest throughout the three worlds her presence within the triple universe.
Salutations to you, whose mass of matted hair is tawny and curled like emerging stalks of grain.

O Mother, who bestows grace upon your devotees, you who delight in the deer-skin and the girdle of human bone, who hold the sacrificial ladle and other implements, who are terrifying at the time of universal dissolution, who are short-statured, ineffable, beautiful with a dark-blue hue, adorned with a garland of severed heads, whose forehead bears a crescent moon, and who possess a wondrous splendor; [I bow to you].
Homage to you, O Mahāmāyā!
I seek the Goddess whose lotus-like pair of feet is worshipped by hosts of gods,
who accomplishes the attainment of desired fruits, and who is the Sovereign Bestower of Knowledge.
They meditate, praise, and offer hymns of praise; from their mouths there constantly issues, for the most part, speech beautiful with pure prose and verse that bestows prosperity.
Thus ends the King of Hymns on the Six-Syllable [Mantra] from the Viśvasāra Tantra.
The illustrious Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, expert in all branches of knowledge,
bearer of the skull-topped staff and the khaṭvāṅga, you who are established as the foremost among all mantras.
He explained the armor-mantra (*kavaca*) of the six-syllabled [mantra] according to its true nature.
Śrī Īśvara said:
"O Goddess, Mahādeva is the god of gods and is proficient in all branches of knowledge.
Having heard those words of hers, the Lord of the World smiled.
He explained the armor-mantra (kavaca) of the six-syllabled [mantra] according to its true nature. The Illustrious Lord said:
Excellent, excellent, O Maheśānī! Since it is for the benefit of virtuous people, I shall relate this great secret armor (*kavaca*), which is difficult even for the gods to obtain.
It is well-guarded in all tantras and concealed among all the gods; it was hidden by the hosts of deities, yet it has been revealed in the Viśvasāra.
In the morning, as well as at midday and especially in the evening;
likewise at midnight, during the night, and particularly in the latter part of the night.
A person should recite the mantra with the Śakti and read the Kavaca;
at that very moment, he attains the siddhi of the deity—of this there is no doubt.
Having meditated upon the Goddess, the practitioner of mantra, for the sake of the mantra's accomplishment, should recite this armor (kavaca) worshipped by the gods,
after first uttering the syllable *oṃ*.
A person should not perform worship or ritual adoration of her; rather, they should merely recite the mantra while constantly reading the armor-verse (kavaca) spoken by Bhairava.
May Maheśvarī, whose nature is *hrīṃ*, protect me upon the head of Hṛllekhā;
may Mahāmāyā, whose nature is *klīṃ* and who is endowed with all the Tantras, protect me.
May she who is the form of Lakṣmī, worshipped in all bodies, always protect me;
may she known as all knowledge in the mouth, the Vaiṣṇavī who bestows success, protect me.
May Sarasvatī, in the form of Śakti, always protect [me] on the tongue;
and may she, in the form of the seed-syllable *ai*, abide in the heart as armor.
And Maheśvarī, whose form is the seed-syllable *huṃ* and whose nature is illusion (*māyā*),
[is located] in the hands, feet, navel, sides, eyes, and nose.
In the belly, the hips, the penis, the private parts,
the two feet, the two hands, the backbone, the shoulder-blade region, and the buttocks;
May the syllable *phaṭ*, the beloved of Śiva in the form of a weapon, protect me at all times;
may the Ḍākinī Varṇinī grant protection for my head.
May Vajravairocanī protect [me] in all limbs; may Chinnamastakā protect [me] always;
may Oṃkāri protect [me] in all limbs, as do the deities of the limbs.
"May the yellow-eyed goddess, the deity of the limbs, always protect me in all my members"—thus, O Goddess, one should recite this; it is the procedure itself in every scripture.
May she in the form of a sword always protect the region of my head;
may Śrīvajrā, whose form is mantra, always protect my crown-lock.
May she who is in the form of a noose always protect [me] in all limbs, and she who is in the form of armor; may Aṅkuśā always protect the two eyes, which are like the moon and the sun.
O Goddess, who causes the destruction of the Asuras, you who take the form of weapons upon every limb—
may Oṃkāra protect me at all times, and may Vikarāla protect me always.
May Atikarāla protect me always; may Mahākarāla protect me always.
Oṃ, may Gaṇapati protect me always; may the Supreme Guru protect me always.
May the Guru protect me always; may Kṣetrapāla protect me evermore.
May Ādhāraśakti protect me always; may this Tortoise protect me forever.
May Ananta protect the heart-lotus at all times;
may she who is the embodiment of the letters protect [me] always; and may Chinnamastā, the beloved of Śiva, protect [me] forever.
Thus has this divine armor, difficult even for the gods to obtain, been told;
it must not be spoken of here or there, but should be guarded with great effort.
It is concealed in all tantras, yet revealed in the Viśvasāra;
it must never be spoken even at the cost of one's life, nor ever to one who is not a disciple.
O Dear One, this armor must not be told to one who is deceitful, devoid of devotion, or cruel;
it must not be told, it must not be told, it must by no means be told under any circumstances.
O noble lady, listen, O friend; the Śrutis were spoken by Śiva in the past.
Therefore, one who knows the ritual procedure [should employ] the mantra, the yantra, and the armor (kavaca) according to the rules.
It must never be given away, nor should it be disclosed; one should never reveal it.
He who recites this armor, so difficult for even the gods to obtain, for one month—
He would become beautiful in person, like another Kuvera;
and he who recites it for two months shall become the abode of prosperity.
He who recites it for three months shall become a vessel for treasures;
when the fourth month has arrived, he shall become the foremost among poets.
When the fifth month has arrived, he shall become a healthy devotee of Śiva;
but when the sixth month has arrived, he shall become a lord of the earth.
When the seventh month has arrived, one who is poor shall become wealthy;
when the eighth month has arrived, one shall be endowed with sons and grandsons.
When the ninth month has arrived, he certainly becomes free from disease;
when the tenth month has arrived, he shall become a lord of all sciences.
"But when the eleventh [chapter] is reached, a person shall obtain the fourfold aims of life.
Thus ends the armor-rite (*kavaca*) of the six-syllabled mantra of the Supreme Deity in the *Viśvasāra Tantra*.
Having reflected thus, one should perform the recitation according to the prescribed rite and offer it;
O Goddess of the Gods, having worshipped the Sovereign of the Suras with this mantra.
Having worshipped Mahāmāyā with perfumes, flowers, and incense, preceded by songs and instrumental music, the preceptor, adorned with ornaments, [should proceed].
Having first uttered the syllable Oṃ, one should recite the "Secret beyond the Secret";
then, having extracted the word "Goptṛ," it is preceded by the word "Gṛhāṇa."
Having extracted that which was composed by us, may it then become a mantra for recitation:
"O Goddess, may accomplishment be mine through your grace, abiding in you."
O Goddess, this mantra has been taught for constant dedication during recitation;
thereafter, the preceptor should perform the dismissal of the yantra with this mantra.
Having recited the root mantra, one should utter the word ending in the dative case;
O Queen of the Gods, one should state the aim for the fruit of the four goals of life and one's own lineage.

Then one should offer "Namo'nantam," as spoken by Śaṅkara. (One should perform one hundred thousand recitations. As with the [number of] lingas, so too for the quarter; the number of lingas has been established by me.
In a Śālagrāma stone, in the Manu-mantra, in a yantra, in an image, and in paintings.
One should worship with devotion and water the book, the Triśikhā, heaven, and the two feet of the Guru, as spoken by Śaṅkara.
One should perform one hundred thousand recitations as the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa);
indeed, for the practice of the Great Knowledge (mahāvidyā), one hundred thousand recitations is the prescribed measure.
This has been declared everywhere in all the tantras by the Lotus-born One:
[with] liquors, meats, victuals, groats, honey, and flesh.
One should worship the Goddess, the destroyer of the Dānavas, with supreme devotion;
having performed the consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) everywhere, the wise person should mutter the mantra.
Having performed worship according to the prescribed rite, one should offer this self-surrender:
"I do not see, I do not hear, I do not think, I do not remember, I do not worship, and I do not take refuge in anything else.
Having abandoned everything, I have taken refuge at Your feet with devotion; O Goddess, protect me and out of compassion grant me [Yourself]."
Success! (p.
40) Whatever is deficient or in excess, whether through ignorance, negligence, or a deficiency in the ritual means—may you forgive all of that.
O Goddess, O treasure-house of compassion, please forgive all of that— devoid of material offerings, devoid of ritual action, and lacking faith and devotion— out of your grace.
Whatever action I have performed, whether great or even small, all of that must be forgiven by the Protector of the World; here I join my palms in reverence.

Then, having offered a handful of flowers, one who possesses devotion should offer all that which occurs in the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, saying: "Obeisance to Śivā, the one to be worshipped by the senses."
Whatever action I perform, whether it be great or even very small, all of that must be forgiven by you, O Sustainer of the World; here I join my palms in reverence.
Then, having offered a handful of flowers, one should recite the non-duality mantra.
The illustrious Lord said:
I shall speak of the contemplation of non-duality; listen, O lotus-faced one, by the mere knowledge of which one becomes Gaṅgādhara himself.
I am woman, I am man, I am Sadāśiva, I am the Supreme Prakṛti;
I am the Puruṣa beyond the wind, I am Nāda, I am Bindu, and I am the Kalās.
I am the Word-Brahman; I am the yoga of action; I am Brahmā, I am Viṣṇu, I am Sūrya, I am Brāhma, I am Vaiṣṇava, I am Śiva;
I am the various powers, I am the asura, I am the sura, and I am intent upon the upward utterance.
I am knowledge, and I am the Vedas; I am the witness of the Vedas, I am the ritual action of the Vedas, I am the yoga of action, and I am the performance of dharma.
I am the grandfather, I am the maternal grandfather, I am the son, I am the guru, I am the preceptor, and I am the sacred tradition.
I am the great devotee of the Lord; I am the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam; I am the Vedas and the scriptures;
I am the meaning of the mantras; I am the hymn of praise; I am the armor-mantra; I am the Thousand Names; I am the Gāyatrī;
I am the seed-syllables; I am the three-syllabled mantra; and I am the fifty-lettered Mātṛkā.

I am the five great elements; I am the principles (tattvas); I am the gross, I am the subtle, and I am the great mountain ranges; I am the sixteen categories beginning with breath control (prāṇāyāma); I am the seers (ṛṣis) and I am the sages (munis);
I am Lakṣmī and I am Śrī; I am the Beloved (Priya) and I am Gaurī; I am the deceased (preta).

I am the Kuṣmāṇḍas, I am the world-protectors, I am the planetary spirits, I am the elephants of the quarters, I am the ten directions, I am above, I am below, and I am the fourteen worlds. Whatever exists therein, I am that; one should perform it with that [realization].
"One should recite the mantra according to the prescribed rite while keeping count according to the rule;
there is no fault in mental recitation—so said the Blessed Lord Hari."
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Viśvasāra Tantra*, in the commentary on *Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā*.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the meritorious rite of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā),
which directly bestows all accomplishments and destroys even the greatest of sins.

O Goddess, it was for the sake of attaining perfection in the state of divinity by the gods, and for the sake of achieving the status of perfected beings by the *rākṣasas*, *pannagas*, and humans seeking liberation.
In a cremation ground, in an empty house, or at a crossroads;

The wise man should recite the Vidyā beginning with Kāmākhyā, or he should recite the one beginning with Lakṣmī;

I shall describe the meditation on Mahākāla, which bestows all fruits:
[one should visualize her] dark-complexioned, with the luster of a great cloud, adorned with a garland of severed heads.
She holds a sword in her right hand,

Let them draw her with two breasts, wearing a single beautiful matted lock upon her head,
laughing aloud, most terrible, accompanied by a roar, and fearsome.
She was surrounded on all four sides by auspicious yet fiercely roaring [attendants];
she had four arms, was terrible, possessed fangs, three eyes, and was jagged like the end of an eon.
Having reflected thus in the mind and having performed worship with diligence,
the practitioner, with a restrained mind, should then perform the outer sacrifice.

then [one should utter] the Goddess in the dative case, ending in -nada, preceded by the Praṇava (Om).
This vidyā has been proclaimed through the offering of a seat to the Goddess;

I shall speak that which was uttered by Bhairava; listen with a well-composed mind.
When [the practitioner] has manifested the mudrā consisting of a garland made of human heads, it becomes [accomplished].

With her two feet adorned by the pair of ears that have heard the Vedas, with her broad and glorious heart-circle encompassing Maheśa, and with her face marked by the crescent moon—her face which, through its immeasurable nature, has burst forth from the limited span of time while she stands in the act of compassion toward the heart—she gazes upon him. Her hands, the instruments of grace, are joined in the ritual of the heart; she looks upon his countenance, which is inscribed with the digit of the moon, as he stands in the sphere of the heart’s activity, his vast and radiant heart-mandala containing Maheśa. Her form, defined by the measure of time yet transcending it, is manifested through her compassionate engagement in the work of the heart.

O Mother, those who recite three times this seed-syllable— Karpūra, devoid of the middle and final vowels, joined with the Moon and the left eye—

To him whose hair is the luster of the rain-cloud of darkness, for those who have attained all perfections. || 1 ||

While the one who has the crescent moon as his crest-ornament, adorned with a most formidable arrow, is reigning supreme.

With her face bathed by streams of tears from both corners of her mouth, she is Kālikā on the right. || 3 ||

O you whose face is revealed, the perfections are held in your own hands.

O Mother, Consort of the Destroyer of Smara, those who recite the mantra beginning with the first letter of the class [Ka], joined with fire [Ra], followed by the very charming Vidhu [Sa] and the pair of Ta-Bhras [Ttha and Tha], then the pair of Kūrca [Ū] and the pair of Lajjā [Sva and Sa], and finally joining the two letters beneath that [Na and Pha] while smiling— those who bear Your own form, O Mother, attain prosperity and grace.
Those with eyes like the petals of a playful lotus become embodiments of desire. || 5 ||

Whether reciting one, two, or even all three of these supreme seed-syllables, which are the ultimate secret, they constantly meditate upon them by joining them with your name and perform their recitation.
For them, Kamalā dwells within the lotus of their eyes, and Vāgdevī resides within the orb of the moon that is their face.
O Goddess, whose neck is adorned with a garland of severed heads, and who is richly endowed with full breasts! || 6 ||
Meditating upon you— whose arms are the lifeless [snakes], whose hips shine with a girdle formed by a multitude of them, who are clothed in the directions,
the creator of the three worlds, the three-eyed one,
dwelling in the cremation ground upon a bed of a corpse’s heart, and intent on the blissful union with Mahākāla.
O Mother, though my mind is dull, I am a poet.
They meditate upon you, the consort of Hara, who have entered a funeral pyre that is exceedingly crowded with heaps of corpses, skulls, and bones, and who—

O Mother, what more shall I say? We are dull-witted; neither the Creator, nor Īśvara, nor even Hari knows Your supreme nature.

O traveler to the hips of all the women of Āpīna, if a devotee, even while engaged in sexual union with a young woman at night,

The poet lives for a very long time. || 10 ||
If one recites [the mantra] while remaining equanimous and composed, and if, on the contrary, one should always meditate upon you while contemplating the unsurpassed great erotic play of Mahākāla,

The multitudes of great siddhis. || 11 ||

O Mother, at the time of creation you bring forth the cycle of existence; you protect the entire world, beginning with the earth, during its course; and at the time of dissolution, you destroy it all.
Therefore, even the Creator, the Lord of the three worlds, the Lord of Śrī, and likewise Maheśa, generally [worship] you.
How can I praise you, even in your entirety? || 12 ||
O Mother, those hosts of gods who serve You with devotion are not deluded; they truly know nothing higher than You.
I have taken refuge in You, the primordial one, who is approached by Hari, Hara, Viriñci, and the other deities—remember me with a smile!
[She who is] intent upon the bliss of the essence of passion. || 13 ||
The earth, the water, the pure wind, and even the sky—you alone, O auspicious Kali, the beloved of Śiva, are everything.
What praise can there be for you, O Mother? By your compassion, may you be gracious toward me who am without refuge. May you be pleased with me.
May my birth become as that of Manu. || 14 ||

Staying in a cremation ground, well-composed, with matted hair, wearing a garment of directions, he becomes Mahākālī at will by means of a thousand flowers of his own emitted semen— each flower being a syllable of your mantra— while remaining absorbed in meditation upon you.

The nectar-like essence of poetry. || 21 ||

Īśvara said:
Listen, I shall proclaim this armor (kavaca), which tears asunder all enemies,
brings about all peace, and is the manifest destroyer of great sins.
It pacifies all diseases, bestows all prosperity,
directly grants the four aims of human life, and destroys even the greatest of sins.

Of this armor (*kavaca*) of the illustrious Śrī Dakṣiṇakālikā, the venerable Mahākāla is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chandas*), the primordial power, the Blessed Lady, is the deity (*devatā*), *drīū* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *svāhā* is the application (*viniyoga*) for the attainment of power.
O Goddess, may *klīṃ* protect my head; O Maheśvarī, may *drīūṃ* protect my crest-lock;
O Maheśānī, may *krīṃ* protect the space between my eyebrows and both my eyes.

Klīṃ protects the opening of the nose; Huṃ, Maheśvarī, protects the tongue; Drīūṃ protects the root of the palate; and Drīūṃ protects the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). On the right, Kālikā, the bestower of all spiritual perfections, protects the heart.
Krim protect the pair of ears; Krim protect the pair of lips.
May *drīṃ* protect the root of the tongue, and may *huṃ* protect the face;
may *huṃ* protect the row of teeth, and may *drīṃ* protect both sides.
O Maheśānī, may *driūṃ* protect me always at the *mūlādhāra*;
likewise on both sides, the two hands, the two shoulders, and the two hips.
In the genitals, the secret place, the hips, the navel, and again in the belly;
in all the elements, the vital breaths, and the sense organs, which are of that same nature.
O Pārvatī, O Goddess of gods, may she who is endowed with the power of Svāhā protect [me] in the great elements, in all beings, at those times, and in every limb.
May Karālavadanā always protect my pair of knees;
may Sadyaśchinnamuṇḍadharā protect my pair of feet.
May she who holds a sword aloft with her left hand protect my fingers;
may Maheśvarī, granting fearlessness and boons, protect me in the cremation ground.
May Mahānēghaprabhā protect Pārvatī in battle and in brilliance;
may Cāmuṇḍā, O Goddess of gods, who grants all perfections, protect her in the forest.

May the goddess Śyāmā always protect [me] from dangers in the midst of enemies; may she, clad in the directions as her garment, always protect me at the king’s gate and during the worship of the gods.
May the Supreme Goddess, wearing a garland of skulls and bearing earrings made of corpses, always protect me in the midst of the wilderness.
May Ghoradaṃṣṭrā always protect me in the midst of water, O Maheśvarī;
may Karālāsyā, the beloved of Śiva, always protect me in the midst of fire.
May she with full breasts always protect me from contact with women;
may she wearing a skeleton-girdle protect me from the midst of spirits, ghosts, and the like.
May she who drinks blood always protect me through her application to the station of the intoxicated;
may she of terrible form and great ferocity always protect me during my meals.
May she who dwells in the cremation ground protect me always in the place of death;
may the goddess Kālī, the bestower of all prosperity, protect me in my home.
May the goddess Kapālī protect me, and may Kurukullā, the great sovereign, always protect my sons during sleep for the sake of all prosperity.
May Kullā always protect me, she who destroys obstacles during travel;
may Virodhinī always protect me in the confrontation with enemies.
May Vipracittā, the daughter of the mountain, always protect me on the mountain;
may the fierce goddess, the bestower of all accomplishments, always protect me at Vāgvāya.
May Ugraprabhā always protect [me] from hunger;
may Parvātmajā protect [me] from sleep, O Goddess of gods; and may Dīptā, the bestower of all success, protect [me].
May the goddess Līlā, the Great Sovereign, always protect me during my growth; may the Great Sovereign named Ghanā protect me, O Queen of Gods, during my sense of shame.
May Karālā, the destroyer of Time, protect [me] from the fear of thieves and disease;
may the Goddess Mātrā always protect me in my home, in the fields, and elsewhere.
May the goddess Śubhrā, the Great Sovereign in heaven and on earth, protect me always;
may Mātrādevī, the bestower of the accomplishment of all goals, protect me always.
May Brahmāṇī, the granter of all desires, protect me in the region of Pātāla;
may Indrāṇī, the Queen of the Gods and bestower of victory, protect me in battle.
May the goddess Cāmuṇḍā, the Great Sovereign, protect me in a foreign kingdom;
may Lakṣmī, the Queen of the Gods and bestower of all prosperity, protect me in heaven.
May Kālī, accompanied by the circle of Yoginīs, protect me always;
for the majesty of this armor is found in the very midst of the three worlds.
O Pārvatī, I have declared the entire armor-mantra (kavaca) along with the meaning of all its mantras;
it is not for wives, nor for sons, nor for kinsmen.
They do not see sorrow; they receive honor from kings.
Whether pure or impure, they shall obtain this armor that fulfills all desires.
By reciting or remembering [this], a mortal becomes capable of both cursing and bestowing grace;
he becomes a sovereign lord named Ānandasindhu, a Virāṭ,
and a mortal master of all waters, capable of both cursing and bestowing grace.
Having obtained the grace of the guru and having acquired the well-guarded knowledge,
Even there, O Goddess, this armor is difficult to obtain in the three worlds;
the Guru is the god Hara himself, and his wife is the beloved of Hara.
For one who worships [the deity] without making distinctions, success is not far off;
having worshipped her according to the sequence previously described by means of the mantra, he should perform recitation (japa).
One shall possess sovereignty and great poetic skill and become a lord of great waters;
there, O Maheśānī, one should always engage in union with women.
A mortal devoted to the fivefold conduct becomes a perfected one (siddha), and not otherwise;
possessed of modesty, the mantra-practitioner should recite [the mantra], for he should not recite the mantra alone.
With his mind focused on nothing else, he should recite the mantra while joined with the yoga of illusion;
[for by this] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the Goddess—the best of gods—[are attained].
O Goddess, upon seeing that practitioner,
those gods who bestow accomplishments in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld become filled with shame.
O Goddess, those gods who are the embodiments of obstacles— whether in heaven, on earth, or in the netherworld— always praise that supreme practitioner upon seeing him.
Seeing that best of practitioners, everyone praises him.
Thus, O Goddess, this armor of Mahākālī has been revealed to you.
Having approached a Guru and obtained this support of the wish-fulfilling tree, which directly bestows devotion and liberation and destroys even the greatest of sins;
Neither by delusion nor by intoxication does a person fail to attain [liberation], nor are they joined with it;
he is perfected on earth as the destroyer of all suffering and calamities. For that king, his enemies—the gods—perish upon his attainment of that friend.
Whoever wears this written [mantra] on the neck or on the upper arm shall achieve success in all undertakings, whatever resides in his mind.
O Maheśvarī, [it should be written] with gorocanā and saffron on birch bark.
For him, there are never mental anxieties, physical ailments, or the burden of suffering and grief.
O Maheśānī, he who especially draws [the diagram] with gorocanā and saffron, or with pure red sandalwood, or with barley-juice (yāvaka), [attains success].
On the eighth day, on a Tuesday, or likewise on the fourteenth day,
O Goddess of the lords of gods, the best of preceptors should draw the image of Durgā.
Especially on the day of the asterism Maghā, Śravaṇā, or Revatī,
when the moon has entered the zodiac sign of Leo and the sun is situated in Cancer.
When Jupiter is in the sign of Pisces and Saturn is in Scorpio,
one should write down the object and hold it while facing northward.
In a cremation ground, in a wilderness, or especially in a deserted house—
at night, indeed, his accomplishment will be unshakable.
O Maheśvarī, one who writes the mantra on birch bark with saffron and washes it with devotion through the yoga of meditation and concentration—
Success will come for him before long; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
The proponent is liberated and the opponent is defeated; no distinction between them is recognized.
The proud are humbled, and Vaiśvānara (fire) indeed cools;
this other group of eight Siddhas, whose form is the perfection of the eightfold conduct, bestows accomplishment.
I bow to you, the destroyer of the fear of worldly existence; I worship her who is beloved by the Lord of the Mountains.
Thus ends the Dakṣiṇākavaca in the venerable Viśvasāra Tantra.
I shall proclaim the varieties of mantras; listen, O lotus-faced one!
By the mere knowledge of which one becomes a bearer of the Gaṅgā (Gaṅgādhara) through praise.
Having extracted the syllable *dakṣaskanda* (the right shoulder) together with the *ratibindu* (the pleasure-drop),
and having mounted it upon the *bindu* (dot) and *nāda* (sound), it is proclaimed as the *mahāvidyā*.
The single-syllable Great Vidyā bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life;
one should recite this Vidyā ten hundred thousand times according to the rules for preliminary practice (puraścaryā).
Likewise, one should recite the vidyā, which is endowed with all accomplishments, during the night;
her worship is as before, and one should perform the ritual acts as before.
One should perform all the rites, such as the placement of the sages (*ṛṣinyāsa*) and so forth, as previously described;
and the wise practitioner should likewise perform the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for this [mantra] as before.
Everything has been spoken by Mahākāla for her just as before; and now, taking up that Great Vidyā consisting of three syllables, I shall explain it.
Then the root-seed, then Māyā, and after that the seed-syllable of Lajjā;
O Dear One, this is the Great Vidyā of Mahākālī, esteemed as Mahākāla.
Now, O lotus-faced one, listen to the five-syllabled vidyā:
having extracted Prajāpati (pra), followed thereafter by that which is mounted upon fire (ra).
One should extract the syllable of Īśāna, joined with the fourth vowel, adorned with the *nāda* and *bindu*,
and joined with the left ear (the letter *śa*).
Having combined the *bindu*, the crescent moon (*khaṇḍendu*), and the *kūrca* seed-syllable, this is known as the *kūrca-bīja*.
Īśa, mounted upon Vaiśvānara and adorned with the *rati-bindu*, [is the mantra].
This is declared to be the seed-syllable of modesty (lajjā), endowed with all the tantras;
the three seed-syllables follow in sequence, and at their end is Vahnisundarī.
The five-syllabled Great Vidyā was taught by the Lotus-born;
O Pārvatī, listen as I shall now speak of the six-syllabled Great Vidyā.

Having extracted the three seed-syllables, one should extract the syllable of the weapon (astra). The consort of fire (svāhā) is declared by the ritual rules; this is the Vidyā that deludes the three worlds.
The eight-syllabled Great Vidyā is now described; listen, O Pārvatī!
A wise person [should recite] the three seed-syllables in sequence, followed again by the three seed-syllables.
This Vidyā, ending with *svāhā*, is said to bestow the fruits of the four aims of life;
now listen, O Pārvatī, as the eleven-syllable Vidyā is described.
One should utter the Vāgbhava heart-mantra, which consists of Prajāpati mounted upon Fire,
conjoined with the fourth vowel and adorned with the Nāda and Bindu.
Having doubled that [syllable] and then appending the word *kālikā* ending in the *ṅi* case,
the Vidyā ending in *svāhā*, O Dear One, is said to consist of eleven syllables.
The seer is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and the meter is declared to be Paṅkti;
the deity is remembered as Kālikā, the power higher than the highest.
The eleven-syllable mantra of Kālikā is very difficult to obtain;
through good fortune one acquires it, and it bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life.

One should recite the vidyā two hundred thousand times for the rite of preliminary preparation (*pūrvasevā*); for other [mantras], it is said by the Lotus-born One that it shall be one hundred thousand recitations per syllable.
I shall describe the meditation upon her; listen, O lotus-faced one, for she was formerly proclaimed by the Sage as the embodiment known as Dakṣiṇā.
Four-armed and black in color, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
she holds a sword in her right hand and two blue lotuses.
Holding a knife and a skull-bowl respectively in her left hands,
she herself is Śivā, wearing a single matted lock that reaches up to the sky.
Always wearing a garland of severed heads around her neck,
she bore a necklace of serpents upon her breast, her eyes red with rage.
Wearing black garments and clad in a tiger skin,
she places her left foot upon the heart of a corpse and her right foot [upon the other].
Having placed herself upon the back of a lion, she herself is a corpse with a lolling tongue;
she is the fiercely terrible Aṭṭahāsā, endowed with a roar and terrifying.
Thus one should constantly meditate upon Kālī, the destroyer of the impurities of the Kali age,
with devoted mantras and through good fortune, sovereignty, happiness, and the moon.
Having bowed to the Guru according to the prescribed rite, one should meditate upon the Supreme Deity.
Now I shall further explain another method characterized by auspiciousness.
Listen with supreme devotion to Kālī, the destroyer of impurities;
first is the root seed-syllable, then Māyā, and after that the seed-syllable of Lajjā.
Then follows Dakṣiṇakālī, and at its end is Vahnisundarī;
this eleven-syllabled Kālī bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
The armor-mantra (kavaca) is enriched with the root-syllable, and at its end is the Mistress of the World (Bhuvaneśvarī);
likewise, it is proclaimed to end with the weapon-mantra (astra) when applied to the right side.
Now I shall proclaim another vidyā consisting of twenty syllables,
by the mere grace of which one may become a Purandara upon the earth.
One should utter the two root-seeds, then again the pair of *kūrca* mantras,
followed by the pair of *lajjā* mantras, and finally the two words ending with the word for awakening (*sambodha*).
As before, there are six [syllables], then the seed-syllable *Tathā*, and at its end is *Vahnisundarī*.
Dakṣiṇā is the seer (*ṛṣi*), Mūrti is the deity, and Paṅkti is declared to be the meter (*chandas*).
The goddess Kālī, preceded by Dakṣiṇā, has been described by the virtuous;
she is the eleven-syllable Vidyā—listen, O Pārvatī.

The root mantra consists of the armor (*kavaca*) and *māyā*, followed by two words ending in the name of a Perfectly Awakened One (*sambuddha*), and concluding with *svāhā*; this vidyā is said to bestow the fruits of the four aims of life.
The seer is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and the meter is declared to be Anuṣṭubh.
Now I shall proclaim another vidyā that liberates one from the three worlds.
Having extracted one's own seed-syllable, at its end comes Vahnisundarī;
Bhairava is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi) for all the Tantras combined.
Asitāṅga, Ururudra, Caṇḍa, Ugra, Krodha, Unmatta,
Kapālī, and Bhīṣaṇa— these are the eight Bhairavas of dissolution.
This is the Mother, the Great Vidyā; listen, O lotus-faced one!
This eight-syllabled Vidyā is well-guarded in all the Tantras.
The two *nīja* seeds, the two *kūrca*s, and the two *lajjā*s,
followed by *svāhā*, is said to be Kālī, who bestows the fruits of righteous action.
Now listen likewise to the five-syllabled vidyā of the Bhairavas:
one's own kūrca, then lajjā, and at the end, vahnisundarī.
The five-syllabled great vidyā is remembered as having Pañcavaktra as its seer;
hear now, O lotus-faced one, the nine-syllabled great vidyā.
The three seed-syllables of one's own [name], the pair of *kūrca* syllables, and then *lajjā*,
ending with *svāhā*— this auspicious *vidyā* is said to bestow all prosperity.
The nine-syllable Great Vidyā is endowed with nine characteristics;
now listen attentively to the eight-syllable Vidyā.
Then one should extract its own seed-syllable, followed by the *kūrca* mantra, and then *māyā*;
with that same [seed-syllable] preceded by *puṃs*, ending in *svāhā*, it bestows liberation.
Now I shall proclaim another [mantra] endowed with ten principles,
by the mere glance of which one becomes the Enchanter of the Three Worlds.
First, the two roots, then the two pairs, then the beard, then the two pairs of modesty.
Furthermore, at the end of that very [mantra], Vahnisundarī [is placed] by him with those same [syllables].
The fourteen-syllable vidyā bestows the fruits of the four aims of human life;
now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe Kālī, the destroyer of impurities.
By whose mere sidelong glance, O Lord of Speech, even you, the supreme one,
[bestows] wealth, grain, a daughter, a wife, as well as horses and elephants.
Whatever one desires in the mind, all that fruit shall be obtained;
there is no knowledge superior to this for sages, which bestows liberation.
O son and friend, listen: this knowledge bestows the fruits of all desires for both householders and ascetics; there is nothing superior to it anywhere.
What is the use of wealth, what is the use of these people, what is the use of sons, wives, or kinsmen, or what use are other worthless conversations, when one’s life may pass away at any moment?
A person need not perform worship or ritual adoration of her; they should merely recite the mantra.
In the Kali Yuga, all supernatural powers (siddhis) will be held in the palm of their hand.
Having extracted the three Brahmās, joined with the drop of passion (ratibindu),
and previously joined with the sound-drop (nādabindu) and the two "beards" of the goddess of modesty (lajjā).
Then, having again extracted [the syllables] in sequence up to the wife of fire (svāhā),
this is declared to be the sixteenfold Vidyā, which is like a wish-fulfilling tree.
O Dear One, her entire worship, including the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and so forth, is as before;
one should first place a triangle and then another triangle upon it.
Furthermore, one should place a nine-cornered [figure] there and install Śivā in its center;
this is proclaimed as the yantra for all forms of Kālikā.
With liquors, meats, female organs, cows, vaijayantī flowers, and gṛñjana roots;
with cocks, buffaloes, goats, nakulas, and likewise with bulls.
One should worship Śivā with well-bred elephants and camels, with meats, honeyed milk-rice, with one's own blood, hair, and flesh, and with one's own semen.
With the *bhaga* and *liṅga*, with discourses on the *bhaga*, and with the *śaktis*, [he worshipped] the leader of the gods;
with various flowers, sandalwood, and various offerings of water.
O Pārvatī, one should worship her who is fond of wine with various kinds of intoxicants, meats, and liquors,
as well as with various flowers and incenses, together with the practitioners.
One should worship the Goddess at night, at all times and always,
in a solitary linga, in a cremation ground, in an empty house, or at a crossroads.
Or on a corpse, or situated upon a funeral pyre, at the root of a kula-tree,
in a "supreme womb," in a "womb-machine," or at the sacred seat of Kālī, by day or by night.
With white flowers of the *svaṣambhu* species, likewise in the maternity chamber,
at the proper time, in the proper place, [he worshipped] the eternal Goddess.
The preceptor should always worship the Goddess according to the prescribed conduct with auspicious offerings, animal flesh, and the instructions of a wanton woman.
O Pārvatī, for him there would be no concern regarding Brahmins, nor any impurity anywhere;
whether in an impure place or a pure one, at all times and forever.
Having performed the *ṛṣinyāsa* and other rites, one should worship the Vidyā day and night;
through recitation, all the deities become pleased while being praised.
O Goddess, there is no one on the surface of the earth whose majesty equals that of the reciter;
everywhere the practitioner is blessed, for he alone is the supreme practitioner.
One should adorn one's own body with divine garments, divine ornaments, and sandalwood paste; having assumed the attire of a woman, the body should become like that of Kālī.
One should always perform the conduct of the Kula, especially month by month;
O Goddess of the God of Gods, I shall subsequently explain all of that with care.
The fourteenth, the sixteenth, the twentieth, and that which consists of the nature of Brahman—
for these, the measure of the *lakṣa* (one hundred thousand) shall be the standard for the rite of *puraścaraṇa*.
For all other vidyās, one hundred thousand recitations are proclaimed;
for all of them, however, the great worship is proclaimed to be accompanied by ritual fees (dakṣiṇā).
There is doubt regarding the form of the eightfold conduct and the form of spiritual accomplishment;
O lotus-faced one, listen as I shall proclaim the Krama-stava.
O Goddess of the gods, the supreme deity of the syllable *nī* is Nārāyaṇa;
O Goddess of the gods, the deity of the syllable *kā* is remembered as Kālikā, the protector of all creatures.
O Goddess of gods, the goddess Trailokyamohinī belongs to the syllable *ka*;
O Goddess of gods, the deity of the seed-syllable *māyā* (hīṃ) is Bhuvaneśvarī.
O Goddess of the gods, the power of Durgā is proclaimed as belonging to the syllable *da*; O Goddess of the gods, Nṛsiṃha is celebrated as belonging to the syllable *kṣi*.
But for the syllable *ṇe*, O Goddess of Gods, the supreme deity is Nārāyaṇa;
and for the syllable *kā*, O Goddess of Gods, the presiding deity is Prajāpati.
But for the sake of the insult (*nikāra*), O Goddess of gods, the deity is Purandara;
it was indeed stated previously for the purpose of the seed-syllable. Now hear that [mantra] ending with the wife of fire (*vahnijāyā*).
O Goddess of gods, Sāvitrī is remembered as the deity of the syllable *sa*;
O Goddess of gods, Varuṇa is proclaimed as the deity of the syllable *va*.
O Goddess of gods, Ananta is proclaimed as the form;
O Goddess, the meaning of the mantra for all [of these] has been told together with the tantra.
At the hour of Brahmā, having risen, the best of practitioners should meditate upon the eternal Goddess;
he should perform the meditation previously described by his Guru.
Having recited [the mantra] one thousand and eight times according to this procedure,
the preceptor should daily recite the Krama-stava according to this same rule.
Oṃ, salutations to the gurus, to the deities, and likewise to that which is beyond them;
having bowed to the one who is higher than the high, who is both transcendent and immanent, and having paid homage according to the prescribed rite to Kṣetrapāla and the deities of the gateway.
Having paid homage to Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, Durgā, Gaṅgā, Godāvarī,
and Bhogavatī, he should then bow to the deity of the site (Vāstudeva).
O beloved, I bow down to Vighnarāja, Vāstvīśa, and Kṣetreśa, as well as to Nairṛta and Brahmā, whose nature consists of the Brahma-karma.
Having propitiated the obstacles according to the ritual procedure, one should then bow to the presiding deity of the site;
having saluted that foundational power (Ādhāra-śakti) who bears two lotuses.
[He saw] Mahāmāyā, blue in color and possessing twelve syllables,
and a tortoise of great body, blue in color and resembling the Himālaya mountain.
I bow to Viṣṇu, endowed with all powers, who has taken the form of a tortoise;
I bow to that Lord Ananta, who stands upon his back.
Salutations to Hari, who possesses a thousand fruits, whose form is like a serpent, who is wise,
resembles the Golden Mountain (Meru), and wears a single earring.
I bow to him who is adorned with thousands of hoods and jewels;
I bow to that god Ananta who stands upon his back.
One should meditate on his armpit as holding a plow that destroys enemies,
and on his left side a mallet endowed with the eleven jewels.
One should meditate upon the imperishable Viṣṇu in the form of a boar situated upon his head—
having a single tusk, a massive body, and a luster like a dark rain cloud.
Upon his tooth, one should always meditate on the Earth who bestows the fruits of action—
the great goddess of blue complexion, adorned with the rays of Saturn.
One should always meditate upon her, endowed with the qualities such as *aṇimā* and established within all sentient beings, with oceans filled with jewels upon her head.
One should indeed contemplate with the mind the earth joined by various mountains;
there, one should contemplate the mountains adorned with [sacred] lineages.
Having paid homage to the elephants of the quarters, one should always prostrate to the yogas,
to the lords of sages, to the seers, and to those who uphold the yoga scriptures.
One should always bow down to the Śākta, Vaiṣṇava, and Śaiva [devotees],
to the mantras, to the deities of the mantras, and to those who are devoted to the scriptures of the mantras.
One should always bow to Candra, to those of the Lunar dynasty, and to those of the Solar dynasty; likewise, one should bow to the great elements, to all beings, and to the constituent parts.
Salutation always to the Gandharvas who sport with flowers;
salutation to the Yakṣas, to the hosts of Bhūtas, and to the Pretas in all rites.
I always offer salutations with devotion to the Śabdabrahmas, O beloved;
repeated obeisance to the Rudras, to the lineages of the Rudras, and to the Bhairavas.
Having offered salutations to the *liṅgas*, to the deities of the *liṅgas*, to the Vedas, to the witness of the Vedas, to the inhabitants of Bhārata, and to the glorious *Śrīmad-Bhāgavata*.
Having paid homage to the Saṃhitās and the Śāstras, as well as those together with their commentaries,
one should always bow down to the Tantras that contain the essential meaning.
Having paid homage to the *Yāmalas*, one should always bow to the Moon and the Sun;
homage, repeated homage, to living beings, to all states of existence, and to those that move upon the earth.

Having paid homage to the immovable ones, one should always bow to the sages; and salutations again and again to the categories of existence, such as the means of valid cognition and the rest, even to those that have been withered away.
Having paid homage to the moving [beings] who are worthy of respect, and having offered salutations again and again to those who are worthy of honor,
one should always bow down to the sages who abide in immobile forms.
Homage again and again to the Brahmins who provide the articles for worship;
having paid homage to the Yoginīs together with their Śaktis, homage again and again!
Having paid homage even to the jewels, one should always bow to the rivers;
having paid homage even to the sacred seats (pīṭhas), one should always bow to the Mothers.
Having paid homage even to all sentient beings, I always offer salutations to the sense faculties;
having paid homage even to the fields, as well as to the guardians of the fields.
Having bowed to the principal mountains and to the various manifestations,
I offer constant salutations again and again to all that has been said and all that remains unsaid concerning them.
I bow to her whose will is truth, who dwells upon all mountains;
having paid homage to Pārvatī, I perpetually offer salutations to the daughter of the mountain.
O Mother, that refuge of kings, which is desired by those who long for their wishes through tears shed during meditation—
that lotus-foot of yours flashes forth in the hearts of those who are truly blessed and worthy of worship in the world of the gods.

O Mother Bhavānī, if the wise take refuge in you with pure devotion, remembering, hearing, or even rolling upon the auspicious, fragrant paste of Ganges mud and saffron, they shall never again experience old age.

O Goddess, your shanks are the supreme primordial nature (prakṛti) of the gods, both high and low; since they are destined for your hands day after day, what other exalted thing could they possibly be called?

O Daughter of the Mountain, [the Lord] shakes the pride of the lords of poets, which is familiar with the beauty of his lotus-like hands, by means of Your shanks; therefore, O Mother, Your lotus-feet are cherished in my heart.
Even Śaṅkara, who has become a woman and whose steps are well-placed, [is subject to you]. O Mother, those who are truly destitute yet constantly chant your name with their minds at your feet—
all the gods, asuras, and hosts of siddhas— constantly roll about through your grace.
Having meditated upon your lotus feet, O Hari, may Śiva— the source of prosperity for all the worlds— become perfected in that which is the supreme beyond the supreme;
thereafter, let this Lord of subjects carry out the creation of the worlds.
What else is there for you? For you, the state of being the fruit of the pair of feet [of the Lord] is itself enough.
O refuge of the gods, among those worthy of refuge, Prajāpati Kaśyapa alone is the Indra;
O Supreme Lady, the prosperity of all speech and the fruit of the lotus-feet of Viṣṇu and Śiva are entirely yours.
May Hari, who is intent on worshipping your feet, reproach the Lord of Sudarśana,
who dwells within the earth in the form of fragrance and is sustained by its waters.
By means of its brilliance, it assumes the form of fire; by means of the wind, it assumes the form of a flower;
as space, it assumes the form of sound; and within the *praṇava*, it bears the form of Brahman.
O Mother, for those whose minds are intent on the supreme good, even the three worlds— along with the moon-like faces of the gods and the Three-Eyed One—
constantly remember his success, yet he does not even think of the entire universe as his own.
O Mother, with your side-long glances, he sports with the entire multitude of lotuses.
For those who possess ascetic power and recite mantras, the truth is indeed not something to be accomplished;
rather, blessed is that universal devotion which you, O Guardian of the Gods, bestow upon those whose minds are fixed on the divine.

You are the sacrifice, you are the oblation, you were Murāri in ancient times, you are beyond the supreme, and you are forever Śrī; O Umā, you are Hari, you are Tārā, you are Śiva, and you are Śivānī.
You are the intellect, you are the mind, you are the goal; you are Bhavānī. You are the man, you are the human being, and you are the activity of men.
You are the accumulation, you are the excellence, and you are the forest for Śivā;
you are the river, you are the stream, you are the goal, and you are the treasure of treasures; you are the daughter, you are the son, and you are the father of householders.
Having fashioned a garland for you from the skulls of Brahmā and the others, those lords of sages obtain the sovereignty over the gods; this is some kind of refuge, and what else could it be?
O Goddess, those who mentally recite "Muṇḍa" for a man and "Khaḍga" for the two arms,
as well as "Vara" and "Abhaya" for the others, become lords of sages, endowed with the powers of the Siddhas.

If one should ever place [the mantra] upon a corpse and recite the beneficial Vidyā within the heart, then one would become a knower of the secret of poetry; at the end, one should take refuge in the pair of feet.
Having meditated upon you with their minds, the world-renowned mother of the worlds becomes the supreme refuge of the worlds;
what other refuge can we have but you?

O Goddess of the gods, those who constantly recite [the mantra] while visualizing its ends encircled by the sounds of jackals would become objects of public censure; yet, O Goddess, they are said to be masters of a hundred treasures.
If those foremost among the knowers of the Vedas recite the mantra while fixing their minds upon the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*) of You, [they attain the highest state].
O Goddess, those people—even a poet among poets, born from his own kin—become subject to public censure.

Having mentally visualized her with disheveled hair, a man who recites this mantra even once while trembling may obtain lordship over the gods and others; hear now, O Kālakālī, what his end shall be upon the earth.
The perfected ones on earth, free from all fetters, chant your three seed-syllables until liberation;
thus, through union with your feet, they become perfected even within three days.
Because of reciting the two mantras born from Your eyebrows, one shall be worthy of worship even by gods and asuras;
everyone attains wealth and scholarship—O Goddess, supreme and yet beyond the supreme, what more could there be?
O Maheśānī, through the awakening of your two-fold modesty, the fourth siddhi shall arise;
by the grace of your address of salutation, even a lord of sages attains sovereignty over men.
(p. 48) Furthermore, O Mother, hear the fruit of that name; the virtuous declare it to be the fourfold aims of life (*caturvarga*).
Moreover, by discarding the three seed-syllables, the Lord of Sages (*munīndra*) attains the state of being the Lord of the Gods (*surāpa*).
Furthermore, O Mother, the Siddhas in the form of Narasiṃha bow down to the pair of *kūrca* syllables;
therefore, by reciting the two *lajjā* syllables, those people attain perfection through their minds.
Having cast this mantra of Satī into the fire, they utter this noble mantra which bestows infinite fruit:
"O Mother, constantly meditating upon and gathering the seats of the fifteen-spoked [wheel], together with the Siddhis,
[we seek] the state of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) whose form is supreme nectar."
Having always meditated upon Kālī and performed the ritual worship along with the specific ancillary rites, one indeed becomes free from the fear of the ocean of worldly existence;
she who has passed beyond the forest of delusion becomes the mother of prosperity at the lotus feet of the Lord.
She, intoxicated, led him toward the dwelling of Śerī, following every step of his path.
You are Śrī, Īśvarī, Kālī, Karālī, and Vikarālikā;
you are Lajjā, Lakṣmī, Satī, Gaurī, Nityā, Cintā, and Citipriyā.
The supreme examination is the ultimate, whose form is supreme;
by those [means], such as perfumes and so forth, which possess the lotuses of the stages of accumulation within the mind, they are endowed with the [noble] states.
Those who, having always bowed and praised [the deity], recite the mantra in their hearts according to the manual of knowledge,
for them there is no fear of the destruction of prosperity within the cycle of existence.
O Goddess, for a moment the mind may arise on the wrong path, yet the retinue [of deities] protects it;
if one recites the mantra and praises it with thirty-three verses.
One should know this supreme vessel of nectar as the best of gods;
by bowing one's head to your pair of feet, one becomes a perfected master of all accomplishments in this world.
Having prostrated, [I praise] those who are worthy of worship by the hosts of gods and asuras, and whose will is unimpeded.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the *Viśvasāra-tantra*, in the commentary on Dakṣiṇakālikā.
Now I shall speak of the Durgā-mahā-mantra; listen, O lotus-faced one! By the mere grace of which one may become Gaṅgādhara himself.
O Dear One, having extracted the final letter of the alphabet (tha), joined with the left ear (va) and endowed with the moon-drop (bindu), this is the seed-syllable of the mantra of Durgā.
Directly bestowing the four aims of human life and destroying even the greatest sins,
there exists no science in this world equal to this one.
What is the use of other idle talk, wherein life is spent in vain?
But that [merit], O Goddess, one obtains as a sixteenth part of the merit from Durgāmaṇi.
O beloved, there is no knowledge in the three worlds equal to the single-syllable mantra,
even without perfumes, without flowers, and without the preliminary performance of fire offerings.
O Goddess, prāṇāyāma grants success even through mere recitation without [other] means;
Jamadagni, Bharadvāja, Bhūṇḍa, Gautama, and Kaśyapa [are its masters].
O Pārvatī, Viśvāmitra, Śiras, Nandi, Kahoḷi, and Tuṇḍika—
these are declared to be the sages (ṛṣis) of the Durgā mantra.
O Goddess of the gods, Nārada is proclaimed as the seer (ṛṣi) of the mantra;
Gāyatrī is declared its meter (chandas), and Durgā is its presiding deity.
The Goddess, who bestows the four aims of life, is established in all tantras;
by her mere sidelong glance, one may become an Indra upon the earth.
Having become wealthy even in this very world, he may bring kings under his control;
through his speech, he would be as wise as another Bṛhaspati.
A Brāhmaṇa shall become a knower of the Vedas, a king shall attain sovereignty,
a Vaiśya shall possess abundance of wealth, and a man shall obtain all perfections.
That great vidyā is manifold; listen to it, O Gaṇeśvarī.
One should recite the vidyā beginning with the *kūrca* [syllable], and at its end, the *vanisundarī*.
Or the wise one should especially recite the Vidyā beginning with *lajjā* (the seed-syllable *hrīṃ*) and ending with *phaṭ*;
or he may recite it joined with the *vadhū* seed-syllable (*strīṃ*) and ending with *svāhā*.
O Maheśānī, the seed-syllable of the bride (Vadhū-bīja) is proclaimed as *Śataviśvam*. Then, one may also recite the mantra joined with *Lajjā* (the syllable Hrīm) and ending with *Svāhā*.
Or else, the sixteen consonants joined with Mārkī (M), Vahni (R),
Tha (THA), and Indu-bindu (the nasal dot) is known as this seed-syllable of Lajjā.
This distinction is proclaimed as the *lajjā* (shame) of the *Mahākālamata*. One should recite the *lajjādyā* vidyā for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life (*caturvarga*).
One should recite [the mantra] beginning with the Vāgbhava syllable, or again beginning with the Praṇava;
or else one should always recite it beginning with the Kāma-bīja and ending with Phaṭ.
In ancient times, Brahmā proclaimed various one-syllable vidyās;
one should always recite that which begins with *lajjā*, or that which begins with *vāk*, or that which begins with *kāma*.

One should always recite [the mantra] beginning with the Praṇava and ending with Phaṭ, especially that which begins with the Kavaca; or else, one may recite it beginning with the Lañjā (Hrīṃ) or joined with the Vadhū-bīja (Śrīṃ).
This Durgā-vidyā, joined with three syllables, is proclaimed;
it ends with "phaṭ" and begins with all the seed-syllables, as declared by the Lotus-born One.
O Pārvatī, one should place the seed-syllables of Indra, joined with long vowels, within one's own body, starting from the heart and so forth, O Pārvatī.
The section on ritual placement (nyāsa) should be as before, and one should perform the rites as before;
one should practice the Vidyā like Kālī and chant the Vidyā day and night.
O Goddess, for twelve hundred thousand recitations, the *puraścaraṇa* rite is prescribed;
herein there is no need for the purification of obstacles such as *siddhi*, nor is there any defect regarding friends and so forth.
One should not employ excessive wind-instruments nor engage in any activity whatsoever,
except at the proper time, in the proper place, and according to the prescribed rules of conduct.
One should worship Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune, with supreme devotion,
using wine, meat, well-prepared cakes, and the flesh of the bhaga, hare, and porcupine.
With songs of the *liṅga*, with the rolling of the vulva, with many cats,
as well as with beef, venison, fish, pork, and rats;
One should worship the Supreme Goddess with fragrant flowers, fresh sprouts, sprinkled water, and various intoxicants, as well as with animals.
One should worship the Vidyā Durgā, the liberator from distress, like Kālī,
with white self-originated flowers and fragrant blossoms.
With barley, black gram, and vermilion combined with red sandalwood,
and with various kinds of meat— those of crows, porcupines, owls, buffaloes, and humans.
One should worship with elephants, camels, vultures, and *khagai* (birds) according to this rite;
then, O Great Goddess, success shall be attained—of this there is no doubt.
One should mutter the Gāyatrī mantra every day according to the ritual procedure of the Goddess—
either beginning with *na* [namas], or beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ), or beginning with *vāgbhava* (aiṃ), following the proper sequence.
Or one should recite the Gāyatrī of the Goddess as recorded in the Tantras, beginning with "Lajjā" and so forth;
immediately after that, one should say "Durgā Devīm" ending in the feminine instrumental case, followed by "vidmahe."

We know her who is the very nature of consciousness, ending with the feminine suffix *ṅi*; we meditate upon her. May that Goddess, having raised [the syllable *tad*] from "that to us," impel us at the end of that.
This Gāyatrī of the Goddess bestows all accomplishments;
one of vast intellect should recite this vidyā four hundred thousand times as the preliminary rite (puraścaryā).
One should recite the mantra of the Goddess, beginning with the *praṇava*, during the offering of her seat;
having first uttered the *praṇava*, one should then say "Vajranakha."

Having extracted the word "siṃha" ending in the nominative case (siṃhaḥ), preceded by the great syllable *maṃ* and followed by the weapon-mantra *daṃṣṭrāyudhaṃ*, one should address it as the seat; then one should say "namo devyai" once more.
As before, there should be the section on the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the body; O lotus-faced one, listen to the meditation according to the Mahākālamata regarding the eternal Goddess.

One should meditate upon the Great Goddess, who has the shoulders of a lion, is mounted upon a lion, is adorned with various ornaments, possesses four arms, and wears a sacred thread made of a serpent.
Clad in red garments, her body resembling the rising sun,
Bhavānīsundarī was attended by hosts of sages such as Nārada and others.
Adorned with the three folds of her waist like a lotus-stalk encircled by three whorls,
she stands upon a jeweled island of gems, provided with a lion throne.
One should meditate upon her, the dweller in the house of worldly existence, as seated upon a full-blown lotus;
or else, one should contemplate Durgā, the destroyer of all difficulties.
Seated upon a lion, bearing the crescent moon, holding a conch, a discus, a bow, and an arrow in her four emerald-like arms, adorned with three eyes, and graced by armlets,
necklaces, bracelets, jingling girdles, and tinkling anklets— may Durgā, the remover of misfortune, protect us.
She possesses earrings that shine with jewels.
One who desires to destroy [an enemy] should recite four hundred thousand times, or even one hundred thousand;
however, when facing a powerful adversary, one should always recite three hundred thousand times.
First, one should perform the preliminary recitation (puraścaryā) of the mantra according to the Sāvitrī rite;
once the mantra is mastered, one should always perform it month by month according to the prescribed rule.
The best of preceptors, following the family tradition, should perform [the rite] according to the prescribed rule;
the one of vast intelligence should deposit everything as before and install the Goddess.
One should always offer oblations to the Great Goddess day by day for the sake of the ultimate goal; having offered bilva leaves with clarified butter, one shall bring the entire world under control.
Karavīra, paṭala, lotus, mango, and that which comes from madhūka;
campaka, nāgamuṇḍa, asafoetida, karmāra, and marīca.
The wise one should always offer *tejapatra*, *guṇḍatvac*, and *mahāmāṃsa*; he should constantly offer the flesh of goats, mice, rams, and so forth.
Once the mantra has been perfected, by constantly offering oblations one may bring the entire world under control;
one should always prescribe the palāśa and lotus flowers for the fire sacrifice (homa).
One shall become Vāgīśvara in person; this was spoken by Śaṅkara himself. O Goddess, what need is there for many other words? Whatever one desires for oneself [shall be attained].
Having performed [this] correctly according to the rite, one becomes a lord of the earth;
what more need be said, O Goddess? One shall obtain the fruit of the four aims of life through many [other means].
I shall now describe the Durgā-yantra; listen, O lotus-faced one!
First, one should draw a triangle provided with nine corners.
Everything should be arranged in three rows and joined together, provided with lotus petals;
the vajra-spear should be accompanied by three lines and adorned with a square enclosure (bhūpura).
Having leveled [the ground], one should draw the wheel according to the aforementioned method and this following procedure;
it should be depicted joined with various weapons and endowed with the *tantra*.
There, one should worship that Goddess, whose form is the primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti);
one should worship Durgā seated upon a lotus, resting on the back of a lion.
The powers beginning with Prabhā are to be worshipped with scents and other offerings in the nine-cornered [mandala]:
Prabhā, Māyā, Jayā, Sukṣmā, Viśuddhā, and again Nandinī.
