Suprabhā, Vijayā, and Sarvasiddhidā are the nine Śaktis;
one should worship them in sequence with these [mantras].
Having first uttered the syllable *oṃ*, and immediately thereafter the syllable *drīṃ ūṃ*,
one should worship [the deities] in their proper sequence, each addressed with its name in the vocative case.
One should worship the goddess Śaṅkhapadmanidhi with supreme devotion, using red sandalwood and other offerings, through union with her on the left and right.
Then, at the conclusion of the worship, one should offer the *arghya* to the Daughter of the Mountain;
furthermore, the deities of the limbs (*aṅgavṛtti*) and the Mothers are to be worshipped within the nine corners.
Brahmā and the other Mothers, adorned with their own ornaments and equipped with weapons such as the vajra, shone forth as the leaders of the world.
One should worship Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune, with supreme devotion;
as before, one should accomplish all [rites] for the attainment of all desired fruits.
The illustrious Lord said:
First, one should arrange a triangle endowed with nine corners,
always accompanied by a city-gate (bhūpura) and a trident (śūla), described as having eight petals and three circles.
There too, one should worship the goddess Durgā, who removes misfortune;
one should worship her beautifully with vermilion and yellow orpiment.
Alternatively, I shall speak of the armor; listen, O lotus-faced one!
By knowing which, all practitioners obtain supreme prosperity.
O Goddess, he who recites the Durgā mantra without knowing the armor (kavaca) does not obtain the fruit of worship and shall go to a miserable state at the end.
Oṃ! May Goddess Umā protect the head; may the wielder of the trident protect the forehead;
may Khecarī protect the two eyes; and may Dvāravāsinī protect the nose.
May Sugandhavāsinī protect the face, and likewise Sādhanī;
may Caṇḍikā protect the tongue, and Saubhadrikā the neck.
Aśokavāsinī is the mind, Vajradhāriṇī has two arms,
the goddess Lalitā is the heart, and Siṃhavāhinī is the belly.
The Goddess Bhagavatī is at the hips; Vindhyavāsinī is on the two thighs;
Mahābalā is on the two shanks; and Bhūtalavāsinī is on the two feet.
Thus you abide, O Goddess, whose very nature is the protection of the three worlds;
protect me in all my limbs, O Durgā, Goddess, salutations be unto you!
Thus ends the Durgā-kavaca in the Viśvasāra-tantra.
Śrī Pārvatī said: O Goddess of the gods, you have truly explained, O Lord of the lords of gods, all those deities, Vedic meters, and sages according to their respective classes.
The illustrious Īśvara said:
Having prostrated before Durgā, who is dark-complexioned and the destroyer of distress,
Dakṣiṇāmūrti resides in the syllable *da* and the Lord of Umā (Śiva) resides in the syllable *u*.
On the half-moon is Śiva himself, the god who is the lord of the three worlds;
Durgā is declared to be the presiding deity, the destroyer of all difficulties.
By means of which one should perform the rites beginning with the seed-syllable (*bīja*), just as a deity performs its own preliminary rites;
now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the thousand names of the Goddess.
Listen with supreme devotion; this has not been spoken by the Veda.

Of this Durgā-vidyā and its thousand-fold Sāman hymn, the venerable Nārada is the seer (ṛṣi), the Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), and the primordial Śakti, the divine Durgā, is the deity (devatā)—she who is Mahāmāyā.
The *viniyoga* (application) is for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life (*caturvarga*).
Oṃ! Durgā, Śivā, Kṣamā, Dhātrī, Lokamātā, Śivapriyā;
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, and likewise Vaiṣṇavī—O Goddess!
Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī, Kamalā, and likewise Caṇḍikā;
the primordial Vāṇī, the deity, the mother of the gods, compassion, and splendor.
Vidyā, Puṣṭi, Tuṣṭi, Kṣudhā, Nidrā, Vibhāvarī,
Mantramāyā, Mahāśakti, Vidyā, and Vidyāvipannagā.
She consists of all mantras, likewise she consists of all sciences;
she is Lakṣmī, she is Vāṇī, she is the source of speech, and she is beloved by the Lord of the World.
She has a melodious voice and a neck like a conch shell; she is devoted to the flute and the lute.
The Goddess possesses rhythmic timing and musical cymbals, and she always delights in various kinds of song.
Nārāyaṇī, Mahāmāyā, Jayadurgā, Jayājanī,
Vijayā, Jayā, Jaitrī, Jayanī, and Jayagāminī.

She is the giver of victory, the giver of happiness, the truthful one, the giver of liberation, and the source of victory and other blessings; she is the humble one, the mother of Viṣṇu, the protectress of the universe, and the one who digests all things.
Brahmāṇī, Vimalā, Raudrī, Jyeṣṭhā, and Jāyā; Vāmanā, Vasanā, Vāsanā, Kroḍā, Kubjikā, and likewise Apsarā.
Urvaśī, Kadalī, Kekā, Kāmākhyā, Kṣamāvatī,
Tīvrā, Vanadā, Dhātrī, Trijagajjananī, and Calā.
Dānapātrī, Mitimitrā, Trāsinī, Trāsavāsinī;
Nimnanābhi, Bhindipālā, Vallabhā, and Vaśadārthinī.

The three-eyed mother of the worlds, the embodiment of truth, memory, and mindfulness; she who is free from forgetfulness and delusion, and who, through her love, is most dear and proficient in the sacred scriptures.
She is the destroyer of wealth and sons, Caṇḍikā, and she whose abode is the lotus;
she is the daughter of Yadu, the maiden of the Yadu clan, as well as the fickle and the restless one.
Tritetrā, Ekanetrā, Dvinetrā, and Sunetrikā;
Poṣaṇī, Poṣakā, and Poṣā—the ritual for the destruction of strength.
She is wisdom, the bestower of intelligence, the giver of wealth, the name itself, the heroic donor, and the embodiment of sacred law;
she is Kālikā, the Night of Time, united with red sandalwood.
With all her limbs marked with saffron and wearing red garments, she has the luster of the color of linseed flowers; she is Gaurī, the benefactress of all.
She is radiant, virtuous, a worthy recipient, the mother of the three worlds, and an ascetic;
she is the daughter-in-law Jayarūpā, who speaks kindly to her son-in-law.
Nītipriyā, Nītiruci, Suruci, and likewise Ruci;
Ratipriyā, Ratikarī, Ratidā, and Rativardhinī.
She whose form is a screen, whose form is great, who brings delight to all beings, and who is Svadhā;
she who is beautiful, whose limbs are beautiful, who is delicate, and whose body is auspicious.
She is a young girl and a maiden, dwelling within the bodies of youths;
she is of noble lineage, well-winged, beautiful-limbed, and of auspicious form.
Kumārī is pleased with her worshiper; Kumārī bestows affection. Kumārī is the servant of the devotee; Kumārī is the giver of happiness.
She who resides in the womb of the maiden, she who bestows enjoyment upon the maiden;
she who is golden and joined with the menstrual flow, whose form is the season, and who is fond of the season.
She is the menstruating one, possessing those qualities, endowed with attributes, and honored for her virtues;
she is both possessed of qualities and devoid of qualities, the source of well-being, and the creative activity that differentiates all attributes.
She is youthful, abiding in youth, dwelling in that which is dear to the young;
she is the maiden established in youth, and she is the worshipper of that which is dear to the young.
She is the young woman, she who moves with the throngs of the young, she who abides in youth, she who has passed through the ages;
she who brings about the various ages, she who stands within the age, and she who is worshipped by those joined in yoga.

She who delights in the refuge of young women, she who is joined with a young woman, she who is the digit of the new moon, she who dwells together with the hand (or the sun), she who is the crescent of the moon, and she who is the crest of the flame.
Āśāpurā, Candrā, Candrakāntipriyā,
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, and Dhṛti.
Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, Aṅgadā, Pūrṇā,
Pūrṇāmṛtā, Kāmadāyinī, and Kāmadā are the digits (kalās) that bestow all desires.

She who possesses manifold forms, she who bestows many boons upon the gods, she who is disciplined, she who is resonant, she who is the shore, she who is the twilight of the shore, and she who is fond of sacred rites.
Arati, Surati, Stutyā, Satyavatī, Sadācasā, Anālā,
Kamalāsthā, Sumālyā, and Māladāriṇī.
She is always to be honored, truthful, and her body is dear to all who are truthful;
she is fond of wine, the bringer of delight, dark-eyed, and the very form of Time.
She causes the exhaustion of all time, she destroys all time;
she is conformable, she is of vast form, she is her own essential nature, and she is devoid of form.
The Mother of the worlds, honored by the worlds, victorious, the progenitor, Jaya,
she who is to be conquered, the giver of victory over all that is conquerable, and the wise one.
She is unattached and well-attached, free from manifold attachments;
she is the conqueror, solitary, wise, knowing the ritual procedures, and the bestower of knowledge.
She is the giver of the path, the maker of the path, the excellent path, and the destroyer of evil;
she is the wife of another, she delights in others, and she takes refuge in those who love the wives of others.
Pramlocā, Kekarā, Kṛtyā, Umlocā, Umāvatī,
Aparṇā, Pārvatī, Durgā, Mṛḍānī, Caṇḍikā, and Ambikā.
She is the source of confidence, the possessor of specialized knowledge, the one who increases the crops in due season;
she is the medicinal herb, the mother of physicians, the healing art, and the healer.
Kalāvatī is Varṇamanī, Medā is Mayā, Pūtanā is Kriyāvatī,
Varṇatanu is Suvarṇā, Rasikā is Ramā.
Kālī is black, devoid of compassion, and she plays with a group of boars;
she is Kākinī, fickle, and likewise fond of the kārṣāpaṇa coin.
Taskā, Śubhrā, Taskasthā, Talpasthā, Sutaplikā, Guhyakālī, Bhadrakālī, Mahākālī, and Kalāvatī.
Atitalpā, Mahātalpā, Sutalpā, and likewise Śoṣikā;
Vindhyacakranivāsī, Sāvitrī, and Bhuvaneśvarī.
She has one side, one eye, and at times she bestows a hundred thousand;
she is the giver of ten million, the embodiment of wealth, and the dweller within riches and grain.
O Durgā, you who possess an invincible form, O Goddess Durgā, salutations be unto you!
You are the embodiment of the syllable Om, the embodiment of Hrīṃ, the Mother of the letters, and the bestower of strength.
She who is the syllable *drīṃ*, the syllable *strāṃ*, and the syllable *huṃ*; she whose form is the seed-syllables;
she who is the syllable *strīṃ* and the syllable *huṃ*; she who consists of all mantras—she is Memory (*Smṛti*).
She is excellent memory, the embodiment of memory, and the bestower of the essence of memory;
the Goddess consists of all the scriptures, and her body is fond of various meanings.
She who brings about many misfortunes, she who is playful, she who possesses hair, she who destroys the enemy;
she who loves wealth, she who creates wealth, she who has three peaks, and she who takes deceptive forms.
Abiding on three peaks, she possesses five peaks and has all peaks as her body;
she is clad in a single garment, has three eyes, is one-eyed, and is the three-eyed one.
Moon-faced Mahāgaurī dwells within the womb;
she resides in the uterus, in the placenta, and likewise among those born of sweat and those born from eggs.
At that time, she was in the form of an egg, with lips reddened by the glow of the sun;
and the illustrious one, abiding in the region of the womb, took the form of a plantain tree.
Iḍā, Suṣumnā, Yogavatī, Gāndhārī, and again Kuhū; Alambuṣā, Hastijihvā, Nalinī, and Niḍāvatī.
Vaikharī is the form of sound, residing within the sequence of the six cakras;
she is the piercer of the six cakras and the source of the supreme nectar.
Abiding in the center of the mantra-maṇḍala, she is the embodiment of Time (Kāla), the source of all qualities;
abiding in the center of the solar maṇḍala, she dwells within the solar maṇḍala.
Aruṇā, Aruṇī, Dṛṣṭā, Sūryakānti,
Divāpati, Tapanī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, and Ruci.
Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, Kṣamā—
the Goddess consists of various elements, and her fruit lies within the various internal elements.
Vahulā, Vahudā, Vijñā, Jñānājñānahāriṇī,
Manojñā, Jñānahāni, Bheruṇḍā, and Bhairavī.
She is Sundarī, Pururūpā, Kātyāyanī, and Pūtanā;
she is the Rākṣasī, the Ḍākinī, the embodiment of the gods, and adorned by the Vedas.
Jarā was an old woman, the mother of an old man, herself standing in old age, and possessing an aged form;
she was Devayānī’s virtuous and worthy vessel, wonderful and of diverse appearance.
Citralekhā, Kuṣmāṇī, the destroyer of Kumbhakarṇa,
the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, and the destroyer of the abode of Viśveśa.
Caṇḍavairī, Vināśī, Kaiṭabhī, Kapaṭeśvarī,
Kapaṭā, Akapaṭā, Kroḍā, Vikṛti, and Kṛtināśinī.
She who destroyed the demon Kaṃsa, she who annihilated the demon Vaka,
she who slew Madhu and Kaiṭabha, and she who brought about the destruction of the abode of Viśvaśa.
The destroyer of Caṇḍavairī and the annihilator [of him], the slayer of Pūtanā’s life, and the destroyer of the demon Keśi;
the slayer of Kālayavana and the annihilator of Jaṭāsura.
She is the slayer of Ariṣṭa and Dhenu, the destroyer of the world's sorrow;
she was proclaimed at the slaying of Kālanemi and resides within all living beings.
Alakṣmī in the form of Lakṣmī, whose very nature is all-powerful energy;
she who is the sacrificial fire for Niśumbha and Śumbha, and the destroyer of Raktabīja.
Vaidāmātā, Sumātā, Sumitrā, Mitrānāśinī, Kauśalyā, Kekayī, Nityā, Mantharā, and likewise Vahūdā.
Sāśvatī, Gāyatrī, Draupadī, Subhadrikā,
Uttarā, Gāndhārī, Jagaddhātrī, and Vapuḥpriyā.
Citriṇī, Kuṣmāṇī, Prabhāvatī, Rātapriyā,
Jvara, Āru, Rudrarūpā, Lomasā, and likewise Rākṣasī.
Hiḍimbā, who had assumed the form of a boar, became compassionate;
she was composed of mind, full of honor, beautiful, and captivating.
She is the enchantress, the embodiment of delusion, and the destroyer of all delusion;
she is the daughter, the worthy recipient, the oblation to the gods, truth itself, and the speaker of truth.
Satyabhāmā, Mānā, Bhuṣaṇā, Bhuṣaṇāvatī, Kukkuṭā, Vāyavī, Venī, Sumānā, and the beloved Rākṣasī.
She who possesses manifold forms, she of many forms, the bestower of much;
Jayā, Durgā, Prabhā, Satyā, she who is adorned with matted locks, and Viṭambikā.
Aticaitrī, Mahācaitrī, Śikhinī,
Kṛpaṇāvatī, Kṛpaṇā, Bhindipālī, Kuntī, and Sundaravāsinī.
She who holds a bow and arrows, she who holds nooses and is the slayer of nooses, she who wields a mace and a club;
the steadfast one who bears a skull-topped staff and follows the path of the arrow and the male.
Gaṅgā, Kāśī, Satī, Sītā, Alakā, Alakapriya,
Cakṣu, Bhadrā, Kapālī, Puṣpā, and Vasundharā.
Furthermore, there are the rivers Karma, Vipāśā, Madanāvatī,
Kāverī, Savitrī, Satyā, Vetravatī, and Vedikā.
And by this very [act], O beloved, Āyurdā, Tuṅgavatī,
and all those many rivers became her kinswomen and daughters.
Ambikā, Girikā, Menā, Gaurī, Sarvajñabhāvinī,
Bhavānī, Kamalā, Lakṣmī, and likewise the beloved of Brahmā’s son.
Nidigdhikā, Spṛhī, Vyāghrī, Vadyā, Vaidyacikitsakā,
Āherū, Atharūpā, Rathyā, and Catvaravāsinī.
She consists of all-knowledge, is truthful, and has the form and color of a cuckoo;
she is of the nature of Śaṅkara, the consort of Śaṅkara, and is fond of the lotus.
She is a Brāhmaṇī, a courtesan, a harlot, and a wanton woman appearing in various guises;
she acts according to her will, goes wherever she desires, and increases the state of passion.
She who is both desireless and full of desire, the beloved mistress of the king of passion,
the beautiful one, Bhairavī, she who is to be praised, worthy of hymns, and fond of the lunar days.
The fifth and likewise the sixth, the eighth and the ninth,
as well as the fourteenth, the new moon (kuhū), Skanda-ṣaṣṭhī, and the full moon.
She who dwells in all the constellations should be meditated upon in the form of the stars:
namely Aśvinī, Bharaṇī, Rohiṇī, and Revatī.
She is the garland of the host of constellations, dwelling in all sacred festivals;
she is the twilight that abides at the three junctions of the day, the bestower of auspiciousness and the granter of blessings.
The eternal ground of perpetual delight, she who is constant and whose very nature is eternal bliss;
the bestower of victory, honored by victory, the one who wears away [all things], and the destroyer of fever.
She is the mother, the giver of birth, and she who has made her abode in the land of her birth;
she is Pārvatī, the dweller in the city, the consort of Śambhu, and she who takes the form of a Daitya.
She was the destroyer of Danu’s sons, as well as Kadru;
she was a celestial maiden, the mother of gods, the wife of gods, and the beloved of Diti.
Aditi is to be known as Suditi; she is the daughter of Danu, whose form is giving.
She is worthy of honor through gifts, the daughter of Danu, non-different [from the Absolute], and whose form is death.
Vadhirā, Vanadā, Viśvā, Viśvamātā,
Valapradā, Kumudā, Gaṇāmbā, Ambā, and Maṅgalacaṇḍikā.
She is the knower of distinctions, established in the state of distinction, and abiding within all principles;
she is Kālarātri, Kujinī, Caṇḍamuṇḍā, and Mahātapā.
Indrākṣī, Paṅgalākṣī, Dīrghanetrā, Sulocanā,
Dīrghaghenī, Mahāghoṇā, Sughoṇā, and Ghoṇarūpiṇī.
She who has beautiful teeth and teeth arranged in pairs, she who possesses the form of many teeth;
she who is fragrant, whose form is fragrance, who possesses manifold scents, and who is sweetly perfumed.

The Goddess is endowed with various musical instruments; she is the embodiment of music, the one who possesses lutes, the desireless one, the lady of the city, and furthermore, the beloved of the thief and the consort of Śaṅkara.
She is the mother of the house, secret, most secret, and well-concealed;
she is the power consisting of all scriptures, imperishable, and the garland of letters.
Driḍhā, Svarūpāṅgī, Tālātālapriyā,
Tanu, Vetrapāṇi, Citrakarī, Vicitrā, and likewise Vidrumā.
Lalitā is the woman who is the very form of blessings; she is the consort of the Yugas, possessing a nature as delicate as the touch of pearls, rubies, and lapis lazuli; she is Rati herself.
She who disciplines, she who is humble, she who bestows gifts, she whose form is generosity, she who is like a river, she who is like a stream;
she who possesses the limbs of a man, she who is a woman, she who is beloved by the supreme man, she who is slender.
Fickle, restless, youthful, engaged in children's play, all-pervading,
she is the natural language of every region and arises from the singing of verses.
Valimātā, Valideśā, Suvali,
Valirūpiṇī, Raktapānā, Raktaruci, Suruci, and Rucirānanā.
Abiding in the midst of all auspiciousness, she dwells within all mandalas;
she is the form of fire, the color of fire, the mandala itself, and the embodiment of fire.
Dhūmrārcis, Rūpā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī,
Suśrī, Svarūpā, Bhavyā, and likewise Havyakavyavahā.
She who dwells in the funeral oblation (kavya), whose form is the funeral oblation, the giver of the funeral oblation, and whose nature is the funeral oblation;
she who is the consumer of the ancestral offering (pitṛbhuj), whose form is the mother, who resides therein, and whose form is that very abode.
She is named Kiṅkarā, the most excellent of her lineage; she is Kapaṭā, possessing a deceptive form;
she has emaciated limbs and the body of a small bird (kuliṅga); she is Vajrāṅgī, born from the Vajra.
Wearing a garland of human skulls, she is of great splendor, beautiful in form yet beyond all forms;
she is Śivadūtī, the Mother of the Dūtīs, the bestower of success, and the beloved of the Siddhas.
Minuteness, lightness, attainment, fulfillment of desires, greatness, as well as sovereignty, mastery, and likewise the power of governing one's own will.
She is the fulfillment of desires, the one who holds a sword, the dweller in half-ruined dwellings,
she who drinks fish, the fish-seizer, the eater of all things, and the consumer of flesh.
She is the practitioner, the life-breath of the practitioner, and the giver of life-breath to the practitioner;
she is humble through her love for discipline, even toward insects and moths.
Kālī is adorned with serpents; she reclines upon the lap of a serpent.
She is the woman lying upon a bed of corpses; she is Bhaismī, Bhāmī, and Kuśāvatī.
Kuśadhā, out of virtuous love, was Sukuśā, having the form of Kuśa;
she of noble lineage was Dīnavatī, beloved and rich in compassion.
Not poor, yet truly poor; endowed with austerity and fond of penance; performing the practice of begging for alms; she is perfection itself, honored by all, and enchanting to the mind.
She is the vomiter, delighted by vomiting, having the form of the seed of the three seeds;
she is seedless, the progenitor of people, and has the nature of the life-force of the world.
The individual soul and the supreme soul, the Self devoid of selfhood,
she who is worshipped, bowed to, meditated upon, accessible through meditation, and the conqueror of wealth.
She is the enemy, the flowing one, the plague, the slayer, and she who is fond of death;
she is difficult to traverse, of formidable form, Durgā, and the destroyer of miserable states of existence.
She is the princess, the king’s consort, the king’s mother, and she who possesses royal splendor;
she is free from the fear of breaking and falling, the source of existence, and she who is dear to the celestial beings.
Bhavānī, the future one, the auspicious, she whose nature is auspiciousness, the remover of fear, she who will come to be, she whose form is existence, Bhavānī, the destroyer of worldly existence.
She who consists of both form and formlessness, death itself, the giver of death, the bestower of form, and the intellect;
she who is dear to thieves, who delights in thieves, and who is constantly saluted by thieves.
She is Vāgdevī (the Goddess of Speech) from whose mouth she issues; she is Māyā, with wide eyes and casting side-long glances;
she is Nāradī and the Mother of the Gods; and her body is dear to the lords of the Dānavas.
She is the victorious one, she who is honored for victory, the giver of victory, and the vehicle of victory;
for among horses Uccaiḥśravas is supreme, while among men the lord of men is supreme.
Vāsanā is the immortal truth among riches, the accumulation of wealth;
she who is named Nandinī among cows is proclaimed as the ringing bell of musical instruments.
The Brahmin woman is eternal, consisting of the letter *a* among other syllables;
she resides in the letter *a*, the letter *o*, the feminine letter *ī*, and the letter *u*.
I am the letter *au* among the series of letters, the learned among those who are wise, and the mind among the senses; I am the form of traditional scripture among all treatises.
She is the gateway to the codes of conduct (ācāra), the beloved garland of Vāmadeva;
the Goddess who dwells in the left side, whose very form is half-woman.
She is the primordial nature of emanation, the first, the supreme-first, and the unconquered;
she is the unconquerable, the victorious, the Bimbī, and the one who knows the body of the universe and its non-universe.
The prostitute Vimuthā was well-disposed toward the trees in the form of Aśvattha;
she is the illusion (māyā) consisting of the cycle of existence (saṃsāra), as proclaimed in the Māyā-śāstra.
She whose garment is a tattered rag, who dwells in the mountain of base metals,
who resides on Kailāsa, the pillar, the weak one, and she who is the goddess of speech.

She who drinks the nectar of immortality, she who is free from defects, she who is beyond the need for recitation, she who is fond of the water-offering (argha), she who possesses vital energy, she who has the form of the dull-witted, she who is perfectly simple, and she who is devoid of all dullness.
She who has manifold names and yet a single name, who is devoid of all names;
she is manifestly composed of the Brahman of light, having the very nature of the Brahman of the Vedas.
She who causes the speech of all beings, she who is established among all beings,
the lute-player, the musician, the courtesan, the flame, and likewise Suruci.
Sunīti, Kayādhu, Hṛtadyuti, and another beyond her;
Cāṇḍālī, Vāyasī, Vālā, and yet another, Acaraṇabhadrikā.
Rasālamātṛkā, or another [form], dwelling in the forest and moving in the forest;
likewise Pṛthivī, Rīti, and Tripadā Sāmagāyinī.

She is devoted to the Sāmaveda, she is the boundary, and she is the destroyer of the Sāmaveda; she is the mistress of the household, she is the support of the family, and her face is the guide for those with evil minds.
Subhadrā, Kuntalā, Dantrī, Śrī, Sallokā, Carā, Vahis;
she is both internal and external, and she wears various garlands.
She is the night, the monthly period, the mother, the knower, and the extent of the matrices;
she is the sweetness of honey among flavors, and likewise the *praṇava* among sounds.
Among colors, the Brāhmaṇa is manifestly the foremost; among grains, Śāli is the best;
among crops, that named Śālikā is supreme; and likewise, among fields, Kāśikā is the most excellent.
The Ganges is declared to be the foremost among rivers, gold among jewels, and Mount Meru among mountains; likewise, my father’s beloved is the foremost among women.
Among rivers, she is the Gaṅgā; at the sacred site (tīrtha), she takes the form of Puṣkara;
her abode is said to be Pulaha, and among hermitages, she is Pārvatī.
Kubera is the lord of the fortunate, and the Lord of Lords is the master of husbands;
he alone is the refuge for those who possess a refuge, and the supreme purifier among men.
She who dispels all darkness is to be known as the one who delights with the nectar of her speech;
she who perfumes with camphor is she whose breath fills the mouth with betel.
Clad in red garments, with a red upper cloth, she is the wearer of rags;
out of love, she is both the ragged one and the delighter of the angry maiden.
Kālī, Kālipriyā, Keli, Krīḍā, Athelā, Kurddhikā,
Ciṭhī, Kuṭhī, Priyakarī, Vendraṭā, and likewise Kandani.
She is the birthplace, she is of noble birth, and she dwells at the gateway of birth;
she is the form of the connection of the channels (nāḍīs), and likewise, she is fond of all flesh.
Śṛṅgā, Rāṅganivāsī, Śṛṅgārabhāvabhāvikā, Candrikā, Candrakānti, and then the action (kriyā) Candrakarī. || 1000 ||
O Goddess, these thousand names were spoken by Nārada;
that Thousand Names of Durgā have now been recounted by me.
Whoever recites even a single verse or a single quarter-verse at dawn indeed becomes a son of Pārvatī himself; this was spoken by Nārada.
For women who are barren, those whose children die, or those who have only one child,
by either reciting or hearing this, Śiva himself shall become their son.
O Goddess of the Gods, by the grace of this hymn, the killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and violating the teacher’s wife— all such sins are destroyed.
Naked, with disheveled hair, having come to the cremation ground and offered a monthly meal as an oblation, one should become eternally devoted.
One should always offer fish that has been cooked, meat that has been cooked, and whatever other substances have been cooked,
together with cooked fish and meat.
Having offered all of that to the Goddess, he should recite the mantra with undivided attention for six thousand times during the portion of the night, remaining intent on dance.
Having returned to his own home, he should offer a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) there to the guru;
thereafter, the preceptor [should worship] the Great Goddess according to this rite.
Before the maiden arrives, those who worship the gods should first perform worship;
[they should worship] beautiful women with delicate limbs, who bestow both worldly existence and liberation.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite, the wise practitioner should perform japa upon that source;
he should then recite it one hundred and eight times daily at the three junctions of the day.
O Goddess, for the wise one who practices in this manner for six months in accordance with the tantra, Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune, becomes manifest before him.
Then the wise one should draw that [diagram] with gorocanā, saffron, lac-dye, sandalwood, vermilion, camphor, and honey.
Holding it on one's arm or head, one shall bring the entire world under control;
having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, and the like, accompanied by songs, instrumental music, and attendants.
The goddesses shall grant whatever special favor one desires through reflection and recitation;
thereafter, one should perform the narrative of the hunt for three days.
Having fed the Brahmins and a most beautiful woman,
one shall then attain great protection for as long as life endures.
He shall become the son of Pārvatī, honored by all living beings;
O Goddess, upon seeing that practitioner, lions, tigers, and other such creatures [shall flee].
They all flee away like deer upon seeing a lion;
once the mantra has been perfected, one should perform the rites for the worship of the gods.
Having brought some excellent clay from the bank of a river,
one should divide it into three parts, such that it amounts to twelve *palas* in total.
The wise man should always dig a trench three parts wide at the edge of the village;
he should then mark out that portion—listen, O beloved, to the procedure for that.
One should dig a pit of one's own height, lined with dried cow dung, sand, and earth, and strewn with leaves of the *aśvattha* tree, accompanied by songs and instrumental music.
Having returned home, the practitioner should bury [the image] with its face turned away;
he should worship Mahāmāyā with songs, instrumental music, and offerings of oblations.
In that regard, one should perform a vigil here; the wise man should sprinkle [the ground] with honey, and he should dig up that soil from within the interior of the house.
Then there shall be suchness, and he shall accomplish success without dependence on external means;
the excellent practitioner should offer the food offering to the deities according to the prescribed rite.
Having fed the practitioners, one should satisfy them with service and other honors;
then, for the sake of accomplishing all goals, there will be great delight on the part of the Goddess.
One should meditate upon the Goddess with supreme devotion through the application of the six rites— [visualizing her] as angry, wicked, likewise trampled, squinting, and filled with grief.
One should meditate upon Niśumbha as the enemy and the Daughter of the Mountain as one's own self;
thus, one shall slay all enemies, even those as formidable as mountains of gold.
Whatever desire one may long for while reciting this unsurpassed hymn,
one attains that very thing perpetually through the grace of Durgā’s feet.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed rite with Svayambhū flowers, white Śukra flowers, barley, and red rice, one shall obtain the unsurpassed accomplishment.
Month after month, one should worship the goddess Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune;
one should honor the daughter of the mountain with fish, meat, grain, and milk products.
Having bathed in water infused with all medicinal herbs, along with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, viḍaṅga, and bakula flowers, one should worship the Supreme Deity.
Having ground together saffron, lotus, and aloe-wood along with gold, combined with various fragrances,
as well as the charcoal from a corpse and the wood of the root-tree;
Having purified it according to the ritual procedure with the root mantra,
the wise practitioner applies the *tilaka* one hundred and eight times.
O Goddess, having seen that *tilaka*, the world shall come under his control;
[this should be done] every day at midnight in a cremation ground on the new moon day of the month of Bhādra.
Having meditated upon her, the daughter of the mountain, one should offer an oblation to the Great Goddess;
he shall become the foremost of all prosperities, indeed like Maheśa himself.
"O Goddess, what need is there for many other [practices]? A man shall obtain all accomplishments.
Thus ends the Thousand Names of Durgā in the Viśvasāra Tantra.
Śrī Īśvara said:
I shall proclaim the hundred names; listen, O lotus-faced one!
By the grace of these alone, there shall always be the favor of Durgā.
Oṃ! She is Satī, the virtuous one, beloved of Bhava, Bhavānī, the liberator from worldly existence;
she is the primordial Durgā, Jayā, Āryā, the three-eyed one, and the wielder of the trident.
She is the wielder of the Pināka bow, the one whose mind is intent, she who performs great penance through Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa;
she is the intellect, the awakening, and the ego; she is the form of consciousness, the accumulated consciousness, and the source of all that is conscious and unconscious.
She consists of all mantras, she is the truth, whose nature is the bliss of truth;
she is the infinite future, the one to be meditated upon, the auspicious one who removes the fear of worldly existence.
The daughter of Asura, the giver of the Vedas, who always delights in the path of contemplation;
she who possesses all knowledge, the daughter of Daksha, and the destroyer of Daksha’s sacrifice.
Aparṇā and Anekaparṇā, Pāṭalā and Pāṭalāvatī;
she who wears garments of fine silk and is resplendent with tinkling anklets.
O beautiful one, you are the immeasurable, the valiant, the cruel, and the beauty of the city;
you are Navadurgā and Mātaṅgī, worshipped by the sage Mataṅga.
Māheśvarī, Aindrī, Kaumārī, and Vaiṣṇavī were seen there,
as well as Cāmuṇḍā, Vārāhī, and Lakṣmī in human form.
Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, Satyā, and Buddhidā—these many [powers] are manifold through love; all are the vehicles of the vehicle-bearer.
She is the slayer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, the crusher of the demon Mahiṣāsura,
the destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, and the annihilator of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
She is the destroyer of all asuras and the slayer of men at all times;
she consists of all the scriptures, is truth itself, and likewise wields all weapons.
Aruṇā, Aruṇī, Sūryakānti, Dāvāpati,
Tapanī, Tāpanī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvalanī, and Rucī.
Suṣumnā is the bestower of enjoyment, all-pervasive, the subduer of adversaries, the sustainer, and the patient earth;
she is the goddess composed of various elements, whose fruit lies within the various internal constituents.
She who slays with many weapons, she who wields many missiles,
she who is both a maiden and a girl, Kaumārī, whose intellect is youthful.
Whether she be immature or mature, the aged mother bestows strength upon him who recites this "One Hundred and Eight Names of Durgā" daily.
O Pārvatī, for such a person there is nothing unattainable within the three worlds—
be it wealth, grain, a son, a wife, a horse, or even an elephant.

Having worshipped the maiden and meditated upon the Goddess, the Sovereign of the Gods, one shall likewise obtain the fourfold aims of life and, at the end, liberation according to the Sātvata tradition.
One should worship with supreme devotion and recite the "Eight Hundred Homages";
O Goddess, for such a person, even the most excellent of all the gods shall grant accomplishment.
Kings attain the state of being worshippers and shall obtain the glory of sovereignty by means of yellow orpiment,
lac, saffron, vermilion, camphor, and the three types of honey.
Having drawn the yantra according to the prescribed rite, the Knower of the Rituals (Śiva), the Foe of Tripura, shall always wear it;
specifically on the new moon day of the month of Bhādra during the night when the moon has entered the asterism Śatabhiṣā.
By writing and reciting this hymn, one shall become a vessel for all prosperity.
Thus ends the hymn "The Eighty-Eight Names of Durgā" in the Viśvasāra Tantra.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, omniscient one, worshiped by the deities!
O Lord, please tell me the ritual procedure for Gaura, the son of Śiva.
Having heard those words of hers, the Lord of the World, the worshiper of the gods, smiled and explained that entire ritual procedure to her.
The illustrious Lord said: "Excellent, excellent, O lady of beautiful hips! The worship of the high-souled Gaṇeśa, as well as his yantra, is hidden in all the tantras."
The greatness of the yellow Gaṇeśa is difficult even for the gods to attain;
through the methods of divinity practiced by the gods and the perfumes of the Gandharvas, it was perfected by himself.
O Maheśānī, what can be said by those with five faces regarding the Lord of the Gods?
O fair-faced one, I know the majesty of this tantra-yantra.
Even with a thousand mouths, Ananta himself could never desire to speak of his greatness, which is difficult even for the gods to attain.
The sages, the ancestors, the gods, the nāgas, the non-nāgas,
and the excellent asuras constantly recite the mantra of the high-souled Gaṇeśa.
I shall explain the extraction of the mantra; listen, O lotus-faced one! Having extracted the seed-syllable of Indra, one should extract one's own seed-syllable.
Adorned with the fourteenth vowel and the bindu and khaṇḍa,
this single-syllable Great Vidyā was proclaimed by the Lotus-born One.
It directly bestows the fourfold aims of human life and destroys even the greatest sins;
yet it must not be given to one who is not a disciple, nor to the cruel, nor to the wicked, nor to one who views others as enemies.
One who desires their own welfare should neither reveal nor cause others to hear [this],
for there is no knowledge equal to the Kākṣara, O beloved of the three worlds.
Now I shall explain meditation; listen, O lotus-faced one!
Without knowing the island composed of the nine jewels within the ocean of nectar—
Its banks were washed by those waves, fanned by gentle breezes,
and crowded with the creepers of the wish-fulfilling trees known as Mandara and Pārijāta.
Having extracted [the seed-syllable], one should meditate upon the Pārijāta tree made of nine jewels in its center, its ornaments reddened by the reflections of gems.
Fragrant and constantly frequented by the virtuous who increase its joy,
beneath it, upon an intellectual pedestal, the Mātṛkā was fashioned within a lotus.
The sixth [mandala] is situated in the non-existent corner (the northwest), possessing eight petals and joined with three images;
it resembles a half-moon and is endowed with filaments.
In a mantra joined with various weapons, one should meditate upon Mahāgaṇapati:

he who has the face of a lordly elephant, is adorned with the moon, possesses the reddish luster of the dawn, and has three eyes; he is constantly embraced by his beloved Rasadā, whose hand holds a lotus, while her own hand rests upon his chest.

I worship Him who, with His hands, carries two seeds, sugarcane, a goad, and a jewel-jars, shining with the luster of His actions; who, with His trunk-like arms, repeatedly wards off the bees that swarm toward His temples by scattering the ichor flowing from them, while His mind is uplifted with joy.
He was emitting the luster of jewels from the mouths of ruby jars held at the tips of his hands, and he was intoxicated with passion for the practitioners.
Having meditated upon that god Gaṇeśa, the son of Śiva, adorned with jewel ornaments and a crest of rubies, one should mutter his mantra.
One who is pure and self-restrained should perform the preliminary rite by reciting [the mantra] four hundred thousand times;
O lotus-faced one, all accomplishments will then be held in the palm of one's hand.
Śrī Pārvatī said: O Lord, O Master of the World, O Teacher of the Universe, you have truly explained the deity of the caste (varṇa), as well as the meter (chandas) and the seer (ṛṣi).
Śrī Īśvara said: O Maheśānī, the primordial Lord of the gods, the God of gods, Sadāśiva, is proclaimed to be the deity of the letter *ga*.
O Queen of the Gods, the leader of the hosts of deities presides over the half-moon;
for the letter Śa, Indra is the presiding deity, the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
O lady with the face of an excellent sage, the primordial power Mahāmāyā is proclaimed as the *ṛṣi* of the mantra of Mahādeva, which begins with the syllable *ū*.
O Dear One, the group of nyāsas is as before, and the worship is as before;
O Goddess, the armor (kavaca) has been told, all of which was taught in the Ādiśāmala.
Everything regarding this very matter is told here; listen to it, O fair-faced one.
Śrī Īśvara said:
Listen, my dear, I shall proclaim the armor (kavaca) which bestows all spiritual accomplishments (siddhi).
Having recited and retained it, one is liberated from all danger.
O Goddess, if one recites [the mantra] without knowing the armor (kavaca) of Gaṇeśa,
no accomplishment shall arise for him even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
Oṃ! Āmeda protects the head, and Prameda protects above the topknot;
Sanmoda protects the pair of thighs, and Gaṇādhipa protects between the feet.
May Gaṇakrīḍa protect my pair of eyes; may Gaṇanāyaka protect my nose; and may Gaṇakrīḍānvita, who brings joy to the head, always protect the pair of my arms.
The creator of the universe is in the belly, and likewise the destroyer of the universe is in the belly;
the elephant-faced one is at the region of the waist, and the single-tusked one is on the hip.
May Lambodara always protect my secret place;
may he, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, always protect me at the pair of my feet.
May Jāpaka protect me always on the pair of knees;
may Gaṇādhipa, the leader of the hosts, who is tawny-hued, protect all my limbs at all times.
O Maheśvarī, whoever should constantly recite this armor (kavaca) of Gaṇeśa, known as "The All-Accomplishing," which destroys all obstacles and impediments;
It directly brings about all accomplishments, directly liberates one from all sins,
directly bestows all prosperity, and causes the destruction of all enemies.
Afflictions caused by malevolent planets, fevers, diseases, and others such as abdominal tumors,
go to destruction instantly through recitation and hearing [this].
O Goddess, this armor bestows wealth and grain and is worshipped by the gods;
O Maheśānī, there is nothing equal to this armor in the three worlds.
O Maheśānī, regarding this Hāridra-kavaca on the surface of the earth,
what is the use of other worthless discourses, wherein one's life would only be spent in vain?
Thus ends the armor (kavaca) of Hāridragaṇeśa in the Viśvasāra Tantra.
O Goddess, many kinds of mantras have been taught by the Lotus-born One;
a wise person should recite one beginning with Lakṣmī, or one beginning with Kāma, or one beginning with Māyā.
One should always recite the mantra beginning with "Lajjā" (the seed-syllable of Lakṣmī) or the mantra beginning with the "Vadhū" (the seed-syllable of Tripurā),
or the Great Vidyā beginning with the syllable "Oṃ," as well as those beginning with one's own specific seed-syllable.
Having joined the sky (the letter *ha*) with the moon (the vowel *ī*), one should drop the middle *bha* and *ra*;
O Great Goddess, this is the seed-syllable of oneself as taught by the Lotus-born One.
That great vidyā consists of two syllables; when joined with the weapon [mantra], it consists of three syllables.
It directly bestows the four aims of human life and destroys even the most heinous sins.
A wise person should always recite this Vidyā, beginning with the syllable *Vāgbhava*, for the sake of scholarship.
Now, O lotus-faced one, listen as I describe Durgā;
she is a manifold Great Vidyā (Mahāvidyā) according to the tradition of Mahākāla, my dear.

One should always recite [the mantra] beginning with Lakṣmī and so forth, or beginning with Vāgbhava and so forth, or beginning with Kāma and bestowing desires, or beginning with Lajjā, or beginning with Naha, or beginning with Kūrca.
Or else, O Goddess, one of vast intellect should recite the Vadhū-bīja and so forth,
which is the Vidya consisting of sixteen consonants joined with the left eye (I) and fire (R).
This is known as the seed-syllable of Lajjā (Hrīṃ), mounted upon the drop of the moon (bindu);
for the sake of attaining success in recitation, one should likewise mutter the seed-syllable of the Goddess (Aiṃ) and so forth.
Mounted upon the *indu-bindu* (the nasal drop) and endowed with the *anusvāra*,
this is declared to be the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the Goddess, spoken by Brahmā in the past.
The three-syllabled vidyā ending in *phaṭ* is concealed in all tantras;
it is declared to be a three-lettered vidyā that concludes with the wife of fire (*svāhā*).
Through enjoyment, one attains the knowledge that bestows all prosperity;
there is no knowledge higher than this, nor any sacred ford more supreme than this.
O Goddess, this crest-jewel of knowledge was spoken by the Lotus-born;
Kaśyapa, Kāhali, Śivānanda, and then Gautama.
Cyavana, Śukra, Śukra, as well as Pulaha,
Kratu, Vasiṣṭha, Durvāsas, Śāntanu, Sagara, and Kṛpa.
All those great-souled ones who are devoted to the Śakti are dedicated to every form of conduct;
they are indeed Śaivas and Vaiṣṇavas, and all of them are worshippers of Śiva.
They alone wander upon the surface of the earth in the form of Śiva;
O Goddess of gods, there is no one else like them for me anywhere on the earth.
The Vidyā consisting of Devakūṭa has been declared by the Lotus-born One,
according to its movement, its time, its location, and its ritual procedure.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Śrīdurgāvidhāna of the Viśvasāra-tantra.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the Vidyā that bestows all fruits;
it directly grants the four aims of life and destroys even the greatest sins.
She is eternally bestowing all accomplishments, likewise the destroyer of all sins;
she is the eternal source of all auspiciousness, granting both devotion and liberation.
The great vidyā Guhyakālī is difficult to obtain even in the three worlds;
this vidyā, whose essence is Devakūṭa, is concealed within all tantras.
I shall declare the extraction of the mantra; listen, O lotus-faced one!
It consists of the first letter of each group [of consonants], mounted upon the deities beginning with Indra, and endowed with Rati and the Bindu.
Then, having rendered it defective, one should extract the syllable *Īśāna*,
conjoined with the left eye (the letter *i*) and fire (*r*), and endowed with the nasal sound (*n*) and the bindu (*m*).
These two forms of Lajjā are said to follow all vidyās;
then one should say "Guhyakālī" or else "Dakṣiṇā."
Furthermore, one should first contemplate the seven seeds in sequence with the intellect;
this mantra, known as Vahnijāyā (the Fire-Wife), is the Trailokyamohinī (Enchantress of the Three Worlds).
There is no knowledge higher than this, no sacred ford superior to this, and no boon greater than this.
Blessed are they, meritorious are they; they are all worshippers of Śiva.
They are all Vaiṣṇavas, knowers of the scriptures, and leaders who provide awakening;
O Goddess of gods, there is none equal to them in the three worlds.
And thus says the Śruti:
When one knows the *kāmarāja*, the *kūrca*, or the vocative address of Guhyakālī,
at all times and on every occasion, one crosses over all murder, crosses over all death, knows all scriptures, becomes wealthy, and in the end goes to the world of the gods.
Through the grace of the Goddess’s feet, one beholds the Goddess within one's own body and accomplishes what is otherwise unattainable.
O Goddess, what more need be said? One shall obtain all perfections (siddhis).
A science similar to this is difficult to find even throughout the three worlds.
In this case, the mantra consists of the *kūrca* (hum), *śakti* (phat), and *svāhā*;
or alternatively, the two syllables *kūrca-vāja* (hum-vaja) and *svāhā* constitute the *śakti*.
The Goddess, whose nature is consciousness and who is stainless, consists of all castes;
she is changeless and of the nature of bliss. At the end of her life, she revealed this to a rogue of her own lineage and to a friend, as stated in the Śruti.
The power (*śakti*) of the three *kāmarāja* [syllables] is Trailokyamohana;
the powers of the two *kūrca* [syllables] are Mūlaprakṛti and Nityā; the power of the one beginning with *jvālā* is Tribhuvaneśvarī;
the power of the first *guhyā* is Dakṣiṇā; and the power of the word *dakṣiṇā* is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, the seer (*ṛṣi*).
Again, likewise for the seeds, Svāhā.
For sound, Śaktikālakā is the destroyer of defilement. On the right is the word *pada* or the secret word; the pin (*kīlaka*) is the letter *ga*, while Mahādevī resides therein.
The leader of the host of deities is [the letter] *u*;
the Great Goddess (*mahādevī*) is in *ū*; Sadāśiva is in *ha*; and the Goddess Īśvarī is in *e*. Such are the deities of the phonemes (*varṇa*).
That great vidyā has been described in various ways by the Lotus-born;
listen to that, O Maheśānī, as it was spoken by the exponents of Brahman.
Likewise, Kāmarāja and Kūrca, at the end of which is Bhuvaneśvarī;
then the secret Goddess Kālikā and the third seed-syllable.
The vidyā ending in *svāhā* is said to be unsurpassed among all vidyās;
having extracted two seed-syllables each, one should then utter them for the purpose of awakening.
Again, in the same manner, there are six seed-syllables, and at their end is Vahnisundarī; this mantra consisting of twenty syllables is proclaimed as the Trikoṇa-vāra.
Then one should utter Kāmarāja, then Kavaca, and then Bhuvaneśvarī; then one should utter the vocative, ending with Svāhā—this is remembered as the supreme [mantra].
The eleven-syllable vidyā becomes ten syllables in nature;
the one-syllable is Kāmarāja, and the three-syllable is Tribījikā.
The six-syllable mantra consists of the six seed-syllables; the eight-syllable mantra is known as ending with *svāhā*.
The two-syllable mantra is the seed-syllable of desire (*kāma*), and the three-syllable mantra is considered to end with *phaṭ*.

The three seed-syllables, followed by the weapon-mantra, constitute the four-syllabled [mantra]. Having rendered the seed-syllables devoid of qualities (nirguṇīkṛtya) and having omitted the word of address, [the mantra is formed].
This vidyā, ending with *svāhā*, is declared to be hidden in all tantras;
this sixteen-syllable vidyā bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
This Vidyā bestows devotion and liberation, brings all the worlds under one's control,
destroys all enemies, and is the very embodiment of the wish-fulfilling tree.
By good fortune one obtains knowledge that is everywhere extremely difficult to find;
such as Parāśara, Vasiṣṭha, Maitreya, and likewise Kaśyapa.
And likewise, O beloved, the King of Kāśī, Aśvapati, Pulastya,
Pulaha, Kratu, and Kātyāyana.
Bodhāyana, Śaṅkhadhara, Stuṇḍa, Kāśyapi, Garuḍa, Śveta, Ketakī, and likewise Kāhala— these are the excellent ones, O lady of beautiful countenance.
Jāta, Niśa, Āsuri, Hari assuming the form of Vāmana,
Sahasrapādahi, Bradhna, Bharadvāja, and Bhāskara;
Viśālākṣa, Surānanda, Dvādaśātman, and Divākara—
these, O Goddess, are the sixteen attendants of Guhyakālī.
The sixteenfold knowledge is difficult to obtain and is concealed within all tantras;
by pronouncing the word "dakṣiṇe," it becomes fifteen syllables long.
The sixteenfold knowledge is secret; even there, O beloved, its teacher is likewise hidden.
Its ritual procedure is easily obtained there, but not anywhere else, O Pārvatī.
By manifesting the two Kāmarājas, the fourteenth Vidyā arises;
the seven seed-syllables were previously taught, and again in the secret [teaching], O Kālikā.
This Vidyā, ending with *svāhā*, is said to be hidden in all Tantras;
it may be either [the Vidya] excluding Kāmarāja, or the sixteen-syllabled one.
Thus, many kinds of vidyās have been proclaimed in various tantras.
Now I shall speak of the Great Vidyā, which is hidden in all tantras;
listen to that which was taught by Bhṛṇḍarāma, O fair-faced one.
Having extracted the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma), one should place two words ending with "Sambuddha" (Namaḥ);
then, at the end of that, one should again provide Kāma, as well as Kūrca and Sundarī.
This nine-syllable vidyā, when combined with the secret word,
becomes a ten-syllable vidyā by uttering the word "dakṣiṇe" [at the end].
Thus, many kinds of vidyās are difficult to find in various tantras;
however, the vidyā spoken by Mahākāla exists in a hundred thousand forms.
One should worship Śivā with the group of nyāsas as before;
one should mutter the vidyā as before, for indeed everything is exactly as before.
One should likewise fashion the seal and the yantra as before;
even for a hundred offenses, one should not strike a woman with a flower.
Whether she be ill-dressed or well-attired, whether she be a maiden or a young woman, one should not revile her either in thought or in speech; having paid homage, one should bid her farewell.
Listen, O Pārvatī, how Bhadrakālī and the other Vidyās are conceptualized:
one should worship all the seed-syllables, beginning with Kāmarāja, in both the preceding and succeeding positions.
One should likewise join Bhadrakālī, ending in the suffix *ṅi*, in the midst of the seed-syllable;
O Dear One, this Vidyā, consisting of twenty syllables, is said to end with *svāhā*.
The goddess Bhadrakālī, of auspicious countenance, bestows the fourfold aims of life;
she is known in a hundred ways as Vidyā, especially in every Tantra.
Then, having extracted the seven seeds of Śmaśānakālikā,
it is universally accepted as ending with *svāhā* according to the sequence of the previous seeds.
The twenty-onefold Vidyā of Bhadrakālī is proclaimed;
one should first extract the seed-syllables, and then the word Mahākālī once again.
At its end, the seven seed-syllables ending in *svāhā* are universally agreed upon;
this twenty-syllable *mahāvidyā* is proclaimed as that of Bhadrakālī.
I shall describe their meditation; listen, O lotus-faced one!
[She is] red, with the luster of a great cloud, and clothed in black garments.
With a flickering tongue, terrible fangs, hollow eyes, and a radiant face,
she is adorned with a necklace and bracelets of serpents and wears the crescent moon as her crest-ornament.
She was scratching the sky with a single matted lock, licking a corpse, and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread; she sat upon a bed of serpents.
And behind it, with a human skull, [he worships] the great forest garland (vanamālā) together with the thousand fruits upon the head of Ananta.
One should know Guhyakālī as being encircled by the hoods of serpents in the four directions;
with the serpent hoods for eighty years, they recognize this as the second bracelet.
The right hand is adorned by the Naga king Ananta,
while on the left, the form of a corpse is fashioned, ending with the beautiful form of a corpse.
One should meditate upon the Goddess as having two arms, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
with her ears adorned by earrings set with the nine gems.
She has a serene countenance, is gentle, and is adorned with all kinds of jewels;
she is the consort of Śiva, attended by hosts of sages such as Nārada.
Having thus meditated upon the goddess Kālī— the one who laughs loudly, the most terrifying, the bestower of the desires of practitioners, and the destroyer of impurities— one should worship her.
Alternatively, one should meditate upon the goddess Guhyakālī, the great source of prosperity—
the four-armed Mahākālī who wears earrings made of skulls.
She has terrible fangs, a formidable appearance, and a complexion like a massive, dense cloud;
she wears a garland of skulls and carries a skull-cup as well as an extremely sharp knife.
And in the right hand, O Goddess, [he holds] the Nāga-group according to the right-hand yoga,
joined with a thousand hoods and adorned by the host of Ananta.
She was chanting the Sāmaveda with a voice transformed by the howling of jackals,
her face quivering from the streams of blood trickling from both corners of her mouth.
Licking a corpse directly, standing in the pratyālīḍha posture,
naked, most terrifying, and attended by various children.
She wears a girdle fashioned from the joined hands of corpses, her face radiant with laughter,
and she dwells within the heart of Mahādeva in the form of a corpse.
And one should thus meditate upon the Goddess Guhyakālī, the Great Sovereign, who fulfills the goals of practitioners with showers of blossoming jewels.
O Dear One, the Vidyā consisting of Devakūṭa is endowed with all the Tantras;
in a different form of meditation, the Vidyā consists of Jīvakūṭa.
Or else, O Dear One, one should meditate upon Kālī, who is regarded as Mahākāla’s consort—
dark-complexioned like a great cloud, and clothed in red garments.
With a lolling tongue, a gaping mouth, and terrifying fangs, she was fearsome yet exceedingly beautiful,
adorned with a pair of earrings made from corpses.
The abode of all loveliness, with two rows of teeth like a string of pearls at her corners of the mouth, she wears a girdle made from the gathered hands of corpses and possesses a smiling face.
She is situated upon the heart of the great god Śavarūpa,
bestowing fearlessness and boons, and holding a sword and a beautiful severed head.
It was adorned with various nāgas possessing a thousand hoods,
fashioned in the form of a corpse by Mahādeva himself in the guise of a corpse-eater.
The right hand was adorned by the Naga king Ananta,
and there were various gods and Gandharvas accompanied by diverse musical rhythms.
One should thus contemplate the goddess, accompanied by Kurukullā and others, who is served by various nāgas and is exceedingly beautiful.
One should worship Guhyakālī, the greatly exalted one, with supreme devotion.
Now I shall describe the yantra; listen, O lotus-faced one! One should first draw a triangle adorned with a hexagon.
Furthermore, one should worship Śivā there in each of the nine corners;
or else, O Daughter of the Mountain, listen as I explain how one should worship her within the yantra.
A triangle, a hexagon, and a beautiful nine-cornered figure;
three circles, along with an eight-petalled lotus provided with its filaments.
This wheel, consisting of fifteen spokes, is mounted upon three enclosures of earth and adorned with the circle of the yoni; it is endowed with all the tantras.
A triangle, a hexagon, and then a nonagon;
likewise, three types [of mandalas] with eight petals, each endowed with three enclosures of earth-walls.

One should worship Bhavasundarī in the midst of that [mandala] with supreme devotion upon a seat of fifteen spokes, O Mother; thus, all great-souled ones, joined with the ritual, are constantly endowed with great perfection and poetic skill.
Their tongues are utterly eradicated and struck down by all afflictions; the power of those enumerations triumphs for a long time.
Now, the powers (śaktis) for the worship of the Goddess are proclaimed:
Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Vipracittā, and Virodhinī.
One should contemplate Ugrā and Ugraprabhā within the hexagon,
as well as Dīptā, Ghanā, Pradīptā, Mātrā, Mudrā, and again Mitā.
One should worship in sequence Nīlā, Nīlaghanā, Ghorā, Aṭṭahāsā, Karālinī, Amitā, Mitā, Mudrā, and Sughorā.
Thereafter, the Mothers beginning with Brāhmī are to be worshipped upon the petals;
in the outer square (bhūpura) are the world-protectors (lokapālas), and outside of that, their weapons.
In the four-cornered Bhūpura, the wise one should worship in sequence;
he should worship Viṣṇu, Śiva, Sūrya, and Gaṇeśa in order.
The wise know the sequence of the five deities according to the ritual procedure of Mahāvidyā;
for the learned one who worships in this manner, accomplishment is not difficult to attain.
One should offer water for the feet and the respectful oblation everywhere with the root mantra;
one should worship Guhyakālī with supreme devotion according to the prescribed rite.
One should utter Sadāśiva ending in the suffix *ṅ*, then again the word Mahāpreta;
likewise, Guhyakālī’s seat and Guhyakālī itself, each ending in *ṅ*.
Then one should say: "Seize, seize my two feet! Kill my enemies!
One should utter "destroy" twice and "devour" twice.
"Turū turū," "padadvandvam," "tat," "sphurasphura," and likewise; "chindi chindi," "padadvandvam," and the two words "siddhiṃ dehi."
One should utter the two armor-mantras (*kavaca*), and at their conclusion, the beautiful goddess of fire (*vahnisundarī*).
Mounted upon the fifty [letters] twice over, one should present them during the offering of the *bali*.
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with Kālī and the secret syllable;
having extracted the Kāmarāja, it should likewise be joined with the King of Mantras.
In that immediately following [verse], one should extract [the mantra] with effort;
having addressed the two auspicious sciences (*vidye*), one should then meditate (*dhīmahi*) upon them.
Having addressed Tāmrāpada, the Goddess then urged him on;
thus, O beloved, the Gāyatrī of Guhyakālī and Kālī has been declared.
In this [practice], there is no requirement for perfected adepts (siddhas), nor any fault regarding friends and the like;
furthermore, it does not involve great expenditure of wealth, as taught by the Lotus-born One (Brahmā).
One should worship Śivā at the proper time, in the proper place, and according to the proper procedure;
having diligently satisfied the Guru, one should recite the vidyā with undistracted mind.
One certainly partakes of all fruits through the satisfaction of the guru;
yet a man who, disregarding the guru’s command, should obtain the vidyā and recite it—
Success does not arise for him even in hundreds of millions of aeons,
[despite] vegetables, soups, cakes, many thick ghee preparations, liquor, meat, milk, foods to be sucked, chewed, licked, and many throat-sliming delicacies, as well as meats suspended from hooks.

One should worship with the flesh of crocodiles, tortoises, cows, iguanas, deer, goats, sheep, porcupines, monitor lizards, and wild cats— these nine sacrificial animals— as well as with burnt fish-flesh, the supreme blood of deer, and ground leaves, flowers, and rice.
I bow to her, who is worshipped by all the wives of the gods.
O Mother, having worshipped the people with offerings of *gṛñja* fruits according to the prescribed rites, and having worshipped the victorious Vaijayantī at night with pure and impure substances,
one should thus fully worship that goddess Guhyakālī, who brings great prosperity.
Having praised with this hymn, one shall accomplish the supreme siddhi.
Therefore, O lotus-faced one, I shall recite a hymn of praise at dawn;
listen, for by its grace high-souled beings attain all perfections.
Śiva said:
Oṃ! Kālī is of great splendor, the sustainer of the worlds, and highly renowned;
she is Sarasvatī, Mahālakṣmī, and the increaser of progeny, fortune, and intelligence.
Bestower of fortitude, bestower of nourishment, Svāhā, Kālī, she who assumes the forms of all desires, intent upon the welfare of all beings, the savior in battle, the Victorious One.
Indvatī, Śaṅkhinī, Pūrṇā, Vidyārājñī, Priyapradā,
Candrānanā, Mahāgaurī, Kūjitā, and Pitavāsavā.
Mahāmāyā, the great illuminator, possessed of great strength and prowess;
the greatly fierce and extremely wrathful one, the slayer of wicked Dānavas.
She is profoundly peaceful, of tranquil form, victorious, and the bestower of strength.
Vidyunmālī, Gadī, Khaḍgī, Cakrī, Cāpodātāyudhā, Jṛmbhinī,
Stambhinī, Bālā, Kālarātrī, and Niśācarī.
The Yakṣiṇī Mohinī, Kṛṣṇā, Praśāntā, and Śāntarūpiṇī;
Brahmāṇī, the Mother of the Vedas, and the dweller on the Snowy Mountain.
Maṅgalā, Śāṅkarī, Saumyā, Jātavedā, Manobhavā,
Karālinī, Mahāvegā, Sādhyā, and Satyaparākramā.
Kāntarī, Draviṇī, Raktā, Naṣṭaśatvavināśinī,
Varadā, Śaśinī, Śāstrasvarūpā, and Mivikramā.
Śavarī, Yoginī, Siddhā, Cāṇḍālī, Amṛtā, Dhruvā, Pūṇyā, Dhanyā, Mahāprīti, Prītidā, and Premavihvalā.
Dwelling in the abode of Kṛtānta, she is formidable, fierce, and a performer of severe and great austerities;
she is devoted to the singular welfare of the world, a refuge, and affectionate toward her devotees.
Vāgīśvarī, Śivā, Sūkṣmā, Sarvā, Nityā, Nagātmajā,
Sarvārthasādhanī, Bhadrā, Goṣṭhī, Dhātrī, and Dhanapradā.
Abhayā Gautamī is supreme; at midnight, Śrī fulfills all desires. Abhayā Gautamī is supreme; at midnight, Śrī fulfills all desires.
All the qualities of Tārā’s name fulfill every aspiration;
these one hundred and eight names have been proclaimed out of a desire for the welfare [of beings].
This secret is wonderful and hidden, difficult to attain even for the gods;
it belongs to the Supreme Goddess at dawn, at midnight, or during the night.
O Dear One, whoever should recite this or cause it to be recited every day for six months,
for them there shall be the attainment of all goals, whatever resides in their mind.
This recitation of the one hundred and eight names, performed with the desire for welfare,
brings about good fortune for living beings and destroys all sins.
The wise person, having become pure and composed, who recites this three times a day, shall pacify all diseases and bring happiness at all times.
In no long time at all, he shall attain the glory of sovereignty;
though suffering, he shall be eternally happy, and though poor, he shall become wealthy.
From this, one becomes possessed of great wisdom and intelligence; of this there is no doubt. One who is bound shall be released from bondage, and one shall be victorious in legal disputes.
They alone fall into servitude—even those with horns and those with fangs;
in battle, in peril, or in a difficult pass, there shall be no safety for one who lacks auspiciousness.
By recollecting these names, one removes all evil;
and that person who, having risen in the morning, shall proclaim them.
He shall be long-lived and possessed of a full lifespan, and he shall never be deprived of splendor;
gods, yakṣas, as well as nāgas, gandharvas, and kaṭapūtanas [shall honor him].
The *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and *piśācas*, the *mātṛs* and the divine mothers—
(what has fallen here?)—
on the slope is Kālikā, the skillful Kālikā, the destroyer of Time.
Klīṃ! May [the deity] protect the region of the throat; and klīṃ! May [he] always protect the sides.

May she who is the syllable *klīṃ* and the granter of all desires always protect [me] on the left side; may she who is the syllable *hūṃ* and the granter of all accomplishments always protect [me] at the pair of breasts.
May Huṃkārī, the Great Goddess, protect me always in the region of the shoulders;
may Drīṃ, who resides in all powers, protect my navel and private parts;
and may Svāhā protect me everywhere—in my hands, arms, and feet.
May the goddess Guhyakālī, of great majesty, protect me in all my limbs;
may Kālī protect me always, and may Kapālī protect me at all times.
May the Goddess Durgā, the bestower of all prosperity, protect me always—at the king’s gate, in distress, and in the cremation ground. May she protect me at all times.
May Kurukullā, the granter of all desires, always protect [me] on the seat;
may Vipracittā always protect for the sake of attaining all accomplishments through the body of the funeral pyre.
May she who is ever opposed [to obstacles] protect me, the bestower of all accomplishments;
may the fierce goddess Mahodayā always protect me on the mountain.
May the Goddess of gods, Māyā of fierce splendor, always protect me in the river;
may Dīptā, whose nature is radiant, always protect me at the royal gate.
May Līlā always protect me in the cremation ground for the sake of all accomplishments;
may Sudīptā always protect me on the journey, destroying all obstacles.
May Adīptā, the destroyer of enemies, protect me always while lying down;
may Vidīptā, the bestower of all accomplishments, protect me always while eating.
May the ever-blue Ghanā, beloved of Śiva, protect me in prison;
may Līlā always protect me through her playful presence in every station.
May Mātrā always protect me from association with women;
may Pramātrā, who dwells by the side of the Goddess, always protect me.
May the Mothers, adorned with beautiful ornaments, protect [us] always;
may she who possesses the radiance of a great cloud, the bestower of all accomplishments, protect in the north.
May she of red complexion always protect [me] in the west, the abode of Varuṇa;
may Mahāmāyā, with a smiling face, protect [me] in the northwest.
Adorned with a necklace of serpents, Harasundarī resides in the northeast;
may she who dwells above, bearing the crescent moon, protect [us].
May Ekajaṭā always protect [me] in heaven, on earth, and in the netherworld;
may Lelihānā always protect [me] in the cremation ground, she who destroys enemies.
May she who wears a girdle of corpses protect me in the abode of the pretas;
may she who bears a garland of severed heads protect me—may she protect me everywhere and at all times.
May Śambhusundarī, with the hoods of serpents upon her head, protect me;
may she who holds the son of the corpse and possesses serpent-like arms protect me forever.
May the Goddess Guhyādikālikā, seated upon the back of a corpse, protect [me];
thereafter, may Śavasutā protect me everywhere with all prosperity.
May the three-eyed one, beloved of Śiva, protect me constantly while in prison; may she, with blood dripping from the corners of her mouth, protect me always in times of danger.
May Aṭṭahāsā Mahāmāyā protect me always in Durgā;
may Mahāmāyā Maheśānī protect me always in the cremation ground.
May Mahāmāyā, who dwells in the cremation ground, protect me at all times in battle,
in the cemetery, in the desolate wilderness, in the terrible fortress, and in bondage with fetters.
In times of distress, in mountain fastnesses, on the banks of rivers and the like,
in prisons, in wildernesses, in heaven, in the mortal world, or in the subterranean realm (rasātala).
In dispute, in the midst of enemies, in an assembly, and always in verbal conflict;
likewise in the midst of foes and upon ships—may Kālikā always protect me.
In heaven, may Brahmāṇī, the bestower of Brahman, protect me, O Goddess of gods;
may Māheśvarī, the daughter of the mountain, always protect me on earth.
May Kaumārī, who assumes a beautiful form, protect me constantly during my youth; may Vaiṣṇavī, the beloved of Viṣṇu, always protect me during my worldly affairs.
May she who grants victory and increases triumph always protect [us] in the midst of people;
may Indrāṇī, the Queen of the Gods and bestower of victory, protect us in battle.
May Cāmuṇḍā, the destroyer of enemies, always protect me in foreign lands;
may Lakṣmī, the bestower of all prosperity, always protect me in the private parts.
May Kokilā, accompanied by the circle of Yoginīs, protect everyone at all times; O Goddess, by the recollection of her armor-mantra, one shall obtain the supreme state.
Whether in an impure place or even in a pure one, the wise and intelligent person, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), should always recite this armor-mantra that grants all desires during the day.
A person of great intelligence should especially recite this at night when unable to engage in sexual union;
within six months, that man shall attain scholarship and skill in poetry.
In battle, in gambling, in dispute, in the midst of enemies during combat, in verbal conflict, and in difficult terrain, the wise man should always recite this armor.
O daughter of the mountain, nothing on earth remains unattainable for him;
his enemies shall become his servants, and he shall always be beloved by all.
O Pārvatī, having obtained the grace of the Guru and reciting this armor-panegyric (kavaca), there is nothing unattainable for that wise man within the three worlds.
One should especially write the vidyā with gorocanā and saffron;
by wearing it on the head or even on the arm, one shall bring the entire world under one's control.
One should write this supreme armor-mantra either in a cremation ground or in a remote wilderness,
specifically using red sandalwood, vermilion, and barley.
One should inscribe this armor, difficult even for the gods to obtain, according to the prescribed ritual at night,
when the moon has entered the zodiac sign of Leo and the sun is situated in Cancer.
When Jupiter has entered the sign of Pisces, the preceptor should diligently write [the mantra];
he should always inscribe the Vidyā in a cremation ground for the purpose of slaying enemies.
One should draw the yantra on funeral ashes for the purpose of killing or subjugating an enemy;
one should draw the yantra on cow dung or on a piece of cloth for the purpose of expulsion.
Then, with a golden needle and one-pointed mind, one should draw the yantra;
one should write it with white jasmine flowers according to this procedure.
Since one should write [the mantra] on Tuesday, the day of Saturn, or on the day of Rāhu for the purposes of killing or inciting hatred,
all those [mantras] residing in the armor (kavaca) become effective for him.
Whether it is worn by the Guru or by Vaiṣṇavas, this supreme yantra is prescribed as that which must be served for the sake of attaining the great siddhis, such as aṇimā and the rest.
Then, by reciting the mantra on a Saturday as well as on a Tuesday at the mouth of the Vāruṇa fire upon a funeral pyre, a man shall obtain all perfections.
Whether in an impure place or even in a pure one, he who recites this supreme armor-mantra shall achieve success in all his aims, whatever dwells in his mind.
O beloved, by the recitation of this armor-mantra (*kavaca*), one gains wealth, grain, sons, a wife, and even an elephant within a year.
O Maheśānī, I am not able to describe the greatness of this armor; what more need be said? A man shall obtain all perfections (siddhis).
Thus ends the Armor of Guhyakālī in the Viśvasāra Tantra.
I shall proclaim the sequential hymn of praise; listen, O lotus-faced one!
Having risen during the *muhūrta* sacred to Brahmā, one should pay homage to the Guru and the deities.
Having first resorted to Vāruṇī, one should pay homage above and below;
one should always offer salutations to the gurus and also to their sandals.
Salutations again and again to the Supreme, who is higher than the high and even higher than the highest;
having paid homage to the Supportive Power (Ādhāraśakti), one should pay homage to the Kula tradition.
Having paid homage to the Dharma-activity, salutations indeed to the King of Tortoises;
constant salutations to Anasta, and repeated salutations to Varāha.
Salutation always to the Earth; salutation, repeated salutation, to ancestral traditions;
salutation, repeated salutation, to the oceans, which are eternally filled with jewels, nectar, and waters.
Homage always to the family trees, and indeed homage to the wish-fulfilling tree; homage again and again to the golden lion-thrones and to human beings.
Then, having paid homage in the four directions, one should bow to all the gods;
one should always offer salutations to the Vedas, and repeated salutations to the meanings of the Vedas.
Homage always to those who move upon the earth; homage again and again to those who move through the sky.
Homage always to the yogas as well; homage again and again to the wombs as well.
Homage always to the ḍākinīs; homage again and again to the Rudras as well.
Homage always to the bhūtas; homage again and again to the pretas as well.
Homage always to those who roam the earth; homage always to the yakṣas, and repeated homage to the obstacles.
Homage always to the sages; repeated homage to the lords of sages.
Constant salutations to the royal sages; repeated salutations to the divine sages.
Homage always to the Haṃsas; homage again and again to the Mūrtis. Homage always to the Bhūtas; indeed, homage to the Mahābhūtas.
Salutations always to the teachers; salutations again and again to those who are like Śaṅkara.
Salutations always to the Vaiṣṇavas, and not indeed to those who are mere illusionists.
One should bow constantly to Māyā; salutations again and again to the Tattvas. One should bow constantly to the Bhāvanās and likewise to the Bhāva-śāstras.
Constant salutations to the bodies; repeated salutations to those who are all-pervading.
Constant salutations to the mantras; repeated salutations to the meanings of the mantras.
And salutations to you, O presiding deity of those [letters], whose nature consists of the phonemes;
constant salutations to your feet, salutations again and again to your feet.
Salutations eternally to the meditations and likewise to the treatises on meditation;
salutations again and again to the hymns, the armor-protecting mantras, and even to the names.
Homage always to the scriptures; homage again and again to their meanings;
homage always to the practices derived from them—thus it is proclaimed as the "Supreme Teaching."
Constant salutations to the tastes, and repeated salutations to the fragrances;
constant salutations to the sacred seats (pīṭhas), and repeated salutations to those who reside therein.
I bow eternally even to the *sattvic* beings; salutations again and again to the *rājasas*.
I bow eternally to the *tāmasas*; salutations again and again even to the *guṇas* themselves.
Homage again and again to the perfected ones who have mastered all branches of knowledge;
having paid homage to the root of bliss, salutations indeed to the one whose stalk is consciousness.
Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the universal reality, the lotus, the petals which are the primordial nature (prakṛti),
the seat of accomplishment (siddhipīṭha), and upon Śiva in the form of a corpse;
Homage, constant homage, to the wheel with fifteen spokes;
homage to Kālikā who resides therein, the secret one whose form is desire.
Salutations again and again to Kālikā, from the powers such as Kurukūṇḍā;
salutations, salutations to you who are known as the Supreme and the Non-Supreme; salutations, salutations to her whose supreme power is Śambhu;
to her of wide eyes, who is worshipped by the hosts of gods, and whose lotus feet are honored by both gods and demons.
O Supreme among the supreme, those perfected ones (siddhas) who have donned a garland of human skulls prevail through their partial manifestations;
some declare her to be gross, while all the sages declare her to be subtle and most subtle.
I bow to you, O Ambikā, O large-eyed one; grant auspiciousness to my home.
By thus kissing this lotus-foot of yours, the perfected ones (siddhas) attain supreme power.
O Mother, by means of your name, may the Creator remove from my mind all sins and all sorrows born of the power of this suffering world, through the rite that grants every fruit.
Thus ends the hymn to the Krama of Guhyakālī in the Viśvasāra Tantra.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Viśvasāra Tantra.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who are learned in all the scriptures,
the fifth Vidyā, preceded by Tripura, was previously described.
Sundarī is remembered as the crest-jewel of all the Siddhas;
he related her entire power in accordance with reality.
Having heard those words of hers, the Lord of the World smiled and related everything that Pārvatī had said, according to the prescribed manner.
The illustrious Lord said:
This [teaching] must never be given to one who belongs to the worldly realm, nor to one who is not a disciple by any means;
nor to one who is lacking in devotion, nor to a rogue, nor to a cruel person, nor to one who speaks with obstinacy.
One should give this [text] specifically to Nindākāra, Sucaka, Devala,
Paṭṭikākhyāyana, and likewise to the village priest.
One should not impart knowledge, especially to a Śūdra who is greedy for wealth, gluttonous, and particularly covetous of food. One should especially not give it to such a person.
The practitioner is proclaimed to be either a king or a prince;
some, however, are renunciants who are solely devoted to yoga.
I bow my head with devotion to my peaceful Guru, who is the manifest form of Śiva seated upon the Yoga-pīṭha, for the sake of attaining the perfection of liberation, desire, and wealth.
Having joined together Brahmā, Ādhāraśakti, and Kālāsura-purandara before him, the Goddess should unite Śivā with them.
