The seed-syllable of the Moon (Candra-bīja) is situated at the beginning of Śiva; the seed-syllable of Śiva is near it;
then the seed-syllable of Mādana (Kāma), the enemy-seed (Śatru-bīja), and at the end of that, Bhuvaneśvarī.
The seed-syllable of Śiva situated within the intoxicant (mādana), then the seed-syllable of Śiva again,
the seed-syllable of the Moon, the seed-syllable of the Enemy, and at the end of that, Bhuvaneśvarī.
One should also join together in one place the syllable of the beak situated at the beginning of Śiva, endowed with the moon-bindu,
and the auspicious seed-syllable of the mountain of the earth.
The seed-syllable of Śiva situated upon the Moon, followed by the seed-syllable of Kāma;
having extracted the Moon of Śiva, one should join it with Bhuvaneśvarī.
Having combined everything into one, it becomes the five-times-five syllable;
this Vidyā, consisting of five peaks, is concealed in all Tantras.
O Goddess, O Beloved, this Vidyācūḍāmaṇi has been declared as the most excellent of all;
out of affection for you, I have told it to you, but it must not be told to just anyone.
I bow to that Great Goddess, the fifth, whose nature is the Self, who is eternal, supreme power, and whose form is consciousness.
I bow down to that very fifth [vow], from which everything has arisen and in which it still abides today, and by which victory shall be attained.
It is an underground chamber, adorned with lines of qualities, beautified by four doors,
possessing three circumferences, sixteen petals, and a pericarp of eight parts.
The enemy angle, the four directions, the eight, the trident, and the bindu—
thus is this great wheel, the abode of the highly auspicious Tripurā.
I bow down to the three wheels of the Goddess, who is seated upon a jeweled throne in the temple of the path of Bhavānī, beneath the eternally imagined tree.
May Indra protect me in the east; may the deity Agni protect me in the southeast;
may Yama always protect me in the south; and may Nirṛti protect me in the southwest.
May Varuṇa protect [me] in the west, and the deity Vāyu in the northwest;
may Dhanada protect in the north, and may Īśvara guard me in the northeast.
May Prajāpati protect above, and the deity Ananta below;
thus may the hosts of deities provide protection for the ten directions.
May Gaṇeśa protect me always; may Kṣetreśa protect me always;
may Gaṇanātha protect me forever; may Durgā preserve me.
May Vaṭuka and Bhairava, as well as Kṣetrapāla, protect [us] at the end;
and may the Lord of Kāmadeva, together with Rati and his wife, always [protect us].
Even while dwelling with my husband in the Nandana grove,
may she protect me at the western gate of Cakra, in the Ratnamandira palace of Bhavānī.
May the treasure of Śaṅkha and Padma protect me at all times;
may the jeweled staircase, resplendent with supreme sovereignty, guard me.
One should guard the western door in the Jewel Mansion with Bhavānī;
Sarasvatī, Mahālakṣmī, Mahāmāyā, and Durgā are for the sake of sovereign power.
Bhadrakālī, Cāmuṇḍā, Svāhā, Śubhaṅkarī, Gaurī,
Lokadhātrī, Vāgīśvarī, and the others are mine.
May all these five, stationed here, provide protection at all times within the mandala of the glorious vessel on the southern side of the wheel.
May the mandala of Fire protect [me] during the worship of the Kula goddess,
as well as those beings who cause heresy, whether they dwell upon the earth or in the intermediate space.
May those who reside in the divine realms perish by the command of Śiva;
may all those five deities on the seat bring about auspiciousness.
May Brahmā, the lord of dwellings and the creator, protect me always.
In the full orb of the sun and fire, blazing with smoke-colored rays and heat, may Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Suśrī,
and Surūpā protect me for the attainment of my desires and goals.
Tapanī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvalinī, Ruci,
Sunandā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Vāriṇī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā.
May these digits of the Sun, residing within the solar orb,
together with them, always grant me [fulfillment], O Āditya.
There, within the orb of the Sun, may the nectar-orb of the Moon—
primordial and the cause of Bhairava-bliss— protect [me] at all times.
Amṛtā, Mādanā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭī, Rati,
Dhṛti, Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, and Aṅgadā.
May Pūrṇā, Pūrṇāmṛtā, Kāmadāyinī, and Surasaṃbhavā—
who abide in the center of the lunar mandala— grant protection at all times.
When the moon, the lord of the stars, has attained a full orb and is filled with nectar,
may he protect me at all times.
O Goddess, within the complete solar orb and the lunar orb,
may Ānandabhairava grant me protection at all times.
There, in the fullness of the full nectar, may the power that is the Vāruṇī digit,
whose form is bliss, grant me protection at all times.
May Rudra, the all-pervading Kālānala, who rests upon the foundation of the frog at the base of all,
and who is the primordial nature of the Yamunā, grant me constant protection forever.
Therefore, may she, by virtue of her function as the foundational support (ādhāra-śakti), grant me protection;
may Kūrma protect me constantly, and Ananta always guard me.
May the Boar protect him while his wheel is positioned upon his head;
may the Earth, the bearer of wealth, who rests upon his tusk, protect him eternally.
May the virtuous ocean always protect me with its jewels and nectar-like waters;
may the island of jewels and the golden mountain grant me protection.
May the Nandana grove protect me; may the wish-fulfilling trees guard me. May the variegated jeweled ground beneath them always protect me.
May the auspicious Ratnamandira protect [me] constantly; may the excellent pedestal protect [me] always;
may the Śvetaputra protect [me] forever; and may the jeweled lion-throne protect [me] eternally.
May Dharma and Jñāna protect those standing at the sides of the lion-throne;
may Vairāgya protect [the throne] eternally, and may Aiśvarya protect it always.
May unrighteousness protect me constantly; may ignorance protect me thoroughly;
may lack of detachment protect me, and may lack of sovereignty protect me at all times.
May Māyā, situated in the center of the lion-throne, protect me;
may Vidyā protect me right there, as well as Pañcanāla at all times.
May Kālikā, whose nature is the ultimate reality (tattva), always protect [me] below and above;
may she protect the orb of the sun and protect the orb of the moon.
May the mandala of Agni protect me, and may Sattva always protect me;
may Rajas protect me eternally, and may the quality of Tamas protect me forever.
May Jñāna, Māyā, Kalā, and Vidyā, for the sake of the self of the principles (tattva) and for the manifestation of power,
always provide protection for the Goddess upon her jeweled lion-throne.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva—
may these five great spirits (mahāpreta) grant protection at all times.
May Svadhā protect Vāsana; may Pretāmbujāsana protect me!
May Devyāsana always protect me; may Cakrāsana always protect me!
May the seat of all mantras protect the sādhya and the asiddha equally at all times:
Īśvarī, Sundarī, Vāsinī, Śrī, and Mālinī.
May all the Siddhas, Īśvarīs, and others, as well as the three beginning with Trirā, protect me—
those who are entirely manifest, hidden, and even more hidden.
The family of the tradition (sampradāyakula) consists of those who have emerged from the Kaula and abide in the supreme secret;
it is known as the secret of the higher and lower, and it abides in the primordial secret.
May these hosts of Yoginīs constantly provide protection:
may Aṇimā protect in the west, and Laghimā always in the north.

May Prākāmyā protect [the practitioner] while dwelling in the northwest; may Īśānī protect him in the northeast; likewise, may Bhaktisiddhi grant protection in the south, and may Icchā protect him in the southwest.
May Prāpti, the bestower of all desires, always protect [me] below;
may Sarvakāmā, who dwells above, always protect [me] above.
May Bhairava Asitāṅga, together with Kāmarūpa and Brahmāṇī, protect me at the eastern gate of the sacred seat.
May Rurubhairava, situated in the southeast direction in Malayā and accompanied by Māheśī, protect for the sake of the accomplishment of the Kulācara.
May Caṇḍaka protect on the mountain, and may Kaumārī together with Yama always provide protection for the sake of the success of the worshippers.
May Krodha, accompanied by Bhairavī, always protect [me] in the south-west at Kulānta, the king of sacred seats (pīṭha), for the sake of attaining enjoyment, desire, and wealth.
May Bhairava Unmatta, together with Vārāhī, always protect me at the western gate; may he grant me protection at all times.
In the great sacred seat of Jālandhara, may the Bhairava Kapālī and the Bhairavī Indrāṇī always provide protection for me in the northwest.
May Bhīṣaṇa Bhairava, who is always accompanied by Cāmuṇḍā at the sacred seat of Uḍḍīyānottara, protect practitioners for the sake of their accomplishment.
May the accomplishment of Saṃhāracaṇḍikā at the sacred seat of Devīkoṭa always protect [me] from the northeast for the sake of attaining the Kulāmnāya.
May the Sarvasaṃmohanī mudrā protect [me] always in the west;
may Drāviṇī protect in the north, and Ākarṣiṇī always in the east.
May Unmāda always protect [her] in the delightful south;
may Mahāṅkuśā always protect [her] in the northwest; may Trikhāṇḍā protect [her] in the northeast; and may [she] protect [her] during movement.
May Khecarī, in the form of the seed-syllable in the southwest, protect from above;
may the Yoginī in the form of the yoni, the Mahāmudrā, protect from below.
May these deities, who eternally abide in the wheel and grant all desires,
always provide protection within the square marked by three lines.
She has the form of attracting desire and the form of attracting the intellect;
she has the form of attracting memory and the form of attracting names.
The goddess Amṛtākarṣiṇī, whose form attracts the body—
these eternal ones, moving through the celestial realms, reside upon the sixteen petals of the wheel.
May the goddesses who grant all desired objects provide protection at all times:
Anaṅgakusumā in the east and Anaṅgamekhalā in the south.
In the west is Anaṅgamadanā, in the north Madanāturā;
in the southeast is Anaṅgarekhā, and in the southwest Anaṅgaveginī.
Anaṅgādaśā is in the northwest, and Anaṅgamalinī is in the northeast;
the eight Anaṅgaśaktis are situated in the eight consonant groups beginning with 'ka'.
May those goddesses stationed on the eight petals provide protection at all times:
the power Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī and likewise Sarvavidrāviṇī.
She possesses the power to attract all things, she brings joy to all,
the goddess bestows all desires, and she liberates from all suffering.
The goddess who pacifies all death, destroys all obstacles,
is beautiful in every limb, and bestows all good fortune.
May those residing on the outer ten-spoked wheel always provide protection—
she who is all-knowing, all-powerful, and the bestower of the fruit of all sovereignty.
The Goddess consists of all-knowledge, she is the destroyer of all diseases,
her very nature is the support of all, and likewise the remover of all sins.
The Goddess consists entirely of bliss and is the very embodiment of all protection;
likewise, the Great Goddess bestows the fruits of all desires.
May those residing within the inner wheel always provide protection;
may Vāgdevī, Vāsinī, and Kāmeśvarī protect me.
May Medinī, Vimalā, Patu, Aruṇā, Jayinī,
and Sarveśvarī— the Kaulikī— always grant me protection.
May the goddesses within the eight corners always provide protection;
and may the deities of the weapons—the noose, the goad, the skull-topped staff, and the sword—be ever present.
May the Goddess, residing within the center of the Śrīcakra, grant protection at all times;
may the Youthful One, whose form is that of the limbs, protect the six limbs situated upon the body.
May the Great Goddesses stationed upon the wheel always provide protection;
[may they do so] within the glorious triangle and at its three corners.
May she who is always sharp protect the center; may Kāmeśvarī protect the left, and Pūrṇeśvarī always protect Vajreśvarī.
May Bhagamālinī protect me at the bathing-pīṭha of Jālandhara;
she who dwells in the Bindu-cakra at the pīṭha of the Sun, Moon, and Fire.
May the illustrious Tripurasundarī, whose nature is that of Brahman,
protect [us] within the Trailokyamohana-cakra, which causes the agitation of all things.
Therein, may the eternal Mistress of the Wheel, Tripurasundarī,
protect [us] in the fourteen-spoked wheel which bestows delightful good fortune.
There, may the eternal Mistress of the Wheel, Tripuravāsinī,
protect [me] in the mobile wheel that accomplishes all aims at the outer door.
May Tripurāśrī always protect me for the sake of my welfare,
within the excellent eighteen-spoked wheel that provides all protection.
May the Goddess Tripuramālinī, the eternal Mistress of the Wheel,
protect [us] within the excellent eighteen-spoked wheel that removes all diseases.
May the perfected Goddess Tripurā, the Mistress of the Wheel, protect me always;
may Tripurāmbikā, the Mistress of the Wheel, grant me protection.
In the wheel consisting of all bliss, situated in the center of the illustrious Tripura,
may the Great Mistress of the Wheel, the illustrious Tripurasundarī, protect me.
May Nityā Kāmeśvarī protect me; may Bhagamālinī protect me;
may Chinnā protect me at all times; and may Bheruṇḍā protect me at all times.
May Vahnivāsinī protect me, and likewise Mahāvidyeśvarī;
may Śivadūtī protect me, and Tvaritā always grant me refuge.
May Kulasundarī protect you, and may Nityānityā protect me;
may Nityā, Nīlā, Patākā, and Vijayā protect [me] at all times.
May Śrī Sarvamaṅgalā, garlanded with flames, protect me eternally;
may Vicitrā protect me always, and may Ṣoḍaśī protect me as the beautiful one.
O Hero, may that Great Vidyā, who takes the form of aesthetic essence (rasa), protect me—
she who is the eternal Mahāsaptamī, the constant bestower of bliss.
May the four goddesses of the pledge, the yoginīs, protect [us] at all times:
may Ḍākinī and Rākinī protect, and likewise Rākinī and Rākiṇī.
May Śākinī and Hākinī, the hosts of Yoginīs stationed in the wheel,
and all the Mātṛkās stationed in the field of battle, grant protection at all times.
May the Buddha protect me in the great square wheel;
may the Lord Prajāpati protect me incessantly in the sixteen-spoked wheel.
Likewise, may Śiras protect me in the eight-petaled wheel;
and may Bhāskara always protect me in the fourteen-spoked wheel.
May the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa always protect me on the twelve-spoked wheel;
may the Supreme Goddess protect me within the center of the eight-spoked wheel.
May the Goddess Śrī Tripurasundarī— the eternal Mistress of the nine wheels, who is the eternal, supreme, and transcendent one— protect me incessantly.
May the fifth supreme goddess, who is to be meditated upon as Mahātripurasundarī, who is the very nature of Brahman, protect [us].
May Nirmālyavāsinī always protect [me] in the northeast;
may Śeṣikā and Sundarī, who dwell on the Vindhya mountain, protect me.
May Kāmakalā protect me constantly; may Mudrā protect me;
may Śakti, who dwells in the Mūlādhāra, protect me at all times.
This protective mantra of Tripurasundarī bestows merit;
it has been taught according to the sequence of worship for the benefit and happiness of practitioners.
Having worshipped Śrī Tripurasundarī according to this sequence and method,
the best of practitioners should always recite the protective mantra.
Having become pure at dawn, or at midnight during the night,
or when a crisis has arisen, or in royal territories that are difficult to traverse.
Whether in water, or while moving about, or in a cremation ground, or on an inaccessible mountain— wherever those three conditions are met, a person should recite it everywhere.
Having meditated upon the Goddess as being present in every limb,
the practitioner should diligently perform the protection that destroys all calamities.
This hymn is marvelous and difficult to find even in the three worlds;
it should be guarded with great effort by one who desires his own welfare.
It must never be given to just anyone; it must never be given at any time.
One should reveal it only to a disciple who is endowed with devotion and is a true practitioner.
One should not give [the mantra] even to fallen practitioners or to kinsmen;
for if it is given, there will be a loss of accomplishment—thus was the ignorant act committed toward Śaṅkara.
The mantras turn away, the beautiful woman becomes angry, and misfortune shall befall him; therefore, one should guard [the mantra] with great effort.
In whosever house this supreme written hymn is found,
even the fickle Kamalā remains there, having become steady.
Therefore, one should diligently honor this text with perfumes and flowers; through such worship, the fruit of worship arises eternally, and by virtue of her presence, one becomes beautiful.
Listen now to the fruit that a practitioner obtains from reciting this meritorious King of Hymns with a well-concentrated mind.
Whoever studies this even once obtains the fruit of worship;
such a practitioner becomes renowned on earth as one who knows the Mātṛcakra.
Devoted to worship, one should recite this for one month in due order;
having become renowned even in heaven, the Goddess shall have a son upon the earth.
Or a devotee who, having written this supreme hymn,
should wear it on the crest-lock, or on the neck, or on the left or right hand.
He shall become the best of practitioners and dear to the Mātṛkās;
he obtains all his desires and attains supreme well-being.
Therefore, one should preserve this with effort according to this rite;
having recited it and caused it to be recited, one shall bring the three worlds under one's control.
To whichever devotee this supreme protective mantra is given,
by wearing it encased within gold, one shall thereafter obtain all desires.

Whatever desires they may long for, as well as those things that grant devotion and liberation, one obtains them here on earth, in the creation, or in the subterranean realm (rasātala); of this there is no doubt.
Upon seeing that supreme practitioner, the malevolent grahas, rākṣasas, and beasts of prey flee from afar; indeed, they are not even capable of harming him.
Poison becomes non-poisonous and evils go to their destruction;
having become like a god in mind and speech, one enjoys abundant happiness.
Therefore, the wise person desiring the attainment of liberation, wealth, and purpose should recite this constantly;
with devotion, one should worship the Goddess and always practice thorough protection.
First, there arises thorough knowledge; one knows a thousand births.
One is not born again in a womb, and there is no further death.
Having assumed the form of a Gandharva and worshipped the Supreme Goddess,
and having recited the protective mantra, one certainly attains divinity.
One without a son obtains a son; the poor obtain wealth;
one accomplishes everything that is unachievable, and certainly attains what is difficult to obtain.
In this terrible abode of extreme suffering, amidst fear and the bonds of fetters,
one who recites [this] there with devotion will certainly be released from bondage.
If one afflicted by a chronic disease should worship the Goddess,
or even correctly recite a single verse, he is immediately liberated from that disease.
Delusion, paralysis, deafness, death, and likewise expulsion—these arise from mere visualization; one shall obtain every accomplishment.
This king of hymns to Tripurasundarī is captivating;
it is a protective mantra that bestows auspiciousness, as proclaimed by Śiva.

One should always meditate upon oneself in this way within the mental lotus: as one who possesses a thousand-petaled red lotus umbrella over the head, showering nectar, and being constantly attended by celestial women;
and likewise, one should meditate on the Blessed Lady, whose face is full like a red lotus, thinking, "I am she."
On this earth, one obtains the entire state of protection;

in the brilliantly clear sky, [one beholds] the beautiful lady who consists of all virtues, with red eyes, seated upon a red lotus, resembling the rising sun, and possessing the luster of red sandalwood.
He who always perceives himself as endowed with all states and all qualities becomes manifestly Śiva,
the God who consumed Madana, and he becomes a sky-walker (khecara).
Thus ends the King of Hymns for the Fifth [Tithi] in the venerable Viśvasāra Tantra.
Now I shall explain meditation; listen, O lotus-faced one, by the mere power of which one shall always become a god manifest.
One should always meditate upon the beautiful Goddess of the gods in the center of the heart-lotus,
which has arisen from the bulb of bliss and consists of the nature of the severed stalk.
The circle of the womb (yonimaṇḍala) is joined with the lines of rajas, sattva, and tamas;
it is a great sixteen-petaled lotus endowed with all the qualities of the principles (tattvas).
In the center of that is an eight-petalled lotus endowed with all the qualities of the principles (tattvas);
in its center is a fifteen-spoked [wheel], and beyond that, a nine-cornered [figure].
One should always meditate upon Sundarī within the yantra consisting of Nārāyaṇa, which has a hexagon situated within a triangle and is endowed with the *bindu* and *nāda*.
The Goddess, the slayer of ten million Dānavas, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
clad in red garments, and adorned with various ornaments.
She bore upon her head a crown fashioned from priceless jewels,
and she possessed three eyes that radiated a splendor equal to ten million suns.
She stands upon the heart of Mahādeva in the form of a Śava,
with feet in the pratyālīḍha posture, terrible, with disheveled hair, and naked.
She is endowed with the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra-rasa), possessed of graceful gestures and emotional expressions,
most captivating as she holds the noose, the goad, the boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Having thus meditated upon the Great Power (Mahāśakti), the beautiful Bhavasundarī, who is served by Anaṅga and others, one should worship the goddess Sundarī, who is most enchanting.

One should constantly enter the intoxication of honey through wines, meats, and semen combined with the three sweets and the three [myrobalans], as well as through substances such as burnt or parched items, and through passionate women.
With intoxicated bulls, mongooses, gavayas, porcupines, mice, and the like;
with cats, *śikyadrava* creatures, various newly born animals, and *ādraka* deer that move with swift speed.
When wine, meat, and other such offerings are prescribed by the Anu [Tantra] for the place of the teeth, worship at night is proclaimed by the renowned as being performed in the fixed abode.
Through various yogas, with young women, and with constant, extraordinary sacrifices,
he always offers oblations into the fire of the womb within that meditative absorption.
Thus, for one who worships the goddess Sundarī, the beauty of existence,
the goddess Aṇimā and the other powers, which are mines of virtues, shall come into his hand.
Without wine, without meat, and without [sexual union with] a woman, one should worship Śivā;
yet perfection is not attained therein even in hundreds of millions of kalpas.
O Goddess, for one who constantly chews upon flesh, bone, and marrow, there will be decline day after day; what need is there to mention anything else?
Alternatively, at that very moment his death would occur, without a doubt;
whether he be an ascetic or a king, he is proclaimed to be one who holds authority.
If a practitioner should worship the beautiful goddess with names other than [her own],
he would devour his brother or even his son as a beautiful woman.
I shall proclaim the sequential hymn; listen, O lotus-faced one!
"Oṃ, salutations eternally even to the gurus," and so forth.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who are proficient in all scriptures;
have mercy, O Lord of the world, for you are omniscient and possessed of great intelligence.
And he recounted to her the substance of her armor according to its true nature.
Having heard her words, the Lord of the World smiled and explained to her that entire armor of divine form.
The illustrious Lord said: I shall proclaim the great lore (mahāvidyā) and the armor (kavaca), which are difficult even for the gods to obtain;
listen to that, which is to be kept secret according to the prescribed rite throughout the three worlds.
By her power, the entire triple world shines forth;
from her everything has arisen, and in her it still abides even today.
She is the mother and father, the mother of the world, and the very embodiment of the world’s protection;
she bestows success upon those who seek it, while the wicked are themselves unsuccessful.
O Goddess, you are the creator of all beings and the very essence of all beings;
in the syllable *ka*, may the goddess Kāminī, the bestower of desires, protect me.
May the Goddess, whose nature is the *mūlādhāra*, protect me in the syllable *e*;
may the Goddess Rati, the bestower of all happiness, protect me in the syllable *ī*.
May Indrāṇī, the beloved of Hara, protect me at the syllable *mā* (the letter *ma*). May the goddess, the beautiful consort of Śambhu, protect me everywhere at the syllable *hrīṃ*.
May Mahāmāyā protect the Vāgbhava syllable on my head with these phonemes;
may the goddess Śivānī, the consort of Hara, protect me at the letter *ha*.
May the Goddess, the destroyer of all sins, protect me in the syllable *sa*.
May the Goddess, the digit of the form of desire (*kāmarūpa-kalā*), always protect me in the syllable *ka*.

May the Goddess, assuming the form of the earth that supports all things, protect me during the syllable *la*. May the Goddess, who shares half the body with Śaṅkara, protect me during the syllable *hrīṃ*.

May Mahāmāyā, whose nature is Śakti, protect me with these syllables. May the goddess Sāvitrī, the bestower of bliss, protect me in the syllable *sa*. May she who is the embodiment of the vowels protect the *kalās* everywhere in the syllable *ka*.
May the goddess Lakṣmī, endowed with all auspicious marks, protect me at the syllable *ka*;
may the goddess Tribhuvaneśvarī protect me everywhere at the syllable *hrīṃ*.
May Mahāmāyā, whose nature is Śakti, protect [me] with these syllables;
may Vāgbhava protect my head, and Kāmarājikā my face.
May she whose nature is Śakti protect [me] in the heart for the sake of attaining the mantra;
may Sundarī always protect, may Sundarī preserve [me].
May the red-colored Sundarī, who always bestows happiness, protect me;
may the auspicious Śivā, beautiful in every limb, protect me everywhere and grant me well-being.
May Sundarī, adorned with various ornaments, protect me always;
may she, who brings joy to the world, protect me everywhere at all times.
May she who consists of all mantras protect me; may she who bestows all good fortune protect me;
may she who consists of all prosperity protect me; may she whose form is supreme bliss protect me.
May the Goddess, beloved of the treasure Śaṅkha by name, protect me at all times;
thereafter, may the auspicious Goddess Padmanidhi bestow happiness.
May the sage Dakṣiṇāmūrti protect me everywhere on the head;
may the sovereign goddess Paṅkti, whose nature is the meter, protect me in the mouth.
May Śaṅkarī, whose nature is a deep and resonant voice, protect my heart forever;
may she who fascinates all protect me, and may she who agitates protect me always.
May she who brings all things into manifestation protect [me]; may she whose form is that of universal attraction protect;
may she who causes universal delight and who eternally agitates all protect.
May she who bestows all accomplishments protect me; may she whose form is that of universal attraction protect me;
may she who agitates always protect me; and may she who holds mastery protect me forever.
May Ākartinī protect me always; may Sammohinī protect me always;
may the goddess Ratī protect me always; may Bhagā protect me at all times.
May Bhagā always protect [the organ of] fortune; may Bhagamālā ever protect;
may Bhagasarpiṇī always protect; may Tripurā protect at all times.
May Tripurāmālinī protect me; may Vālā protect me at all times. May Māheśvarī always protect me; may Kaumārī protect me at all times.
May Vāsinī protect me always; may Mahāsiddhi protect me always;
may Sarvavidrāviṇī protect me; and may Gaṇanātha protect me forever.
May Goddess Durgā always protect Vaṭuka; may she protect him at all times.
May Kṣetrapāla always protect him; may Ādhāraśakti protect him.
May Ananta protect [me] always; may Varāha protect [me] always;
may Pṛthivī protect [me] always, as well as the golden lion-throne.
May the ocean of red nectar protect me constantly at all times;
may the one whose vehicle is the moon protect me, and may the wish-fulfilling tree always guard me.
May the white parasol always protect me; may the Jewel Island always guard me;
together with the Nandana grove, may it protect me for the sake of all spiritual accomplishments.
O lotus-faced one, may the world-protectors, Indra and the others, protect you always;
may their mounts always protect you, and may their weapons protect you at all times.
May the missiles protect [us] at all times; may the Yoginīs protect [us] at all times.
May the Siddhas always protect [us], O Goddess, and may you grant all perfections.
May the Goddess, beautiful in all her limbs, protect me everywhere and at all times;
she is the Goddess whose form is bliss, whose nature is consciousness, and whose essence is pure awareness.
And may Sundarī, the beauty of existence, protect me always and everywhere—
on the road, in a temple, in a terrible place, in danger, and on an inaccessible mountain.
In the forest and in the wilderness, O Sundarī, she is auspicious everywhere;
this is called the armor (kavaca), and the extraction of the mantra, O Pārvatī.
Whoever, having risen at dawn, recites this with self-restraint and purity during the three junctions of the day,
for him there shall be the accomplishment of all aims, whatever resides in his mind.
With gorocanā and saffron, or even with red sandalwood,
and with white self-arisen flowers, [one should worship] during the periods of Mars, Saturn, and Venus.
In a cremation ground, or in the wilderness, or in an empty house, or in a temple of Śiva,
having worshipped the Yantra and the Kumārī according to one's capacity and under the guidance of the Guru;
Having worshipped her in that source, and especially the preceptor’s wife,
and having worshipped and praised Vidyuti according to this rite;
Having worshipped the young maiden, one should have the *yantra* retained by the Guru;
and having worshipped it in her vulva and having satisfied the Guru’s wife.
Then, having offered an oblation to the Goddess with men,
cats, mice, mongooses, buffaloes, and black ants, one should worship according to one's means.
Having worn it upon the neck, the head, or the arm— situated in the middle of gold—
on an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable constellation, and likewise during the rising of a noble zodiac sign.
Having worn this armor, a person shall obtain all perfections;
indeed, the majesty of this armor cannot be described even in hundreds of years.
But I am able, O Great Goddess, to describe its fruit as it unfolds:
for him there is no fear of thieves, nor is there any affliction from disease.
Therein, there is no fear of famine, nor likewise any oppression;
it pacifies all obstacles and destroys all diseases.
It provides all protection for living beings and bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
it must never be spoken or given away here or there.
Having received the mantra according to the prescribed rite, the wise person should worship it constantly;
even therein, I consider this armor (kavaca), which is the very form of the deity, to be difficult to obtain.
Having obtained the grace of the Guru and acquired this well-guarded lore, one also acquires the armor; even that substance is difficult to find within the three worlds.
Whoever, being restrained and pure, should recite this verse or this hymn, for him there shall be the accomplishment of all aims; so it was spoken by Śaṅkara.
The Guru is the manifest God Hara, and his wife is the beloved of Hara;
for him who worships them without making any distinction between them, success is not far off.
The disputant becomes mute; the patron acts as a servant; the king behaves like a slave;
the proud man is humbled; and even fire becomes cold for one who knows all things.
I worship and salute that beautiful one, the beloved of Śambhu, who destroys the fear of existence; she is another set of eight Siddhas whose form is the perfection of the eight kinds of food.
Thus ends the Armor of Tripurasundarī in the Viśvasāra Tantra.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, O Mahādeva, you who are expert in the secret scriptures,
please tell me truly the hundred names of Sundarī.
The illustrious Lord said:
"O Goddess, you have asked well, O goddess who brings an end to the afflictions of the gods.
Listen attentively, O Goddess, to the hymn of a hundred names that is being proclaimed."
The practitioner who, having risen early in the morning, recites this with a well-concentrated mind, will directly attain all prosperity and destroy all obstacles.
Having become pure, the supreme practitioner should enter there upon the seat;
all his obstacles flee to the ten directions.
Having concentrated the mind upon the Goddess, who dwells in the pericarp of the heart-lotus,
one should recite the auspicious hymn spoken by Kārttikeya, which bestows all prosperity.
Śrī Kārtikeya said: Oṃ! She is the beautiful one, the supreme sovereign, Bhavānī, the lotus-faced;
she whose abode is the lotus, the great lotus, Lakṣmī, and the eternal Nārāyaṇī.
She is Brahmāṇī, whose form is Brahman, the consort of the Supreme Brahman;
she bestows all spiritual perfections, is Truth itself, holds a noose in her hand, and wields a bow.
Holding a goad and a sword in her hands, she wears various ornaments;
she is the bestower of the eight supernatural powers and is devoted to the Yogaśāstra.
She is auspicious, the giver of desires, and the bestower of all objects of longing;
she is the Great Illusion, the Great Measure, and the destroyer of great delusion.
The yakṣiṇī Hiṅgumāstā is Tārā who dwells in emptiness;
she consists of the fiftyfold divisions of phonemes and is eternally composed of all syllables.
Bhairavī, Sundarī, Bhārā, Kālikā, Citrarūpiṇī,
Ekā, Anekā, Mahetyā, and she who is always the essence of all mantras.
She is Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭkāra, the bestower of all desires;
she is Anaṅgakusumā, Anaṅgamadanā, and Madanāturā.
Anaṅgamekhalā, Anaṅgā, Kāmabījeśvarī, Kalā;
Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, and Ruci.
Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī,
Kṣamā, Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣyā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, and Dhṛti.
Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrīpateraṅgadā,
Pūrṇā, Pūrṇāmṛtā, Kāmadāyinī, Śambhusundarī,
Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, and Visphuliṅginī.
She is of beautiful fortune, compassionate, tawny-hued, and the carrier of offerings to the gods and ancestors;
she is pleased by the flowers of the Self-born One, resides in semen, and is beloved by Śukra.
Abiding in the *bhaga*, having the form of the *bhaga*, and adorned with a garland of *bhagas*—
thus has this divine and auspicious hundred names of the Goddess been told to you.
Having meditated upon the goddess Sundarī, whoever should recite [this] with a well-composed mind, endowed with faith, once, twice, or thrice a day;
The practitioner who, having become pure and being well-composed, should recite this,
shall become the most excellent of practitioners, like another Gaṇeśa.
Whatever one desires arises;
that best of practitioners who recites this at midday for one month shall obtain every such fruit.
Having worshipped the Great Goddess Sundarī, whose essence is Tripura,
he shall become the foremost of all prosperity, like another Kuvera.
The supreme practitioner who recites this at the proper time for two months,
and having recited it for three months, shall become possessed of a son if he was previously sonless.
He who recites [this] for four months shall become a supreme lord of speech;
he who recites it for five months shall obtain a lost kingdom.
He who recites it in the sixth month will always be born wealthy;
when the seventh month has arrived, he shall attain the state of Śaṅkara.
Whoever recites this for eight months in a cremation ground or an empty temple, the destruction of all enemies shall occur for him; there is no doubt about this.
When the ninth month has arrived, he becomes skilled in all yogas;
when the tenth month has arrived, he becomes a wish-fulfilling tree for those who desire.
In the eleventh [chapter] he has the form of Rudra, and in the twelfth he is the Lord of Siddhis;
thus, whoever recites this hymn after having worshipped the Queen of the Gods.
With vermilion, red sandalwood, various beautiful flowers,
as well as dūrvā grass, bilva leaves, kuśa grass, sandalwood, and saffron.
Having performed worship, one should offer the *arghya* oblation to Sundarī Bhavasundarī;
there one shall obtain all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*), as spoken by Kārttikeya.
Having worshipped with vermilion, yellow orpiment, lac, gorocana, and other substances, and having performed the recitation, one should then recite the "Hundred Homages" once more.

Whoever, being well-composed, should recite this daily at dawn, or at the three junctions of the day, or at midnight, or again and again at twilight; ||| on a bed of *śaṣpa* grass, he shall always [attain success].
By the teaching of Śaṅkara, there shall be the complete accomplishment of all [aims] for him who has written [this] on birch bark with gorocanā and other substances, O Dear One.
There, the best of practitioners, having worn [this], shall obtain all accomplishments.
Thus ends the Śrī Tripurasundarī Stotra in the Viśvasāra Tantra.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, expert in all scriptures!
Have mercy, O Lord of the world; you are the knower of dharma, O high-minded one.
"O Supreme Goddess, she who dwells in the Great Lotus Forest, whose form is the bliss of the cause,
and who is the mother for the welfare of all beings," he said.
Having remembered Mahātripurasundarī with the Vāhana-mudrā,
one should invoke the Vidyā with the auspicious gesture of salutation and compassion.
Having meditated upon Mahātripurasundarī in the center of the wheel according to the previously described method, the lords of practitioners should then commence the worship.
Having meditated thus and placed a flower upon his own head, that practitioner,
having washed both hands, should again perform meditation.
Having formed the tortoise-mudrā with both hands, being pure and restrained in speech,
[he should worship] with saffron, flowers, agallochum, and most enchanting sandalwood.
Having prepared a flower combined with musk and having meditated upon it,
one should contemplate the Goddess who has arisen from the *mūlādhāra*, her form perfected as *kuṇḍalinī*.
The Goddess consists entirely of splendor; she brings about the destruction of all dualities.
The Goddess is the embodiment of all speech and likewise the piercer of the six cakras.
Having brought [the deity] through the path of the breath and established her in the center of the mantra according to the previously mentioned procedure, one worships the venerable Tripurasundarī.
Having invoked them, the wise one should worship with various fragrant ointments and various kinds of food offerings,
as well as separate oblations for each.
Having worshipped Sureśvarī according to the prescribed rite with raw and cooked vegetables and excellent soups, one shall obtain the perfection spoken of by Śaṅkara.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
"O Lord of Devas, tell me of the yantra of Sundarī, who is of the nature of Tripurā.
Śrī Īśvara said:

I bow to the Wheel which possesses a central point, a triangle, an outer eight-spoked figure, and an outer primary corner; which is joined with another fourteen-cornered figure; and which consists of a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, a sixteen-petaled lotus, a circle, a square, and a four-faced city-gate.
Thus, having worshipped the beautiful lady of Śrīmātrapura within this Great Wheel (Mahācakra), one attains great siddhi; there is no doubt in this matter.
There too, one should worship the nine very beautiful goddesses:
Anaṅgakusumā, Anaṅgamekhalā, and Madanā, as well as [the others].
Anaṅgarekhārūpiṇī, Anaṅgānaṅgamālinī,
and Śaśirekhā— these are declared to be the nine powers (śaktis) of Sundarī.
Then, by this sequence, one should worship the sixteenth power,
namely Sarvasaṃkṣobhiṇī and likewise Sarvātidrāviṇī.
She possesses the power of universal attraction and is the cause of universal delight;
she is the agitator of all and likewise the deluder of all.
She possesses the power to paralyze all, she is the one who effects the paralysis of all;
she is the goddess who accomplishes all aims and bestows all prosperity.
She adorns all things with virtue, she bestows all accomplishments,
she grants all prosperity, and furthermore, she makes everyone dear.
She is the performer of all auspiciousness and likewise the bestower of all desires;
she is the liberator from all suffering and the destroyer of all death.
She who is beautiful in every limb and the bestower of all prosperity—
a man shall obtain perfection after worshipping her according to the prescribed rite.
Śrī Pārvatī said:
"Have mercy, O Lord of the World! You are omniscient, O high-minded one.
She who was previously mentioned as Sundarī is renowned as Lopāmudrā."
He explained her power according to the ritual rules as it truly is;
having heard those words of hers, the Lord of the World laughed.
He taught that lore, the unsurpassed among all lores.
Śrī Īśvara said:
I shall declare the great lore which was spoken by Brahmā in the past.
Listen to that, which is to be kept strictly secret here according to the prescribed rite throughout the three worlds.
By her power, the entire triple world shines forth;
in her everything was born, and in her it remains even today.
Mother and father are honored by the world, being the very embodiment of the world’s protection;
they grant success to those in the worlds of the perfected ones, while wicked beings are like swords [to them].
She who brings benefit to all beings, she whose own nature is that of all beings,
and she who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon ascetics and householders alike.
Because this [mantra] grants liberation to those who are compassionate and truthful, I shall describe the extraction of the mantra; listen, O lotus-faced one!
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Śiva, one should extract the seed-syllable of Śakti;
then the Kāma-bīja situated upon the Earth (L), and at its end, Bhuvaneśvarī.
One should join there the seed-syllable of the Sun, the seed-syllable of the Moon, followed by *svāhā* and *ahaṃsat*,
and therein [join] that Goddess Māyā, the Sovereign of the Three Worlds.
The supreme goddess Śakti,
conjoined with the seed-syllable of Śiva and united with the Hṛllekhā seed-syllable, is the Vidyā Tripurasundarī.
This fifteen-syllable vidyā is concealed within all tantras;
there is no vidyā equal to it, and it is difficult to find even throughout the three worlds.
Oṃ! May Lopāmudrā protect my head; may she who rides upon a lion protect my forehead.
May Kṛṣṇā protect my eyes; may Bhāratī protect my nose.
May the dweller of Kailāsa, the greatly exalted one, protect the pair of ears;
may the dweller of the face protect [the face]; may the dweller of the tongue and the upper palate protect [them].
May Lalitā protect my neck on all sides; may Piṅgalākṣī protect my heart;
may Dhūmrā protect both my flanks; and may Prāntaravāsinī protect my hips.
May Nitambakusumā protect the genitals;
may Valadāyinī always protect the private parts; may Mitā protect the shanks; and may Tvaritā protect [them].
May Mahāmāyā protect the circle of the knees, and may Lalitā protect [them] from all sides;
may Lopāmudrā, the sovereign of the gods, always protect the pair of feet.
May the goddess Lopāmudrā, the sovereign of the gods, protect me in all my limbs;
may the goddess Lopāmudrā, who brings great prosperity, always protect me in the eastern direction.
May Sundarī protect [me] in the southeast, the south, the southwest, and likewise the west; and in the northwest, the north, and the northeast as well.
May Lopa-mudrā, the beautiful one who bestows happiness, protect you always.
Thus has this divine armor (kavaca), which grants both worldly well-being and liberation, been told to you.
It directly brings about all auspiciousness and destroys great sins.
(Folio lost here. Oṃ, of this *Sahasranāmastotra* of the venerable Śrī Lopāmudrā Tripurasundarī, the Blessed One...

Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi), Anuṣṭubh is the meter (chandas), Ādyāśakti is the primordial power, and the Blessed Lady Śrī Tripurasundarī is the deity; this is the application (viniyoga) for the attainment of the four aims of human life by me. Oṃ, Aśokavāsinī, Āśā, Ādityā, Anurūpiṇī.
Blisses are immovable and immortal; these blisses bestow the wisdom of food.
Āsurī, Alpadā, Śokā, Aśokā, Śokanāśinī, Jayadā, Jitvarā, Yāṅgī, Sukhadā, Śubhadā, and Śubhā.
Manoharā, Mānaśrī, Supālā, Pālinī, and Mahī.
Indrikā, Dīpikā, Kṛṣṇā, Śobhanā, Priyā,
Kāstāvāsinī, and Kṛṣṇā, who possesses a luster equal to that of the moon.
She is camphor, agallochum, and musk; her intellect purifies the three worlds;
she is day, night, and the twilight; she is the great sacrifice and has the form of the moon.
The single and manifold Great Illusion, the Goddess, the Blessed One Kuhū;
she is Aruṇā, the Victorious, the Conquerable, the Conqueror, and the Bestower of all desires.
Bestower of honor, proud, venerable, and worthy of respect, she of great intelligence;
a great meteor, bestower of auspiciousness, secure, and dweller upon all mountains.
Bheruṇḍā, Kurukundā, Kālikā, Vindhyavāsinī,
Nṛmuṇḍahantā, Śastā, and she who wears a garland of severed heads.
Accompanied by latent impressions, she dwells there, intent on the dance of the hungry ghosts;
she is Sundarī, Bhairavī, Ghorā, Pūrṇā, Ghṛṇadā, and Ghṛṇā.
She is the Narmadā, the daughter of Nandin, worthy of praise, and the one to be lauded;
she is the essence of power, the giver of arms, wisdom, and the bestower of all desires.
She is Aindrī, Māheśvarī, Brāhmī, Kaumārī, Kīrtikā, Akali, Rohiṇī, the bestower of auspiciousness, Śvetāṅgī, and she who possesses auspicious marks.
Of noble lineage, she is the source of great security, the bestower of peace, and the increaser of well-being;
she is the deluder, the nourisher, the one satisfied by forbearance, and the one who dries up the mind.
She who is fond of pleasure, the remover of passion, the giver of delight, and the garland of joy;
she is Kaulinī, the bestower of the Kali age, Kalkī, and her body is as dear as the jasmine flower.
She carries [all things], she bestows victory, she is the conqueror, the destroyer of defeat, and she whose characteristic is victory;
she is victory itself, the victress, the triumphant, the source of union, the noble lineage, and the family.
She who knows the mantra is beautiful, truthful, and the giver of beloved food;
she causes hunger and thirst to be agitated, yet she is the destroyer of all agitation.
Nalinī, Nālinī, Nālī, Vāhinī, Ramamānasā,
Māṃsapriyā, Māṃsaruci, and the great Madyapānā.
Helā, Nīlā, Mahāśālī, Dhurjyā, Siṃhavāhinī, Vāyasī, Pūtanā, Kṛtyā, Trailokyabhāvinī, and Rati.
Padminī, Padmahastā, Padmasthā, Padmavāsinī,
Mahāpadmā, Supadmā, Stambhinī, and Śumbhunāśinī.
She has one eye, she has squinting eyes, and she has three eyes; she is the bearer of the trident, the wielder of the trident, the tawny-eyed one, the lotus-like one, and the giver of death.
She is the giver of honor, the one worthy of honor, the destroyer of pride, and the one who causes distress;
she resides in semen, is honored by semen, is the destroyer of semen, and the deluder of semen.
She whose chest is semen, who creates semen, who is served by semen, who is exceedingly seminal;
she who deludes with semen, whose mind is semen, and whose form is the cleansing of semen.
She is the great semen, full of semen, served by semen, and exceedingly seminal;
she is the life-force of the self-arisen flower and is filled with self-arisen flowers.
She is pleased by the worshipper of the Self-Existent (Svayambhū), she bestows delight upon the Self-Existent,
and she is the channels (nāḍīs)— Iḍā, Piṅgalā, and Suṣumnā— who grant auspiciousness.
Gāndhārī, Hastajihvā, Pūṣā, Ālambusā, Matā, Śaṅkhinī, Citriṇī, Vānī, Valinī, Valahānanā, Vaikharī, Kekarī, Kekā, Lalanā,
and Mārgavāhinī.
Mārgadā, Mohinī, Nandā, Manmathapriyavādinī,
Ānandabhairavī, Kālabhairavī, and Kulabhairavī.
She is established as Vaṭukābhairavī, she who abides in strength, the deity of strength;
she is of noble lineage, radiant with jasmine-like earrings, Kāmākhyā, and she who is worshipped by Kāma.
Viśeṣajñavivādā, Vidyujjihvā, Vasundharā, Āvālikā, Vasudā, and the various Kamalavatīs.
Svāhā, Śālā, Mālā, Āryā, Vaipāyinī, Kṛpā, Vāmācāravatī,
Vāmā, and Vāmācāravilāsinī.
Sumati and Kumati, intent on the slaying of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa; the lioness of Niśumbha and Śumbha, the destroyer of Raktabīja; Cāmuṇḍā, Carcikā, the most excellent, who causes manifold emanations.
Śobhanā, Śubhākampā, Kampaśākhitalasthitā,
Yuvatī, Keṭabhī, Jyotsnā, Sumanā, Vimānā, and Mahā.
Pīḍā, Pīḍākṣayakarī, Kahoḍā, Yāminī, Śuci,
Vāruṇī, Indrāṇī, and Sāvitrī, who is the very form of Brahman.
Citriṇī, Citrarūpā, Mayūrapucchadhāriṇī,
Vāyasī, Bhujagā, Bhogā, Kadru, and Vinatā are virtuous.
Guḍāpretā, Viśālākṣī, Satī, Sādhvī,
Virūpiṇī, Vikadru, Śobhanī, Caṇḍī, Pracaṇḍā, and Aticaṇḍikā.
Karālī, Karālākṣā, Vikarālā, and Karālikā;
the destroyer of Daityas and Dānavas, Paiśācī, Yakṣiṇī, and Yati.
Gāndhārī, Gaganā, Gamyā, established in all seeds;
she who grants desires, Tvarā, Citrā, and Vicitracitrarūpiṇī.
She is fearless and the remover of fear; she bestows auspiciousness and destroys inauspiciousness;
she is lightning, the mother of physicians, the poet of the wish-fulfilling tree, and ritual action itself.
Rādhikā, Rūpiṇī, Satyā, Lakṣaṇā, Revatī, Maghā,
Sudantā, Śubhadantā, Adbhūtā, and Aruṇā spoke.
She whose great laughter flashes like lightning, who is bliss personified in the form of Kalki,
who possesses various jewel-lotuses, who is a lotus-pond, and whose abode is the lotus.
Vimboṣṭhī, Lalitā, Cokṣā, Tīkṣṇāṅgī, and Sarvasiddhidā;
Sarvāṅgasundarī, Piṅgā, Padmarūpā, and Manogati.
Viśālā, who dwells at every crossroads with her radiant forbearance;
Nārasiṃhī, Vārāhī, Akulī, Nakulī, and Dhvani.
She who holds a trident in her hand, the vast one, the conqueror, the giver of victory, and the victorious;
she who is the form of death, the remover of death, the giver of time, and the one garlanded with time.
She who bears various weapons, she who is cool, she who destroys all the Daityas;
she who is Svāhā, Svadhā, and Vaṣaṭkāra; she who bestows sacrifice, she who enjoys the sacrifice, and she who possesses all qualities.
Śaramā is immortal, primordial, the destroyer of great illusion;
she is the science consisting of missiles and weapons, dwelling afar and residing in the inaccessible.
The river Sindhu consists of all things, she is the primordial source of all, the bestower of all,
the fierce one, Tārā, Yaśodā, Nīlā, and the blue Sarasvatī.
She is victorious, the night, as flickering as lightning, the one who utters sweet flatteries;
she is the embodiment of fortune, of great form, possessing manifold manifestations and a body of radiant light.
Susīmā, Mahāsīmā, Ameyā, Khecarī,
Kriyā, Sūryakānti, Candrakānti, and Priyaṅkarī.
She who bears a garland of skulls, she who sports in all the scriptures,
she who possesses knowledge, she who is the earth, she who is the Gaṅgā, she who is Kāśī, and she who is Satīpurā.
Nagadā, Maradā, Rājalakṣmī,
Manāgapi, Vimanas, Sumanas, Śambhu, Śāmbhavī, and Haṃsarūpiṇī.
Mātā, Pitā, and Vipulā, who moves with the gait of a lordly elephant;
Līlā, Mālā, Tathyā, Subhakṣyā, and Atirāgmitā.
She who possesses sons, she who is the form of a son, the dear child, the one devoted to her calf,
the knower of danger, the one beyond delusion, the formidable, and the lunar day of deception.

She who is asleep, awake, and fast asleep; she of pure eyes and expansive body; she who utters the sound "huṃ"; she whose form is the seed-syllable; she who utters the sound "drīṃ-ūṃ"; and she whose form is the seed-syllable.
Hrī, Śrī, Gāṅgī, Gāndhārī, Suguṇā, Vipulāstanī, Kamalī, Yuvatī, Satyā, Stavanīyā, and Māmadohṛtā.
She is Śitalā and Suśīlā, the giver of wind and she whose form is wind;
she is fond of bulls, mounted upon a bull, and has a bull as her vehicle.
Hūti, Niti, Sunīti, Kailāśavāsinī,
Kṛti, Kālarūpā, Karālā, Amitā, Asitā, and Sitā.

Sunīti, Suruci, Kānti, Kṛṣṇā, Akṛṣṇā, and Kṛśāṅgikā.
Vajrāṅgī, Vajrahastā, Guruhastā, Sarasvatī, Atasī, Kulaṭā, Ceṣṭā, Bhartārā, Noḍinī, and Bhūtā.
She who speaks much, she who is affectionate, she who is well-devoted, and she who is compassionate toward her devotees;
she who is tender toward her children, she who is abundant, she who is the shore, she who is a maiden, she who is Gaurī, and she who is Rohiṇī.
She is a young woman with tremulous eyes, with restless eyes, of auspicious and slender form;
she has a long nose, is unevenly toothed, bestows a pair [of boons], and has teeth set in pairs.
Avajā, Gojā, Kṣatriyā, Vijayā, Jayarūpiṇī, Śaṅkhinī, Ṭiviṭitvā, Kṣaṭvi, and Ghāṭī Svarūpiṇī.
Having become embodied and then withdrawn from it, she is past all worldly ties and devoted to her Lord;

Ceṣṭā, Śānti, Śāmbhavī, Carcikā, Caṇḍarūpiṇī, Kulaṭā, Yuvatī, Vanyā, Sarvāṅgasundarī, and Sudhā.
Kekarākṣī, Kṛśāṅgī, Śaśī, Tāmasī, Dayā, Gāndhārī, Vivaśā, Viśvā, Vikaṭākṣā, and Kaṭākṣiṇī.
She is gentle, like the moon, or Lalitā with four faces;
she is Kārtikī, Kulajā, Kuntī, Kuntarūpā, and Kumudvatī.
Possessing a radiance equal to the sun's brilliance mingled with the lunar orb, she was as flickering as lightning; large-eyed, beautiful-eyed, and lovely of gaze.
She has the eyes of a deer, she is fawn-eyed, she is of restless gaze, and she is the restless one;
she is the trembling one, the great delusion, and the destroyer of great intoxication.
A Yakṣiṇī of noble birth or one possessing a noble lineage, appearing in the form of a Yakṣa;
she is Kākinī and Bhallukā, and she has vanished in the form of Ojarūpiṇī.
Cicituṭā, Visarpiṇī, Vitānī, Vipulānanā,
Hiḍambā, Durghaṭā, Jñeyā, Vakāsyā, and Priyavādinī.
Kairātī and Koṇarūpā, adorned with the family of Kukkuta;
Śānta and Śāntirūpā, Sumatī and Sumanapriyā.
She has tawny eyes and three eyes; she is ruddy and the bestower of victory.

Vetālī, Vipulā, Mohā, and Mahāmohavivarjitā;
Anantā, Satyavādī, Nityā, and Nityasvarūpiṇī.
She whose garland is the *liṅga*, who is adorned with a garland of *bhagas* around her neck;
she whose limbs are *bhagas*, the sister, enjoyment itself, delusion of the *bhaga*, and whose very self is the *bhaga*.
Kātyayanī, Jaganmātā, Sumātā, Madanāvatī,
Vipāśā, Sukeśā, Hemā, Aninā, and Pulopamā.
Indrākṣī, Vāruṇī, Yakṣā, Yonimudrā, Dhanapriyā,
Anaṅgakusumā, Anaṅgamekhalā, and Madanāturā.
Ambikā, Hrādinī, Durgā, Svarūpā, Hūṃ-svarūpiṇī,
Suṣumnā, Iḍā, Yogavatī, Bhairavī, and Vaṭubhairavī.
Kālī, Vālī, Gālī, Susamā,
Sāmagāyinī, Gāyatrī, Yamunā, Yāmā, Sasatvā, and Varadāyinī.

Dāntī, Kumbhahantā, Ahaṃkārākṛti herself,
Jīvā, Parātmā, and likewise Kuṇḍalinī are so remembered.
O life-breath of women, you who dwell in the sacrificial pit of the womb;
you are the Gaṅgā, the hundredfold splendor of Kāśī, the exquisite beauty, the most beautiful, and the maker of splendor.

She is the existent one, the true, and the perfectly true; she is the agitator of the assembly, the one from whom the world arises, the flower-like, the object of desire, the sovereign of the king of desires, and action itself.

she is the garland of letters, the garland of mantras, consisting of all mantras, the auspicious Śivā.
Adorned with every ornament, colored by the kalamañjīra,
she is the movement of the five elements, the embodiment of love, and dwells within the great elements.
She who possesses evil intent, who is difficult to attain, who is hard to sing of, and who dwells in inaccessible places;
she whose sovereign power is vast, yet who has vanished, perished, and whose path is bowed down.
The Goddess Nirmālyavāsinī, Śeyikā, and Sundarī; likewise Caṇḍeśvarī, Vijayā, Ugracaṇḍā, and Pracaṇḍikā.
She is known as Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā, Caṇḍī, and the goddess Caṇḍadevī; she is Mātulānī, Pipāṭhī, Rākṣasī, Yoginī, and Javā.
Kuśalā, Kuśalyā, Kuntī, Kumudā, Kṛpā,
Haṃsamukhī, Śucimukhī, Vinatā, Lalitā, and Tridhā.
Vaṅkṣu-mudrā, Revatī, Kāverī, Savitā, Amṛtā,
Girikā, Vānarī, Vālā, Bhūṣaṇā, and likewise Uṣitā.
Bhānumatī, Citralekhā, Viśākhā, Śikhinartakī, Mohinī, Toṣiṇī, Stutyā, Stavanīyā, and Subhāvinī.
Kiṅkiṇī, Caṅkinī, Citrā, Yoginī, and Yogadāyinī;
