She is the knower of the meaning of all truths, as well as the embodiment of all scriptures;
she is Mālāvatī, with a serpent in her hand and a snake serving as her sacred thread.
The Ḍākinī, Varṇinī, Ghorā, Vajrapuṣpā, Tilottamā, Asitā,
and Kurukullā, who are the very nature of the wheel of the bindu.
She is Heat (uṣmā) and the drinker of heat (uṣmapā), whose nature is the Sound-Brahman (śabdabrahman);
she is the ascetic woman (tāpasinī), the night of destruction (niśārātri), and the one who differentiates the sounds of resonance (nāda).
Rastoru, Caturākārā, Kumārī, Vṛṣabhāsurī, Śarmiṣṭhā, Yādavī, Yajñā, and she who is the embodiment of all powers.
Then the Ācāryā, as well as the noble Aṅkuśī and Tomarī;
the goddess Kuṇḍātmikā, who is Kuṇḍā, the performer of sacrifice, and the beloved of sacrifice.
She whose abode is the Ṛg, Sāman, and Atharva Vedas, who is the very embodiment of the branches of the Veda,
the lovely maiden Śatākṣī, and likewise Hṛtadyuti.
Dhātrī, Kartrī, and Indrī—the auspicious daughters of the King of Kāśī—and the Yoginī Ākāśavāsinī reside within my wisdom; this is the offering (bali).
Vetālī, Ripuṇā, Śvetā, as well as Guṇavatī, Mati, Praphullā, Phullarūpā, and likewise Kulavatī and Kulā.
Phetkāriṇī, the mother of mantras, who dwells in the nasal vowel (anusvāra),
she who brings bliss to her devotees, worthy of praise, and the auspicious one to be lauded.
Arpaṇā, Niścalā, Lolā, Vidyā, Vidyāvatī, Vibhītikā, Mṛtyu, Māriṇī, and Mṛtyunāśinī.
Immeasurable, like the tamarind tree, skillful, slender-limbed, with thin arms and a whip-like waist;
she is of heroic stride, rare, unblemished, and always spreading like a diamond-studded carpet.
Sundarāṅgī, Surāṅgī, Kuraṅgī,
Śaralālikā, Nagīśvarī, Akāmā, Avaśā, and Graha-anu.
She is the deluder and the non-deluder, the immortal one, the earthen, and she whose form is wine;
she is the one who causes trembling, the one who cuts through, the embrace, and she who dwells within the form of the hair.
She is the syllable Kūrca, the form of Time, dwelling in the wheel of the Bindu;
she is Viṣaṇā, Viṣayā, Vaiśyā, Kṣatriyāṇī, and the compassionate Kṛpāvatī.
Born from the bulb of bliss, she is bliss itself; her eyes are rays of light.
She is the unreal form, the barbarian, and the Veda that is exceedingly fond of speech and conduct.
Pramoṣā, Premnā, Apremā, Sādhakā, Bhakti, Raktapā—
this is proclaimed as the Thousand Names of Lopāmudrā.
By the mere grace of her, one becomes Nārāyaṇa himself;
the sonless obtains a son, and the destitute becomes wealthy.
A king attains victory, a Kṣatriya woman becomes blessed with virtuous sons,
a Vaiśya shall have an abundance of wealth, and even a mute person shall become a skilled poet.
One becomes free from disease, wealthy, and liberated from chronic ailments;
having touched two women in their menses, one should recite this vidyā day and night.
Like Kuvera, he becomes unsurpassed in wealth;
having become intent upon the wives of others, he should recite the vidyā day and night.
With authority and with his mind, that very wise Śrī Sadāśiva himself should always perform the sacrifice of the messenger (dūtīyāga) day after day.
By touching, seeing, praising, and reciting the Mahāvidyā of a woman in her menses, a man shall attain all perfections.
One who seeks dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa should recite [the mantra] in a supreme womb;
having adorned his hands with self-manifested kusa-grass rings, the wise one should always recite it.
One should worship the Goddess with supreme devotion, especially with white flowers;
one should worship the Mother of the World with white, self-originated blossoms.
With single-minded concentration, one of vast intellect should draw the yantra upon a birch leaf using yellow orpiment, saffron, lac,
sandalwood, and fragrant pastes.
One should draw the yantra in an empty dwelling according to one's ability and with all sincerity;
having meditated upon that beautiful consort of Śambhu, one should worship the Goddess according to the prescribed rite.
Having worshipped, one should wear the yantra; [one should worship] Kumārī, the daughter of the Mountain.
On the night of the new moon of the month of Bhādrapada, one whose life remains for three quarters of a day should offer a bali-oblation.
A skilled practitioner should offer liquor along with cocks, mongooses, rams, buffaloes, mice, men, burnt fish, and burnt substances.
There, the one of vast intelligence should recite [the mantra] one thousand and eight times;
then he should utter the words "Come, come" and offer it to the Goddess.
One should constantly sip a handful of water used for washing the vulva;
such a person shall become the foremost among the prosperous, like another Kuvera.
He shall possess a lifespan like that of Mārkaṇḍeya, be free from fever and grey hair,
have eloquence like Bṛhaspati, and be comparable to Madana in beauty.
If one should always worship the Goddess without wine and without meat,
accomplishment will not arise for him even in hundreds of millions of eons.
The best among all possessors of knowledge, of noble lineage, and pleasing to behold—O Goddess, what else need be said? By means of this vehicle, a man shall obtain the fourfold aims of life.
Thus ends the Thousand-Name Hymn to Tripurasundarī in the Viśvasāra Tantra.
Now I shall proclaim the great vidyā, Sundarī, consisting of sixteen syllables,
by whose mere sidelong glance one becomes Nārāyaṇa in person.
The kingdom may be given, Śiva may be given, but the sixteen-syllable [mantra] must not be given;
for each single mātrā of Sundarī is Śiva himself, the bearer of the Gaṅgā.
What is the use of wealth, what use of people, or even servants and kinsmen?
Through mere knowledge and realization alone, one becomes the supreme Gaṅgādhara.
He is indeed a Vaiṣṇava, he is a Śākta, and he alone is always a true Brāhmaṇa;
he is the best among all possessors of knowledge, a yogi who increases spiritual accomplishments.
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall describe the most beautiful extraction of the mantra;
listen with supreme devotion for the sake of accomplishing all desires and goals.
This manifold knowledge was told by the Lotus-born One to Nārada during the Pādma Kalpa; now, in this very place, I am telling it to you.
When the vidyā of Lakṣmī and Nārāyaṇa begins with the seed-syllable *śrīṃ*,
or when the vidyā begins with *lajjā* (the seed-syllable of Lajjā), one shall become honored by the gods.
Having brought saṃsāra under control, one shall become personally dear to Śambhu;
or when passion and the other [afflictions] become the Vidyā, she becomes the sovereign of the three worlds.
She is declared to be Brahmāṇī when she is joined with Vedavyāsa;
and when that beautiful woman is joined with Śivaprāsāda, she is likewise so designated.
Then that very [Vidyā] shall be eternal, bestowing the state of Maheśvara;
thus was the Vidyā described by Śiva in manifold ways during the Kṛta Yuga.
The Great Vidyā is proclaimed in many ways according to the differences of regions;
now I shall describe the Great Vidyā that bestows the abundance of all accomplishments.
By whose mere sidelong glance one becomes the sovereign of the three worlds—that is Mādana; that day is Śakti; and within that is Bindumālinī.
Situated in the center of the seed-syllable of Indra (Aim), joined with the flaming syllable (Ra),
conjoined with Māyā (I) and the Mistress of the Bindu (H), she is placed above all.
O Goddess, this is that Vāgbhava, which bestows the state of Lord of Speech;
it is the seed-syllable of Śiva, divided threefold according to the sequence of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
The first [syllable] is devoid of the pair [of bindu and nāda]; it is the syllable of Madana (the letter *ma*) without the arrow (*i*).
Again, one should join the seed-syllable of Indra (*la*) situated below the letter *śa* of Sthiti.
Likewise, O Maheśvarī, even below "Namaḥ Śivāya" is the blazing sun (ra),
conjoined with the fourth vowel (ī) and adorned with the bindu, the crescent moon, and the half-moon.
Thus it is: this great seed-syllable is the king of desire, of great success;
it has *māyā* as its seed, O Great Goddess, and is the intoxicant joined with the enemy.
O fair-faced goddess, having extracted the seed-syllable of the Moon alone,
O Goddess, one should abandon the sequence of emanation and proceed instead by the sequence of purification.
By means of the yoga of the sequence of withdrawal, one should extract the seed-syllable of Śakti;
this is declared as Śrī in all tantras by the Lotus-Bearer.
Beyond this, there exists no higher great knowledge (mahāvidyā) in the three worlds;
it is the embodiment of all knowledge and bestows both heaven and liberation.
The Goddess is the bestower of all desires and is the very embodiment of all desires;
just as the vital breaths follow [the soul], so too does the sixteenth [digit].
She whose form resembles vermilion, who is beautified by three eyes,
and who is seated upon the heart of Mahādeva in the form of a corpse.
The Goddess, wearing a garland of severed heads and having a serpent as her sacred thread,
is adorned with various ornaments and attended by Siddhas and Gandharvas.
One should always meditate upon Pārvatī, who is naked, most formidable, with disheveled hair and a large belly, and who is the abode of all beauty.
And those other mantras and so forth that have arisen from her limbs—
great, great, great vidyās, great mantras, most great!
The origin of her limbs was described by the Lotus-born One;
just as among the Purāṇas the Mahābhārata is said to be the most excellent.
Just as the Śrīmad Bhāgavata is declared among the Pāramahaṃsya scriptures,
so too is Nārāyaṇa-Nara the embodiment of non-dual realization.
Among bipeds, the best is the foremost of the twice-born; among constellations, the moon;
among the senses, the mind is the best; and among mountains, the Himalaya.
Just as the Gaṅgā is among rivers, as the knower of the Vedas is among Brāhmaṇas,
as Śambhu is among Vaiṣṇavas, and as the Āgama itself is among the scriptures;
Among the sciences, this is the Great Science (Mahāvidyā) proclaimed by Śrī;
herein there is no requirement for supernatural powers (siddhi) and the like, nor is there any obstacle from friends and so forth.
In this place, there shall be no consideration regarding food; there is no restriction concerning location;
there is no great expenditure of mental effort, nor is there any outcaste status whatsoever.
One should worship Sundarī with supreme devotion in every way;
then, [one should draw] a hexagon, a nonagon, and thereafter a triangle.
One should draw the yantra upon one another, adorned with the circle of the yoni,
provided with eight petals and the lines of passion, existence, and darkness.
One should contemplate the great powers, Anaṅgā and the others, within the petals here;

one should worship the goddess Sundarī, whose nature is Śrī, in the triangle. One should always perform the placement [of mantras] upon the body of the beautiful woman with the previously mentioned groups of nyāsas.
One should install the supreme goddess, who is known as consisting of the nine wombs;
having installed her in the form of a womb, one should meditate upon that Great Goddess.

One should always perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) consisting of the nine wombs upon the body of the daughter [of the Guru] according to this method; O Goddess of the Gods, this is known as the nine-womb essence.
Having performed the placement of the supreme Vāgbhava seed-syllable from the navel upwards,
one should always place the Kāma seed-syllable from the heart down to the navel.
One should always place the seed-syllable of Śakti from the head down to the region of the heart;
for one should then place the first and second [syllables] upon the two hands with the supreme [devotion].
The third is known as the essence of both, consisting of the non-vagina (navayoni);
one should place the three seed-syllables again in sequence upon the head, the support, and the heart.
One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) consisting of the nine wombs according to this procedure;
one should place them in sequence using the three seed-syllables through the application of the proper order.
One should form a triangular shape like a vulva at the ears and the chin;
then one should form it at the shoulders, the mouth, the eyes, and the nose.
One should place [the syllables] on the two shoulders and then on the two sides of the chest;
they should be at the knees, the base of the arms, the feet, and the private region.
One should then perform the placement [of mantras] consisting of nine yonis upon the two sides, the heart, the throat, and the two breasts;
this is the authoritative method for the Great Vidyā.
One should likewise perform [the worship] for Chinnamastā, Kālikā, Sundarī, and Śrīvidyā; this is remembered as consisting of the nine yonis.
Then one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) beginning with Rati according to this procedure:
having placed Rati at the mūlādhāra, one should then place Prīti in the heart.
One should place the incense of the roots and so forth upon the head in both reverse and direct order,
[worshipping] Amṛteśī, Yogeśī, and Viśvageśa again and again.
One should then place these [syllables] in sequence upon the crown of the head, the mouth, the heart, the secret place, and the two feet, arranging them two by two according to the prescribed rule.
The root seed-syllable is declared to be each [deity's] own initial letter joined with the nasal bindu;
one should place the mind-born [syllable] on the head according to the rule by means of Īśāna.
One should place Tatpuruṣa, joined with Makaradhvaja, in the mouth;
one should place Aghora in the east, and then Kandarpa in the heart.
One should place Manmatha, conjoined with Devādya and others, in the secret organ on the left;
and Sadyojāta, together with Kāmadeva, in the pair of feet.
Then one should contemplate oneself as having five faces, like Śiva;
[one should place] those [mantras] upon the faces facing upwards, east, south, north, and west.
One should perform the placement with the intellect according to the previously mentioned procedure for Hṛllekhā and the rest;
then, having encased the [syllables] beginning with the Kāma-bīja with the Hṛllekhās.
The instructor should contemplate the five-faced one with this color:
like a pearl, a yellow cloud, a pearl, and the color of barley.
By means of the upward sequence and through the practice of clockwise rotation,
it is joined with the syllables *bhuṇḍa*, *vyoma*, and *agni*, and endowed with the long vowels.
The presiding deity of the mouth is conjoined with the drop (bindu) and the nasal point (indu);
alternatively, it consists of the five short vowels preceded by the syllable Oṃ.
Sprinkling [the water] in reverse order, one should perform the placement again and again;
O Goddess, one should place the five forms according to the sequence beginning with the head.
One should place Drāviṇī, preceded by *krīṃ*, on the head; Kṣobhiṇī, preceded by *hrīṃ*, on the feet;
Vaśīkaraṇa, preceded by *klīṃ*, on the mouth; and [Khecarī], preceded by the seed-syllable *hūṃ*, on the secret place.
Again, in the heart, one should place Ākarṣiṇī joined with the Bhṛṇḍa [mantra] from heaven and so forth;
likewise, Sammohinī follows in sequence—this is declared to be the deposition of the letters (varṇanyāsa).
The five stars beginning with Subhaga are located in the forehead, between the eyebrows, the face, the throat, the navel, and the two foundations (the feet).
One should place all [the goddesses], beginning with Kāmabījā, who are devoid of intoxication and delusion;
Subhagā, Acyā, and all the others, as well as Subhagā and Bhagā.
Then Bhagasarpiṇī, followed by Bhagamālinī;
then Anaṅgā, Anaṅgakusumā, and again Anaṅgamekhalā.
The letters are the primary deities, free from the agitation of all intoxication by the bodiless Love (Anaṅga), adorned with ornaments and the like.
Holding a garland of skulls and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, they are bestowers of auspiciousness;
[they embody] Vāgbhava, Kāmarāja, Varuṇa, and [the seed-syllable] joined with Indra.
This third [syllable] is said to be mounted upon the drop (bindu);
it is declared to be the seed-syllable of Lajjā, conjoined with the six seed-syllables.
The fifth seed-syllable, consisting of the lunar seed joined with heaven (Svarga), has been told to you;
the preceptor should briefly install these seed-syllables beginning with Subhagā.
One should place the vowels on the head, the forehead, the ears, the two eyes, the pair of nostrils, the pair of cheeks, the pair of lips,
the teeth, and the mouth; [and likewise] on the chin, the throat, the two sides, and the pair of breasts.
On the two lower arms, on the two elbows, on the two hands, and on the region of their backs.
Then at the navel, the secret place, the thighs, the knees, and the shanks;
thereafter at the buttocks, the soles of the feet, and finally on both toes of the feet.
The preceptor should assign those letters beginning with *ka* to these locations:
again, he should assign them to the waist, the neck, the throat, the heart, and the secret place.

Then, one should place the syllables beginning with the seed-syllable of Kāma (Klīm) according to the prescribed ritual upon the ears, the cheeks, the head, the mouth, and the two great eyes of the Rākṣasa.
Having encased [the mantras] beginning with Māyā in both reverse and direct order,
the preceptor should then perform the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa) according to this procedure.
The Guru should place those [syllables] beginning with *mā* upon the body in reverse order, by the mere placement of which the knowledge of reality arises.
One should perform [the ritual] up to the *kṣānti* [syllable], and thereafter I shall explain it according to its true nature (*tattvataḥ*):
first the *praṇava*, then the one beginning with *kāma*, and again the *māyā* and *kūrca* [syllables].
The preceptor should place the phonemes in their respective locations according to this procedure;
the preceptor should place them with the *anusvāra* and ending in *namaḥ* in their appropriate positions.
The instructor should place the word "paraṃ" ending in the dative case in its proper location;
then, he should contemplate the individual soul (*jīvātman*) and the letter *ma* upon all the limbs.
One should personally contemplate the syllable *bha* for the self of vital breath (*prāṇātman*) in all limbs;
and one should personally contemplate the syllable *va* for the self of intellect (*buddhyātman*) in the heart.
The letter *ka* is situated in the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the letter *pa* is situated in the mind (*manas*);
there, the preceptor should place them in the heart according to this procedure.
One should always contemplate the word "parā" and the word "śabdārtha" everywhere; one should always place the syllable *na*, which is the essence of sound, upon the pair of feet and on the head.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) by uttering the syllable *dhakāra* for the essence of touch at the mouth;
one should contemplate the syllable *dakāra* for the essence of form at the heart.
Then one should place the letter *tha*, whose essence is taste (*rasa*), upon the *liṅga*;
thereafter, one should place the letter *ta*, whose essence is fragrance (*gandha*), upon the pair of feet.
O Pārvatī, one should place the syllable *ṇa* in the ear for the self of hearing,
and one should contemplate the syllable *ḍa* in both eyes for the self of sight.
One should again place the syllable *ṭha*, the essence of the tongue, upon the tongue;
and one should contemplate the syllable *ṭa*, the essence of the sense of smell, upon the nose.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the letter *ña* upon speech for the self of speech;
thereafter, one should place the letter *ṛ* upon both hands for the self of merit.

One should then sequentially place the syllable *ja*, whose essence is the lotus, in the region of the anus; thereafter, one should place the syllable *ha*, whose essence is the feet, in the location of the feet.
One should place the letter *ca* on the genitals for the self of the generative organ (*upasthātman*),
and perform the placement of the letter *ṅa* on the head for the self of space (*vyomātman*).
One should sequentially place the syllable *gha* at the region of the navel for the self of passion (*rāgātman*),
and one should perform the heart-assignment (*hṛdinyāsa*) with the syllable *ga* for the self of splendor (*tejasātman*).
One should sequentially place the syllable *tha* for the water-self (*jalātman*) in the secret region,
and then place the syllable *ka* for the earth-self (*pṛthivyātman*) on the two feet.
In the same manner, one should place [the letters] up to the letter *kṣa* by means of this yoga and according to this rite.
One should place the letter *ya* in the heart for Saṅkarṣaṇa, who is the soul of the Puruṣa.
One should place the syllable 'ra' in the heart for Pradyumna, the soul of the universe;
and one should place the syllable 'la' for Aniruddha, whose nature is cessation (nivṛtti).
Again, one should place the syllable *va* in the heart for Nārāyaṇa, the Self of All,
who is joined with the three lunar mandalas and endowed with the sixteen digits (*kalās*).
One should place the letter *ya* upon the body, as is approved in the Tantras;
furthermore, one should place it at the heart for Vāsudeva, the Supreme Self.
One should perform the placement of the letter *sa* for the self of semen according to this procedure;
and the letter *ha*, which is prescribed for the heart for the Sun, is sanctioned by the Tantras.
One should place [the letter] for Nṛsiṃha, whose nature is wrath, upon all the limbs and the skin;
the letter *kṣa* is proclaimed to be pervasive among all the phonemes.
Those who know the principles of ritual assignment (nyāsa) declare this to be the *tattva-nyāsa*; without the application of its various groups [of syllables], success can never be attained.
Having thus recited it, one should then perform the sixfold placement (ṣoḍhānyāsa). O Goddess of the gods, I shall hereafter describe the sixfold placement that follows.
Having thus performed the installation of the body (*nyāsatanu*), one should worship the eternal Goddess;
thereafter [worship] Anaṅgā, Anaṅgamadanā, and Kāmeśvarī.
One should worship Bhagamālinī and Bhagā as these Śaktis; or else, one may worship the Śaktis beginning with Icchā, as they are endowed with all the Tantras.
He who worships these principal female deities in their proper order— Rati, Ratipriyā, and Nandā— who hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, shall attain success.
One should worship all [the goddesses] upon the body of the Goddess, adorned with the ornaments of the Goddess;
all [of them], beginning with the seed-syllable of Kāma (Klīm) and ending with "Namaḥ," according to the Tantric tradition.
One should utter the word "Citsvarūpām" ending in the feminine suffix *ṅī*, followed by "vidmahe";
then, having pronounced "Jālandharīm," one should utter "dhīmahi" immediately thereafter.
Having extracted that from us, O Goddess, may the Goddess inspire us.
This is the Gāyatrī of the King of Mantras, esteemed by Śiva.
One may recite the mantra beginning with *kāma* (Klīm), or one should recite the Vidyā beginning with *māyā* (Hrīṃ) for the attainment of dharma, kāma, and artha;
or one may worship the Vidyā beginning with *kūrca* (Hūṃ), or even that beginning with the seed-syllable of the *vadhū*.
Gāyatrī is proclaimed to be the foremost of all mantra-vidyās;
beginning with Oṃ and ending with Namaḥ, these vidyās are for the purpose of distinguishing the seats.
One should utter Sadāśiva ending in the suffix -Ṅ, followed by the word Mahāpreta;
then the seat of the Goddess (Devī-āsana) in the dative case, and at its end, the Heart mantra again.
Regarding the offering of the mantra-seat, it was said by the Lotus-born One:
"The Śaktis beginning with the seed-syllable of Kāma, who bestow auspiciousness, are to be worshipped."

One who worships according to the ritual procedure in the four directions of the seat should worship in the yantra at the left corner her whose luster is equal to that of a drop of passion (ratibindu).
One should visualize Prīti, who stands in the southern corner, holding a noose, gentle in appearance, overwhelmed by intoxication, and possessing a luster like molten gold.
One should worship her who stands before [the deity], red in color, adorned with red flowers and other ornaments, holding a goad and a gesture of salutation with her two arms.
One should worship her as she gazes upon the bow and arrows;
one should worship the deities of the heart and other limbs of the Goddess within the hexagon.
For all mantras and yantras, the one known as Mūrti is the Dakṣiṇā;
alternatively, Mahādeva is remembered as the Ṛṣi of all vidyās.
Having thus worshipped according to the rules with hymns and recitations,
[one should offer] wines, meats, *vaṭakas*, excellent cakes, vegetables,
[meat from] buffaloes, gayals, cows, camels, and female jackals.
With lions, tigers, piercing [beasts], porcupines, forest-dwelling black antelopes, rhinoceroses, and śalyas;

with boars, human-beasts, and common cattle; and constantly with fish and meat—whatever he always describes, those men who speak of it as being of the nature of heaven describe that very thing otherwise.
Svārā, Śaṅkara, and Śaṅkarāyā—
one should worship all of these with the attendants of Hara;
for it has been proclaimed by Nārada and others that without such worship, the attainment of knowledge never occurs.
One who always worships the Goddess with the five things beginning with the letter *ma*— burnt fish, parched grain, meat, what is to be licked, and what is to be drunk— is honored by the wise.
Having worshipped especially with white *svayambhū* flowers the Supreme Power (*paraśakti*),
and having performed recitation (*japa*), one shall always obtain the fourfold aims of life.
Whoever recites [the mantra] one hundred thousand times according to this procedure for preliminary practice (puraścaryā),
all supernatural powers (siddhis) will be within the palm of their hand during the Kali Yuga.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the most beautiful King of Yantras,
by knowing which all practitioners attain supreme Śiva.
One should always draw a triangle joined with a *bindu* in front;
then a hexagon, and after that, a nonagon.
Thereafter, one should [draw] the shape of the womb by means of both reverse and direct order;
it consists of lines for rajas, sattva, and tamas, possessing eight petals and a pericarp.
One should draw a Bhūpūra, adorned with lines of qualities, according to this procedure;
O Bhadanta, one should fashion a very beautiful mandala in the shape of a womb (yoni).
In the midst of that, one should worship the Goddess together with her own retinue;
indeed, the best of practitioners must certainly offer the bali-oblation.
If one should worship Sundarī without making an offering,
that beautiful woman shall cause even his flesh, bones, and marrow to be given away.
One should worship the Supreme Deity with white *svayambhū* flowers,
and with fragrant white flowers endowed with fragrance.
One should worship with supreme devotion using perfumes, flowers, food, and water;
for if there is a lack of food, the housewife becomes angry with the master of the household.
Without the offering (bali) and the spear (śakti), she becomes angry as Bhavasundarī;
one should worship the Yantra in the Yoni-kunda, especially with red flowers.
That practice of the Yugas which I have described should not be performed at night; it should be done in a cremation ground, in the wilderness, or in an empty temple.
One should recite the mantra according to one's own capacity for the attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life;
one should worship a young girl daily and always praise the young girl.
Having worshipped her according to the prescribed rite— whether she be ill-clad or beautifully attired— with vermilion, red garments, and excellent ornaments;
Having fed [the guest] with the thought that they are goddesses, and having paid obeisance, one should dismiss them.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the armor (kavaca) which grants all desires;
by the mere knowledge of which the Goddess comes within the range of one's vision.
At dawn, at midday, in the evening, and at midnight,
a person should bow to the Guru according to the prescribed rite and recite the armor-verse (kavaca).
One should always visualize Sundarī upon a thousand-petaled lotus, bowing to her in front, on both sides, above, and below.
I worship Sarasvatī, who holds a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
having recollected the deities of the phonemes, the wise one should recite the armor (kavaca).
May the goddess Kāminī, the bestower of desires, protect me at the syllable *ka*.
May the goddess Maheśvarī, whose form is Śakti, protect me at the syllable *e*.
May the goddess Bindumālinī, of auspicious countenance, protect me at the syllable *i*;
may the goddess Indrāṇī, the bestower of all accomplishments, protect me at the syllable *ma*.

This, O Pārvatī, has been declared as the armor (kavaca) and the extraction of the mantra;
he who, having become restrained, pure, and disciplined, recites it at the three junctions of the day, [attains success].
Whatever is held in his mind shall achieve every purpose;
[this is accomplished] with gorocanā, saffron, barley-juice, and red sandalwood.
With white *svayambhū* flowers,
when [the planet] Mars or Saturn is present, one should perform it in a cremation ground, a wilderness, or likewise in an empty dwelling or a temple.
Having worshipped the mantra with the preceptor and his consort,

Having worshipped, worn, and praised [the deity] according to this rite,

Then, having offered an oblation to the Goddess with human beings, cats, mice,
cocks, buffaloes, and rams, and having worshipped according to the prescribed ritual;
Having placed it within gold, one should wear it on the neck, the head, or the arm, on an auspicious lunar day, under a favorable constellation, and likewise during the rising of a noble zodiac sign.
And having worn this armor, a person shall obtain all accomplishments;
as for the majesty of this armor, I could not describe it even in hundreds of years.
But I am able, O Great Goddess, to describe its fruit:
that there is no fear of thieves there, nor is there any fear of disease.
Therein, there is no fear of famine, nor likewise any oppression by bandits;
it pacifies all obstacles and is the supreme bringer of peace for all.
It pacifies all death, destroys all diseases,
provides protection for every living being, and bestows the fruits of the fourfold aims of human existence.
It should never be spoken of here or there, nor should it ever be given away;
having received the mantra according to the prescribed rite, the wise person should constantly recite it.
Even there, I consider it difficult to obtain the armor in the form of a deity,
having received the grace of the Guru and attained the well-guarded lore.
Even there, it is rare; it is rare throughout the three worlds—that one who, being self-restrained and pure, should recite even a single verse or a single quarter-verse.
For him, there shall be the accomplishment of all aims; this was spoken by Śaṅkara:
"The Guru is the god Hara himself, and his wife is the beloved of Hara."
For one who worships without making distinctions, success is not far off: the disputant becomes mute, the patron floats [on a boat], the king acts as a servant, the Guru becomes short,
and the fire indeed becomes cold.
I worship that other group of eight Siddhas, whose form is the perfection of the eightfold conduct;

Thus ends the Śrīvidyā-kavaca of the venerable Tripurasundarī in the illustrious Viśvasāra-tantra.
I shall proclaim the Krama-stava; listen, O lotus-faced one!
By the mere knowledge of which one becomes Nārāyaṇa himself.
"Having risen during the *brāhma* hour," and so forth.
Now I shall describe the Great Vidyā known as Tripurapūrvikā,
who is Bhairavī, called Sarvasiddhā, and the bestower of the fruits of the four aims of life.
The Goddess, whose form is bliss, is the destroyer of all obstacles;
she is the eternal primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), endowed with all the Tantras.
There is no knowledge equal to this, which is difficult to obtain even for the gods in the three worlds;
it is the knowledge that bestows virtue, wealth, and desire, and destroys all enemies.
Through the gods, one attains divinity; through the gandharvas, one obtains fragrance; and for those desiring pleasure as well as the wealthy, she grants their own heads and bestows liberation.
I shall proclaim the extraction of the mantra; listen, O lotus-faced one!
Having extracted the seed-syllable of Śiva, it is joined with fire and the moon.
O Supreme Goddess, one should extract that which is joined with the twelve vowels;
conjoined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*, it is proclaimed as the *vāgbhava*.
Having explained it according to the sequence of stability, the Kāmarāja is now described:
the letter *ka* is enriched with the seed-syllable of the Moon (*candra*), and above that is the seed-syllable of Śiva (*śiva*).
The seed-syllable of Indra situated in the letter *ka*, followed by the seed-syllable of fire, mounted upon the point of delight (*ratibindu*); this is known as the King of Desire (*kāmarāja*).
The seed-syllable of the Moon, situated upon Śiva and the others, adorned with the fire-bindu and mounted upon the vowel *manu*, is proclaimed as the "conjunction" (*saṃsarga*).
This Śrīṃ is proclaimed as the foremost of all vidyās,
just as butter is among curds, or as a Brahmin is among bipeds.
Just as the Gaṅgā is among rivers, just as Hari is among the gods,
and just as Śambhu is among the Vaiṣṇavas, so has she been celebrated.
The assignment of seed-syllables (nyāsa-varṇa) should be as before, and the worship is remembered to be as before;
the worship of Sundarī was thus described by the Lotus-born One.
In the yantra consisting of nine wombs and joined with the powers such as Rati and others,
the Mothers beginning with Brahmā are to be worshipped again in the openings of the petals.
Outside that, O fair-faced one, one should worship with supreme devotion the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons within the Bhūpura, just as one would worship the Sun.
The preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) of Bhairavī is characterized by its specific qualities;
for the performance of the preliminary rite, one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times.
One should worship Śivā, who is clothed in red garments, adorned with various ornaments, and holding a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
One should worship you, the Goddess, according to the proper conduct, like Sundarī— Śivā, who wears a garland of severed heads as her lower garment and whose eyes are blood-red.
She is seated upon the heart of the great corpse Sadāśiva,
standing in the tribhaṅga posture, with full and elevated breasts.
The great power Anaṅgā and the others are most enchanting when served;
one should worship that goddess according to the prescribed ritual, just like Sundarī.
Without sacrificial gifts, without fire oblations, and without feeding the Brahmins,
one should worship the goddess Bhairavī and also the secret Tripurā.
One should proclaim the Vāgbhava [syllable] joined with the Bindu and conjoined with Lohita; likewise, one should proclaim Śrīkaṇṭha conjoined with Lohita and conjoined with Laṅa.
One should visualize the great preta Sadāśiva as joined with the syllables *he* and *sau*; beginning with *Oṃ* and ending with *namaḥ*, one should then [place] the seat of the Goddess in the heart.
By the offering of his own seat, the Lotus-born One declared the Vāgbhava [seed-syllable]; one should extract the word "Tripurādevī vidmahe.
Having extracted "Kāmeśvarīm," one should then say "dhīmahī" followed by "tat."
Then, having lifted him up while he is still moist, one should speak and impel him.
O beloved, this Gāyatrī is declared to be Tripurā for the purpose of worship;
one should always recite it either beginning with the Vāgbhava syllable or beginning with the Kāma syllable.
The wise practitioner should constantly recite the mantra four hundred thousand times as the preliminary rite (puraścaryā);
however, if he recites the vidyā without having first recited the Gāyatrī, [the practice is fruitless].
Success in knowledge does not arise even in hundreds of millions of aeons;
Gāyatrī is proclaimed as the supreme among all mantra-knowledges.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the armor (kavaca) that grants all desires;
by its mere grace, one becomes a god—of this there is no doubt.
The seer (ṛṣi) is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and the metre (chandas) is declared to be Paṅkti;

The placement of the sages (ṛṣinyāsa) for all the syllables of the mantra has been performed previously.

Now the Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), Bhairavī, associated with Tripura, is being described.
And by the grace of which knowledge a person may obtain the fourfold aims of human life.

Thus has this divine armor, which grants all desires, brings prosperity, removes fear, wards off death, and bestows peace, been recounted to you.
The greatness of this armor, which shatters existence, brings about accomplishment, increases prosperity, and fulfills all aims, cannot be told by me even in hundreds of years.
But I am able, O Great Goddess, to describe its fruit:
a man shall obtain through this armor the fruit of worship, recitation, and praise.
The Great Goddess [should not be revealed] to one who is deceitful, devoid of devotion, or a slanderer;
nor to one with missing limbs, nor to one with redundant limbs, nor to a liar.
One should not display the divine praise; by showing it, one becomes a destroyer of Śiva.
The armor that has the form of a god must not be spoken of here or there.
Whether in impurity or purity, a person should recite this at all times;
for him, the service of the great siddhis, such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest, is ordained.
O Maheśvarī, [one should write] on a birch-bark leaf with gorocanā and saffron,
using lac, red sandalwood, and even flowers from the *svarambhu* tree.
Having written [the mantra] with a golden stylus on the forehead, or on the earth, or on the lip,
in a circular form, his success shall be unshakable.
Whether on the head, or on the left, or on the right ear, or on the lower lip—
he, by that very act, is as one who has bathed in all sacred fords and been initiated into all sacrifices.
For whomever this armor is upon the body, success is difficult for others to attain;
he who should draw it at night in a deserted dwelling or likewise in his own home.
O Maheśvarī, having become pure, one should draw the yantra during the night;
O Maheśvarī, on Sunday, Tuesday, Thursday, or Friday.
One should meditate upon the auspicious Yantra that bestows all prosperity, as instructed by the Guru,
on either the eighth, the ninth, or even the fourteenth lunar day.
One should draw the yantra at night; then its accomplishment is unfailing. Alternatively, the preceptor should diligently draw it on the tenth or the sixtieth day.
When the Moon has entered the sign of Leo, the Sun is situated in Cancer;
when Jupiter has entered the sign of Pisces, and Saturn is situated in Scorpio.
Having written it, you should wear the yantra while facing north,
diligently in a cremation ground, a wilderness, or an empty dwelling.
If one draws the yantra at night, its accomplishment will be unshakable;
upon seeing it, the disputant shall be silenced, and the king’s conduct shall be properly undertaken.
One who is proud becomes hunched and attains total dullness; one who is cold toward Vaiśyas becomes a fire and attains victory everywhere.
I am not able to fully comprehend the greatness of this armor;
I have merely described here the fruit of its recitation, worship, and chanting.
Therefore, a person should recite this armor-mantra with every effort;
having attained his desire before long, he will certainly become a sky-walker.
That mortal who here recites this with a heart exceedingly moistened by devotion shall obtain the fruit of recitation that is to be enjoined;
he quickly becomes the supreme abode of all prosperities, a foot upon the crest of the crowns of kings.
He possesses fortune, he is fortunate, and he is long-lived.
Thus was this hymn of the armor for peace spoken by Śaṅkara;
there is no knowledge higher than this, and no mantra higher than this.
There is no knowledge higher than this, nor any sacred ford superior to this,
from which everything has arisen and in which it still abides even today.
O Maheśvarī, who desires dissolution, all this shall go to dissolution;
I bow to the goddess Tripurā, Bhairavī, the liberator from worldly existence.
This [work] directly bestows all accomplishments and destroys great sins.
Regarding this *Śrī Tripurā-nāma-bhairavī-sahasra-nāma-stotra*, the Blessed Lord Śiva is the seer (*ṛṣi*),
the *paṅkti* is the meter (*chandas*), and the primordial power, the Goddess Tripurabhairavī, is the deity (*devatā*) for the sake of attaining all prosperity and success.
The Second Yoga:
Oṃ, the Goddess Tripurābhairavīśānī, who dwells in the perfection of yoga,
who consists of all mantras, and who bestows the fruits of all powers.
The auspicious Goddess, whose nature is the support of all, bestows every prosperity;
she is the Yoginī, the Mother of Yoga, and the one who impels the attainment of yoga.
She is the object of meditation for yogis, the mother of yoga, and she who sports in both yoga and non-yoga;
she is playfulness, sport, and likewise divine dalliance, setting in motion the very form of time.
Kālamātā, Kālarātri, Kālī, Kamalavāsinī,
Kamalā, Kāntirūpā, Kāmarājeśvarī, and Kriyā.
Kuhū, she of deceptive form, Kapaṭā, she of deceitful appearance; Kumadā, Carcikā, Kāntā, and Kālarātri, who is ever beloved.
Ghorarāvā, Ghorarūpā, Raṇadā, Ghṛṇā, Kṛpā, Ghargharā,
Ghoriṇī, Ghurṇā, and she who is ever fond of terrible sounds.
The mind should be meditated upon as having a terrible form, rich in manifestations, and bestowing the sound of a water-pot;
it is like a bell with a gurgling resonance, always fond of the sound of a bell.
Subtle, subtler, gross, and exceedingly gross, O Great-minded One;
emaciated, full of being, as well as terrifying, setting forth a dreadful roar.
She who is of the nature of delusion, the remover of fear, the giver of fear, and the destroyer of fear;
the Goddess who dwells in the cremation ground and resides in the abode of the cremation ground.
She whose seat is a corpse, whose food is a corpse, whose body is a corpse, who is both auspicious and inauspicious;
she who feeds on corpses in the region of the throat, and who is enchanted by the bracelet of a corpse.
She has prominent teeth and beautiful teeth; she is both truth and untruth, dwelling in the realm of mystery.
She is the embodiment of truth, the seizer of truth, and the destroyer of those who speak falsely.
She whose intention is truth, whose perception is truth, who dwells in both attachment and non-attachment;
she who is unattached, free from attachment, the Suṣumnā, who deludes all attachments.
Māyā is the Mother, the Great Māyā, who delights in great intoxication;
she is fond of drinking wine, devoted to intoxication, and the destroyer of those who revile wine.
She wears a garland of flowing blood, dwells upon two skulls,
always drinks the river of flesh, is intoxicated with great liquor, and possesses excellent meat.
She who carries flesh, she who supports flesh, she who eats flesh, she who devours flesh;
she who drinks blood, she who delights in blood, she whose mouth is red, and she whose eyes are red.
She who removes redness, she who loves redness, she who destroys the affliction of redness;
she who drinks blood, she who delights in redness, she whose body is red, she who is intensely red.
She who possesses the flowers of the Self-Existent, she who is pure, she who is more blissful than the flowers of the Self-Existent,
she whose food is the flowers of the Self-Existent, and she who destroys the censure of the Self-Existent.
She who delights in the self-manifested flower, she who originates from the birth of the self-manifested,
she who takes away the self-manifested flower, and she who brings an end to those who revile the self-manifested.
She wears red garlands and red flowers; she is adorned with blossoms of red flowers.
Her limbs are anointed with red sandalwood, and she worships with red sandalwood.
She is the fish, the beloved of the fish, the garland, the eater of fish, the great prosperity;
she is the one whose food is fish, who desires fish, and who destroys those who revile the fish.
Kiṅkarākṣī, likewise Krūrā, Krūrāsatyavināśinī,
Krūrāntā, Kuliśāṅgī, Vajrāṅgī, and Vajrasambhavā.
She possesses a vajra-body, she wields the vajra, and she dwells within a vajra-skeleton;
she draws in the deep navel, she bestows fear, and she removes fear.
She who bestows fear, she who is formidable with fear, the most terrifying, and she who roars with a fearsome sound;
she who is beautiful, the auspicious one, the truthful, the secure, and likewise the bringer of security.
Her parting is adorned with vermilion, her form resembles vermilion,
her nose is brightened by pearls, and she possesses a beautiful, well-defined nose.
Svarā, Lambodarī, Dīrghā, Dīrghaghoṇā, Mahotkaṭā, Kuṭilā,
Cārvavā, Caṇḍī, Caṇḍanābhi, and Caṇḍikā.
Aticaṇḍā, Pracaṇḍā, Mahācaṇḍā, Caṇḍaveginī, Caṇḍālī,
Caṇḍikā, Cāṭu, Śabdarūpā, Calā, and Camu.
Campā, Campāvatī, Caukṣṇā, Tīkṣṇapriyā, Kṣiti;
Jaladā, Jagadā, Yogā, and Jagadānandakāriṇī.
She who is worshipped by the world, the mother of the world, the earth, and the patience of the world;
she is victory, the victorious one, the progenitress, the conqueror, and likewise the bestower of victory.
She is the Mother, the Sustainer of the World, known as Jayā, whose very form is victory;
she is the Mother of the Universe, honored by the world, Jayā, the auspicious bringer of triumph.
Jayanī, Jayamātā, Jayā, Vijayā, Janā;
Khḍginī, Khaḍgarūpā, Sukhaḍgā, and Khaḍgadhāriṇī.
She whose form is the sword, who holds the sword, whose limbs are the sword, who is fond of the sword;
she who bestows the sword, whose illusion is the sword, and who is born from the body of the sword.
Khaḍgā, Khaḍgadharā, Khelā, Khaḍginī, Khaḍgamuṇḍalī;
Śaṅkhinī, Cāpinī, the Goddess Vajriṇī, Suṣaṇī, and Mati.
Rāgiṇī, Bhindipālā, Pāśī, Aṅkuśī,
Śavī, Dhanuṣī, Ṭaṅkinī, Carmī, Dantī, and Karpamālikā.
Mudgarī, she whose form is the *hallā* plant, Tūṇī who dwells in battle,
Tṛṇālayā, Tṛṇaharā, and she whose form arises from grass.
She who is without grass yet has the form of grass, whose limbs are like cotton and who is fond of cotton;
the Goddess who wields various weapons and from whom various weapons originate.
She who takes away and bestows millions, she who grants gain and dwells within gain;
she who removes gain and produces gain, she who possesses gain and whose very form is gain.
She is the supporter of the earth, the giver of wealth, the blessed one, the one of auspicious form, the sustainer, the bow;
she possesses the bow, she whose sound is like a bow, she who honors the bow, and she who is wealthy now.
Dhuraśabdā, Dhanāmānyā, Dhanyāṅgī, Dhananāśinī,
Dhanuhā, Dhanalābha, Dhanalabhyā, and Mahādhanuḥ.
She is perfectly peaceful and of tranquil form, dwelling upon the path of the breath;
she is the sky, served by the hosts of deities, and the increaser of coming and going.
She is the one to be gone to and the act of going; she is the remover of disease and the increaser of disease.
She is stability and the destroyer of stability; she is the art that brings an end to stability.
She is the giver, the one who provides shelter, the beloved, the most dear, the bestower of what is dear, she of lovely complexion;
she is the destroyer of what is dear, the auspicious one dear to all, she whose love is dear, and she of the lovely body.
She is the giver of what is dear and the one who brings about what is beloved; she resides in the abode of the Beloved.
She is perfectly steadfast, of stable form, the bestower of stability, and the increaser of firmness.
Cañcalā, Capalā, Cālā, Capalāṅganivāsinī,
Gaurī, Kālī, as well as Chinnā, Māyā, Mānyā, and Mahāprabhā.
Sundarī, Tripurā, the auspicious one, the dweller in Tripureśvara;
the goddess who destroys Tripura, the destroyer of the life-breath of Tripura.
She is Bhairavī, abiding in Bhairava, the beloved body of Bhairava;
she is the limb of Bhairava, the performer of Bhairava’s deeds, and the most cherished consort of Bhairava.
The beautiful Tripurā, the auspicious one, who dwells in the Lord of Tripura;
the Goddess who destroys Tripura, who brings about the destruction of the life-force of Tripura.
She is Bhairavī, abiding in Bhairava, the beloved body of Bhairava;
she is the limb of Bhairava, the performer of Bhairava’s deeds, and the most cherished consort of Bhairava.
She is Kāladā and Kālarātri, as well as Kātyāyanī and Kriyā;
she is Kriyahā, Kriyadā, Kraivyā, Kriyaprāṇa, and Kriyākathā.
She is Hrīṅkārī, Kamalā, Lakṣmī, Śakti, Svāhā, Vibhu, and Prabhu;
she is both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, the son who bears the name of the father and possesses the form of a man.
She is Puruṣāṅgī and Pūruṣī, as well as the one who assumes the form of Prakṛti;
she is the Supreme Person (Paramapuruṣa), Ramā, Nārāyaṇī, and Satī.
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
as well as Vārāhī, Cāmuṇḍā, Indrāṇī, and Haravallabhā.
Bhairavī, Māheśī, Kṛṣṇā, and Kātyāyanī;
likewise Rākṣasī, Ḍākinī, Citrā, Vicitrā, and Vibhramā.
Haṃsinī, Rākinī, Bhītā, Gandharvī, Gandhavāhanā,
Kekarī, Koṭarākṣī, Nirmāṃsā, and Śuṣkamāṃsikā.
Lalajjihvā, Sujihvā, Vāṇadā, and Vāṇadāyinī;
Candrā, Candraprabhā, Candrī, and she who is intent upon the splendor of the moon.
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati,
Dhṛti, Śaśinī, Candrakānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, and Vargadā.
She is the Fullness, the one of full nectar, the wish-fulfilling creeper, and the burner of the world-cycle;
she possesses the hand of the Kalpa-tree through her beautiful luster, yet her body brings about the destruction of the eon.
She is named Kalpa, she is fit for the aeon, and she is the binder of those who bind the aeon;
she has a pure face, a face like a hungry ghost, a face like a meteor, and a great face.
Sūryā, Sūryaprabhā, Sūryā stationed within the solar disc,
Sūryakānti, [the one] named Sūryā, and Sūryabhāvanā.
Tapanī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jālinī, Ruci, Sunandā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhinī, Dhāriṇī, and Kṣamā.
She who is the beginning of the ages, the destroyer of the ages, the one to be yoked, the giver of fitness, and the increaser of fitness;
she who dwells in the center of the circle of fire and resides within the circle of fire.
She is the form of the fire-mandala and is known as the fire-mandala;
she is beloved by fire, belongs to the class of fire, has fire as her food, and is of excellent conduct.
She is the splendor of fire, the arrows of fire, the giver of fire, and the destroyer of fire;
she is the activity of fire, the consumer of fire, the Time, and she is eternally established within fire.
Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī,
Suśrī, Svarūpā, Kapilā, and likewise Havyakavyavahā.
The Goddess of manifold splendor, the consort of the Supreme Brahman;
the Goddess consisting of the light of Brahman, whose very nature is the Supreme Brahman.
She is the female form of Puruṣa, she is Puruṣī, the beloved body of Puruṣa;
she is named after men, she is worthy of merit and honor, and she is the one who increases the limbs of Puruṣa.
Unborn and sinless, breathless and likewise without decay;
the snatcher of the life-force of the constellations, and the one who honors the constellations as ornaments.
She is worthy of being honored by the hundreds of thousands, the taker of the hundreds of thousands, the hundreds of thousands herself, and the one whose very nature is the hundreds of thousands;
she possesses the limbs of Puruṣa, she is the abundance, and she is eternally a portion of Puruṣa.
She who possesses beautiful flowers, whose hands hold flowers, who takes flowers, who is fond of flowers;
she who loves flowers, who seizes flowers, and who is worshipped by those who bind garlands of flowers.
She who is honored by flowers, she who destroys the affliction of flowers;
she who is the stars, she who possesses beautiful stars, she who is worthy of the stars, and she of great prosperity.
She who possesses a great garland, she who is highly honored, the Great One, the worshiper of the Great,
the most worthy, the one to be revered, the Great Mistress of Mahākāla, the Magnificent.
She is the Great-Faced One, the one worthy of homage, and the dweller in Mahālaṅka;
she is the Mistress of the Great Conch, Mīnā, Matsyagandhā, and Mahodarī.
Lambodarī, Lamboṣṭhī, Namranimnatanudarī,
Bimboṣṭhalakṣanāsā, Lambā, Ghoṇā, and Sulambakā.
Atilambā, Mahālambā, Sulambā, Lambavāsinī,
Lambahā, Sulambī, Lambasthā, and Lambapūjakā.
Vilambā, Mahālambā, Sulambā, and Vṛhattanu;
Caṇḍaghaṇṭā, Mahāghaṇṭā, and she who always delights in the sound of the bell.
She who loves music, who delights in music, who is the foremost among the gods, and who destroys [the cycle of] music;
she is Ramā, Ramā, Rāmā, the delightful one, and the one of auspicious nature.
Exceedingly beautiful, the giver of delight, the plantain-stalked, with thighs like plantain stalks, possessing the splendor of Rāma’s consort,
the beloved of Rāma, held by Rāma, with limbs as lovely as Rāma’s, she who delights in amorous play.
Ratipriyā, Ratimatī, Ratisevyā, Ratipriyā;
Surati, Kurati, Śobhā, Viśobhā, and Śobhanāśinī.
She is beautiful, greatly beautiful, exceedingly beautiful, and auspicious;
she is alluring, greatly alluring, very alluring, and the one who binds with desire.
She is the limb of greed and yet barren of greed; she is the destroyer of greed and the annihilator of greed.
She is fond of greed, possessed of great greed, and the reviler and censurer of greed.
Dwelling in the limbs of greed, she is the fragrance, the foul odor, and the destroyer of odors;
she is attached to fragrance, worshipped with fragrance, sweetly scented, and the essence of the fragrance of love.
She who is foul-smelling and putrid-smelling, yet exceedingly fragrant and sweet-scented;
she of great fragrance, worthy of exquisite perfumes, the destroyer of that which destroys all scents.
Padmā, Padmāyatī, Premṇā, Padmagandhā, Sugandhikā,
Padmālayā, Padmakarā, and she whose vehicle is borne by the lotus-bearer.
She who abides in the lotus, she who is the source of the lotus, she who sports with the lotus, she who possesses a beautiful lotus;
she who brings an end to the lotus, she who carries the non-lotus, and she who makes beloved the love for the lotus.
She who censures the lotus-eyed, she whose vehicle is the contentment of the lotus,
the goddess who holds a red lotus and is ever fond of the red lotus.
She who possesses the fragrance of red lotuses, she who dwells in red lotuses,
she who protects the abode of red lotuses, and she who is enchanting with red lotuses.
She has eyes like red lotuses and assumes the form of a red lotus;
she is a woman, the sovereign mistress of Nārāyaṇa, and the beloved of Nārāyaṇa’s abode.
Residing in the body of Nārāyaṇa, she is the delight of Nārāyaṇa;
residing in the body of Nārāyaṇa, she dwells in the mind of Nārāyaṇa.
Born from the body of Nārāyaṇa, she is the beloved form of Nārāyaṇa;
she belongs to Viṣṇu, is worthy of worship by Viṣṇu, and is the abode of the portions of Viṣṇu.
She is the one to be worshipped by the worshipers of Viṣṇu, her body abiding within the portion of the Vaiṣṇavas;
she is to be worshipped by Hara, she is the most excellent among those dear to Hara, and she is the forbearance of Hara.
The destructive Kuhū resides within the body of Hara, is intent on the worship of Hara,
has arisen from the body of Hara, and dwells within the limbs of Hara.
She is the worshiper and the one to be worshipped by Hara; she is intent on the salutation of Hara;
she has emerged from the body of Hara; she is the play of Hara; and she is the eternal movement.
The beautiful Gaṅgā is free from conflict, unattached, and the destroyer of attachment;
she is self-born, solitary, difficult to attain, and the increaser of the body that is hard to reach.
She who dwells in the fortress, whose form is the fortress, and who resides within the body of the fortress;
she who is joined with the wind, who acts through the wind, and who worships those who worship the wind.
The Goddess, assuming the form of wind, moving along the path of the suṣumṇā,
resides within the body, is the very form of the body, is to be meditated upon as the body, and possesses an excellent body.
She is the form of the channels, residing in the channels, the channel-like one, with a face like a small tube;
she is both Iḍā and Piṅgalā, dwelling within the Suṣumṇā.
O Maheśānī, you who perform what is dear to Sadāśiva, who assume the form of Mūlaprakṛti,
who are Amṛteśī, and who dwell within the limbs of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).
She is the creator, sustainer, and destroyer, who prevents dissolution and calamity;
and by means of the principle of the great dissolution, she effects both creation and withdrawal.

She is always the utterances *svadhā* and *svāhā*, the conventional usages, and the beloved of both the sacrificial offerings (*havya*) and the ancestral oblations (*āhavya*). She is the locus of the offering, the consumer of the offering, and she is born from the very body of the offering.
The cow is the plaything for the sacrificial oblation; she is the source of form, born of beauty, fragrant, Nandinī, meritorious, the limb of sacrifice, and born of sacrifice.

She who abides in sacrifice and whose body is sacrifice; she who is born from a womb and dwells in a womb; she who is not born from a womb, yet being virtuous, truthful, and of excellent intellect; she who is the slender form of the unchaste woman.
She is Ahalyā and Gautamī; she is Videhā, the destroyer of the body;
she is Gāndhārī, Draupadī, Dūtī, Śivadūtī, and the beloved of Śiva.
Tripureśī, Paurṇamāsī, Amāvāsyā, Caturdaśī, Pañcamī, as well as Ṣaṣṭhī, Navamī, and likewise Aṣṭamī.
The eleventh and twelfth lunar days, as well as the day of the week, are terrifying in form;
the solar transits (saṃkrānti) are the form of the month, and she is the form of the season, beloved of the seasons.
The Supreme Self is of two forms: Ghaṇṭikā, who assumes the form of a staff, and Mahākālī, who is Yāmarūpā, the twilight, and the destroyer of the twilight-demoness.
She is the three-watch night, she who has the form of Yama, the daughter of Yama, and Yami forever;
she is Mātaṅgī, she whose form is the bank, the noble-born one, and the destroyer of the lineage.
The beloved of the Kula, the jar-shaped one, the jar-bodied, the increaser;
the swift one, the mother of the Kula-possessors, the one not far away, the ruddy dawn.
She is the rivers flowing to the ocean, she is peace, she is the form of peace, and she is perfect tranquility;
she is hope, thirst, hunger, and agitation, dwelling in the very form of agitation.
The river flowing to the ocean, peace, the Vedas, sacred tradition, splendor, the earth, day and night, and the bodies composed of the five elements— all these are indeed excellent forms.
Taṇḍulā, Chinnamastā, she who has the serpent as her sacred thread,
Varṇinī, Ḍākinī, Śakti, Kurukullā, and Sakulikā.
Pratyaṅgirā, Aparājitā, Ajitā, Jayanāśinī,
Jayā, Vijayā, and Mahiṣāsuraghātinī.
She is the slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha, the destroyer of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, the killer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, and the one who brings about the destruction of Raktabīja.
Kāśī, Kālyanivāsī, Mathurā, Pārvatī, Aparṇā, Caṇḍikā, Devī, Mṛḍhanī, Ambikā, and Kalā.
White, black, and red-colored, with forms like the crescent of the autumn moon—
Rukmiṇī and Rādhikā are thus proclaimed as the attendants of Bhairavī.
By reciting the names of the Goddess one thousand and eight times, even one who is burdened with great sins is liberated; there is no doubt in this matter.
The killing of a Brahmin, the drinking of liquor, theft, and sexual intercourse with the teacher’s wife—
these constitute the ten great sins (mahāpātaka), as well as the secondary sins (upapātaka).
By means of the hymn spoken by Gālava, pride perishes at that very moment—
whether one recites it correctly, even a single verse, or even merely remembers it.
Whether one recites it oneself or causes it to be recited, one is immediately released from bondage—
at the royal gate, in fear, in a fortress, in danger, or in a mountain pass difficult to traverse.
O Maheśvarī, whether in a wilderness, on a mountain, or among people;
when faced with the danger of fire, in a state of fear, or agitated by the threat of lions and tigers.
By reciting or remembering it, a mortal becomes the destroyer of all calamities;
the childless obtains a son, the poor becomes wealthy, and the dull-witted becomes wise.
A Brahmin devoted to all the scriptures shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices;
he attains the power to paralyze fire, wind, and water, as well as the power to arrest the movement of the sun.
O Maheśvarī, killing, causing hatred, as well as eradication,
subjugation, and all supernatural powers (siddhis) arise right here.
Having become pure at dawn, at midday, and at the onset of night,
whether one recites it oneself or causes it to be recited, one shall obtain the fruit of all desires.
O Maheśvarī, it should be worn on the left hand by women and likewise on the right hand by men, on Sunday, Tuesday, Thursday, or even Saturday.
Or one may draw it on a Saturday; then one shall obtain the fruit of all accomplishments, whether in a wilderness, in a cremation ground, or at night during the hour of midnight.
The preceptor should diligently draw [the mandala] in a deserted dwelling or even in a house,
when the sun has entered the sign of Leo, when Jupiter is in Sagittarius, and when the sun is situated in Cancer.
When Jupiter is in the sign of Pisces, the practitioner should write [the mantra] with effort;
or, having seen the vulva of a woman in her menses, he should always write it while stationed there.
One should carefully draw [the design] using white *svayambhū* flowers, fragrant sandalwood with a sweet scent, and musk from the navel of a deer.
Having written it and having recited it, one should preserve it with a single-minded focus;
and having worshipped a young maiden as well as adorned women.
Having worshipped with one's own flowers, perfumes, sandalwood, and cloths,
one should worship with vermilion and red flowers through the yoga of devotion.
Alternatively, one may worship the deities with a girl up to ten years of age;
there, one shall obtain the fruit of all desires even at that very moment.
In this [practice], there is no dependence on the attainment of supernatural powers (*siddhi*) and the like, nor is there any concern regarding friends or enemies;
it bestows accomplishment through mere recitation (*japa*), without the great expenditure of wealth.
At all times and on every occasion, one should offer an oblation with six thousand prostrations according to the prescribed rite and worship Śivā daily.
Day and night, one should offer oblations of white *svayambhū* flowers and worship the goddess Pārvatī, the consort of Bhairava, accompanied by Tripura.
One should constantly feed ten or twelve Brahmins upon regaining a lost kingdom, as well as during the fourfold assembly of the virtuous.
One shall be liberated from chronic disease; in the fifth [month], one becomes a preeminent poet;
in the seventh, one attains the power of moving through the sky (khecaratva); and in the eighth, one becomes like Bṛhaspati.
In the ninth [year], there is the attainment of all success; in the tenth, one becomes honored by the world;
in the eleventh, one brings kings under one's influence; and in the twelfth, one becomes a lord of the earth.
Whoever recites it even once obtains the fruit of worship;
likewise, whoever, being self-controlled and pure, recites even a single verse correctly.
He obtains the fruit of that worship as spoken by Bhairava;
he becomes long-lived and endowed with joy, especially through the yoga of Brahmā and Indra.
O Maheśvarī, she resides either at the Saubhāgyaśobhana pool during the Siddhayoga,
or on the fifth lunar day, or likewise on the sixth, wherever she may be.
In that regard, there should be no doubt, nor any defect such as being a woman and so forth; for what need is there for many [conditions]? The goddess shall obtain the fulfillment of all desires.
Thus ends the *Sahasranāmastotra* of Śrī Tripurabhairavī in the venerable *Viśvasāra-tantra*.
Now, O Great Goddess, I shall proclaim the Vidyā of Mahiṣamardinī:
one who desires a son obtains a son; one who desires a kingdom shall attain a kingdom.
One who desires shall obtain their desires, and one shall attain the fruit of all accomplishments (siddhis) by means of buffaloes,
bulls, goats, rams, cocks, perfumes, incense, corpses, animals, flowers, milk-lamps, and bilva fruits.
With śāka trees, crows, pecas,
madana-araṇa-vināca-uṣmas, guñjas, guñjāriṇīs, and flowers as red as wine from the intoxication of honey; with cloves, bakula blossoms, and dhūsta trees that destroy the barbarians.
A man [should worship] with Aśoka, Pāṭala, Kunda, and Kuruvaka flowers,
as well as with lotuses born in water or on land, especially when anointed with the three sweets (trimadhu).
With *āmiṣa*, *urumāla*, *ocra*, and likewise *kuruvaka*;
with *śālvalka*, *vānara*, *aśva*, and likewise *mṛganābhi-mṛga*.
With pigs, red flowers, red vegetables, milk-rice (pāyasa),
fresh butter, jaggery, and likewise products derived from jaggery.
One should offer oblations to the Goddess every day and always worship a young maiden;
one should constantly satisfy the young maiden, and by that, everything will always be accomplished.
One should always offer a row of jackals, as well as beef and cow-flesh;
one should worship the Goddess every day with beef, including the bones and marrow.
Always in a cremation ground or a desolate wilderness, with perfumes, parched grains, and sesame seeds,
one should remain upon a corpse, on a funeral pyre, or at the mouth of a fire-pit.
One should constantly worship the Goddess, the Vidyā Mahiṣamardinī,
whether situated upon a corpse, on a funeral pyre, on a bed, or even during sexual union.
Whether in an impure place or a pure one, the teacher, with undistracted mind, should worship the Vidyā according to the previously described method of ritual placement (nyāsa).
One should worship the Goddess with self-manifested flowers through the yoga of devotion;
having especially prepared a yantra, one should worship that auspicious Śivā there.
The best of practitioners, having consumed the sacrificial oblation, should recite the vidyā with devotion;
there is no doubt that he will achieve the immobilization of water, wind, fire, the sun, and the moon.
Upon seeing the most excellent practitioner, the disputants depart shorn of their luster;
and the destruction of the wicked occurs very soon, within seven days.
O beloved, diseases go to destruction within seven days;
what is the use of saying more here? One shall obtain the fruit of all one's desires.
Now it is said: "O lotus-faced one, listen to the extraction of the mantra.
O Goddess of gods, the knower of the ritual should indeed utter that which is preceded by twenty among the points of contact."
Having extracted the word *mahiṣamardinī*, one should then apply the word *svāhā* after it;
this eight-syllabled mantra is known as the *vidyā* of Mahiṣamardinī.
One should recite the mantra of Mahāmahiṣamardinī beginning with the Praṇava;
or one should always recite the mantra beginning with the Praṇava or with the word "Kāma."
One should always recite [the mantra] beginning with Māyā and the Kūrca seed-syllable,
or likewise that beginning with Vadhū and the Kavaca seed-syllable.
Without seed-syllables, the Great Vidyā is proclaimed as "seedless";
at all times and in all places, the wise one should recite it beginning with "Kāma."
For the sake of desire, one should recite that Mahiṣamardinī beginning with the seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja);
for the purification of speech, one should recite that Goddess beginning with the Vāgbhava syllable.
The ten-syllabled mantra should always be recited; the ten-syllabled mantra should be praised and served.
O beloved of the three worlds, there is no knowledge equal to the ten-syllabled mantra.
The two seed-syllables are joined in pairs, with each pair occupying a single position;
likewise, the Praṇava and Māyā constitute the ten-fold Vidyā.
Thus, many kinds of vidyās have been described in various tantras;
beyond these is the Mahāvidyā, which is difficult to obtain even in the three worlds.
When creation was destroyed, when all things mobile and immobile had perished,
and when the cosmic egg had become one, it was long ago tormented by Mahiṣa.
The Vidyā Mahiṣamardinī, born from the body of Sundarī,
is the Great Goddess for the destruction of the Dānavas and the Nāgas.
And those of evil intent who have arisen for the sake of destruction—
[she] named Mahiṣamardinī is the protector of all sentient beings.
O Maheśānī, O Pārvatī, listen as the meditation upon her is described:
she stands in the tribhaṅga posture, crushing the demon Mahiṣāsura.
She is endowed with a mass of matted hair, with the crescent moon as her crest-ornament;
she has the luster of a dark cloud, is dark-complexioned, and is adorned with jeweled earrings.
The goddess has three eyes and eight arms; her lotus-like hands hold a vajra and a conch, as well as a sword, a shield, an arrow, a trident, a noose, and a goad.
She holds a bow and arrows, rests upon the shoulders of a lion,
and likewise has her left thumb slightly raised above the buffalo.
Her body was thus half-emerged and pierced by the trident,
while her face was adorned with betel leaf mixed with pieces of camphor.
Adorned with various ornaments, wearing a serpent as a sacred thread,
graced with necklaces of serpents, and possessing the prowess of great power.
Having thus meditated upon the Goddess, who is exquisitely beautiful with a pair of pillars as graceful as plantain trunks, one should worship her by the name Mahiṣamardinī.
Then the preceptor should perform the ritual placement of mantras (mantranyāsa) according to this procedure:
"O slayer of Mahiṣa, Hūṃ" is proclaimed as the heart-mantra.
"HŪṂ PHAṬ" for the enemy of Mahiṣa is proclaimed for the head;
furthermore, one should place the dual form "mahiṣahiṃsāya" on the crest-lock (śikhā).
"Hāṃ" is proclaimed as the pair for slaying Mahiṣa, serving as the armor; "mahiṣahanayugmaṃ" is declared as the pair of eyes.
"Mahiṣaṃ chedaya-dvandvaṃ" is the pair [of arms], and "mahiṣaṃ ca vada-dvayam" is the pair [of feet].
Having uttered "māraya" twice and again "kuṭṭaya" twice,
one should then pronounce the sounds "hūṃ phaṭ" and perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) over all the limbs once more.
Having thus performed the ritual placement according to the rule, one should recite the mantra for the seat:
the Praṇava, the pair of Kavacas, and again the pair of Māyā and Lajjā.
One should offer the [deity] whose weapons are diamond-claws and fangs, ending in the suffix -ṅe, as well as the lion-throne,
together with armor and weapons, at the end of the heart-mantra.
This is the end of the *asnyakta-āsana* (the seat of unshed [offerings]), as told by the Lotus-born One;
O lotus-faced one, now hear this mantra for the offering of the *bali*.
Come, come! Seize the pair of feet, seize the pair of feet!
O Goddess, accept this offering from me, [consisting of] the two feet of a buffalo.

One should utter the two words *sādhaka*, followed again by the two words *khādayat*; then one should say the phrase "grant the state of all accomplishments" (*sarvasiddhipadaṃ dehi*), and thereafter utter the word *svāhā*.
This mantra for the offering of the sacrificial oblation (bali) is proclaimed for the Mūrdhanī [vessel].
Now I shall describe the auspicious yantra that bestows all prosperity:
one should first draw a triangle, and after that, a nine-cornered figure.
The lines of rajas, sattva, and tamas adorn the circle of the womb;
it is a great eight-petaled lotus, complete with its filaments.
One should duly cast the lotus stalk, the line of the tusked one, the mountain joined with the trident, the half-moon, the bow-position, and the arrow.
One should construct a yantra endowed with various weapons according to this procedure.
Now, O Pārvatī, listen as the goddesses who constitute the components of the worship are described:
Durgā, Āryā, Prabhā, the one known as Kaṇaka, and Kṛttikā.
These are declared to be the Abhayās; one should worship them in sequence within the hexagon.
All are dark-complexioned, holding swords in their hands, and overwhelmed by my amorous play.
On the eight petals, O Goddess, beloved of Hara, these are to be worshipped; listen:
Prabhā, Māyā, Jayā, Sukṣmā, Viśuddhā, and likewise Nandinī.
Suprabhā should be understood; she should be known and worshipped according to this rite:
having first uttered the *praṇava*, one should then say "to Jātavedas."
One should utter the word *śūlavāmapada*, then say *somamarātī*;
one should utter the word *nidahāti*, and then again the word *vedasan*.
One should recite "paviṣadatu padam," then "durgāṇi ca padam" again;
thereafter, one should recite "viśvānāveva sindhuṃ ca duritātyagniḥ."
The preceptor should encircle the yantra with the *bhūpura* using this mantra;
for the rite of *puraścaraṇa*, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times.
One should worship the auspicious Mahiṣamardinī daily with the offering of bali;
he shall become the very source of all prosperity, [like] Mahiṣamardinī herself.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall declare the armor (kavaca) that grants all desires,
by the mere grace of which one becomes Sadāśiva himself.
Having first uttered the syllable *oṃ*, the practitioner of mantra should daily recite the armor (*kavaca*) for the sake of attaining the mantra and for the accomplishment of the mantra’s phonemes.
Oṃ. For the *kavaca* (armour) of Mahiṣamardinī: the Lord Great Sage is the seer; the *anuṣṭubh* is the metre;
the primordial power, the Blessed Goddess Śrī Mahiṣamardinī, is the deity; the application is for the attainment of the four aims of human life (*caturvarga*).
Klīṃ! May the Goddess Kāminī, the bestower of desires, protect my head.
May the goddess Mardinī, the sovereign of the gods, protect me in the syllable MA.
May the goddess Sāvitrī, the destroyer of time, protect me at the letter *i*;
may the goddess protect me at the letter *ni*, in the heart, and on the arms and sides.
In the navel, the genitals, the anus, the throat, the two ears, the two cheeks,
as well as in the crest-lock, the armor, the pair of feet, and the pair of shanks.
May she who is endowed with all powers protect me in every limb, Svāhā! May Kāmādyā protect me, Svāhā! May Mardinī Śivā protect me in every limb, Svāhā!
May the ten-syllabled Great Knowledge (Mahāvidyā), Mardinī, protect all my limbs;
may Mardinī protect me constantly, and may Mardinī always guard me.
May Mardinī protect me constantly in the kingdom, as well as in the fortress, on the boat, and in the midst of fire; may Mardinī always grant me protection.
May Durgā, the Great Goddess, protect me; may Āryā always protect me. May Prabhā, the Great Sovereign, protect me; may Kanakā protect me at all times.
May Kṛttikā protect me constantly; may the Siddhas always protect me. May Prabhā protect me; may Mahāmāyā protect me; may Māyā always protect me.
May Jvarā protect [me] always; may Sukṣmā protect [me] at all times; may Viśuddhā protect [me] forever;
may Nandinī protect [me] constantly; and may Suprabhā protect [me] at every moment.
May Vijayā protect me everywhere; may the nine Śaktis protect the limbs of the Goddess;
may the Śaktis protect me constantly, and may the Mudrās always protect me.
May the Yoginīs protect me constantly; may the Khecarīs protect me at all times. May the Ḍākinīs protect me constantly; may the Siddhas always protect me.
"May the Goddess Mahiṣamardinī protect [me] everywhere and at all times.
Thus has this divine armor, so difficult to obtain, been recounted to you.
This should not be spoken of here or there, but must be guarded with great effort;
it has been concealed in all the scriptures and revealed here in the Viśvasāra.
Knowledge is easily obtained everywhere, O Maheśvarī, but this great armor is difficult to obtain; it is not for the deceitful, the faithless, or the slanderer.
When a limb is missing or when there is an extra limb, or when one speaks falsely regarding a cruel matter,
one should not display the armor that grants all desires as a divine object for praise.
O Maheśānī, that which was spoken by Śaṅkara must not be told here or there;
if it is given to them, the siddhis will perish in due course.
The mantras turn away and, having uttered a most terrible curse, bring misfortune upon him;
therefore, one should protect them with great effort.
O Maheśvarī, having written [the mantra] on birch bark with gorocanā and saffron during an auspicious conjunction, it should indeed be worn upon the Brahma-thread.
The venerable one [should act] during Siddhiyoga, or during the Karanas Vava, Balava, Kaulava, Vaṇija, under the asterisms Śravaṇā, Revatī, or Punarvasu.
In the Uttarā-yogas, as well as in the three Pūrva-yogas,
or under Aśvinī or Rohiṇī, on the third or ninth lunar day (tithi).
On the eighth or the fourteenth day, or on the sixth or the fifth lunar day;
or on the full moon day, one should likewise worship Durgā at night in a wilderness.
In a place with a single linga, in a cremation ground, in an empty dwelling, or likewise in a temple—
with flowers that have grown spontaneously, or even with those offered by a Guru or Vaiṣṇavas.
Furthermore, having written [the mantra] with white or red flowers, or with sandalwood mixed with red [pigments],
upon a funeral ember or a cloth from a cremation pyre, one who should wear it;
All perfections shall belong to him; so it was spoken by Śaṅkara.
Having worshipped the maiden and having offered the Devīsūkta, [he attains success].
Having recited it, he should feed Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and possess wealth and wives;
and for three days, he should perform the narrative known as Ākheṭaka.
Then there shall be for him great protection and armor that grants all desires; for him there shall be no mental afflictions, no physical diseases, and never anywhere any suffering, grief, or fear.
Upon seeing him, the disputant shall be silenced and the king shall act like a servant;
he who is pure and disciplined should recite this daily for one month.
During the day he should be one who eats sparingly, and at night he should be devoted to his strength;
he should always recite [the mantra] six thousand times every single day.
Within six months or three months, one certainly becomes a sky-walker;
the sonless obtains a son, and the poor man becomes wealthy.
The king shall become free from disease and endowed with strength;
he should constantly recite this vidyā according to the prescribed rite upon his organ when it is in the state of *rajas*.
Thus, the wise one who performs this is indeed the illustrious Sadāśiva.
Thus ends the *Mahiṣamardinī-kavaca* in the *Śrī-viśvasāra-tantra*.
The illustrious Lord said:
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall proclaim the thousand names of the Goddess,
