by the mere knowledge of which one becomes Sadāśiva himself.

For this *Sahasranāmastotra* of the Illustrious Mahiṣamardinī, the venerable Śrī Sadāśiva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the *anuṣṭubh* is the meter (*chandas*), the venerable Goddess Mahiṣamardinī is the deity (*devatā*), *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*), and the seed-syllable of desire (*kāmabīja*) is the application (*viniyoga*) for the attainment of the fruit of the four aims of life.
Oṃ! Fame, beauty, contentment, nourishment, fortitude, peace, action, compassion, wisdom, joy, the supporter, modesty, fortune, and eloquence.
Prītiratika, Śavākhyā, and likewise Nārāyaṇī;
Mādhava, Govinda, Viṣṇu, and Madhusūdana.
Trivikrama, Vāmana, Śrīdhara, Kamalāsana, Hṛṣīkeśa, Padmanābha, and thereafter Dāmodara.
Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha; Nivṛtti, Saṃpratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti, and Indirā.
Vāpikā, Recikā, and Mocikā beyond her;
likewise Sūkṣmā, Sūkṣmatarā, Mṛḍāṇī, and Yāminī.
She is all-pervading, of the nature of space, the undissolved form of Śrīkaṇṭha;
she is exceedingly subtle, the supreme form, the immortal goddess Amareśvarī.
Arvī, Śobhā, Vibhūti, Tithi, Śasthānaka, Hara, Vāṭaśa, Bhautika, Sadyojāta, and Anugraheśvara.
Akrūra, Mahāsena, Ṛddhi, Sṛṣṭi, Samunnati,
Smṛti, Medhā, Kānti, Lakṣmī, Dyuti, Sthirā, and Tithi.
Gati, Jarāyujā, Pālinī, Śānti, Īśvarī, Rati, Kāmikā, Vasudhā, and again Hrādinī.
Furthermore, there are Pratidīrghā, Tīkṣṇā, Raudrī, and Bhayā;
then Nidrā, Tantrī, Kṣudhā, Krodhī, and another, Kriyotkārī.
Mṛtyu, Sītā, Śvetā, Aruṇāsitā,
Anantā, and Krodhī— these are the five mantras of Caṇḍeśa.
Śiva, Rudra, Kūrma, Netrāsura-vitānana,
Ajeśa, Sarvasomeśa, as well as Aṅguli and Dāruva.
Ardhanārīśvara, Kāmī, Umākānta, Sureśvarī,
Āṣāḍhī, Kuntikā, Gaṇa, Caṇḍa, and Parāparā.
Heruṇḍa, Mahākāla, and thereafter Kālīśa;
Bhujaṅgaka, Pinākīśa, Khaḍgīśa, and Kuśa as well.
Akṣobhya, Atama, Śrīmīna, and likewise Nandina;
Śivasamvartaka, Pūrṇā, and the goddess Virajā.
Śālmalī, Lolākṣī, and Vartulākṣī after her;
then Dīrghaghoṇā, Sughoṇā, and again Dīrghamukhī.
Śucimukhī, Vidyāmukhī, Kālī, and Sarasvatī;
likewise Sarvasiddhi, Gaurī, and Śivā, the dweller in the three worlds.
The knowledge of the three worlds consists of mantras whose supreme essence is the power of mantra;
the power of the Self is the Mother, the Creeper, Lambodarī, who is beyond that.
Drāviṇī, Nagara, Khecarī, Mañjarī,
as well as Rūpiṇī, Viriṇī, Kākorī, and Pūtanā.
Bhadrakālī, Yoginī, Śaṅkhinī, and likewise Vajriṇī;
Kālarātri, Kujinī, Kapālā, and Vajrayā.
Jayā and Vijayā, as well as Sumukhī and Īśvarī; Revatī and Mādhavī, and likewise Ghāyasī and Vidāriṇī.
Sahajā, Lakṣmī, Vyāpinī, and likewise Jayā; Durgā, Prabhā, Satyā, Vāṇī, Caṇḍā, and Vilāsinī.
Vijayā, Vijayā, Viśvā, Vinandā, Sunandā, Smṛti, Ṛddhi, Samṛddhi, Śuddhi, Bhakti, Buddhi, Mati, and Kṣamā.
Vāmā, Kledinī, Klinnā, Vasudhā, and another, Vasudā;
Parāyaṇā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Sandhyā, Prabhā, and Niśā.
Amoghā and Vidyutā, as well as Sarvaśāstramayī;
likewise Cakrī, Gadī, Śārṅgī, Khaḍgī, Śaṅkhī, and again Halī.
Muṣalī, Śūlī, Pāśī, and Aṅkuśī; furthermore, Mukunda, Nandaja, Nandī, Nara, Naraka-jit, and Hari.
The one worthy of praise, the eternal abode, the protector, the descendant of Śūra, the heroic Janārdana;
the sustainer of the earth, the universal form, Vaikuṇṭha, the Supreme Person, and Śiva.
Vali, Valānuja, Vāla, Vṛṣaghna, Vṛṣīvala,
Haṃsa, Varāha, Vimala, and thereafter Nṛsiṃha.
The Goddess consists of all scriptures; Śivā consists of all mantras;
she consists of all letters, is worthy of praise, and has the nature of eternal bliss.
She is the embodiment of color and form, consisting of consciousness and bliss, and likewise composed of all knowledge;
she is the Great Vidyā, the Great Mantra, the Great Prosperity, Intellect, and Action.
The Goddess is gross, subtle, and extremely subtle; she is proportionate and vast-bodied; she is Śivā, composed of the light of Brahman and composed of the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī,
as well as Vārāhī, Anantā, Rudrāṇī, and Cāmuṇḍā is the seventh.
Mahālakṣmī, aṇimā, and laghimā after that;
then vasitva, gāyatrī, and likewise kāmāvasāyitā.
Vimalā, Utkarṣiṇī, Jñānā, Kriyā, Satyā, Mahodayā,
Prabhavī, Satyānugrahā, and the ninth, Saha-pūjakā.
She belongs to a great lineage, is known as noble, is a pure woman, and is dear to Śiva;
she is intelligence, wisdom, splendor, truth, knowledge, intellect, and the bestower of fortitude and understanding.
She is the Sovereign of All, the chaste and virtuous Satī, the daughter of Dakṣa,
Aditi, Smṛti, Śruti, the Great Knowledge, the Secret Knowledge, and the Ancient One.
Vyāpinī, Śālinī, Pāvanī, Kledinī, Dhāriṇī, Mālinī, Haṃsinī, and Śastrinīśvarī are to be known [as such].
She is radiant, unsteady, and fickle; she is a woman with shapely hips.
Holding a trident and a noose in her hands, she has beautiful hands and three eyes.
Rare is the compassionate one who consists of all-knowledge;
she is the soul of time, the bearer of the source of beings, and the power consisting of wisdom.
She is the active one, composed of color, and indeed the illusory power;
she consists of the Vedas, possesses celestial chariots, and is the very nature of the power of existence.

Victory to you, O Mother of the world, whose form is manifold manifestation, who is love itself; victory to you, O Jātī, Ambikā, Vāgbhavī, Durgā, the embodiment of intellect, and the one of great wisdom!
Karālī, Vikarālī, Uṣā, Uṣā, Sarasvatī, Śrī, Durgā, Āśā, as well as Śraddhā, Medhā, Kānti, Mati, and Sukhī.
The noble one is Kheṭakarūpā; the Vidyā is remembered as Hrīḥ together with Puṣṭi;
and there are Prajñāsinī, Vāṇī, Kuhū, and Kapaṭarūpiṇī.
Rudravīryā, Mahāvīryā, Prabhā, Nandā, Kṣudhā, Kṛśā,
Poṣaṇī, Udbhidā, Satyā, Sabhā, Śubhakarī, and Sahā.
Kālarātri, Mahārātri, Bhadrakālī, Kapālinī, Vikṛti, Kuntimūrti, Sendukhaṇḍā, and Śikhaṇḍinī.
She is the destroyer of Niśumbha and Śumbha, the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura;
she is Indrāṇī, as well as Rudrā, whose body is half that of Śaṅkara.
She is Nārī and Nārāyaṇī, the auspicious one who is the triple void;
she is Ahlādinī and Ambikā, manifesting in thirty-two forms.
Piśācī with a wheel in her hand, Rākṣasī, Yoginī, Jarā,
Vṛddhamātā, Vṛddhatallā, adorned with beautiful ornaments.
Śitāṅgī and Śuklavarṇā, Raktāṅgī and Raktabhūṣaṇā,
Piṅgalākṣī and Viśālākṣī, as well as Samṛddhi and Vṛddhi.
Śraddhā, Svāhā, likewise Bhikṣā, Māyā, Saṃjñā, Vasundharā,
Trilokadhātrī, Gāyatrī, Sāvitrī, and Tridaśeśvarī.
She is of her own nature and of many forms, the mother of the aggregates, the beloved of Acyuta;
she is Vimalā and Malā, as well as Aruṇī and Dāruṇī.
She is primordial nature (prakṛti), transformation (vikṛti), birth, nourishment, maintenance, and withdrawal;
she is the twilight, the mother, the virtuous one, the swan-like one, the maker of the path, and the supreme Jina.
The divine mother is the blessed Devakī, whose abode is the lotus;
she is three-faced and five-faced, the crusher of both gods and demons.
Long-lipped, with hair reaching her waist, many-headed, and wolf-bellied; Rādhā, Uccārgā, Apatyakulirekhā, and Gaṇātmikā.
Gaganā, Gāṇarekhā, Pavanavegā, and likewise Svadhā;
Bhuvanapālā, Gaṇakrīḍā, Madanā, and Madanāturā.
Anaṅgānaṅgamadanā, Mekhalānaṅgarūpiṇī,
Anaṅgākusumā, and Vilvarūpiṇī, who bestows fearlessness.
Bhakṣobhyā, Satyavādī, Vahurūpā, Śuci, Smṛti,
the one named Varadā, Vāgīśā, Aparāṇadharā, and Śivā.
Jvalajjihvā, Mahājihvā, Sarvajihvā, Mahāprabhā,
Dhāriṇī, Mālinī, Daṃṣṭriṇī, and Ūrdhvakeśinī.
She who knows the flavors, the connoisseur of aesthetic delight, the beautiful one, the consort of Murāri, the giver of essence, the delight itself;
she who is Siṃhikā, the worshiper, the performer of all deeds, and the destroyer of all that is done.
She is the speaker of speech, the eloquent one, the youthful, and the abode of compassion; she possesses pure luster, beautiful splendor, and is endowed with all forms of radiance.
Vibhūḥ, unnati, kānti, sṛṣṭi, kīrti, samunnati,
vyuṣṭi, utkṛṣṭi, ṛddhi, and Lakṣmī, the bestower of all prosperity.
Śrī, the bestower of all auspiciousness, the beloved of Hari, should be meditated upon;
she is indeed Brahāṇī, Rudrāṇī, and the eternal refuge of Rudra’s prowess.
Bhuvaneśvarī is the Great Vidyā, the unsurpassed bestower of all knowledge;
she is to be known as Jayā, Vijayā, Ajitā, and Aparājitā.
Nityā, Vilāsinī, Dogdhrī, Sughoṇā, Vanamālinī,
Gaṇāmbā, Gaganāmbā, and Śāntyatītā— this is the mantra of Ambikā.
Vāgbhavī, Śambhuvanitā, and Ramā— endowed with these three seed-syllables,
Tvaritā, Navadurgā, Hṛllekhā, and Gaganā are ever-present.
Raktā, Karālā, Lolā, Ghargharī, Ghūrṇanāśinī,
Kṛcchrā, Ghṛṇācāndā, Sugandhā, and Gandhanākulī.
Kuṇḍalī is both beautiful and misshapen, possessing a radiance equal to lightning and fire;
she pierces the six cakras and is colored by the supreme nectar.
Ḍākinī, Rākinī, Citrā, Vākinī, and likewise Lākinī;
Kākinī, Śākinī, and Hākinī are the goddesses of the wheels.
Residing within the lunar disc at the center of the thousand-petaled lotus,
she is Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, and Dhṛti.
Śaśinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, Aṅgadā, Pūrṇā,
and Pūrṇāmṛtā— these bestowers of desires reside within the solar disc.
Tapanī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci, Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Dhāriṇī, Bodhinī, and Kṣamā.
She who abides within the solar disc, she who is born from the solar disc;
she who stands in the midst of the fiery disc, she who dwells within the fiery disc.
Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī,
Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, and likewise Havyakavyavahā.
Hūḥkāri, Khecarī, Caṇḍā, Chedinī, Kṣepiṇī, Kalā,
Kṣemakārī, Viśālākṣī, Vikaṭākṣā, and Mṛgākṣikā.
Kṛdaṅgā, Mṛganetrā, Dīrghanetrā, and Manobhavā; Tantrā, who consists of various strings, and Śaśī, who consists of various weapons.
She who has three thorns, whose body is like that of a bull, the destroyer of all enemies;
she who is endowed with all ornaments and wears every kind of decoration.
She is the beloved woman, the beautiful one, the embodiment of desire, the one who possesses desire, and the bestower of freedom from desire;
she has a pure face, a dark face, a single eye, and a formidable countenance.
She has squinting eyes and is ruined; she is distinguished by her stainless arts;
she possesses many kinds of forms, many shapes, and deformed appearances.
Ratīsvarī, Ratiprīti, Viprīti, Prītimañjarī, Carmati, Sumati, Kāla, Vituṣṭi, and Tuṣṭi.
Vīṇā, Veṇu, Mṛdaṅgā, Śrī, Sallokeśvarī, Mayī,
Paramaiśvaryarūpā, and likewise Virūpākaraṇī.
She is the embodiment of all bliss and the cause of all delight;
she possesses three peaks and five peaks, and she is the one whose form consists of all peaks.
The sixteenth is the fifth; the fifteenth is again the seventeenth;
the eighteenth is the moon-bearer, the lunar one, and likewise the beloved of the moon.
Eternal, stainless, moist, causing moisture, possessed of passion,
consisting of the substance of passion, causing melting, and possessing the luster of the petal of a blue lotus.
Hṛllekhā, Kledinī, Klinnā, the destroyer of all agitation;
Rāgī, Rāgavatī, Retā, Madanā, and Madanāvatī.
Mekhalā, Drāviṇī, Satyā, Smaraṇā, Vismṛtā, Lakṣmī,
Hemaprabhā, Tanvī, Padmākṣī, and Padmalocanā.
She has long shanks, beautiful shanks, and great shanks;
she is large-bodied, with the luster of a dark cloud, dark-complexioned, black-hued, and possessing her own natural form.
The Goddess, whose form is the seed and whose form is the individual soul, resides within all living beings; she consists of all principles and brings about the manifestation of the Kula.
The Goddess consists of all sacred seats (pīṭhas); she is the subtle power (kalā) within the entire realm of existence.
She is the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā), the auspicious Goddess Padmāvatī, who bears the half-moon mark.
Navadurgā, Durgā, the destroyer of the demon Durga,
Svapnāvatī, Viśālākṣī, Citralekhā, and Śāṅkarī.
Lopāmudrā is to be honored by him who has overcome the affliction of passion;
likewise Prabhā, Māyā, Jayā, Durgā, Viśuddhā, and Nandinī.
Suprabhā, Vijayā, Viśvā, Vinadā, Sunadā, Tvarā,
Supratiṣṭhā, Pratiṣṭhā, and Rasalābhasvarūpiṇī.
Āryā, Bhūri, Mahiṣī, Mardinī, accompanied by Mahiṣa,
Kalavyākhyā, Kānanī, Kṛttikā, and Kālanāśinī.
She is the Yoginī, the Mother of Yoga, united with Yoga, and the one who endures through the ages; she is the source, the destiny, the praiseworthy, the one worthy of praise, and the enchanting one.
Śūlahastā, Hastā, and likewise Carmacāpadharā;
Saudāminī, Sudyamā, and likewise Sarvaratnamayī.
Āryā, Durgā, she named Bhadrā, Kālikā, and likewise Kalā;
Bhadrakālī, Kapālī, she named Kṣemā, and Kṣemabandhakā.
She whose womb is the Veda, whose great womb is vast, whose limbs contain the essence of bliss, and who possesses beautiful eyes;
she who is barren to the fire of time, yet resembles the fire of time itself.
Vibhīṣaṇā, Bhīṣaṇā, Subhīmā, Atibhīṣaṇā,
Atiprītiparākhyā, Uttarā, and Uttarapriyā.
Salutations to Namottarā, who is immortal by day and night;
to Punarvasu, the Mistress of Yoga, the Mistress of Universal Yoga, the Mother of the Universe, and the Bestower of Wealth.
She is of great strength, known as Valā, the giver of strength, and the bestower of power;
she is Vālikā, Taruṇī, Vṛddhā, Kaiśorī, and Yuvatī for all time.
Drāviṇī, Kṣibhiṇī, Kṣobhā, Kṣamā, Kṣobhā, Kṣamā, Kṣayā,
Ākarṣiṇī, Mohinī, Sammohinī, and Sadāgati.
Subhagā, Bhagākhyā, Bhagasarpiṇī,
Anantarā, Bhagamālī, Bhagāṅgī, and Bhagamālāvibhūṣaṇā.
She who possesses the marks, she who wears a garland of marks, she who is worshipped by the bodiless one (Kāma) and by Aṅga;
she who is honored by the Bhaga, she whose limbs are the Bhaga, she who is pleased by the Bhaga, and she whose very essence is the Bhaga.
The thousand-eyed one, arising from the beginning,
is filled with the power of will (*icchā-śakti*), the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), and the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), beginning with action.
The manifold, the manifold creator, the creator consisting of mantra,
the moon, the power of will, knowledge, and action, the beloved, the bestower of desires, and the new-moon night.
Rati, Ratipriyā, Nandā, and the ninth, Manonmanī;
Unmādā, who is cherished by the intoxication of passionate love, and Madāmadavilālitā.
The fish, devoted to truth, lovers of meat, and ever-devourers of great flesh; those whose nature is intoxication, possessed of great passion, eaters of flesh, and consumers of meat.
Sadāśiva’s beloved is Icchā, who is established within all;
she is Kumārāṅgī, Kumārī, Sukumārī, and Vilambinī.
Mahotsūksmā, Karālāsyā, Ṣaḍaṅgayuvatī,
Satī, Ākarṣiṇī, Drāviṇī, Khecarī, Mañjarī, and Śubhā.
Mātaṅgī, worshiped by sages, resides in the abode of Mataṅga;
she is the one who draws near, the one who withers, the nourisher, the attractor, and the ordainer.
Raudrī, Praśānti, the one called Śuddhā, Kriyākāntā, Śubhodayā,
Mohinī, Pramathā, Caṇḍā, Bhāvinī, and Bhavamocanī.
She is the lightning-creeper known as the crane, beautiful and radiant with bliss;
she is the power of consciousness (cicchakti) who is both of dull intellect and great intellect, and whose form is peace.
Śyāmā, Gāyatrī, Śyāmāṅgī, and likewise Virodhikā; Varṇinī, Vadana, Vandhyā, and she who is devoted to all debates.
Tīvrākhya, Jvalinī, Nandā, Bhogadā, Kāmadāyinī, Ugrā, Ugraprabhā, Tejovatī, and Satyānanākṛti.
She is a maiden with the form of a child, the ornament of all sentient beings;
she possesses the moon and has the luster of the moon, the giver of wealth who bestows riches.
She is delight, she is immersion, she is the drop, the peace of all, the bestower of auspiciousness;
she brings about abundance, she is secure, most secure, and the attainment of secure power.
Delighted by the self-arisen flowers, she worships with the blossoms of the self-arisen;
her smile is like the self-arisen flowers, and she is filled with the blossoms of the self-arisen.
Suṣumṇā, Yogavatī, Gāndhārī, Naravallabhā,
Liṅgamālā, Liṅgagīti, and Bhagamālāvibhūṣaṇā.
The Goddess is the nectar of the bhaga and liṅga; she is auspicious in nature, the nectar of the bhaga and liṅga, delighted, possessing excellent marks, and having the form of the bhaga.
She is the sister, the garland of the *bhaga*, residing in the *bhaga*, the auspicious bestower of the *bhaga*;
she is the abode of semen, the form of semen, the great semen, and the one possessing exceeding semen.
She is exceedingly white, served by the seed (śukra), born from the body of Śiva;
she is the form of the Great Utterance (mahāvyāhṛti), as well as Svadhā, Svāhā, Sudhā, and Dhṛti.
She who finds supreme delight in offerings to gods and ancestors, the performer of the Yajus, the beloved of the Yajus;
she whose abode is the Ṛg, Sāman, and Atharva Vedas, and who is worshipped in all the Vedas.
She who is beyond the Vedas, the mother of the Vedas, the embodiment of the Vedāṅgas, the worshiper of the Vedas,
she who is praised by Vedic knowledge, the stainless one, and the bringer of auspiciousness.
Bestowing security, with limbs smeared with saffron and lips deeply red,
she wears red garlands, has crimson limbs, and bears the form of red sandalwood.
Her nose was adorned with pearls, she possessed beautiful teeth set closely together,
she was full of delight, profoundly deep, and endowed with all excellent qualities.
The Goddess, wearing a garland of severed heads, stands in the pratyālīḍha posture;
she is honored by the universe, honored by the world, the conqueror, the victorious, and the triumphant.
Sundarī, Bhairavī, Viśvā, Purabhairavī,
Kāminī, Pururūpā, Lākinī, and Putrarūpiṇī.
Rākiṇī in the form of a son, and Śākinī in the form of a son;
she who is unborn, born of the sacrificial rite, born of the cow, born of the mountain, and the daughter of the mountain.
Vāsanī, Vandhyarūpā, Guhyakālī, Mahāprabhā, Suprabhā, Virajā, Satyā, and she who is eternally truthful— Sadāsatyavatī.
Gāndhārī, she named Naraka, Narakāntā,
Narākṛti, Rukmiṇī, Satyabhāmā, Rādhikā, Kumudā, and Kṛśā.
Kumudāṅgī, Kaumadī, Padmanetrā, Priyambadā, Pūjakā,
Pūjakaprītā, Ṭiviṭnvā, and Suṭīvikā.

She who bears a sword, she who is auspicious, she who is beloved, she who has a single tusk, she who is the source of the hosts of beings; she who is deceitful, she who wears a tattered garment, she who is dark-hued, and she who dwells upon all mountains.
Vindhasthā, Vāmanā, Vindhyā, she who dwells upon the Vindhya mountains,
Urvaśī, Kālikā, Kaikā, Viśvarūpā, and Vasundharā.
Vibhīṣaṇā, Itibhīṣaṇā, Caṇḍī, Vilāsinī, Vetravatī, Viṣaṇṇā, Vimalā, and Mānadāyinī.
Honored by the world, the sustainer of the world, the earth of the world;
unconquerable, agitated, possessing universal forms, and revered by the universe.
She is insentient yet abiding within consciousness, possessed of excellent intellect, and full of passion;
she has a face like a swan, beautiful eyes, three eyes, and wide vision.
Kurukulvā, Sukulvā, Asitā, Amitā, Sitā;
Mudrā, Mudrāsatī, Haṃsī, Siṃhasthā, and Śaśiśekharā.
Aśokavāsinī, Revā, Sukhāsyā, Suranāyakā, Śāmbhavī, Śāṅkarī, Māyā, Kālakṣayakarī, and Karā.
Animā, Bhāvinī, Indrā, Jinamātā, Jineśvarī, Ajinā,
Kuttivasanā, and Vyālayajñopavitinī.
She is Carvikā, the speaker of flatteries, the one with a virtuous family, and the fair-faced one;
she is Vajreśvarī, the mother, and the destroyer of all seeds.
She is the destroyer of all suffering, free from conflict and devoid of duality;
she is difficult to aspire to, difficult to propitiate, difficult to contemplate, and difficult to transcend.
She who disciplines the undisciplined, she who brings about the destruction of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa,
she who is the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura, and she who is the destroyer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha.
She is the Queen of the Queens of Kings, the seed-syllable that brings about the destruction of all the wicked;
she is the Yakṣiṇī, the Yoginī, the object of yoga-meditation, the sacrifice, and that which is the goal.
She is of noble lineage, the consort of Śambhu, the power of Śambhu, and the beloved of Śambhu;
she dwells in the triangle, is eternal, Bheruṇḍā, and the beauty of the Kula.
She is the abode of all enjoyments, preceded by all enjoyment;
she is worthy of worship, highly precious, great, and a speaker of truth.
She dwells in the cremation ground, she is meritorious, the giver of merit, and the bestower of merit;
she is the generous one, the one who removes [suffering], the one to be led, the triple-sacrifice, the great, and the earth.
She is the mistress of the lion-throne, the lineage-born, Totalā, equal to Tulasī; she is fond of Hālāhala, the playful one, residing in the linga, and the worshiper of the immortals.
She who dwells in the sacrificial pit, she who resides in the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*, she who inhabits the *kuṇḍa-golaka*,
she who delights in the *kuṇḍa-puṣpa*, she who is well-pleased, and the bestower of joy.
The maiden is clever with clever love, and her skill resides in cleverness;
she is a maiden possessed of worship, a maiden who observes the vow of celibacy.
She who abides as a youth and is a maiden, she who dwells in the womb and whose essence is the womb;
she who is skillful and of noble birth, likewise fortunate and highly blessed.
Sumitrā, Lakṣmaṇā, Queen Damayantī whose nature is self-restraint,
Madayantī, Draupadī, as well as Susthā and Kuśātmikā.
She has five topknots, she is Menakā, the sister of Maināka, and lightning;
she is not five-faced, she is the three-eyed one, and she is Smṛti, the beloved of the five-faced one.
Her vehicle is adorned with bracelets fashioned from the staffs of the lords of nāgas;
she eternally resides on an island of jewels and dwells upon a lion throne.
Clad in an elephant hide, adorned with anklets,
wearing silken garments, her hands radiant with a necklace of gunja berries.
Clad in a tiger skin, wearing a serpent as her sacred thread,
with a tilaka-mark of self-originated flowers, she dwells on the Vindhya and Kailāsa mountains.
Vinītā, Valimātā, Kuntī, Kekā, Kṛpāvatī, Kumudvatī, Kṛṣṇadehā, Śambarī, and Upavītinī.
Vinītā, Khaḍgarūpā, Piṅgalākṣī, Priyavratī,
Brajāṅgī, Vrajadehā, Vajrahastā, and Vivasrakā.
She is sky-clad, stationed on the battlefield, the white water-lily, and fond of the white water-lily;
she is the practitioner, the life-breath of practitioners, and the one who brings an end to hell.
She is knowledge, knowledge, the great knowledge, the great mantra, the most great;
she is the syllable Oṃ, capable of accomplishing for practitioners whose minds are either capable or incapable.
She follows the left-hand path, she is the left-handed one, the stainless one, and the one whose bow is made of reeds;
the virtuous lady holds the flower-arrows and wields a bow of sugarcane.
Manobhavā and Amanasthā, having praised Manu, the Great Manu;
and Manu’s daughters Devahūtī and Svarṇadī, the auspicious worshipper.
This is the Thousand Names of Mardhinī, spoken by Śiva;
whoever, having risen early in the morning and become pure, should recite it day and night.
At night, at midnight, and especially during the twilight,
the preceptor, having performed the ritual placement of mantras on the hands according to this procedure, [should proceed].

Having sipped water according to the rule and become [pure], one should always perform the placement of the mantra-syllables, beginning with the seed-syllable of the body, in both direct and reverse order.
Facing westward, one should place the mantra seven times and recite the hymn known as the *Sahasranāma*, which is the means for attaining liberation.
Having recited the armor-armor (kavaca) there— whether in a cremation ground, a wilderness, or an empty dwelling— one should then mutter the mantra six thousand times.
Having offered a sacrifice with the blood of a cock, a mouse, a ram, a buffalo, and even a human, one should recite the mantra with undistracted mind.
"Seize, seize my two feet; likewise, devour my two hands!
Having addressed my enemies thus, destroy them both!"
Then the wise one should first utter "Grant success," followed by the pair of feet ending with *dviṭha*;
thereafter, he should recite the mantra until fear arises.
For him, there shall arise the great siddhi beginning with atomization (aṇimā), and then he may dwell [there],
consuming burnt fish, burnt meat, and blood-vegetables day and night.
Having offered [the oblation] in a cremation ground or a remote wilderness according to the ritual procedure, one should recite the mantra;
within six months, one will become eloquent and another Great Lord (Maheśa).
One should always worship Mardhinī with white flowers from the Svayambhū [tree];
one should always recite the narrative known as Ākheṭaka for three days.
At the time of the *puraścaraṇa* rite, one should first perform it for three days;
then the Goddess Mardinī, who is worshipped by the gods, will become pleased.
One should recite the mantra day and night at all times with diligence;
one should always perform the daily rites, placing the mantra at the beginning of each action.
He alone is indeed blessed as a Vaiṣṇava, and he alone is likewise a Śākta;
one should mutter the mantra at night and offer the bali-oblation at night.
O Goddess, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds equal to them;
having been touched by two women in their courses, one should recite the mantra day and night.
In a cremation ground, a wilderness, or an empty dwelling, one should recite the mantra day and night with intense devotion until the mantra attains accomplishment.
One without a son obtains a son; one without wealth becomes wealthy;
and one who is diseased becomes strong—of this there is no doubt.
One who recites this hymn for one month shall regain a lost kingdom;
he who recites it for two months shall become the foremost among kings.
The wise one who recites the seventh [chapter] shall possess sons and be happy;
[this is done] with yellow orpiment, saffron, and red sandalwood combined.
One should worship the daughter of the mountain, the Great Goddess who is fond of incense and lamps,
according to the prescribed ritual with red sandalwood, dūrvā grass, and saffron.
One should always offer the *arghya* to Mahādevī three times every day;
even while being devoted to another's wife, one should recite the mantra with undivided attention.
Within six months, one shall attain whatever success resides in one's mind—
everything that pacifies all misfortunes and is endowed with all accomplishments.
It pacifies all sins, destroys all suffering, and pacifies all death; it was spoken by Śaṅkara.
O Goddess of gods, by the grace of this hymn, you become [the purifier of] all— brahminicide, the drinking of liquor, theft, and sexual intercourse with the teacher’s wife.
He is of noble birth, he is wise, he possesses true intellect, and he is honored by all—
he alone is eternally victorious for whom the Goddess is beloved.
A man who always rejoices in the bliss of the Goddess shall become one who is eternally blissful;
month after month, he should worship the Great Goddess according to this rite.
On the ninth day, on Tuesday, and on the fourteenth day, on Saturday,
one who is devoted to faith should worship the Goddess with animals, birds, and other offerings.
There, the best of preceptors should recite the Devīsūkta as before;
he should worship a young girl there, beginning with one year of age up to ten.
Then Mardinī, accompanied by Mahiṣa, becomes well-pleased with extensive ornaments, perfumes, and the like, such as vermilion and sandalwood.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) according to the previously mentioned procedure day and night;
there, one should recite the mantra by one's own capacity for as long as it lasts day and night.
One should offer liquor from jar after jar, especially the Vaijayantī;
by means of the fire-oblation one may bring all kings under control, and thus one should perform the oblation.
One may attract the daughters of the gods and even bring Keśava under one's control;
[so too] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and the gods, the best of the immortals.
O Goddess, seeing that practitioner, they praise him while filled with joy;
one should practice the Vidyā like Kālī, and one shall obtain the fruit like Kālī.
"One should not worship the Goddess with Vaiṣṇava rites, nor should one adore her with Tulasī;
the vessel for the *arghya* offering should not be a conch—so it was declared by the Lotus-born One."

One should worship Śivā with the vessel of Viśvāmitra, that is, an earthen vessel. One should always offer [oblations] consisting of dust, meat, and the likes, prepared by servants and drunkards, along with flowers, flower-products, human heads, rams, and great boars.

With *guñjā* seeds, with the powers and exploits of Śakti, with pure and impure things, with drinks, with fruits to be chewed, and furthermore with parched grains, one should always satisfy the Blessed Lady.
Devoted to worship, they offered various substances night after night during their rites; O Beloved, for them there was never any sorrow or fear on the surface of the earth.
And having touched or seen the Supreme Goddess while they were menstruating, [they were purified].
If one recites it daily for six months, one becomes like another Kuvera.
And Pāṣaṇḍa was like another Bṛhaspati in his poetic skill;
he was the foremost among those possessing all branches of knowledge and was comparable to Madana in beauty.
In this world, intoxication is a foe as powerful as the wind, difficult to conquer;
yet, having emerged from every peril, it attains the state of being beloved by all.
O Goddess, by the grace of Mardinī, one obtains all the fruits of the Rājasūya, Rājapeya, and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Having seen another's wife engaged with another man, or having touched her,
one who recites this mantra daily amidst women or within a maternity ward [is purified].
Having fashioned an image of Manu with sandalwood and red sandalwood according to the prescribed rite,
one should duly worship the goddess Mahiṣamardinī there.
Having offered an oblation of Javā flowers, Vajra flowers, and especially Droṇa flowers, along with the flesh of fish, as well as the meat of the nakula, gavaya, and ruru deer;
One should recite the mantra six thousand times at night or at dawn, using a porcupine quill, a lizard, a tortoise, a buffalo horn, and a rhinoceros horn.
O beloved, the Blessed Goddess Durgā shall always be pleased with him who recites your beautiful mantra every day while offering a bali-oblation.
He shall become the son of Pārvatī and a worshiper of all sentient beings.
Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Thousand Names of Mahiṣamardinī," in the venerable Viśvasāra Tantra.
Now I shall proclaim the supreme Vidyā, Bhavānī, who liberates one from worldly existence;
by the mere knowledge of which one becomes Sadāśiva himself.
A sonless man obtains a son, and a poor man obtains wealth;
by the grace of the Goddess’s pair of feet, one attains the status of a king.
A Brāhmaṇa attains the Veda; a Kṣatriya becomes victorious;
a Vaiśya becomes a master of wealth; and one shall obtain all perfections.
I shall proclaim the extraction of the mantra; listen, O lotus-faced one!
By the mere knowledge of which, one becomes the supreme Lord of Speech.
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, [he beheld] Maheśvara, the God of gods.
The Lord was seated, absorbed in meditation, his lotus-like face serene,
his pair of feet colored by the crest-jewels of gods and demons.
Having prostrated before the god, Nandika spoke with palms joined in reverence.
Śrī Nandi said:
"O God of gods, O Lord of the universe, I have a great doubt. O Master who is affectionate toward His devotees, I wish to ask about a certain secret."
O Lord, of which deity is this hymn being recited by you day and night?
Is it the Supreme Reality, or is there something else even higher than the High?
Thus questioned then by Nandika, the Lord Śambhu, the Teacher of the World, spoke— the Blessed Īśvara whose lotus-face was blossoming like a flower with unfolding petals.
The illustrious Lord said: "Excellent, excellent, O best of the Gaṇas, that you have questioned me! I shall tell you even that secret which is to be concealed from Skanda."
Formerly, at the end of the kalpa, desiring to create the worlds, the power known as Mūlaprakṛti— consisting of the three guṇas and possessing hidden consciousness— [manifested].
Once that [universe] has arisen through the Great Principle (mahat) and the other evolutes who know it,
some power called "consciousness" remains embracing me.
Then, from that which is born of causal volition, the auspicious Dhīṣṭāsinī arises;
thereafter, the supreme power known as Icchā unfolds.
Then, moreover, the Power known as Speech, consisting of sound—
the Mother of the World, the Mother of the Vedas, Sarasvatī— manifested.
Śrī, Brāhmī, Vaiṣṇavī, Raudrī, Kaumārī, Pārvatī, Śivā—
she who bestows success, she who bestows intelligence, she who is peaceful, and the giver of all auspiciousness.
Out of favor toward her, I have praised the Goddess herself with thousands of names, O Queen, you who are worshipped by the living beings of the three worlds.
Satisfied by this hymn, she entered into me alone;
from that time forth, the supreme state of sovereignty was attained by me.
By his grace, I have created this entire world of moving and non-moving beings,
including the gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas.
Together with the earth, the oceans, the mountains, forests, and groves; together with the constellations, planets, and stars; and accompanied by the assembly of the five elements.
With this hymn consisting of a thousand names of Nandin,
I always praise the supreme and non-supreme Śakti, who bestows grace upon me.
Having spoken thus to the supreme god, the lord and teacher of all that moves and is stationary,
Nandin bowed his head and addressed the Supreme Lord.
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Protector of the world, Teacher of the universe!
I am your devotee, I am your servant; please grant me your grace.
This meritorious hymn of praise to the Goddess is difficult to obtain even for the gods;
O Lord, I wish to hear it, as well as whatever power she possesses.
The illustrious Īśvara said:
Listen, O highly fortunate Nandin, to this auspicious king of hymns,
which consists of a thousand divine names and bestows spiritual perfection as well as the bliss of liberation.
Having risen early in the morning, one should recite it with purity and concentration;
endowed with faith, one should do so three times a day—for there is no praise higher than this.

Of this *Śrī Bhavānī Sahasranāma Stotra*, the Lord Mahādeva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chandaḥ*), the Primordial Power (*Ādyā Śakti*)— consisting of three seeds and being threefold— is the deity; its application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of attaining my own skill in poetry, great scholarship, and all spiritual perfections (*siddhi*).
Oṃ; this Vidyā of Bhavānī, consisting of the three seed-syllables of Vāgbhava, Śambhuvanitā, and Ramā, was proclaimed by the Lotus-born One.
The seed-syllable of Śiva, situated upon the Moon and possessing Fire, the Vāgbhava syllable, and the Bindu;
Gaganam joined with the Moon and the Kāma-bīja possessing Fire.
The seed-syllable of desire (Kāma-bīja) conjoined with the void (Ākāśa), possessing fire (Vahni) and mind (Manas), joined with fire and union;
the crescent moon (Indu-khaṇḍa) endowed with the bindu and conjoined with Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
Below that is Mādana, below that is Śakti, and at the end of that is the garland of Bindus;
the Moon is situated within the seed-syllable of space, and below that is the letter of generation.
Joined with Māyāvindheśvarī and stationed above all,
this is that seed-syllable Vāgbhava, which bestows the state of mastery over speech.

Having divided the seed-syllable of Śiva threefold according to the sequence of emanation, maintenance, and dissolution, one should remove the first two [syllables] from the beginning; below the first [syllable] is the vowel of Madana (the letter *u*).
Furthermore, one should join the seed-syllable of Indra (L) situated below Śiva (H);
likewise, O Maheśvarī, one should place the abode (M) below Śiva, conjoined with fire (R).
Joined with the fourth vowel and adorned with the bindu and nāda—
such is this great seed-syllable, Kāmarāja, which brings about great prosperity.
O Great Goddess, O fair-faced one, having applied the seed-syllable of Māyā joined with the intoxicating [letter] and the enemy [letter],
and then the seed-syllable of the Moon alone;
O Goddess, having performed the sequence of emanation, one should then extract the seed-syllable of Śakti by means of the sequence of purification through the yoga of the sequence of reabsorption.
This [mantra] called Bhavānī-vidyā was spoken by Śaṅkara;
having worshipped and recited it, one should chant this auspicious hymn.
The great goddess, mother of the world, Mahālakṣmī, beloved of Śiva;
the illusory power of Viṣṇu, the auspicious one, the peaceful one, the perfected, the unmanifest, and Sarasvatī.
She is forbearance, peace, splendor, moonlight, Pārvatī, the beloved of Śaṅkara;
she is Tripurā, Nandinī, Nandā, Sunandā, and she who is praised by the gods.
She is the science of sacrifice, the great illusion, the mother of the gods, and the sustainer of the deities;
she is affection, Pṛthā, the renowned one, Mṛḍānī, and the dweller of the Vindhya mountains.
She is the perfected lore, the great lore, the Earth, and she who is served by Nārada;
she is the beloved of the Destroyer of Cities (Śiva), Splendor, the Desirous One, and the lotus-eyed one.
She is the delighter, the great lore, Durgā, the destroyer of misfortune;
she is the perfected lore, the great lore, the light, and she who smiles with blooming lotuses.
She is the difficult-to-attain, rare knowledge; she who dwells in the city of the virtuous;
she who is without leaves (Aparṇā); the illusory power of Śambhu; she who is full of love; and she who speaks with gentle words.
Aparṇā, Śāmbhavī, Māyā, Mādarā, Mṛdubhāṣiṇī, Nārāyaṇī, Mahānidrā, Yoganidrā, and Prabhāvinī.
She is the Prajñāpāramitā, the humble one, Tārā, the honey-sweet virtuous lady;
she is joined with the ocean of bees and honey-makers, the delighter who dwells within the lion.
Royal Fortune is the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*, she who brings nectar, whose essence is nectar;
she is statecraft, the three Vedas, commerce, and the science of government in action.
She is the source of all emergence, the deliverer, the perfected one, the immediate path, and the supreme refuge;
she is the ocean, the Mandākinī, the Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the Sarasvatī.
The Godāvarī, the Vipāśā, the Kāverī, the Śatadru, the Sarayū, the Candrabhāgā, the Kauśikī, and the auspicious Gaṇḍakī.
The Narmadā, the Karmanāśā, the Carmāvatī, and the Vedikā; the Vetravatī, the Vitastā, the Varadā, and the Naravāhanā.
She is the virtuous wife devoted to her husband, the chaste one, the one with beautiful eyes, the dweller in Daṇḍa;
she is the one-eyed one, the thousand-eyed one, the one with beautiful hips, and the one garlanded with fortune.
She is the leader of the army, the banner, the well-arrayed host, and she who desires heaven;
she is the one with the standard, compassion, Rambhā, the lute, and she who is fond of the fifth note.
She is the beloved of the supreme and subordinate powers, the triple energy who bestows Brahman;
she is Aindrī, Māheśvarī, Brāhmī, Brahmāṇī, and the proclaimer of Brahman.
The Blessed One is Desire, the Cow, the Crow-Cow, the Compassionate One;
she is the Holder of the Thunderbolt, the One with the Thunderbolt in Hand, Caṇḍī, and she of fierce valor.
Gaurī, golden-hued, the performer of maintenance and destruction,
both one and many, the Great Sovereign, the hundredfold, the many-formed, the Great-Born.
Adorned with the earth as her armlet, she dwells in the sequence of the six cakras;
she pierces the six cakras, and is dark, black, yellow, and tawny.
She is hunger, she is Kṛṣṇā, she is fever, she is old age, she is youth, and she is the abode of Varuṇa;
she is the digit, the minute measure, the hour, and the blink of an eye—the very form of Time.
Kṣemā, Kṣamāvatī, Kṣāntā, Aditi, Diti, Mati,
Svarūpā, Sunāsā, Cakṣusparśavatī, and Kriyā.
She who loves fragrance, she who is sweetly scented, she who is pleasant to the touch, she whose movement is delightful,
she who is musk, she who has the eyes of a deer, and she who dwells in the perfume of camphor.
Padmayoni, Sukeśī, Aliṅgā,
Bhagarūpiṇī, Yonimudrā, Mahāmudrā, Khecarī, and Khagagāminī.
Madhuśrī, Mādhavī-vallī, Madhumattā,
Madodgatā, Mātaṅgī, Suprahastā, and Puṣpavāṇeṣucāpinī.
Raktāsvaradhara is one who holds milk and wears red flowers as an ornament;
Dhīrā Mahāśvetā is one who holds white sounds and is beloved by the Vasus.
Well-attired, holding a spear in her hand, adorned with necklaces of pearls,
fragrant with camphor, youthful, a lotus-like woman, she whose abode is the lotus.
She who wields a sword, she with a discus in hand, she armed with a spear and an iron club,
she bearing a bow, she with a noose in hand, and she holding a trident and granting boons.
Holding a wine-jar in her hand and mounted upon an excellent peacock,
the heroic goddess carries superior weapons and is intoxicated with the pride of the drink of heroes.
Vasudā, Vasudhā, Vācā, Jayā, Śākambharī,
Śivā, Vijayā, Jayantī, Sustanī, and Śatrunāśinī.
She is the pregnant power of the Vedas, the bestower of boons, the bearer of excellent gifts,
Śītalā, Suśīlā, and the dweller within the seizing spirits of children.
Kumārī, Suparvadyā, Kāmākhyā who is worshipped by Kāma,
Jālandharī, Dharā, Anantā, and she who dwells in Kāmarūpa.
The truthful one who possesses the seed of desire, devoted to the true Dharma;
the subtle deity like a pillar, subtle and the awakener of the intellect.
She who has a six-pointed and a three-pointed [yantra], who has three eyes, whose banner bears the bull,
who is fond of bulls, who is mounted upon a bull, and who is the slayer of the demon Mahiṣāsura.
Kālī, who removes the pride of Śumbha, is fashioned resembling a blazing fire;
she is adorned with a skull and wears a garland of skulls.
Kapālakuṇḍalā is long, the messenger of Śiva, and possesses a deep resonance;
she is the bestower of supernatural powers and intelligence, eternal, and the awakener of the path of truth.
The earth rests upon her shell-like neck, providing her with shade;
she is Kuṇḍalinī, containing the world within her womb, reclining in the form of a serpent.
The lotus-stalk of the navel, from which seven lotuses emerge, has its root in the *mūlādhāra*; it is without support and makes its abode in the sacrificial pit of fire.
The stone-faced Vāyukuṇḍamukhī is without support and without refuge;
she is the nourishment of the body, the nourishment of the mind, and the nourishment of the self, arisen from the vital breath.
She is the mother of medicinal herbs and physicians, the potency of substances, and the sovereign power;
she is the object of knowledge for physicians, the practice of healing, the most wholesome diet, and the destroyer of diseases.
She is the hunt, the eater of deer-flesh, the deer-skin, and the deer-eyed;
she is born of speech, multiform, the form of slaughter, and arisen from slaughter.
Her form is praised by the elders among the bards; she is the liberator from the prison of rebirth;
she is Ambikā, Bālikā, and Ambā; she is pure and worshipped by virtuous people.
She is Kaulinī, whose form is the Kula; she belongs to her own Kula and is worshipped by the Kula.
She is unconfused by the revolutions of the Kālacakra, she is the delusion itself, yet the destroyer of wandering.
She whose form is a cave of bliss, the sovereign goddess of the three seed-syllables;
she is the garland of clouds with its musical instruments, the beautiful rain that causes the crops to flourish.
She whose form consists of the letters A, I, U, and E;
she who is the syllable Hrīḥ, whose nature is the seed-syllable, and who dwells in the vowels as the syllable Hrīṃ.
She is the power consisting of all syllables, garlanded with the letters of the alphabet;
she is the color of vermilion-red and is fond of the vermilion tilaka mark.
Delightful and possessing delightful seeds, she manifests the subjugation of the world;
she is the subduer of kings, to be served by kings, and the rite that effects the subjugation of kings.
She is the queen, honored by the king, known by the king, and praised by the king;
she is the power consisting of the king's dharma, worshipped by the four castes.
The accomplishment consisting of all dharmas is concealed in all tantras;
it consists of the Brāhmaṇī, Kṣatriyā, Vaiśyā, Śūdrā, and those born of excellent castes.
Devoted to the path of the Vedas, Māyā dwells upon the left side of Śiva;
O Goddess, devoted to the path of the Vedas, you are Vidyā who deludes the entire universe.
She is the science consisting of missiles and weapons, the perfect memory, and the upholder of dharma;
she is tradition, the supreme revelation, the eldest, the most excellent, and the dweller in the netherworld.
Amedhyā, Satyamedhā, Bhadrakālī, Aparājitā,
Gāyatrī, Satkṛti, Sandhyā, Sāvitrī, and she who rests upon the three steps.
She who is the three junctions of the day, the three steps, the supporter, the one with beautiful lotuses, the singer of the Sāman hymns;
she who is the Pāñcālas, the girl, the youthful maiden, the eternal play of childhood.
Garbhāvavādharā, Asūnyā, Garbhāśayavināśinī,
Surārighātinī, Kṛtyā, Pūtanā, and Tilottamā.
She is possessed of the power of modesty, eternal, Bhavānī, the destroyer of sin;
she wears silk garments, she is song, she is beautiful melody, and she has charity as her sphere of action.
The lute-string consists of the seven notes: ṣaḍja, madhyama, and dhaivata;
it possesses melodic sequences (mūrcchanās) established within the musical scales (grāmas), remaining self-abiding and dwelling in its own proper stations.
Laughing with loud, piercing laughter, she is a preta devoted to the dance of pretas;
fond of song and delighting in instrumental music, she bestows contentment, nourishment, and forbearance.
She is the culmination, the one who loves sacrifice, and the sacrifices that set the world and the scriptures in motion;
she is the time of fierce fever, the uneven one, and the destroyer of the sacrificers.
Viṣāri, Nāgadamini, Kurukulvā, Mṛtodbhavā,
Bhūtāhārā, Bhūtarakṣā, Bhūtaveśā, and Vilāsinī.
She is the destroyer of Rākṣasas, the night of the Rākṣasas, and she who is endowed with the hunger of heroes;
she is the wheel-shaped one, the moonlight, splendor, the radiance of the sun, and the wanderer of the night.
The Ḍākinī, Śākinī, Siddhā, Hākinī, and Rudhirapriyā; she who rests upon the white and the black, the goddess Kamalānanā who delights in union.
She is praised in the Vedas as the one who assumes the form of a guru, the heavy one, death, the skilled Mārī, the slayer of Rākṣasas, the Rākṣasī, and the mother of the gods.
Resembling the lunar disc and established within the lunar disc, she possesses the powers of atomization (aṇimā),
levitation (laghimā), extension (prāpti), irresistible will (saṃspṛhā), and the ability to assume any form at will (kāmarūpiṇī).
Bestower of the eight supernatural powers, mature, destroyer of wicked demons,
beginningless and endless, she is Contentment herself, possessing four arms and four faces.
She is composed of the fourfold awakening, the peace that bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
she resembles the kāśa flower, with eyes like autumn saffron.
She is the past, the present, and the future; she is born of the mountain and dwells upon the mountain.
She delights in the left-hand path, she is the beautiful one, and she resides on the left side of Śiva’s body.
She who delights in the left-hand path, the nourisher, Lopāmudrā, the awakener;
she whose eyes are the moon, sun, and fire, and who is worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva.
She is the auspicious one, the lotus-born, the desirable, the pure, and Maṅgalacaṇḍikā;
she is the purified self, the supreme self, and the contemplation of the creator of all beings.
She is Maṅgalā, Suśīlā, and the awakener of the supreme path;
she is Dakṣiṇā, Dakṣiṇāmūrti, Sudakṣā, and the beloved of Hari.
Dākṣāyaṇī, destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, daughter of Dakṣa;
Yoginī, absorbed in yoga, the limbs of yoga, and destroyer of [worldly] meditation.
The form of Nārasiṃha wears the yogic belt; she is the supreme goal of the liberated, of noble birth, and the bestower of the fruits of the three aims of life.
She is the giver of wealth, the giver of dharma, the auspicious one, the granter of desires, and possesses the splendor of lightning;
she is the witness, the giver of moments, and her nature is both manifest and unmanifest.
She is the sacrificial rite, the daughter of Kaṭyāyana, the pure, the auspicious, and the possessor of a multitude of splendors;
she is of beautiful fortune, of noble fame, the garment, Kālikā, and the destroyer of time.
The lineage of the seed is joined with the awakening of the Seed of Blood;
she is the seed of the world, the life-force of the world, and the one who desires the welfare of the three worlds.
Kratu, Kātyāyanī, Svacchā, Śubhagā, Dyutivargiṇī, Suśrī, Sukīrti, Vasanā, Kālikā, and Kālanāśinī.
She who makes the moon shine, who acts as the rays of the moon, who is the sixteenth digit born from a hundred thousand [parts],
she who is devoted to that state, the Yakṣiṇī worshipped by the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
Citriṇī, Citrarūpā, Vicitrā, and Citrarūpiṇī;
Cāmuṇḍā, who holds a severed head in her hand and is intent on slaying Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa.
The eighth, eleventh, full moon, ninth, fourteenth, the new moon,
and the lunar digit of Hasta— these are the Earth who holds the full pitcher.
She is fearless, yet she is Bhairavī; she is both terrifying and formidable. She is Tripurabhairavī, the Great Fierce One, the Wrathful One, and she is worshipped by Mahābhairava.
Nṛmuṇḍā, Hastinī, Caṇḍā, Karāladaśanānanā,
Karālārī, Karālā, and Ghoraghargharanādinī.
She has red teeth and hair standing erect, and is as crimson as the bandhūka flower;
she is Kādambarī, free from thirst, a native of Kaśmīra, and fond of saffron.
Kṣānti, Vahūsuvarṇā, Ratirbahūsuvarṇadā,
Mātaṅginī, Varārohā, and Mattamātaṅgagāminī.

She is a swan, possessing the gait of a swan; she is a female swan, while he is a male swan. Her hair is flaming, her face is like the full moon, she is dark-complexioned, possesses a beautiful smile, and wears earrings shaped like wheels.
She is ink, the pen, that which is to be written, the beautiful writing, and dear to the scribe;
she holds a conch, has a conch in her hand, holds water in her hand, and is the deity of the waters.
Kurukṣetra, Kāśī, Mathurā, Kāñcī, Avantikā,
Ayodhyā, Dvārakā, Māyā, Tīrtha, and the bestower of the Tīrtha-hala.
Tripuṣkarā, Aprameyā, Svarūpā, Rūpavardhinī, Tejasvinī, Sutīkṣṇā, Baladā, and Baladāyinī.
The unmanifest and the manifest-formed, the divine knowledge of Śambhu,
the auspicious daughter of Śambhu, the daughter of Manu, and the progeny.
She is earth, water, fire, ether, the Great Principle (mahat), time, and the quarters of space;
she is the power consisting of all time, perceptible to all who hear.
The desire consisting of all-knowledge, which brings about the awakening to half of all reality,
is the state of waking, deep sleep, dreaming, and the fourth state (turiya).
Hastening yet moving slowly, languid and gladdened by the fragrance of the palace,
the drinking hall was filled with vessels for wine and intent upon food and drink.
Her eyes were slightly reddened and rolling, and she spoke with somewhat indistinct words;
she was the fulfiller of hopes, the initiation itself, skillful, and honored by those who have been initiated.
She is the consort of the Nāgas, the daughter of the Nāgas, the possessor of coils, the beloved of the serpent-king;
she is the science consisting of all scriptures, perfect memory, and the practitioner of dharma.
She is Śruti, Smṛti, and Medhā; she is the preeminent Pātālavāsinī;
she is Mīmāṃsā, Tarkavidyā, Subhakti, and Bhaktavatsalā.
Birth is non-birth for one who is not of noble lineage; it is profound and devoid of intrinsic being.
Her form holds the serpent-noose; she is the sustainer of the *nāgas* and wears *nāga*-earrings.
Sucandrā resides in the center of the moon, dwelling within the corners of the wheel;
she is the Vidyā consisting of all mantras, supreme among the syllables of all mantras.
Madhuśravā, Śravantī, Bhrāmarī, Bhramarālayā,
Mātṛkuṇḍalamadhasthā, and Mātṛmaṇḍalavāsinī.
The Vidyā consisting of all mantras, the fair-faced one who destroys the sound of existence,
she who has transcended and exists as Bhavānī, the cluster of blossoms of love.
The power that possesses all happiness, which destroys [the cycle of] food,
is the cause of meritorious beings and the one who carries them across the ocean of the *bhaga*.
Akrūra, Grahavatī, Vigrahā, and Graharājatā;
Rohiṇī, Dutagarbhā, Kālabhū, and Kālavartinī.
Kālī, free from blemish, she who is designated by sixty-four names;
she is the ancient one and of ancient hue, yet ever-new and the beloved of the Supreme Lord.
The Ajā constellation increases joy and passion;
the Pañcarātri, Nāga, Pañcā, and Pañcaśleṣā dispel fear.

A row of five [women] possessing the five lumps, residing in the five places; one who has recently given birth, one longing for a male, one who has miscarried, and one who has recently miscarried—these are excluded.
She is the power that transcends passion and semen; she is the membrane that bears the embryo;
she is the knower of the three times, the one who embodies the three times, the triple-formed, and the dweller in the city.
Arogā, Śivatatvā, Kāmatatvā, and Rāgiṇī;
likewise the eastern, the far-eastern, the western, the northern direction, and the intermediate directions.
Ahaṅkṛti, Ahaṅkārā, Balajāyā, Balapriyā, Kṛṣakā, Kāmadhenī, Suśraddhā, and Śraddhadevatā.
Mātrāmātā is Mahī; Tṛpti is the mother of the father, that is, Pitāmahī;
Snūyā is Dauhitrinī; Putrī is Naptā; Pautrī is Śiśupriyā.
She who flows from the breasts, the stream of milk, the source of the universe, and the one who suckles;
she who holds the infant in her embrace, the swing, and she who delights in playing upon the swing.
Urvaśī, Kadalī, Kekā, Viśalyā, Śikhinartinī,
Khaṭṭāṅgadhāriṇī, Khaṭṭā, and Vāṇapuṅkhānuvartinī.
In the great ocean, the term *vartinī* refers to a good path, a spy, a moat, a ditch, and an exit; while *velā* refers to a circular rampart, a shoreline, and a boundary.
She is the nourisher and the witherer, the unattached one, she of long hair and beautiful eyes;
she is the graceful, the fleshy, and the slender one who bears the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
Intoxicated by drinking human blood, adorned with human skulls and bones, she delights in the game of dice; Sārā is her beloved, and Śārikā speaks pleasant words.
Śāmbhavī, Gāruḍī, Vidyā, Vāruṇī who is worshipped by Varuṇa,
and Vārāhī, who holds a severed head in her hand and has uprooted the earth with her tusks.
The Śālagrāma stone is of terrifying form yet generous, an image resting within an image;
it is of beautiful form, the very embodiment of a treasure, and pure.
Memory, which consists of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), and the cultivation of excellent impressions;
Prakrit, the regional dialects, verses (*gāthā*), songs (*gīti*), and riddles (*prahelikā*).
Iḍā and Piṅgalā, as well as Suṣumnā who has the form of the sun;
Śaśisūryā, who resides in the sun; Hrādinī, who has the form of nectar.
The Goddess is of corresponding form, of vast form, of subtle form, and established in the heavy;
she is both stationary and moving, bestowing the fruits of performed actions.
She dwells within the body that has transcended sense objects; she is without distinction, having conquered the senses;
her nature is consciousness, she is the bliss of consciousness, and she is the very essence of the Supreme Brahman.
Changeless, free from enmity, and characterized by detachment, it is the speaker of truth;
distinct from the knowledge of the Puruṣa, it is the manifestation that bestows isolation (kaivalya).
She is solitary, a yoginī, wise, and of great learning;
she is effortless, composed, and uniquely honored by all the world.
She is service, she who loves service, she who is to be served, and she who increases the fruits of service;
she is the power possessing all happiness, the most auspicious among all auspicious things.
Thus, this Thousand Names of Bhavānī, spoken by Bhava,
he who recites it after rising in the morning, having become pure and composed;
And the man who, with a steady mind and endowed with faith, should listen constantly— whether once a day, twice a day, or thrice a day.
Completely liberated from all suffering and free from greed and anger,
he is illustrious, renowned, blessed, a protector of his sons, and honored by the world.
One who is handsome, endowed with virtues, and possessed of power and vigor,
always obtains a superior, steadfast, auspicious, and beloved wife.
Freed from all sins, he attains an increase in wealth;
he enjoys constant happiness with his kinsmen and wife, and experiences great festivals for his sons and grandsons.
Delighted and served by many pure-minded attendants,
the Brahmin has reached the further shore of the sciences, and the Kshatriya is victorious in battle.
A Vaiśya, rich in the desire for wealth, and a Śūdra shall obtain happiness;
one desiring a son obtains a son, and one desiring wealth obtains wealth.
One who desires objects of pleasure obtains those objects according to his wish; one who desires the Dharma attains the inexhaustible Dharma;
and one who desires a daughter obtains a daughter endowed with beauty and virtue.
His fields shall yield abundant crops and his cows shall give much milk;
for him there is no misfortune, no calamities, and no fear from kings or enemies.
An unwholesome thought does not arise; he attains the status of a leader of his lineage;
and demons, malevolent spirits, and the like do not afflict him.
Neither Piśācas nor Ḍākinīs, nor Bhūtas, Bhavyas, or Jambhakas [shall harm] children who are overcome by infantile seizures; it brings peace to such children.
And when there is a division among many in their affection, the cultivation of friendship is supreme;
[yet] Nandin was bound with firm iron fetters in the inaccessible abode of Śiva.
A mortal who stands, listens, or recites this is liberated; there is no doubt about this.
He shall experience no unpleasantness from his wives, nor from his sons, nor from his daughters-in-law.
They do not see sorrow, for they become worthy of honor by kings;
the blind man gains his sight and is no longer afflicted by eye diseases.
The deaf man regains his hearing, and the mute man acquires auspicious speech;
and the woman whose fetus falls is born with a stable pregnancy.
Śrāvaṇī and Vahūbharmā liberate by themselves those who are afflicted with leprosy,
whose bodies are decayed, and who are devoid of hair, nails, and skin.
By reciting this mantra, those who are pure and have conquered their senses, and who recite it one hundred times, become possessed of divine bodies.
Those who are childless shall obtain sons; there is no doubt in this matter.
Those who are seized by great diseases or afflicted by the two kinds of fevers should perform the ritual bathing.
The child who has mastered what was heard becomes a master of divine speech, like a lordly elephant;
through reciting and hearing this, they become possessed of divine bodies.
Those mortals who always recite [this] especially on the eighth, the ninth, and the fourteenth days, shall certainly not be partakers of suffering.
Restraining his diet for nine nights, firm in devotion, with senses conquered,
the wise man, being pure, should remain in the presence of her image within the temple of Caṇḍikā.
If a wise person recites the Ekādaśī hymn one hundred times, he shall be free from fear;
the Goddess herself will grant him his desired boon.
In the beautiful mountain-pīṭha of the Siddhas, the abode of the gods and the field of the Siddhas, success is attained through recitation and hearing; it cannot be otherwise.
He who, sleeping on the ground with his senses subdued, recites this one hundred times,
even he beholds the Goddess in a dream in her embodied form, bestowing boons.
Those supreme persons who recite it a thousand times will possess the power of poetic composition in Sanskrit and mastery in the exposition of the treatises.
O Pārvatī, their power is manifested even without study,
their forms doubled by the crest-jewels reflecting the glow of their claws.
And those great lords perform expiations for all of them;
[this is done] on an auspicious day by writing with saffron upon birch bark smeared with yellow pigment (rocanā).
When the deity has been restrained, one should maintain [the practice] after having worshipped the young maidens and having fed those who are hungry with milk, sugar-candy, and various foods.
Those kings who are honored by other monarchs become possessors of fame and illustrious;
for such a ruler, there is no fear of enemies or of wicked men.
And beautiful-eyed women, though pure in their passion for pleasure, are heard to be impaired when afflicted by desire, even while standing in bodies overcome by youth.
The pure man who, having written it, wears it on his head or neck,
shall enjoy a lifespan of a hundred years and shall not encounter any adversary.
Or those for whom [the names] Ketu or Dundhubhi are inscribed upon their armor in battle—
[those who are] overwhelmed by illusory armies, though possessing splendor, yet deprived of their vital energy.
Having conquered those who are senseless, deluded, and deprived of weapons,
they overcome the fear of enemies and attain victory in battle.
Nor those who practice sorcery, serpents, and the stake of dispute in battle;
nor *ḍākinīs*, *yātudhānas*, the great pestilence (*mahāmārī*), and *śākinīs*.
Bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, rākṣasas, sky-dwellers,
and the like do not enter the house or the body where this [image] is kept or drawn.
For him, no fear arises here from weapons nor from floods of water;
it is the supreme destroyer of the strength of the wicked and the sinful.
O Mandūraka, whoever, being composed, recites this in a spacious cow-pen for the sake of pacifying faults and warding off malevolent planets—
They do not see the messengers of Yama, nor do they undergo the torments of hell;
in the end, they attain the eternal world of Śiva.
In all terrible afflictions, this hymn— which wards off all suffering and bestows all auspiciousness— should be recited by those who are composed in mind.
This meritorious Thousand Names of Umā was spoken by Rudra and directly revealed by Nandikeśvara; it bestows the four aims of human existence.
This secret must not be disclosed; it should not be given to just anyone, but only to one of noble lineage, who is well-composed, and who possesses devotion to Durgā.
Alternatively, one may give this meritorious hymn, which bestows the fruits of all desires, to a beloved disciple, a son, or likewise to a friend.
There is no mantra higher than this, no hymn of praise higher than this;
there is no knowledge higher than this, and no holy place or boon superior to this.
Blessed are they and performers of meritorious deeds,
who, having resorted to her even once, worship Maheśvarī, she who is honored throughout the world.
May she who is the deity of deities, who is worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods,
be the granter of boons in this world and the source of all auspiciousness for the virtuous.
Thus ends the hymn of the thousand names of Bhavānī in the venerable Viśvasāra Tantra.
Now, O Maheśānī, I shall describe the great vidyā of Sarasvatī, who bestows mastery over speech and grants the fruits of the four aims of human life.
For one by whose mere knowledge Vṛhaspati becomes manifest, there is no need for ritual worship or adoration; he should always simply recite the mantra.
Without flowers, without perfumes, without fire-offerings, and without oblations,
a man who is a skilled poet should worship the supreme goddess Vāgbhavī.
The mantra-practitioner who recites [the mantra] every day, by day and night, for six months—
should always, at all times, recite it with constant discipline.
Having become pure, one should recite this vidyā once day and night;
he shall become like Śrī Varṇī on earth, truly Gaṅgādhara himself.
Having extracted the twelfth vowel, adorned with the *nāda* and *bindu*, one should know the syllable *bhū*; this is the supreme single-syllabled *vidyā*.
One should extract the seed-syllable of fire (ra) conjoined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*;
conjoined with the sixth vowel (*ū*), it is proclaimed as the second [syllable].
Having extracted the seed-syllable of the Moon, one should then join it with the "excellent" [letter];
mounted upon the fourteenth vowel, it is adorned with the nasal sound (nāda) and the bindu.
That great vidyā of three syllables bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
O Goddess, this vidyā was [revealed] in ancient times by Brahmā in the Ādiyāmala.
It is declared to be the crest-jewel (cūḍāmaṇi) of all vidyās;
O Goddess of the gods, there exists nothing equal to it in the three worlds.
Vasiṣṭha and other sages are its ultimate refuge;
the sage is Dakṣiṇāmūrti, and the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh.
Her presiding deity is declared to be Vāgbhavī Sarasvatī;
now I shall describe another, so listen, O lotus-faced one!
In ancient times, the goddess Vāk, whose form is existence, was proclaimed by Brahmā;
she is composed of the elements and enriched by Bindu and Nāda, and is further like the moon situated within Brahmā and Indra.
The seed-syllable of the Moon, joined with heaven (the letter *u*), adorned with the Bindu and Nāda, mounted upon the fourteenth vowel; this is Bhairavī in the form of a child.
This speech, renowned as Vāṇī, bestows the four aims of human life;
by the Lotus-born One, it was employed to restore Svargavān from his curse.
She possesses the splendor of a thousand rising suns, wears a red silken garment, and a garland upon her head;
her breasts are smeared with red pigment, and she holds a rosary, the Vidyā, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting mudrā.

I bow to the goddess who smiles like Mukunda, who possesses three eyes, whose hands bear the marks of the crescent moon, who is red in hue, who wears a triple dot (bindu) on her forehead, and who is crowned with a jewel resembling the cool-rayed moon.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the goddess Bālā Tripurabhairavī;
one should worship the Vidyā Bālikā, together with the Tantra, using the Śrī-mantra.
The placement of its syllables and its entire fruit have been declared by the Lotus-born One;
now hear the rule for the practice of that three-syllabled Sarasvatī.
Eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) and avoiding meat, the practitioner of mantra should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
he should bathe three times a day and perform the fire-oblation (homa) every single day.
Then one should offer oblations to Mahādevī day and night;
by that, O wise one, one becomes like another Śukadeva.
In his assembly, speech arises consisting of lotuses;
it is white in color, seated upon a white lotus, and adorned with various ornaments.
She holds a pen and an inkwell, is the wisdom-seal (jñānamudrā) who bestows fearlessness,
stands in the tribhaṅga posture, and is adorned with all ornaments.
One should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times during the rite of *puraścaraṇa* for the sake of Śivasundarī, who is endowed with fresh youth and possesses a smiling face.
First, one should inscribe a triangle, adorned with a hexagon;
then, a nine-cornered figure provided with three lines should be placed there.
Situated in the center of the yoni-maṇḍala is an eight-petalled lotus with a pericarp;
again, one [draws] a sixteen-petalled lotus, and again three enclosures of the earth (bhūpura).
It possesses four gates and is joined with vajra-spears, being most beautiful;
everywhere it is surrounded on all sides by garlands of colors, making it exceedingly lovely.
The Yantra enclosed within the Gāyatrī bestows all prosperity;
one should worship therein the Goddess Vāgdevī, the beloved of Śiva.
One should worship Bhuvaneśvarī, who is enveloped by the letters of the Mātṛkā;
one should utter the Goddess of Speech (Vāgdevatā) ending in the suffix -ṅe, followed immediately by "dhīmahi."
Having extracted that seed-syllable (tad), one should speak the Goddess and impel her;
this indeed is the Gāyatrī as it was proclaimed by Brahmā in the past.
One should always recite the mantra beginning with Kāma, or that beginning with Bhava, or that beginning with Lakṣmī;
or one should always recite the Vidyā beginning with Māyā, or that beginning with Lajjā.
The wise man should recite either the *vadhū-bīja* and so forth, or the *kūrca-mantra* and so forth;
this is declared to be their *gāyatrī*, which he should always recite preceded by the *praṇava*.
One should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times as the preliminary rite with undistracted mind;
one should worship the Goddess either like Sundarī or like Kālī.
Then one should perform the offering of the sacrificial oblation (balidāna), the ritual placement (nyāsa), and the conduct (ācāra) as before;
one should perform the conduct as before and, with a concentrated mind, worship the Vidyā.
In this matter, there is no requirement for perfected beings (siddhas) and the like, nor is there any defect regarding friends and such;
and as for the sacrificial oblation, it should be barley and nothing else—so it was declared by the Lotus-born One.
Having first uttered the Vāgbhava seed-syllable, then the Lajjā-bīja thereafter;
having uttered the Lakṣmī-bīja, then the Kāma-bīja thereafter.
This knowledge consists of the four aims of life and bestows the fruits of those four aims;
there is nothing equal to this knowledge even in the three worlds, and it is difficult to obtain.

Gaurī, resembling a garland of campaka flowers, with a smiling face, beautiful, surpassing the three worlds in splendor, holding a lotus, a conch, the gesture of fearlessness, and the boon-granting mudrā in her lotus-like hands,
adorned with noble necklaces and various ornaments, [I salute].
It is better indeed to serve one who is honored.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the auspicious Goddess who embodies the four aims of life;
with supreme devotion, one should honor Śāmbhavī, the beloved of Śiva.
He would become the son of Pārvatī; and this was spoken by Śaṅkara:
[he should offer] liquors, meats, along with flowers, and fried and roasted items on all sides.
With burnt *sikyā* seeds, burnt meat, and especially burnt fish,
along with *svayambhū* flowers, semen, and a mixture of *jārā* and lac;
One should worship the Goddess with vermilion, red flowers, and also with *kuruvaka* blossoms, along with a spear, for the attainment of all prosperity.
One should utter the Vāgbhavī [seed-syllable] ending in the feminine suffix -ī, followed by "vidmahe";
thereafter, one should utter the Kāma-bīja ending in the feminine suffix -ī, followed by "dhīmahi".
Having extracted that from it, one should then recite "tanno devī" and "pracodayāt";
this is declared to be the Gāyatrī, which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life.
Likewise, the mantra beginning with the seed-syllable, conjoined with the Kāma-bīja,
should be recited four hundred thousand times as part of the rite of preparatory practice (puraścaraṇa).
At the conclusion of his work, he should satisfy Śambhusundarī with wealth, grain, and other offerings;
according to his ability, he should recite the vidyā at all times, day and night.
One should worship Bhairavī daily, just as one worships Tripurabhairavī;
first, one should arrange a triangle, and then a nine-pointed figure joined with six [angles].
A triple reflection [mandala] with eight petals provided with filaments,
an outer enclosure (bhūpura) enriched with lines of qualities, and equipped with thunderbolts and tridents.

One should worship the beloved of Viṣṇu upon the seat endowed with the nine powers. Of this four-syllabled armor (*kavaca*) of the Mother of Śambhu, the venerable Śrī Sadāśiva is the seer (*ṛṣi*), the Anuṣṭubh is the meter (*chanda*), Vāgbhavī is the deity (*devatā*), Vāgbhava is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and Lajjā is the power (*śakti*).

The application (*viniyoga*) is for the sake of attaining all perfections and the abundance of my mantra-composition and scholarly eloquence, [using] the *Ramākīlaka* which is of the nature of *Kāmarāja*, as the armor (*kavaca*).
May Oṃkāra protect my head; may Vāgbhavī, the bestower of all accomplishments, protect [my forehead].
May Aiḥ protect the space between my eyes, and may Śaṅkarī protect my pair of eyes.
May Vijayā protect me in my home; may Jayā always protect me. May Śivadūtī always protect me; may Sundarī protect me at all times.
May Bhairavī protect me everywhere; may Bheruṇḍā protect me at all times.
May Kālikā protect me eternally, and may Kālarātri protect me always.
May Navadurgā protect me always; may Kāmākhyā protect me at all times. May the Yoginīs protect me always, and may the Mudrās protect me always.
May the goddesses stationed upon the wheel, the hosts of yoginīs, always protect me in all undertakings and at all times,
in every action and for all purposes.
May Lakṣmī, the goddess of gods, protect me for the sake of all prosperity.
Thus, O Goddess, I have narrated to you this armor-mantra (kavaca) which grants all desires.
O Maheśvarī, if one desires one's own welfare, one should not speak [of this] anywhere to one who is deceitful, devoid of devotion, or a reviler.
One should never show [the Linga] when it is deficient in limbs or has extra limbs; O Goddess, one should not show it while praising it, for by showing it thus, one becomes a destroyer of Śiva.
One should bestow this supreme armor upon one who is of noble birth, possessed of great enthusiasm, devoted to Durgā, a Vaiṣṇava, and pure.
One should bestow this armor, which is endowed with the essence of all tantras, upon one's own disciple who is devoted, peaceful, and likewise wealthy; so it has been said.
On a Saturday or a Tuesday, one should draw the yantra, complete with all its constituent parts, using red sandalwood paste and barley gruel.
One should draw the divine armor with auspicious *svayambhū* flowers,
using one's own semen and the semen of others, combined with various fragrances.
With gorocanā, saffron, or even red sandalwood,
on an auspicious lunar day and under a favorable yoga, on the day of the asterism Śravaṇā or on a Sunday.
Under Aśvinī, Kṛttikā, or especially Phalgunī;
likewise during the Indrayoga, the Śubhayoga, and the Śukrayoga.
O best of men, one should never [perform this] during the Kaulava, Vavaka, or Vanija karanas;
nor in an empty dwelling, a cremation ground, or especially in a desolate place.
Having written it and having recited it, one shall bring the entire world under one's control;
or one should wear it on the head or on the arm according to this rite.
Having worshipped according to the prescribed ritual with red sandalwood, dūrvā grass, and especially saffron, as well as fragrant flowers and perfumes;
Having worshipped the maiden, one should sacrifice to the eternal Goddess;
one should worship the Supreme Deity with fish, meat, and the flesh of crows and porcupines.
Having fed the Brahmins with excellent preparations such as ghee and especially well-prepared cakes, one should worship the Supreme Goddess.
There, one should perform the Ākheṭaka narrative for three days;
then there shall be great protection, as spoken by Śaṅkara.
Through killing, defiling, and so forth, they obtain [their goals]; of this there is no doubt.
He shall become the son of Pārvatī, standing at the forefront of all scriptures.
The Guru is Śiva himself, and his wife is the beloved of Hara;
one should worship the Goddess as non-different from him, and for such a person, spiritual perfection is not far off.
The mortal who here constantly recites this, with his mind focused on the syllables, shall obtain the fruit of recitation that is easily mastered;
he becomes one whose feet are elevated by the splendor of the crowns of kings, and who is the very embodiment of all auspicious marks.
Long-lived!
Thus ends the armor of Sarasvatī in the venerable Viśvasāra Tantra.

Thus, the *Tantrasārādi* was compiled, edited, and published by Śrī Rasikamohana Caṭṭopādhyāya, son of Ānandamohana Caṭṭopādhyāya, a resident of Butunī village under the jurisdiction of Māṇikagañja, which is part of the Ḍhākā district.
The Great Tantra named Viśvasāra, a compendium of the various Root Tantras, is completed.
